Title: Speech to the Parliament of the Republic of Macedonia
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Address by The Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia Dr Ljube Trpeski to the Parliament of the Republic of Macedonia, Skopje, April 1998 Address by The Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia Dr Ljube Trpeski to the Parliament of the Republic of Macedonia, Skopje, April 1998 Respected, In 1997, the trend of economic activity began in the Republic of Macedonia in 1996. The real increase in gross domestic product of 1.5%, although twice as high as last year, is below expectations. However, it is significant that the trend of positive economic growth is still maintained, especially given the difficulties facing the Macedonian economy in the first half of 1997. In the first half of 1997, there was a deepening of unfavourable movements in the external trade balance started in 1996, with the deficit in the exchange of goods abroad of 214.3 million exceeding the long-term capital inflow into the country. Due to the inability to further increase short-term debt towards abroad, it defined the financing of the deficit by reducing the foreign exchange reserves of the monetary system on a permanent basis. In such conditions, the stability of the exchange rate as the main objective of monetary policy was maintained in two ways: a/ through the sale of foreign exchange on the foreign exchange market and the reduction of foreign exchange reserves of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia. Thus, foreign exchange reserves in the first six months of 1997 were reduced by 11.7 million, as amounted to the central bank's net foreign exchange rate defense sales and; b/ through an automatic increase in the degree of restriction of monetary policy. In accordance with the adopted monetary strategy, the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia did not neutralise the monetary effects of unissued primary money on the basis of foreign exchange transactions, as this would question maintaining the stability of the exchange rate. Such a policy, characteristic of 1996, allowed the stability of the exchange rate to be maintained in the first six months of 1997, but at the same time determining too much tension in monetary frameworks. The burden of maintaining a stable but overestimated exchange rate thus fell entirely on monetary policy, causing the loss of foreign exchange reserves, high and long-term unsustainable monetary contraction and high real interest rates. Thus, negative rates of cash mass growth, which were first registered at the end of 1996, persisted in the first six months of 1997. At the end of June 1997, the M1 monetary mass achieved a negative inter-year rate of 3.3%, while the m2-denar cash mass in the same period achieved a negative increase of 0.2%. At the same time, the real interest rates of banking rankings remained at a high level of over 20% per year. Such conditions definitely confirmed that the established starting level of the exchange rate of the denar in relation to the German mark (27 denari per German mark) is unbalanced, i.e. that the defence of the estimated exchange rate causes high and unsustainable economic costs. For these reasons, a one-off devaluation was carried out in early July 1997 (July 9, 1997), establishing the exchange rate of the denar at 31 denar per German mark. The stability of the exchange rate at the newly established level was maintained without more serious problems in the second half of the year, in the face of foreign exchange surpluses in the foreign exchange market, improvement of balance of payments and acceleration of monetary growth rates. The effects of devaluation in the direction of recovering monetary growth, reviving exports and filling foreign exchange reserves were felt in the first months after the adjustment of the value of the domestic currency. This does not mean that the effects of devaluation, especially on exports, are completely exhausted, as the improvement in the price competitiveness of the Macedonian economy is expected to have an effect with a certain time delay, i.e. in the first half of 1998. Expectations in this regard are supported by the fact that the degree of nominal devaluation (16.1%), in fact, it also meant a degree of real devaluation of the denar, given that the adjustment of the value of the domestic currency was accompanied by adequate measures in income policy, by which the salaries of employees of all incompletely privatised companies were virtually "frozen". However, it should be borne in mind that the slow character of restoring trust in the institution austerity and in the banking system, On the one hand, and the need to dynamise investments, on the other hand, will define the continuation of the structural imbalance between austerity and investment in the coming years and on that basis will maintain the high level of deficit in the current account of the balance of payments of the Republic of Macedonia. It is of utmost importance that despite the adjustment of the external value of the domestic currency, its internal value in 1997 retained stability, which has been its feature for continuity for three years. Thus, with a time series of inflation rates of 9.2%, 0.2% and 4.5% in the last three years, the Republic of Macedonia is at the top of the most successful countries in transition, and very close to developed industrial countries. Permanently maintaining a low and stable inflation rate as an orientation of economic policy holders in the long term is certainly the most favourable macroeconomic ambition for reviving investment activity and achieving dynamic economic growth. Fiscal policy continued in 1997 with adjustments aimed at reducing the volume and structure of revenues and costs towards the country's needs at the level of development achieved. Due to the underwriting of revenues in the first half of 1997, conditional on the deterioration of liquidity and profitability of economic entities, measures were taken in mid-1997 to further reduce budget expenditure and improve revenue collection. The implementation of these measures allowed the public sector deficit in 1997 to be maintained at a low level of 1.8% of GDP, which is significantly below the Maastricht criterion. A healthy fiscal policy, in addition to being a necessary condition for narrowing the balance of payments deficit, is also in the function of the envisaged narrowing of the role of the public sector and leaving more room for private sector action as a long-term strategy. The transition process certainly carries numerous trials and social costs, the most pronounced of which are the problem of high unemployment and low living standards of the population. Solving these problems, such as generating them, it is a long-term process whose dynamics can be accelerated by accelerating structural reforms in companies, greater wage flexibility, labour market reforms, austerity reaffirmation as a condition for reviving domestic investment, a more aggressive and organised performance to attract foreign investors, etc. A positive impact in alleviating these problems is the influx of foreign funds for structural adjustment and private sector development, In 1997, 18.4m was withdrawn from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and 8.4m for the development of small and medium-sized enterprises from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. Private sector development credit funds on the basis of these, as well as on newly agreed credit arrangements, remain to be withdrawn next year. During 1997, the process of restructuring companies, a key element on which the success of post-privatisation reform depends, took place slowly. In 1997, due to the insufficient level of domestic accumulation and the scarce influx of foreign capital in the form of direct investment, the defensive way of restructuring companies continued in 1997, which consisted mainly of laying off the surplus of workers. This resulted in an increase in the number of unemployed, while the number of companies in bankruptcy and the mutual debts of business entities increased. This imposes the need in these domains, which in 1997 was done less than expected, to work more intensively in the next period, in order to replace what was dropped and to catch up with more advanced transition countries. The issues that began or continued to be resolved in 1997, and remain open to resolution in the next period, are also being added to the problem of recapitalisation and modernisation of the banking system. The issue is expected to be resolved by the impending entry of several foreign financial institutions into the territory of the Republic of Macedonia, which will also allow competition in the banking system to increase. In the direction of restoring the trust of savers, creating healthier and more liquid banking institutions, is also to start the functioning of the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (March 1997) and the Interbank Money and Securities Market (November 1997). Thus, the Republic of Macedonia has almost completely rounded off its own financial system, whose good positioning and functioning are prerequisites for achieving lasting economic development. D-R Ljube Trpeski Governor

Title: 55-year-old IMF and World Bank Assembly in Prague
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Address by The Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia Dr. Ljube Trpeski at the 55-year-old IMF And World Bank Assembly in Prague, September 2000 Address by The Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia Dr Ljube Trpeski at the 55-year-old IMF and World Bank Assembly in Prague Allow me to welcome you from Prague, the host country to this year's Millennium Assembly of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. I hope that all the beauty she has and carries Prague will be an additional motive for the more successful work of this gathering. Since gaining its independence, the Republic of Macedonia has implemented complex macroeconomic stabilisation programmes, structural reforms and institutional reforms to create a stable, modern, efficient and market-oriented economy. The total reforms of the financial system are also integral to the reforms of the financial system, of which the degree of development of the Macedonian economy depends largely. Namely, a healthy, competitive banking system and an adequate institutional and regulatory framework are prerequisites for mobilising financial resources and effectively allocation of credit assets, increasing savings and investments, creating an optimal structure of interest rates, for efficient transmission of monetary signals and for low fiscal costs. All this has a positive impact on macroeconomic stability and the degree of economic growth. At the same time, this is particularly important for transition countries and developing countries, where the capital market and the financial market in general are underdeveloped and do not provide alternative financial instruments. The basic assumptions for the existence of a healthy and modern banking system are the existence of a healthy macroeconomic framework, quality internal corporate governance and adequate economic infrastructure. In terms of infrastructure, there are two essential elements: an institutional framework, which includes a legal, administrative and political structure for the management of economic and financial transactions and; structure of financial markets, as an operational framework in which banking institutions operate. Efficient banking is based on a legal system that will facilitate the implementation of financial contracts, the collection of loans and the realisation of the collateral. Banks must be able to collect the demands they have been given, which requires quality bankruptcy procedures and adequate protection of ownership rights. On the other hand, an administrative structure is also needed that can apply the laws and ensure correct and swift judicial proceedings in resolving financial disputes. Macedonia's banking system stemmed from the former SME's banking system. At the time of monetary independence, the banking system of the Republic of Macedonia had a classic oligopolic structure, dominated by two of the largest banks, which owned over 80% of the banking market. The main function of the banks' operations was inversely set instead of their main goal of profits they were placed in the service of their main shareholders, who were also the largest debtors, i.e. credit beneficiaries. The derogation of the underlying function of banks and the development of a "culture of non-payment of liabilities", have caused impaired performance of banks' operations, expressed in the concentration of large amounts of dysfunctional placements in their credit portfolio (over 70%), reprocessing, high costs, poor geographical dispersion, debtor dominance in management bodies, absence of credit policies and internal procedures, etc. The externally imposed problem of freezing old foreign exchange deposits, which remained trapped in the Central Bank of the SME, further violated trust in the banking system, resulting in low levels of austerity and financial intermediation. The monetary authorities' attempt to break the oligopolic structure of the banking system by setting a very low capital threshold in the first years after monetary independence resulted only in the formation of the so-called "monetary independence". dwarf banks" that could not realistically violate the dominance of Macedonia's two largest banks. The conditions in this domain have improved significantly during this year. Namely, the sale of the largest and only state bank in the Republic of Macedonia Business Bank a.d. foreign investors, the sale of Credit Bank a.d. Skopje to a foreign investor, the announcement of the sale of the third largest bank , Tobacco Bank a.d. Skopje to investors from Germany and Slovenia, are undoubtedly major steps in creating healthy competition, as an integral part of the process of restructuring the banking system. From a systemic point of view, the basis of the reforms of the banking system from the so-called "second generation", is the adoption of a new Law on Banks in July 2000. The main intensity in preparing the new legal regulation was to achieve an optimal balance between strict regulation of supervisory aspects and leaving a high degree of liberalisation in which the competitiveness, ability and creativity of individual banking institutions will be expressed. The adoption of this modern legal text sublimes the joint one-year efforts of expert teams from the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia and the Ministry of Finance, as well as the experiences and suggestions of eminent foreign experts from the World Bank. The new banking act was drafted on the basis of the European Union Directives on Banking and Insurance of the So-Called "Banking and Insurance". "White Book" and the so-called "White Book". "The 25 Basel Principles for Efficient Banking Supervision." Given that the Republic of Macedonia's entry into the European Union is a long-term goal of the Government of the Republic of Macedonia, the start of harmonisation of legal regulation in the banking sphere is only a good start to this process. In addition to the legal texts of developed European countries, solutions in this area have been consulted in several advanced transition countries. The basic principles and changes adopted by the new Bank Act focus on several points: a more liberal procedure for licensing a bank and acquiring shares with the right to manage; a higher degree of liberalisation of more legal solutions; strengthening supervisory standards regulating the ongoing operation of banks; strengthening corporate governance in banks and introducing a so-called "principle of four eyes"; strengthening the procedures for the operation of banks; defining post-rict and detailed corrective measures that the Central Bank is obliged to take towards banks that do not comply with the legal provisions; strengthening the role and responsibility of the Management Board in banks, etc. The adoption of the new Bank Act, the sale of Business Bank a.d. Skopje, changes to the legal regulation aimed at improving financial discipline, as well as the adoption of a new Securities Act giving banks the opportunity to operate in the capital market, are part of agreed activities with the World Bank arrangement intended to restructure the financial sector and companies (FESAL 2). But reform activities do not end with these major projects. From an institutional point of view, the FESAL 2 arrangement also envisions a significant organisational change a separate unit has been established within the Directorate of Supervisory for dealing with problembanks within the NBRM. This unit has already been formed and will have the task of monitoring the operation of banks. In addition, if a bank is threatened with liquidity or solvency, and meets the criteria to be defined as a "troubled bank", it will be immediately placed under special supervision (monitoring) and corrective measures will be taken towards it. Other reform activities aimed at improving the state of the banking system include the envisaged adoption of a new Foreign Exchange Act by the end of 2000, which plans to introduce a greater degree of liberalisation in this area, while maintaining the necessary caution. The last major reform project in the financial sphere to be implemented in this and in the first half of 2001 are payment reforms, which envision the introduction of the so-called "real-time gross alignment system" (RTGS), and banks will be given a major role in the execution of payment turnover. This will allow banks to have a better insight into the liquidity of clients, which will improve the cash-flow management process and affect the creation of a healthier and more liquid banking system. Thank you. D-R Ljube Trpeski Governor

Title: Canvas reform seminar, Ohrid
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Welcome speech by The Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia Dr Ljube Trpeski at the canvas reform seminar, Ohrid, 09-11.02.2001 Welcome speech by The Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia Dr Ljube Trpeski at the canvas reform seminar, Ohrid, 09-11.02.2001 Dear guests, Dear colleagues, Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great honor and pleasure to welcome you and wish you success in the work of the first daily seminar on the reform of the country's payment system. The importance of the country's domestic payment system for the economy requires a cautious approach to its changes. Mutual contacts made through such seminars and other forms of communication should help consider the details related to the realisation of a comprehensive reform, such as the reform of the payment system in Macedonia. In addition, it is necessary to define very precisely the working functions of the new payment system, the impact of the old system of business entities, and the business habits it generated, the migration period from the old to the new payment system, etc. Payment turnover in the previous period was carried out on the basis of laws corresponding to the conditions of management and the types of capital ownership (mostly social) during that period. But overall social, political and economic changes in the country have imposed the need for reform of the payment system, as a significant segment of the banking system in the Republic of Macedonia. Further development of social relations in the country and a clear orientation towards a market economy, with a specific capital ownership, require a proper change in the country's payment system, which will give a full expression of the connection and mutual interest of business banks and their clients. Reasons for the reform I hope that, among other things, the reasons for reforming the payment system, as well as how to overcome them, will be discussed at this seminar. I would like to point out that with the new payment system, banks will be given the opportunity to work in new conditions, establish immediate contacts with their customers, develop a new range of banking services based on mutual competition, and thus raise confidence among domestic and foreign partners. Also, creating payment system infrastructure compatible with international financial structures, acceptable and understandable to international investors, will achieve one of the objectives of harmonising the Macedonian financial system with European Union regulations. It is a significant prerequisite for the Republic of Macedonia's rapprochement with the European Union. A significant occasion for payment system reform is the rapid development of technology and technology. Namely, the extremely rapid progress of informatics and telecommunications is causing changes in payment systems. The changes go to integrate payment turnover into the range of services offered by the banking system. The separation of this function outside the banking system, as has been the case so far and is still the case in the Republic of Macedonia, has generated and still generates a delay in changes and, accordingly, a delay in the development of banks. Purpose Starting with the need for reform of payment turnover in our country, with fare financial assistance, a Feasibility Study for Payment System Reform in the Republic of Macedonia was prepared during 1999, which was later adopted by the Government of the Republic of Macedonia. In accordance with this study, the main characteristics of reform are the following: payments to be made through commercial banks on a competitive basis; payment turnover to be carried out as a pure financial function; legal and natural persons have the opportunity to work through more than one account, in several banks; alignment in the central bank, in real time (promptly), on a gross basis (so-called RTGS system); the establishment of a low-payment clearing institution that will work on a net basis and a change in the legal regulation, not only for payment and commercial banks, but much more broadly. Such a reformed payment system in the Republic of Macedonia is expected to result in the following goals being achieved: Increasing the bank's responsibility and controlling its customers, including liquidity management by the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia and commercial banks; Direct responsibility of banks to the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia through supervisory procedures; Separation of common tasks, such as controlling and transferring them to the relevant institutions; Reducing the risk of interbank transactions; Providing opportunities for competition between banks in the payment system, through their service and price; Creating financial infrastructure that will be compatible with international financial structures and easily understandable to international investors that will provide the ability to attract foreign banks and investment. NBRM interest The efficient functioning of the payment system is of great importance to all financial entities in each national economy, especially the Central Bank as a monetary policy holder. One of the central bank's main tasks is to maintain the global liquidity of the economy at a level that ensures normal flow of commodity-cash transactions, without jeopardising price stability and the exchange rate of the national currency. In addition, the lower the efficiency of the payment system, because the alignment process lasts longer or is less secure, the more cash there is in payment turnover. Consequently, the central bank's efficiency in managing the monetary offer will be lower. Therefore, the increase in the efficiency of the payment system minimises cash in paid turnover, hence the central bank's control over the cash table is greater. Greater central bank control over monetary mass does not allow monetary policy to be conducted more efficiently. Such a situation usually determines the great interest of central banks in establishing the most efficient paid system. A brief review of the development of modern payment systems suggests that in order to ensure an efficient payment system, almost all central banks are operationally involved in the alignment of interbank payments. The existing configuration of payment systems in developed countries reflects a solid association with banking systems an association that has worked very well in the past and now. Activities of the NBRM In order to meet the obligations of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia in payment turnover, we have approached more activities. First, we are actively preparing to introduce a alignment system between banks that will work on the so-called RTGS principles real-time gross alignment. To that end, with fare financial assistance, we have concluded an agreement to acquire a ready-made system and expect it to be functional in mid-May this year. In addition, we were preparing to define the rules of operation of the Alignment System, which will be delivered to banks by the end of February this year. The rules will provide for banks to be able to join by two different methods: using the international banking network SNIFT and with the so-called "private network" between banks and the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia with the help of Macedonian Telecommunications. More details about this system will be given to you during these days. Furthermore, we are preparing to distribute cash to 10 regional centres from where other payment carriers will be able to supply. The presence of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia at these remote locations from the headquarters will help to securely and in a timely manner the issuance of the cash, in accordance with the needs of the payment carriers and through them to the participants in the payment turnover  all natural and legal persons in the country. In addition, we are preparing for the function of the state's service bank in payment turnover in the country. To that end, the Single Treasury Account will be opened at the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, through which the Treasury System at the Finance Ministry will be able to make paid turnover for the other state authorities participating in payment turnover. Finally, we are preparing to meet the obligations that will follow the adoption of the new Law on Paid Turnover, such as: decision-making on the standard for account construction, awarding leading numbers to banks and prescribing criteria for issuing and withdrawing permission to perform paid turnover. Some of these decisions will be presented to you at this seminar, while the rest are expected to be presented in March 2001. We will also be ready for additional decisions, together with the Finance Ministry, to specify the steps of reform. Conclusion The reform of the payment system imposes the need to carry out numerous activities, in several institutions. They must all be completed so that payment turnover can take place in a secure and transparent manner. I ask you for a lot of attention in fulfilling your part of the obligation, in order to preserve and improve the trust of the country's banking sector. I thank you for your attention and wish you a successful job over the course of these three days. I hope that this will contribute to a more successful round-up of reform and the installation of the payment system in Macedonia in line with the payment systems of developed countries. Thank you! D-R Ljube Trpeski Governor

Title: Forum of the Business Bank
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Speech by The Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia Dr. Ljube Trpeski at the Forum of the Business Bank, 27.02.2003 Speech by The Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia Dr. Ljube Trpeski at the Forum of the Business Bank, 27.02.2003 "In 2003, more relaxed monetary policy" Ladies and Gentlemen, Let me first thank the organisers of this forum for inviting me to be one of the speakers. Within the time I have been given, allow me to explain the basic characteristics of monetary policy implemented by the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia. Monetary policy in the Republic of Macedonia in all years after independence is one of the key instruments of macroeconomic policy. The main objective of monetary policy in the Republic of Macedonia is to maintain price stability. Price stability is one of the main elements of total macroeconomic stability and a fundamental prerequisite for healthy and sustainable economic development. The National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, as a central bank in the first years after independence, implemented a monetary policy aimed at realising the disinflation process. To mention that in 1992 on monetary independence day, average inflation was 1690%. The National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia managed to take down hyperinflation of single-digit inflation in a relatively short time. Since 1995, the Republic of Macedonia has had inflation that moves around the average of inflation in the Member States of the European Union. If only the inflation level criterion is taken, we are ready to join the European Union. By October 1995, the National Bank of Macedonia had implemented its crunch goal -price stability through a strategy of targeting the cash table. But from October 1995 to the present day, so this year it has switched to targeting the exchange rate. So the de facto fixed exchange rate all these years is the main nominal anchor of economic policy and defends itself with all economic policy instruments in which monetary policy is key. Why did you resort to changing strategy? Because for a small and open economy, such as Macedonia, the fastest and most effective way to achieve and maintain price stability is by maintaining a stable exchange rate. The Republic of Macedonia is a school example of this. The question arises as to how long that policy should persist and whether it is not time to move towards a leadership fluctuating course. And if there are discussions, especially in academic circles about the need to fluctuate in certain margins, however, and in the last arrangement we agreed with the IMF, the policy of a de facto fixed exchange rate remains, which will defend itself with all economic policy instruments. And to all current and potential investors, I can tell you that the ambition in which you will invest in the Republic of Macedonia will be price stability and stability of the exchange rate. The biggest temptations for the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia in maintaining the price stability and stability of the denar exchange rate were in 2001 and partly in 2002. In 2001, because of the war, fiscal policy was very expansive. If we at the central bank did not respond properly, there was a risk of the country returning to the hyperinflation zone. I am proud that in 2001 only using market instruments typical of each central bank, without the use of administrative measures, we were able to maintain both price stability and exchange rate stability. 2001 was a school example of how a systemic banking crisis could easily have taken place, as the population began to raise their deposits en masse. And that's what we were able to get through. We do so in a close co-operation between the central bank and commercial banks. Last year was easier, although in that year, the main burden of maintaining price stability and exchange rate stability was monetary policy. You know, in an election year, usually the fiscal policy governed by the government is looser than usual. But that is why here is the central bank with its instruments to neutralise that expansion and we have succeeded in doing so. And if we say that we ended the year with inflation below 2%, then we will find that the National Bank of Macedonia has fully responded to the task. This year, in 2003, the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia significantly facilitated the task of implementing monetary policy, because fiscal policy took its share of responsibility. That budget and fiscal policy are returning "on track" allows monetary policy to be much more relaxed. This relaxation is reflected in the reduction of the escont rate, in the reduction of the lombard rate, in reducing the rates of the obligatory reserve, in the possibility that banks will use liquidity loans with the central bank during all days of the month, etc. This designed monetary policy will make it easier for the private sector to come to loans to banks and i hope for lower interest rates. Credit activity will, however, allow GDP growth to grow by 3% by keeping inflation low up to 3%. Such an economy and, in particular, monetary policy, I hope will be attractive enough to challenge your interest in investing in the Republic of Macedonia. In terms of investment opportunities in the banking sector in the Republic of Macedonia, I would like to first point out that unlike some countries where certain barriers to investing in the banking sector are being put in place, especially from neighbouring countries, you could make sure that we do not have such prejudices. The largest investors in the banking sector in the Republic of Macedonia are from neighbouring Greece and we see it as an advantage. Our strategic goal is, one day, to be members of the European Union as soon as possible. Our strategic goal is our national currency as quickly as possible to experience the fate of your drachma. With your help, we can achieve this strategic goal faster. There are a number of small banks in the Republic of Macedonia that need recapitalisation. One way to invest in the banking sector is in existing banks. You can also start banks from a new one if you don't want to invest in an existing bank. D-R Ljube Trpeski Governor

Title: Conference of Clearing Institutions
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Welcome speech of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia Dr Ljube Trpeski at the 8th International Conference of Clearing Institutions, 18-20.09.2003 Welcome speech of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia Dr Ljube Trpeski at the 8th International Conference of Clearing Institutions, 18-20.09.2003 Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great honor and a pleasure to address this international conference attended by representatives from about 25 countries and international organisations, as well as on behalf of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, to welcome you to our country and to wish you a successful course at the conference. Given the topics to be discussed at this conference, I can certainly find that the effects of the conference will be positive not only for clearing institutions, but also more broadly for banks and other participants in payment systems. The National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia belongs to a group of central banks with a distinct degree of independence in relation to the executive branch. Its main goal is to maintain price stability. It achieves its goal by implementing the central bank's basic functions: - implementation of monetary policy; - maintaining financial stability and - functioning of the payment system. These three basic functions depend on each other. In this sense, the payment system plays a stoic role for financial markets. It is the main channel for liquidity distribution. Hence, the stable and efficient functioning of the payment system is a necessary condition for effective implementation of monetary policy. On the other hand, monetary policy operations help to properly operate the payment system, supplying liquidity for its smooth operation. The efficient functioning of the payment system allows safe and timely completion of financial transactions, creating a significant contribution to the performance of the national economy. Given that the payment system is one of the most vital components of financial and economic infrastructure, it can be assumed that any irregularities in its operation can quickly expand and create instability throughout the financial system. The payment system exposes participants to risks and can be a channel for transmitting shocks from one part to another of the financial system. On the other hand, the stability of the financial system significantly affects the successful operation of payment systems. Precisely because of these roles, the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia pays great attention to the security and efficiency of the payment system and is the initiator of reforms in the payment system. Thus, two years ago, a major reform of the country's payment system was implemented in the Republic of Macedonia and a modern payment system was built, which corresponds to the new states of the market economy. The new payment system strengthened the competitive component of banks, increasing the efficiency of banks and the entire banking system as a whole. At the level of a bank, more efficient liquidity monitoring and management is allowed. This reform also increased the efficiency of monetary policy making. On the other hand, if the fact that a legal entity may have multiple accounts in several banks in the new paid system is taken, diversification of the risk of an aspect of a legal entity is possible, which is a significant benefit to the financial system in general. The efficient and stable functioning of the payment system, the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, achieves them through the following functions: -Operational function, -Monitoring function, the regulatory function, and -Development function. The National Bank exercises its operational function as the owner and operator of mips Macedonian Interbank Paid System. It is a real-time gross alignment system (RTGS system). The operations in the system are carried out by participants in accordance with predefined MIPS Rules of Operation. In addition, the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia is a bank of the state and is run by the Only Treasury Account. Here I would like to point out that the functioning of the MIPS system is largely harmonised with the Basic Principles of Systemically Significant Payment Systems. This is not only an assessment of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, but is also confirmed by the FSAP Mission (May-August 2003) which gave very good assessments of mips' compliance with the Basic Principles and the IMF Transparency Code. At this point, the fsap mission's remarks are being overcome, which are primarily about building a backup system in a remote location as well as changing some legal provisions. I would like to point out that macedonia's Interbank Paid System fully covers its costs by operating, while achieving a minimum transaction price. In addition to regular operation, we were honored to present our RTGS system to representatives of eight different central banks from Europe, Africa and Asia who were and are in the implementation phase of their RTGS systems. I am proud to point out that the National Bank of Macedonia is one of the few institutions in the country that has been able to provide technical assistance to other central banks. Systemic risk is the main reason for the closer interest of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia in the field of monitoring payment systems as a second significant function. The principles used in assessing a secure and efficient payment system in monitoring are developed and codified in a report issued by the Bank for International Alignments (Basic Principles for System Important Payment Systems). The National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia has accepted these principles as a guide to its own supervisory activities. With their help, the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia ensures that all types of risks in the payment system are reduced. A significant place in payment systems in the Republic of Macedonia is also the Clearing House -KIBS, which is the largest private payment system. It works on the principle of deferred net alignment for processing low-value payments. Its proper development is a contribution to the overallity of payment systems in our country, which the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia follows within its function of monitoring payment systems. The National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia has an iRegulation function in the country's payment system. This function is achieved through decision-making, instructions and solutions in the field of payment systems. The development function of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia in Payment Systems is in monitoring and introducing new standards in operation, monitoring development trends and creating an ambition to implement them in payment systems in the Republic of Macedonia. Dear Ladies and Gentlemen, Allow me to express my satisfaction both from the topics treated at this international conference and by delegated lecturers from different institutions in Europe. Payment systems play a key role in the country's monetary stability and are therefore paid adequate attention. In this regard, I hope that this conference will also shed light on new knowledge from this area that will be useful to all of us. At the very end, I want to wish you all a pleasant and happy stay in our city and bring with you pleasant moments and new experiences. D-R Ljube Trpeski Governor

Title: Banking Conference organised by Pexim, Ohrid
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Presentation by The Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia Dr. Ljube Trpeski at the Banking Conference organised by Pexim, Ohrid, 27-29.11.2003 Presentation by The Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia Dr. Ljube Trpeski at the Banking Conference organised by Pexim, Ohrid, 27-29.11.2003 "The prospects and challenges of the Banking System of the Republic of Macedonia through the prism of comparative analysis with the banking system of central and southeast European countries" Since the monetary independence of the Republic of Macedonia, a series of reforms have been implemented in the banking system that have paved the way for the construction of a stable, secure and market-oriented banking system to meet the challenges of building a market economy in the Republic of Macedonia. There are assessments, which come primarily from international financial institutions, that reforms made in the financial system, i.e. in the banking system as its spinal column, are on the pedestal of the total economic reforms in the Republic of Macedonia. The result of the reform commitments taken is reflected, above all, through the level of stability and security of the banking system achieved. Such a finding is unequivocally confirmed through the increasing confidence of the public and citizens in Macedonian banks whose reflection is the growing trend of deposits collected. This grows the total financial potential of banks, which is one of the main prerequisites for effectively performing their basic function financial intermediation between financially surplus and financially deficiency economic subjects. But it should be noted that much remains to be done on the road that departs from stable banks and moves towards efficient banks that will be able to support the country's economic development more strongly. However, it is interesting to take a brief comparative look at the characteristics of the Banking System of the Republic of Macedonia with the banking systems of some of the countries of Central and Southeast Europe. I would like to start by pointing out that unlike many other countries in this group who have faced systemic banking crises during the transition process and reform of the banking sector (Czech Republic, Estonia, Croatia, Bulgaria, etc.) the Republic of Macedonia has avoided this. The high capital odds of Macedonian banks, the strict and prudent approach of Macedonian bankers in terms of the disposal of the cash raised, the strengthened banking supervisory, and the stable macroeconomic ambition have provided a very stable solvency and liquidity position for banks. This allowed banks to pass both the most difficult exams the Kosovo crisis in 1999 and the political security crisis in the Republic of Macedonia in 2001. Thanks to their high liquidity, at the time banks responded to increased demands for deposit payments, setting another solid pillar in building confidence in them. The analysis of the performance of banks in the Republic of Macedonia indicates that one of the main characteristics in this domain is the high capital adequacy coefficient which, with a state of 30 On June 9, 2003 it was 26.7% and at the very top compared to other Central and Southeast European countries, where the average is somewhere about 15%. After separate countries in this region, this indicator with a state of 31.12.2002 ranges from 11.6% in Slovenia and 14.2% in the Czech Republic, to 25.2% in Bulgaria and 30.4% in Serbia. The reasons for the high capitalisation rate of banks in the Republic of Macedonia may continue to be located in the following: -a relatively more conservative approach of banks in the placing of free funds in the form of loans in the economy. For illustration alone, the liquid ity of Macedonian banks, in the form of deposits in foreign banks, continues to have a dominant participation, with about 35% in the structure of the asset. These placements according to regulatory treatment are generally less risky, which also requires a lower risk ponder in calculating the adequacy of capital; -a relatively sympathetic structure of banks' liability, with higher participation of their own funds, versus a relatively smaller deposit base and other types of other sources of funds, which is particularly characteristic of smaller banks. Namely, the average participation of Macedonian banks' own funds in their total financial potential is 20%, versus the level of about 10%, which is a feature of the banking systems of other Central and Southeast European countries As efficiency in financial intermediation increases, a drop in the capital adequacy rate should be expected. Namely, the increase in lending volumes, off-balance sheet activities and the inclusion of financial derivatives should also lead to higher risk assets affecting the reduction of this coefficient as an indicator of the solvency position of banks, which, if too high, means that their efficiency in financial intermediation is low. The financial intermediation coefficient in the Republic of Macedonia analysed as the ratio of the total assets of banks to GDP is about 40% which is relatively low. Thus, this coefficient in countries such as the Czech Republic, Slovenia, Slovakia, etc., moves above 100%, while the average in EU member states is about 250%. In the Netherlands, for example, the share of assets in GDP is over 350%. Only Italy and Greece have a financial intermediation rate of less than 150% and is at the level of the highest financial intermediation rate achieved in transition countries. In the context of the analysis of financial intermediation, the indicator of the participation of net domestic loans as a percentage of GDP should also be taken into account. It can generally be concluded that approved net domestic loans represent a relatively small part of the GDP achieved in the national economies of central and southeast European countries. At the end of 2000, the participation of net domestic loans in the GDP of the Republic of Macedonia was 23.1%, versus 50.4% (Croatia), 49.9% (Slovenia), 79.6% (USA) and 134.9% (Euro Zone). However, the credit activity of Macedonian banks during the first half of 2003 saw moderate monthly positive dynamics. Gross credit rankings for non-financial legal entities and the population increased by 4.6% during the first six months of this year. Such a trend in credit activity still speaks to banks' conduct of cautious credit policies. From the point of view of the fixed-term structure of loans, certain positive movements may be observed in the direction of further intensifying long-term lending to the population and companies. In the period analyzed, long-term loans increased by 13.8%, versus a 4.3% decrease in short-term loans. This is about gradually intensifying long-term lending, which began in 2002, and as a strategy of banks, persisted in 2003. This is particularly characteristic of long-term lending to the population, which increased by 26.3% during the first six months of this year, while the increase in long-term credit rankings in companies was 9.6%. According to the purpose of long-term loans to the population, those approved for residential construction prevail. One of the main problems of transition countries is the credit risk manifested by the generation of high-risk rankings. This was particularly characteristic in the initial period of restructuring of banking systems, when this problem was mainly manifested through: -the existence of accumulated poor rankings made by banks before the start of reforms. Most transition countries, at the beginning of reforms, approached cleaning up the balance sheets of banks from these rankings by state intervention; -further generating new problematic rankings, which was due to inadequate credit risk management systems by banks, macroeconomic instability of countries and the underbuilt legal and institutional framework (inefficient court procedures for collecting demands, low financial discipline, etc.) Over the last decade, all transition countries have adopted the necessary regulation to regulate banks' credit risk, such as: methodology for classifying the asset according to the level of risk, determining the percentage of reservation required according to the risk category, and defining prudential limits limits limiting the bank's credit exposure to individual clients, insiders and shareholders to a certain level. Based on experience knowledge and guidelines coming from Basel, these standards are subject to permanent review and compliance by regulators in order to achieve more adequate credit risk control. The level of high-risk rankings in the Republic of Macedonia is still relatively high, although significant progress has been made since the monetary independence of the Republic of Macedonia. On 30 June 2003, credit exposure to banks in the Republic of Macedonia classified in B, D and D was 16.1%, versus 44% at the end of 1995. By comparison, the lowest participation in high-risk rankings, according to data with the state of 31.12.2002, was observed in Bulgaria (3.6%), Croatia (5.8%), Slovenia (about 7%). This rate is double-digit in Poland (20.5%), Serbia (24.3)%, etc. Further strengthening the internal credit procedures of banks as well as improving the overall economic and political ambition in the Republic of Macedonia should lead to a continuation of the already started trend of reducing the level of high-risk rankings, which will also mean a more efficient allocation of financial resources in the Macedonian economy. One of the characteristics of transition countries, including the Republic of Macedonia over the last decade, was the opening of banking systems to foreign investors and the permanent increase in the number of foreign banks in these countries. The positive effects of foreign capital entry in these countries are multiple: -the entry of foreign capital is followed by the possibility of providing other more efficient foreign sources of bank financing, which in turn can result in a reduction in active interest rates; -the entry of foreign capital is also followed by the introduction of new banking products, know-how, the establishment of new systems and approaches to risk management; -all of the above affects the increase in competition between banks and the initiation of processes for their enlargement, through merger and annexation; -the entry of foreign strategic investors creates the possibility of opening up national economies towards foreign, primarily Western European markets and creates the potential for possible future membership of these countries in the European Union The banking system of the Republic of Macedonia has a relatively low level of foreign capital compared to the other countries in the region analysed. Over the past two years, foreign capital participation in the total capital of Macedonian banks has been retained at a level of about 44%. After separate countries, foreign capital participation in total capital with a state of 31.12.2002 ranges from 19.4% in Serbia, 32.5% in Slovenia, to 82% in the Czech Republic, 90.2% in Croatia and 78.4% in Poland. One of the acute problems of the Banking System of the Republic of Macedonia over the past years has been the low profitability of Macedonian banks. The main indicators of banks' profitability, the rate of return on assets and the rate of return on capital of Macedonian banks, have a negative omen over the past years, or are at a completely low level compared to other transition countries, especially euro zone countries. By comparison, over the last decade, the average rate of return on the capital of banking systems of separate euro zone countries ranged between 5% and just over 10%, versus the average rate of return on the capital of banking systems from Central and Southeast Europe, which has long had a negative sign to positive sign and reach the level of about 5%. After separate central and southeast European countries, the capital return rate with a state of 31.12.2002 ranges from 3.04% in BiH and 6.7% in Poland to 16% in Bulgaria and Croatia and 22% in the Czech Republic. The average return rate of the asset is about 1% in most countries in this region. With a state of 31.12.2002, this indicator ranges from 0.4% in BiH and 0.5% in Poland, to 1.5% in Croatia and 2% in Bulgaria. According to the latest data on 30 July 2003, these profitability indicators of Macedonian banks have a negative omen. This stems from the stated loss in the operation of 5 banks, concluded on 30.06.2003. If the analysis and quantification of these indicators exempts banks that have worked with loss, the asset return rate and the return rate of the other banks, which otherwise represent 66.1% of the total financial potential, are 2.46% and 11.4%, respectively. One indicator on the basis of which banks' efficiencies are measured is the ability to control operating costs in relation to banks' assets. As of 31.12.2001, the highest participation in these costs was recorded by Bulgarian banks of 4.5%, while the lowest participation in Czech banks was 2%. In euro zone countries, the average share of operating costs in banks' assets is about 2%. According to the latest data on June 30, 2003, the share of operating costs in macedonian banks' assets is 2.1%, which is within internationally acceptable frameworks. Furthermore, the analysis can only be limited to the amount of salary costs and other employee-related costs as the highest component of operating costs. While banks in euro zone countries have seen a trend of reducing these costs in recent years, there is still a reverse trend among banks from transition countries. The average participation of these costs in euro zone banks' assets ranges around 1.0% (19932000). On the other hand, during the same period, these costs in transition countries increased and reached a level of about 1.8% in 2000 compared to banks' assets. According to the latest data on June 30, 2003, the participation of salaries in macedonian banks' assets is 1.15%, a satisfactory indicator of efficiency. From the comparative analysis of the state and performance of the Banking System of the Republic of Macedonia with those of central and southeast European countries, it can generally be concluded that banks in the Republic of Macedonia have a stable solvency and liquidity position throughout the past period. The main road to the banking system of the Republic of Macedonia is the path to achieving greater efficiency, a higher rate of financial intermediation, however, with the need to control and limit the level of banking risks within acceptable frameworks. Here, in particular, I would like to emphasise the necessity of permanent monitoring, control and measurement of credit risk. Namely, the increase in financial intermediation and, above all, the credit activity of banks expected in the coming period should be followed by all necessary preventive mechanisms to prevent the generation of new risk y loans. One of the risks banks face is operational risk, the basis of which is, among other things, the setting of information systems and standards for their security. Modern and modern information infrastructure prevails mainly in Macedonian banks. There is no process or banking operation performed in our banks, and in a segment of it it does not depend on its exit from the computer. In most banks, certain employees perform daily operations on 2 or 3 computers. Dependence on technology is evident in the normal execution of daily banking services. In order to successfully regulate and manage operational risk, the efforts made by the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia through the introduction of a supervision of information systems and the imposition of minimum standards necessary to ensure the security of banks' information systems are also made. Of the supervisory controls (IT Supervisory) so far, the finding is that the largest number of banks, together with programming houses, have developed programs that correspond to their size and complexity and the type of activities they carry out. The general impression is that Macedonian banks will focus on integrating their information systems into one in the coming period, in order to improve efficiency in the execution and maintenance of systems. However, certain weaknesses have also been found. In most banks, the role of internal and external auditin this segment is still insufficient, and thus the management board and bank management's awareness of the problems, shortcomings and risks in this domain. In the coming period, one of the main challenges we will face is the implementation of the New Basel Capital Agreement, known as Basel 2. From the analyses and experienced knowledge carried out internationally, especially by the Basel Committee for Banking Supervision, the introduction of Basel 2 will be a real revolution in banking operations and the management of risks in banking worldwide. The new capital framework is extremely complex, as it regulates several aspects of the bank's operation, such as: -credit risk -methods of reducing credit risk, -operational risk; -interest risk; -other market risks; -internal procedures of banks in terms of monitoring, measuring risks and determining the necessary capital; -market discipline, i.e. presentation of data in public; -supervisory monitoring process. All these elements of the New Capital Agreement will also require adequate information support from banks for identifying, measuring and monitoring credit, market and operational risk, creating a time series for the creditworthiness of the bank's creditworthiness, a time series for metered losses from operational risk, etc. It is also necessary to create certain institutional prerequisites for the implementation of this project, rather than affirming the place and role of credit rating agencies in the Republic of Macedonia. It is of particular importance to make efforts by the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia and commercial banks to start preparatory activities for basel's implementation sooner 2. This is necessary to encourage the total integration of the Republic of Macedonia, both in global financial flows and in relation to its aspirations for Membership in the European Union. D-R Ljube Trpeski Governor

Title: Promotion of gold coin - 60 years ASNOM
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Promotion of gold coin -60 years ASNOM, 30.07.2004 Promotion of gold coin -60 years ASNOM, 30.07.2004 Dear friends! On Monday, in less than three days, it does not stop, mark and mark the 60th Second August after the highest state body of power in the recent history of the Macedonian people, known as ASNOM, was constituted so many years ago. As is known, the people's "representatives, regardless of nationality, religion, gathered on that day, gender, race and political party affiliation, which have been given evidence, they accept the struggle for the independence and freedom of the people of Macedonia and the people's liberation struggle of all other peoples in Yugoslavia, and in addition are irreconcilable enemies of the occupier and his helpers" (Art. 3 of the ASNOM Decision). They gathered and began the constitution of the dream state of thousands of their predecessors. They gathered and informed the fundamental rights of the citizen of democratic Macedonia-thorough benchmarks on which the new state will be built, including: (quote from the adopted Declaration) 1. All citizens of the federal Macedonian state are equal and equal before the laws, not looking at their people, gender, race and religion; 2. Each citizen is guaranteed security for personality and property, guaranteed the right to property and the honorary initiative in business life; 3. Every citizen is guaranteed freedom of religion and freedom of conscience; 4. All citizens are guaranteed freedom of speech, press, gathering, agreement and freedom of society; 5. The right to choose and be elected to all electoral bodies in the people's government, etc. From then on, to this day, it did not suit and did not go as written. There were both "equals" and "much more equal" before the laws. There was and was a distorted, abused right to the right to freedom of conscience, the right to the agreement and freedom of association. There was and was a gross abuse and absolute negativity of the right to property and the right to the honorable (private) initiative in business life. There is much that has been promised, and it has not been achieved. But the country was evolving, however. Until the culmination of the crisis of the recent system, Macedonia grew as an identity. A sense of pride and not only the feeling, but also the reality of having their own institutions, national freedom -after decades and centuries of enslavement, occupation, oppression, was far above the dissatisfaction with smaller and greater breakdowns, deviations and negations from the recorded and a little cited by the ASNOM Declaration on the Fundamental Rights of the Citizen of Democratic Macedonia. Therefore, in all the past decades, the sense of community, the sense of coexistence has grown. We could have said with great confidence: We, our homeland, our society. Therefore, 8-September 1991 was at least seemingly, so easily possible. There was nostalgia, for many, due to the disintegration of the former SME, there was also euphoria and exaltation from the return of the previously delegated functions to the Federation -euphoria and exaltation from the act of building a completely independent state, an independent member of the O.N. State with all the "aim", i.e. all attributes. Therefore, joy spilled over the constitution of the first pluralistic Parliament. Therefore, songs were sung and ora were seen in the late night hours of September 8th. Cameras were shining, cameramen, journalists on the day of the introduction of their own money, on the day of the promotion of their own, independent army. Our national and state identity seemed to explode, despite some ethnic communities feeling the moment for an internal interethnic redistribution of collective power and influence at the time. Those days, those years, that basis, that support, that membership of the O.N., in the IMF, the WTO, etc., that today with the right to explicitly seek equal membership in NATO and the EU, would not have been possible without many knowing and unknown heroes throughout our centuries-old networks. In particular, they would not have been possible without the ASNOM and the ASNOMs. Without those who "accepted the struggle for independence and freedom of the people of Macedonia and who are nevertheless irreconcilable enemies of the occupier and his helpers". In Their honor, for Their glory, for the glory of Their winning spirit, for their statehood perseverance, for Their eternal memory, for the eternity of their work, we forged this jubilee gold coin. On the avers is the panoramic representation of part of the Monastery of St. Father Prohor Pchinski and its endsthe place where they made the historical decisions. The place that even today is a captured consciousness, anti-Asnomic, anti-civilisational prevents us from visiting it. And, of course, contrary to the expectations of such consciousness, both place and event gain more in their excitement and historical magic. The gold-plated reversal, at the centre itself, illustrates the cover of the ASNOM Manifesto. And it doesn't matter how much that gold coin weighs. For ASNOMICS, for this achievement, it is important how much we, today's generations, weigh. How much it weighs on our ability to defend ASNOM and develop it by settling in the present and future as a nation and a constant state, as a people capable of fighting a fight and getting a fight for the lives of their citizens no less good than those who can best. Both before ASNOM and asnom to this day, one is crystal clear. To be wrong in choosing the system and internal editing it is correctable. I believe that we have asnomic power and that we have a future with that. I believe that we will have strength and mind, or I would say, if we can, smart courage, resist all and today's and future temptations: through the permanent progress of human rights and possible, long-awaited economic progress to increase our individual and state achievements. Let's prove that we are for a cultural competition with everyone and that our place is among the best. The National Bank will protect the ASNOM spirit and be a bank equally in the interest of all citizens. Above all, through stable currency and low inflation. And as for the gold coin, I recommend -buy it. It's not every year for a six-decade jubilee and there are no other gold coins like that. There are only five hundred in accordance with the rare courage of asnomics. And I thank Biljana Unkovska for the design and goldmak for the workmanship. Thank you for deciding to be together tonight. Mr Petar Goshev Governor

Title: CEF Meeting
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Address by Governor Petar Goshev at the CEF Meeting -06 May 2005 Address by Governor Petar Goshev at the CEF Meeting -06 May 2005 Welcome to Macedonia and on behalf of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia. Feel at home. You watch and hear for yourself that there are still external entities that Macedonia wants for its first home. The report does not remind us that the CEF was founded by the wise and useful decision of the Government of Slovenia (2001), which is also joined by five other countries: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Macedonia, Serbia-Montenegro. And that in 2003 CEF was joined by Bulgaria, Moldova and Romania, making together nine entity countries that now have about 59 million inhabitants. The report also does not remind that the CEF was founded to address issues related to the development of public finance management capacity (to address issue of capacity development in public finance), in southeast European countries. But the Programme (Business Plan) tells us that CEF has treated and treated issues from the field of monetary policy, exchange rate, macroeconomic management as a whole, financial programming, banking, etc. So the CEF is neither left only in europe's narrower south-east, nor on the initial focus of the issues -capacity development in public finance management, which is very good for support, but also another proof that: you may know where you will start or where you started, but it is harder to know where you will end up. In any case, CEF is formed to improve our knowledge on specific, extremely important issues that directly or indirectly affect the growth and development of the economy and the well-being of citizens, in countries for which regional approach recognises similar background and similar needs. How much do we need CEF-type initiatives? From continuing and improving the work of CEF and the like? I always use the most synthetic indicator as a possible argument GDP or GNP. This group of states, tentatively speaking, of CEF, without Slovenia has a population of 56.6 million, with a total gdp of 146.9 billion in 2003. The first has 10.98 million inhabitants, the second 10.06 million inhabitants. The two, along with 21 million inhabitants, achieved 319.8 billion in GDP, and the 8 countries with 56.6 million inhabitants achieved only 146.9 billion. Looking for an answer to the question of major differences in the level of development and differences in growth rate dynamics, scientists and researchers have long and widely discussed which element in any form in Cobb-Douglass' production function (in a narrower or wider variant) is a larger or smaller source of income growth: whether it is the accumulation of physical and human capital, whether it is a so-called total factor productivity, whether it is economic and political institutions, geographical characteristics, etc. There is no doubt that attitudes, scientific conclusions are more convergence and gravitate towards the meaning of capacity, functionality, rationality of the so-called institutional factor. That convergence, with different accents, seems to me to reflect elhanan helpman's following lines in the very fresh, extremely highly rated work, titled "The Mystery of Economic Groth". He says: "My tale of growth economics is organized around four themes: First, the accumulation of physical and human capital is important, but it explains only part of the variation across countries in income per capita and its rate of growth. Technological and institutional factors also affect the rate of accumulation of these capital inputs, and they are in some sense more fundamental. Second, total factor productivity is at least as important as accumulation. To understand its determinants we need to understand what shapes the accumulation of knowledge, in particular, the incentives for knowledge creation. Third, growth rates of different countries are interdependant, because knowledge flows across national borders Fourth, economic and political institutions affect the incentives to accumulate and to innovate, and they so affect ability of countries to accommodate change.           : "countries that start with similar endowments can follow different developmental paths as a result of differences in institutional structures, because institutions affect the incentives to innovate and to develop new technologies, the incentives to reorganize producton and distribution in order to exploit new opportunities, and the incentives to accumulate phisical and human capital. For these reasons institutions are more fundamental determinants of economic growth than R&D or capital accumulation, human or physical " Following this course of reflection, four years after the founding and operation of cef what we can say, and through the experience of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia is as follows: CEF successfully accomplishes its mission of an educational institute for this part of Europe. CEF successfully disseminates cross-border knowledge and expertise, influences the process of exchanging positive experiences, reduces knowledge differences and positive practices. CEF has a solid intensity of work (86 seminars with 1,500 participants not a small job). CEF has a good program, useful for participants. He makes a good choice of topics in consultation with founders and donors. CEF engages solid lecturers, so apparently due to the choice of topics and lecturers, despite the possibilities for our employees to attend other seminars in reputable centres of Europe and the world  they have never lost the interest and desire to seek training and training of seminars organised by CEF. CEF's work contributes visibly to facilitating and improving co-operation and exchange of experience between central banks in the region. Joint meetings raise mutual awareness of each central bank's institutional capacity, people get to know each other, and this opens the channel of permanent professional communication outside seminars. Employees of the Central Bank of the Republic of Macedonia know what issue they should consult the Central Bank of Slovenia on, after which with the Central Bank of Bulgaria, Croatia, etc. CEF facilitates the harmonisation of domestic central banking and total financial legislation with the same from the EU, thereby helping us to faster adopt the standards needed to achieve our goal of Membership of the European Union. CEF contributes to strengthening the institutional capacities of economies in the region, to creating a good institutional framework as an important condition for more dynamic economic growth. In this way, CEF becomes a component of such an important growth factor, the so-called total factor productivity, which if not today, in the years before us we may also be able to decompose it with our quantitative part. Therefore, the Central Bank of the Republic of Macedonia will participate in its full capacity in improving the work of the CEF in the future and naturally requires more seminars with topics of central bank competence. At CEF we are used to, CEF needs it, CEF has proved useful and successful and therefore we will continue to support its development because of common needs. Mr Petar Goshev Governor

Title: Opening of a Workshop on "High Level of Cash in Circulation in the Republic of Macedonia" at the NBRM
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Address by The Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, Mr Petar Goshev, opening a Workshop on "High Level of Cash in Circulation in the Republic of Macedonia" at the NBRM, 14.04.2006 Address by the Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, Mr Petar Goshev, and the opening of a Workshop on "High Level of Cash in Circulation in the Republic of Macedonia" at the NBRM, 14.04.2006 Respected, For centuries, economists have been preoccupied with the issue of growth. They've been studying continuously since Adam Smith's days. Thus, they continuously analyze the cost per unit of product, the time required for a unit of product, the net value that remains after deduction of all types of costs. It would be displaced to ask whether the different amounts of cash in circulation for the same or different GNP values, the relationship between cash and cashless transactions in payment transactions, the speed of payments and the like affect costs, the efficiency and effectiveness of the economy. Because, more than famous is: -that printing and distributing the cash costs money; -that, saving and securing the cash costs money through costs for space, people, insurance; -that, the holders of the cash, with the act itself have opportunistic costs, because, a short definition of the cash, as the most liquid part of the M1 cash mass simply states: These are banknotes and coins that do not carry interest; -that, keeping cash ready at home, or transferring them to bags or bags carries risks -both for money and for "postmen"; -that keeping cash done outside banking and other financial institutions directly reduces financial intermediation, weakens lending to companies and the population, shortens the support of the real sector; -that the high amount of cash, as an autonomous factor, makes liquidity planning difficult by both the central bank and the banks themselves, etc. Therefore, if all this is known and accurate, it would be irresponsible, not to analyze this process and not to ask ourselves: -why is the cash in circulation in the Republic of Macedonia comparatively still at such a high level? -why are the network and cashless payment instruments developing slowly or insufficiently quickly or with a greater delay compared to most comparable countries? -who are the main generators and supporters of the high level of cash? -are there, from the list of causes of high level of cash such that can be removed in the short term, others in the medium term, third who require permanent activity, in order to try through this segment  the amount of cash in circulation, to enter an input to improve the efficiency of the economy? -which institutions and according to the type of jurisdiction should, or are obliged on this issue today, to do more!? Confident that the new appropriate activity of the relevant institutions aimed at this segment could help, we have agreed that several people from the central bank will previously prepare a certain analysis that will re-update the issue of the ratio of cash and cashless transactions in payment transactions of the Republic of Macedonia. You have this analysis ahead of you, which can be both more comprehensive and deeper and somewhere more precise! But in any case, we believe that a provocation for a contentdebate is enough. Why, among other things, really provoks us to ask ourselves: -can the competent institutions finally tighten forces to reduce the grey economy, which almost everyone claims to be the main maintainer of the high level of cash. But through a concrete, state strategy and operational plan of measures and activities that will definitely result in faster integration of grey into the official economy? -can we, should we coordinate better, as competent institutions and agree that, however, it should intervene in the legal regulation, that it also has misdemeanors and contradictions and that we should do so an hour sooner? -can we be indifferent to the fact that over 12 billion denari a year, so over 1 billion denari a month pension money with bags and postmen is blown to the end users, that the worse is distributed and other billions, it was those for cash salaries, for wine, for fruit, for tobacco or for any other payments, and all that to justify it with our mentality, habits, culture, etc.? Definitely, Macedonia, however, is not so ignorant, inadaptable to modern trends. -can we, should we open a comprehensive debate about the "concept of blocked accounts"? Living companies with blocked accounts that have not settled obligations for months and years, and trustees and the state do not implement a collection procedure from what such companies have left or have? How much does this concept stimulate work in cash, grey economy, tax evasion, sluggishness in the relocation of production factors, non-dynamic, non-creativity? etc. Aware that these issues are issues from the domain of several institutions in the country, we, as a central bank, as one of the responsible payroll entities, as the only authorized issuer of cash, as an institution that spends both on their production and their storage and distribution, have allowed ourselves to invite you all to this debate or, more specifically, with some of you to organize this one-day workshop together. I, on behalf of the central bank, thank you for being all here.
