Especially to individuals who, in their own name and on behalf of institutions, have been reluctant to prepare presentations and presentations that will help us all dive deeper into the causes of the relatively high level of cash in circulation in our country as well as for other weaknesses in the payment system, for, ultimately, we are more easily identifying the measures we needs to improve the situation. I hope that this joint activity of ours will not only end in another exchange of opinions, but that through the next analysis of cash in circulation and as a result of institutional interventions, we will find significant improvements not only as a result of the evolutionary act of changing awareness and habits. Moreover, all previous reforms and improvements in this sphere are the result of intervention by the competent institutions. I wish inventive and useful discussion and a pleasant working day in the premises of the National Bank! Thank you! Mr Petar Goshev Governor

Title: Welcome speech at annual award on the occasion of the 15th anniversary of monetary independence, Skopje
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Welcome speech by The Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, Mr Petar Goshev, at the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia's annual award on the occasion of the 15th anniversary of monetary independence, Skopje, 26.04.2007 Welcome speech by The Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, Mr Petar Goshev, at the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia's annual award on the occasion of the 15th anniversary of monetary independence, Skopje, 26.04.2007 Dear ladies and gentlemen, I am honored to welcome you today, when, for the first time, the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia awards the Annual Young Researchers Award for Best Work in the Field of Macroeconomics. Today's award is, in fact, a round-up of the formal procedure that began in September 2006  by the adoption of a proper decision by the Council of the National Bank and the publication in November of that year  of the Competition in several daily newspapers and professional journals in the Republic of Macedonia. As this year's first award of the MacroeconomicS Young Researchers Award coincides with the end of 15 years of monetary independence of the Republic of Macedonia, Allow me, before i announce the winners of the award, to look back on today's jubilee, extremely important for the statehood of the Republic of Macedonia. As a direct participant in the events of 1991 and 1992, I can, even after fifteen years, speak very detailedly and specifically about this turbulent period filled with high hopes. But since in October last year we already marked another jubilee -60 years of central banking on the territory of the Republic of Macedonia -incorporating the imminent assessments for the last 15 years, Just briefly, for reminder, I once again want to emphasize the meaning of today, leaving, understandably, more space for the presentation of the works of our young authors. On 26 April 1992, the first multiparty Assembly of the Republic of Macedonia, in the face of constant political and military pressures on the rounding of our sovereignty, passed the Law on the Monetary Unit of the Republic of Macedonia. On the same day, in co-ordination with the Assembly, the then governor, Mr Borko Stanoevski, in this building, signed the Decision to release the value vouchers of the National Bank of Macedonia, which introduced the Macedonian national currency denar. The acts adopted today 15 years ago were part of this thorough break with the past, embodied in the final and irreversible entry of the Republic of Macedonia into the society of states that possess all the attributes of the modern notion of state sovereignty and independence. Over the past one and a half decades, the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, as part of the total economic system, I am convinced that you share my opinion, successfully performed the functions assigned by law. It is not a foul, but a notoriety fact, that stable denar, low and stable inflation, as well as a stable banking system are provided. These are benefits confirmed by all international financial institutions, and all competent analysts, standing by the thesis that these are necessary prerequisites for sustainable economic development. These results are the product of the fact that the National Bank is continuously working to elevate its professional capacity and permanent efforts to gradually approach the central banks of developed countries. In modern conditions of a dynamic environment, the functions of central banks are becoming more sophisticated and in this context, the National Bank seeks to flexibly respond and face all new challenges. Thus, in addition to classical functions related to monetary policy and exchange rate regime, Today, the Bank plays an active role in the development of financial markets, the establishment and development of the reformed pension system, the development of a banking supervisory based on the risks, analyses and assessments of total financial stability in the country, as well as the promotion and development of the application of economic modelling. This shows that the past 15 years, in addition to laying the foundations for modern central banking, and overcoming several crisis periods, have been marked, among other things, by the development of the National Bank in all spheres of its operation. In this regard, the introduction of the practice of awarding the National Bank Annual Award for Best Work by young macroeconomic researchers is part of our commitment to due evaluation of their research efforts, as well as their knowledge and expertise that are more than required for the development and strengthening of the institutional capacity of our economy. And with this award we actually want to show that we believe in the potential of young macroeconomists in our country, wanting to support them in their scientific research work. Our country has different types of economic problems. But there is also personnel potential that has ideas and suggestions for viewing and overcoming them. The awarding of this award focuses on some of that potential, in fact the most promising of young and capable staff whose scientific research work should be encouraged and supported in all possible ways. We are particularly pleased that at the outset this initiative meets our expectations. Namely, the Evaluation Board, composed of: Dimitar Bogov -Vice Governor, who is also chairman of the Board, Dr. Goran Petreski, Associate Professor of the Faculty of Economics in Skopje and external member of the Council of the National Bank and Dr. Aneta Krstevska, Director of the Directorate of Research at the National Bank, finds: that we have received a solid number of submitted papers -16; that the majority of those papers, i.e. 9, are of good quality, dedicated to current macroeconomic topics served by the application of current macroeconomic research methods. And, because there are final winners or winners in every match, so is this one. And, now most importantly, especially for the participants in the competition. Based on a review of the papers that have arrived, the Board unanimously declared that this year's NBRM Award for Best Work in the Field of Macroeconomics is awarded to the author whose work bears the title: Calculation of the fundamental equilibrium exchange rate of the denar. It is clearly an extremely current topic for transition countries, including the Republic of Macedonia. According to the characteristics of the work, we believe that the awarding of this work will set a high standard for the awards that would be awarded in the coming years. The author of this work and the first winner of the Annual Award of the National Bank is Branimir Jovanovic. I invite him to receive the award. In addition to the above work we declare best, the Evaluation Board also unanimously declared that another work deserves special attention, namely the work under the headline: Model of sustainable unemployment rate for transition countries, with a look back at the Republic of Macedonia. As the headline shows, labour is dedicated to one of the biggest problems of the Macedonian economy, unemployment. Given the serious approach and quality of work, the Board proposed to consider awarding a second prize, which the National Bank Council has pleasedly accepted. Thus, based on supplementing the Decision on the Annual Award of the National Bank, we are awarding a second award to author Dimitar Nikoloski, whom I also invite to receive the award. Finally, I would like to thank all participants in the first Competition for the Annual Award of the National Bank and congratulate them on their efforts to participate in the Competition. We all, along with other new participants, encourage them to apply to the next Competition for the Annual Award of the National Bank. The best work will be awarded again. I believe that in this way we will have the opportunity to promote more young macroeconomist researchers and at the same time enrich professional literature with quality scientific papers. After this, I would not want to take more than the time provided for the presentation of the papers of the award-winning authors. This is their day. Once again thank you for your presence today, congratulations on the award-winning authors, and let all of us be happy with the jubilee -15 years of monetary independence! In addition, let's indulge in the presentations of the award-winning authors and the president of the Evaluation Board. Mr Petar Goshev Governor

Title: Press conference
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Press conference of the Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia Mr Petar Goshev, Skopje, 26.12.2007 Press conference of the Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia Mr Petar Goshev, Skopje, 26.12.2007 Respected, On my behalf and on behalf of my associates, allow me to welcome you to this already traditional New Year's eve meeting. Another year is behind us, each with his vision of her, and normally, again with the next one before us, with new expectations, hopes, puzzles, etc. I will look back briefly, from the point of view of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, and what ends in a few days for the coming year. I. 2007 analysed from the point of view of the economy's achievements, is definitely positive, successful: - With the expected highest real GDP rate of over 5 percentage points; - With an average inflation rate of about 2% or slightly above two; - With a stable exchange rate held; - With a relatively low current account deficit-expected to end with -2.3 percentage points from projected GDP; -With gross foreign exchange reserves amounting to 1,564.6m euros on 15.12.2007, which means a 150m-euro increase compared to the end of the previous year or security of 3.8 monthly imports of goods and services planned for next year; -With a continued trend of further interest rate cuts, i.e. the price of capital. The Central Bank's interest rate was reduced, in November, to 4.66%, and the average active interest rate of banks, for all types of loans and all maturities, was reduced to 9.98%. II. The ambition to pursue monetary policy in 2007 was favourable: -We had continuously good foreign exchange inflows in the foreign exchange market ,"the results in the external trade with the world was better than 2006, especially in the first half of the year, and the increase in so-called private transfers covering the lion's share of the chronic trade deficit continued; -We had a highly disciplined budget ary policy, which is likely to end in a budget surplus, which is strong support for monetary policy; -Continued the increase in the credibility of monetary and fiscal policy, which have a strong impact on the creation of positive expectations of market participants; -The world economy has seen another year of extremely high economic growth - expected GDP growth of about 5%. This allows: -Maintaining exchange rate stability and another year at a low general level of economy prices; -Maintaining the competitiveness of the Macedonian economy in foreign markets, because we have made it clear: a mild depreciation of the real effective exchange rate of the denar; increase, as I said, on exchange reserves; slightly faster labour productivity growth in terms of real wage growth; -interest rate cuts; and -creating conditions for dynamic growth of monetary and credit aggregates. Monetary and credit aggregates are expected to record the following growth rates by the end of the year: private sector loans -37.5% (i.e. to reach 36% of GDP), the broadest cash mass -32%, deposits of about 35% and primary money 17.8%. And, if there are any more, who ask if monetary policy supported economic growth in 2007, it should only look at these figures because they are 2, 3, 4, and even more times above nominal GDP growth. So the answer is, more than YES! III. In such conditions, one of the most regulated economic activities, and at the same time, in line with world trends the most closely monitored -banking, has also historically achieved the best results: -Total deposits of non-financial persons reached 150 billion denari (2.5 billion euros) on September 30, 2007, or more than the same period last year by 32.6%. 58% of these are deposits of the population. This is the most convincing illustration of the increasing trust of savers in the banking of the Republic of Macedonia; -The annual private sector loan rate is 41.4 (October 2006/October 2007), and the annual rate will end at about 37%. Within these frameworks, loans approved to the population increased by 56.4% to 43.2 billion denari (about 705 m euros), and to companies 71.8 billion (about 1.2 billion euros); -Financial intermediation, expressed as participation in total assets, gross loans and total GDP deposits, is progressing rapidly, reducing the lag behind other comparative economies: total assets, gross loans and total GDP deposits, in the same order reached 67%; 37.5% and 48.6%, and on 31.12.2006 they were: 57.4%; 29.6% and 41.3%. So, in all three indicators, 810 percentage points growth in GDP, which is an extremely high dynamic! The fact that such dynamic lending growth is as follows: -Improving the risk profile of banks; -The profitability and efficiency of banks is increasing. For example: their profit in the first 9 months is higher by 56% compared to the same period last year; The return rate of the asset from 1.7% increased to 2%, and the rate of return on capital from 11.1% to 30.09.2006 increased to 15.8% to 30.09.2007; -The adequacy rate of capital remains almost double (17.2%) than the minimum prescribed (8%); -In 2007, about 77m euros of direct investments (share buybacks of about 46m euros, about 4m euros in reinvested profits, about 27.4m euros in recapitalisation and a subordinated deposit) entered banking. This is without portfolio investment in the banking sector. At the same time, a significant restructuring process occurred. Non-financial sector shareholders were replaced by shareholders from the financial sector all from abroad, with greater experience in banking and finance and much greater financial potential than previous ones. These investments, along with some others in preparation, will increase credit potential, the range of financial products and services and no doubt competition in banking, with the ultimate benefit to companies and the population. IV. For 2008, economic growth views have already been made no less than the year's, meaning above 5% and an inflation rate that will gravitate around 3%. There are strong arguments for accelerated economic growth to continue. But potential risks must also be closely monitored. Monetary policy will also focus in 2008 on maintaining exchange rate stability and preventing an undesirable level of inflation growth. To continue and increase the sustainability of economic growth and the tolerant level of inflation, the following matters: -Not to have a more significant deterioration in the conditions of exchange with the world. This means that no further major jump in the price of energy occurs; -Do not continue to reduce the demand and prices on the world market for our main export products; -To calm the food market, not believing that, when it comes to agriculture and the overall food sector, a repeat worldwide within another unfavourable year, as this was; -To continue political and security stabilisation in the region, which implies resolving the Kosovo issue in the best possible way. But at the same time: -Let's continue with disciplined monetary and fiscal policy as before, which I have no doubt about; -To continue to further improve the conditions for economic activities, by further deepening structural reforms, which have evidently begun to result in increased performance of the economy; -The movement of real wages does not exceed productivity growth and/or real GDP growth. In. In 2008, we will continue to develop the operational framework of monetary policy. We also plan to introduce shorter-term treasury records than the current 28-day, and introduce longer-term than 28-day ones, with the intensity to manage liquidity more efficiently in the system. Together, we will improve the auction mechanism in terms of increasing competition and efficiency. Depending on foreign exchange market movements, balance of payments and inflationary pressures, we will also react by including other monetary policy instruments, all in the function of maintaining macro-economic stability, as it is definitely the best ambition for sustainable economic growth. We. In June 2007, the European Commission assessed the sector in the field of financial services in the Republic of Macedonia. In addition, it rated the Banking System of the Republic of Macedonia as the most developed segment of the country's financial system, both in its financial situation and assortment of products and services, as well as from the perspective of the regulatory framework and progress in the overall reform processes. She positively assessed the adoption of the new Banks Act, saying it was a major step towards implementing European regulation. However, it does not satisfy us at all. The promotion of banking requires continuous work, moreover, as with everything else. In 2008, all by-laws arising from the new Banks Act will be adopted by the end of March. A key emphasis, among other things, will be placed on: -The decision on corporate governance in banks, which will lay down the basic principles for good corporate governance in banks; -The decision on the methodology for determining the adequacy of capital, with essential news on how banks' own funds are calculated, by installing appropriate accounting standards based on international financial reporting standards. This rounds out the application of BASEL I and enters into force of the New Capital Agreement BASEL II; -The decision to manage credit risk, then the Decision on the risk management methodology that lays down the basic principles to be met by banks in the introduction and application of the concept of risk management. In 2008, as part of the implementation of the New Capital Agreement BASEL II, a new methodology will also be prepared to manage the risk of changing interest rates, resulting from the portfolio of banking activities, as well as the inclusion of operational risk in calculating the adequacy of capital. There will be numerous other regulations and activities all in the function of more efficient risk management, all in a function of greeting and a more competitive banking sector of the Republic of Macedonia. I am convinced that we will have a successful year: with new investments in banking, with improved prudential principles, which will be the backbone of supporting economic growth. Respected! Markets and the human body are interconnected. The reason is simple. The markets and markets are operated on by man. Therefore, the key words in their functioning are sensitivity, health, stability, in any sense. Hence, to have a successful year of economic and personal plan, we need a healthy and stable environment, in the country, a closer environment and beyond. To that end, congratulating you on the new year, I wish you personal health, and a healthy environment for a fair match in the never-completed process of the battle to increase people's well-being. Mr Petar Goshev Governor

Title: Press conference in Skopje
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Press conference of the Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia Mr Petar Goshev in Skopje, 29.12.2008 Press conference of the Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia Mr Petar Goshev in Skopje, 29.12.2008 Respected, On my behalf and on behalf of my associates, allow me to welcome you to this traditional New Year's eve meeting and briefly reflect on the challenges the National Bank faced in the year ahead, as well as the challenges facing us in the coming 2009. I. The world economy will remember 2008 after high oscillations in food and energy prices and the global financial and economic crisis, which this year gained dramatic proportions. Rarely before, global movements in 2008 are characterized by high variability. In a period of just over a year, the global economy of a solid growth phase and galloping prices of food, energy and metals, a recession-phase dive and rapid price reductions of primary products. In 2008, the ambition in which we pursued monetary policy characterized: increased inflationary pressures; continued deepening of external imbalances, and an increased level of uncertainty produced by the global crisis. This says that in 2008, as the Central Bank we faced stressed challenges, and, in our opinion, successfully dealt with them. But let me look back, a little more specifically, although what we have been through this year is no stranger to us.  Since the second half of last year and especially the first half of 2008, we have been preoccupied with the inflation movement, dominantly caused by external factors. Let's recall, during the first quarter of the year we had higher annual inflation rates, more than a decade unnoticed in our country, which inevitably did not force us to take appropriate monetary measures to prevent the transfer of the initial effects of the rise in food and energy prices on inflation in the medium term. The measures taken, along with the gradual stabilisation of food prices globally and the reduction in oil prices, resulted in a calming of inflation, which began to feel as early as the second quarter of the year, and more pronounced than the third quarter here. The average inflation rate in January 2008 was 8.7%, while the annual inflation rate in November was reduced to 5.2%. In December, we expect it to be reduced below 5%, and the average will fall to about 8%. This is how we expect it to end 2008 in terms of inflation.  Macedonia's economy continued to grow in the first three quarters of 2008. The main growth boosters are personal and investment consumption. But as our economy is highly open, the global crisis is expected to have a negative impact, primarily on the real sector of the economy, especially noticeable in the last quarter of the year. In October and November 2008, industrial production saw an annual decline, primarily caused by reduced foreign trade, which in these two months has an annual growth rate of (0.2) and (-2.0), versus the average for the 11 months of the year of 21%. Given such situations in the industry, along with the slowdown in personal consumption and investment, in general restraint conditions, it does not expect a significantly lower economic growth rate (about 2%) in the last quarter of the year. In any case, due to a solid increase in the first three quarters and in 2008, the economy will achieve a real GDP growth rate of about 5%.  In 2008, there was again an expression of an extremely unpleasant structural problem of our economy: the trade, namely the current account deficit of the balance of payments. Thus, inflation care was replaced by concerns about this fact. In the current account of the balance of payments, we registered a significant deepening of the deficit. As of September, the deficit reached 567m euros, versus the same period from 2007, when it was only 83m euros. The main reasons are: the deterioration of the trade balance (by 625.2m euros, or 83.3%) and reduced net inflows based on private transfers (by 6% compared to the same period last year). Reduced external demand in the last quarter of the year, caused by the global economic crisis, has an additional adverse impact on the current account balance. Therefore, we estimate that the current account deficit for the whole of 2008, which takes into account the possible consequences of the global financial and economic crisis on the balance of payments, as well as the latest movements and projections for oil and nickel prices on world stock markets, points to a current account deficit of 14-15% of GDP.  In 2008, the "remediation" of the current account deficit was carried out from the capital and financial account. In the capital and financial account, we had an increased influx of direct investment and a sharp decrease in banks' net foreign exchange assets. It was the inflows from these sources that allowed favourable foreign exchange market movements for most of the year, despite: (1) the deteriorating trade balance, (2) reduced inflows from private transfers and (3) high outflows on the basis of dividend payments to foreign companies. In such circumstances, gross exchange reserves have remained at the level since late 2007, providing over three monthly average coverage of imports of goods and services from the following year.  By saving the private sector in banks, we can be satisfied. However, the final rate of private sector deposit growth in banks will be lower than last year's, as in November, it is 15.2% year-on-year, as opposed to last year's growth of 29.7%. As the year went on, so the growth rate slowed. The main reason was the fear that the global financial crisis would not spill over into Macedonia, and I must say, not the small number of unmeasured statements that have increased such fear. The latest quarter also caused reduced economic activity. Also, as the year passed, the exchange savings stakes grew faster than denarii. Again, the dominant reason was of a psychological character, driven by higher inflation and unfounded rumors that persistently spread about the exchange rate. Credit growth versus a gradual slowdown (especially in loans to the population) and in 2008 will show high growth (about 35%), as it is 37.8% high in November, an obvious fact that suggests that monetary policy strongly supported economic activities this year. This is what the growth rates of almost all monetary units speak of. II. The banking system was not directly affected by the global crisis. It is the orientation of Macedonian banks to traditional banking activities that focus on the domestic market, the absence of using structured products and the execution of complex financial activities, the low dependence on foreign sources of funding has contributed to maintaining its stability. However, during 2008 the National Bank took several measures to prevent risks in the banking system: tightening the treatment of banks' demands on the basis of credit cards and overstepping transaction accounts, in determining the solvency of banks; limiting intensive credit growth to the population; monitoring of banks' exposure to abroad; daily deposit monitoring; etc. Of course, the measures adopted by the National Bank Council, which concern a prescribing obligation for banks to maintain a minimum level of liquidity, separately in denari and in foreign exchange to cover their obligations to be delivered over the next 30 and 180 days, are particularly important. As is known, we have also allowed excess foreign exchange funds to be placed by banks in the country, i.e. in instruments of the National Bank in foreign exchange. Total 2008 was another successful year for banking in the Republic of Macedonia. Three new foreign strategic investors have entered banking. At the end of November 2008, 14 banks were owned by foreign shareholders and participated with about 84% of the total capital of the Banking System of the Republic of Macedonia. The participation of financial institutions in the ownership structure of ordinary shares issued by banks continues to increase. (from 60.4% at the end of 2007 to about 67%).  The role of the banking system as a financial intermediary continued to grow. The share of the asset in GDP reached about 70%, which is 10 percentage points higher than last year. Such positive dynamics contribute to reducing the lag relative to other countries in the wider region.  Although at the end of the third quarter of 2008, the first signals of an increase in the risk of the banking system's credit portfolio were expressed, however, it calms the fact that on an annual basis, the participation of high-risk bank placements (V, D and D) in the total credit portfolio continues to decrease. At the end of September 2008 it was 5.7%, versus 6.4% in September 2007.  Although with a reduced level, banks continued to operate profitably and efficiently. In the first nine months of 2008, the Banking System of the Republic of Macedonia made a profit of 15.8% compared to the same period last year. By comparison, the profit achieved in the first nine months of 2007 was 56% higher compared to the profit achieved in the same period of 2006. The asset return rate (ROA) was 1.9%, (down 0.1 percentage point compared to the first nine months of 2007). The rate of return on capital (ROE) in the first nine months of 2008 was 16.5%, (0.7 percentage points more compared to the same period since 2007).  The liquidity of banks in the Republic of Macedonia is solid, but we are seeing a downward trend. It is particularly positive that the capital position of banks fully covers the identified risks. The adequacy rate of capital (as a basic measure of bank stability) is almost double (15%) than the minimum prescribed (8%).  Additionally, all simulations made on a regular basis by the National Bank show that the banking system manifests a satisfactory degree of resistance to various hypothetical shocks. What do we predict for 2009?  2009 is a very difficult year for projections. Uncertainty from the depth and duration of the global economic crisis remains in its entirety, and this brings great uncertainty to countries whose economies are open, and especially small, as is the case with ours. However, it is certain that we will face a slowdown in economic growth, compared to 2009. According to our current projections, it will be a success if our economy grows between 3-4.5%.  It is also certain that the trend of inflation reduction will continue. The slowdown in inflation is expected to affect: -Stabilizing import prices with the greatest impact on our price index (food and energy prices); -Reduced personal consumption (due to slower growth in household loans, reduced opportunities for wage and pension growth; and the uncertain dynamics of private transfers). Following these assumptions, in 2009 we expect the average inflation rate to range from 2.2-3.4%, and on the annual (December 2009 /December 2008) at an interval of 2.35.6%.  The current balance of payments account deficit will remain at a high level of about 10-11% of GDP. The fact that this level of deficit, if achieved, would be slightly lower than the final one for this year (2008) does not mean simultaneously relaxing the pressures of the foreign exchange market, primarily due to the extremely uncertain movements in the capital and financial account, from where the above gap should be covered.  The expected slowdown in economic activity, the decrease in exchange inflows, the refrain from saving under the influence of the global crisis are likely to require a slowdown in cash mass growth, which is currently estimated at 10-11%. In the face of slowing growth in primary sources of bank financing, uncertain surroundings, reduced and more expensive access to external sources of funding, it is realistic to expect a slowdown in credit growth that would not be significantly above the stated rate of cash mass growth, of course under the above assumptions. What will be the focus of the NBRM in 2009?  And, in 2009, we will continue to implement the strategy for maintaining a stable exchange rate, which has proved to be very successful in maintaining price stability as a basic monetary goal. According to the above, in 2009 we will need to analyse the movements related to the country's balance of payments, since price fluctuations, as it is obvious that the biggest challenge for economic policy holders will be the current account deficit and movements in the capital and financial account of the balance of payments. The state of payment imbalances, their sustainability in the short and medium term will be the main determinant of character, i.e. the position of monetary policy. In particular, these questions will depend on whether monetary policy tightens, whether it remains the same or deepens. One thing is certain, the National Bank will use all instruments available to maintain a stable exchange rate, as a direct goal of achieving its core low inflation target. Of course, monetary policy will have more room for flexibility if other policies do not elude this very important issue of the country's macroeconomic stability.  In 2009 we will continue to closely monitor the state of banking. We have a stable banking system and that must not be called into question. All types of risks will be regularly monitored and all necessary measures will be taken appropriately.  For the last few years, we have worked hard to strengthen the institutional capacity of the National Bank. The process of permanent education and organizational promotion was very intense. The work of the supervisory, economic research, statistics, payment operations, central banking operations and the management of exchange reserves is important. Operational and all other risks in all segments of the National Bank's operation are continuously reduced. For some of these achievements, you can read notes in all important documents of the IMF, the World Bank, the European Commission. And in 2009 we will continue to strengthen the institutional capacity of the National Bank, deeply convinced that the difference between us and the best is less and less. There are no major challenges expected next year. I believe we will deal with them successfully. Thank you for the good co-operation we've had this year. I look forward to good co-operation in 2009. Congratulations to you in 2009. I wish you many joyful moments, tranquility and creativity that you have not reached before! Mr Petar Goshev Governor

Title: On the occasion of the Award of the Annual Award of the NBRM and the 17th Anniversary of Monetary Independence, organised in Skopje
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Opening address by the Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, Mr Petar Goshev, on the occasion of the annual award of the NBRM and the 17th anniversary of monetary independence, organised in Skopje, 29.04.2009 Address by the Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, Mr Petar Goshev, on the occasion of the Award of the Annual Award of the NBRM and the 17th Anniversary of Monetary Independence, organised in Skopje, 29.04.2009 Respected, Let me warmly congratulate you, to express my great gratitude for taking the time part of today to share it together. Of course, this is the case, the action in the past is such, so especially in this period of every current year, and want not to? let us not remember on April 26, 1992. In fact, that day the Assembly of the Republic of Macedonia adopted the "Law on the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia", "The Law on the Monetary Unit of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia" and "The Law on the Use of the Currency of the Republic of Macedonia". This established the basic legal framework for the functioning of monetary power and the introduction and use of its own national currency. It actually formed a special institution, with full legal legality, which we call the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia. From that day on, the institution began to deal with inflation and hyperinflation, depreciate shocks of an economic and political nature to austerity, build and maintain confidence in financial intermediaries in the face of overall transformation, namely rereplacement of each other's social system with fundamentally different basic principles of positioning and functioning. Through hyperinflation, it reached an institution with the right capacity for strategic formulation and operational achievement of monetary policy to ensure one of the most important public goods  maintaining price stability. Through quasi-banks and shocking savers, we have reached today's modern banks. Through the former SOC (Social Bookkeeping Service), among other things, extremely suitable for political control over economic subjects, we have reached today's modern and efficient paid system in the country. Thus, this troika of very decent shots, which represent the reputational legitimacy of the Central Bank, along with the maternal but upward trend of the application of the rule of law, has become the basis for financial stability that we have had for many years as a general condition an indispensable assumption of successful total economic activities. To deliver more than a decade of price stability, stability of the exchange rate, as well as maintaining a stable banking system, in the face of numerous internal and especially external security and political shocks our country was going through, is not immodest if I say it is a result of respect that belongs to everyone who worked and works at the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, of course, together with the other institutions without which these results would not be possible. No doubt, in order to be a successful modern central bank, it should be available to well-educated employees. Good economic researchers, good supervisors, good connoisseurs of central banking operations, good lawyers and organizers, good leaders of teams working on the appropriate tasks should be held. Making good selection and investing in permanent education, I have full responsibility, and why would I hide, I can proudly say that the National Bank has such staff in increasing numbers. Some of them can be compared to the most successful of the most successful countries in the world. However, knowledge should be constantly improved, never enough where it is most. Today's global economic crisis, which began rightly where economic science is rightly said to have reached the farthest and deepest, is unfortunately once again confirming it, mercilessly increasing the world's great poverty, especially in developing countries and the least developed. New painful, "tectonic" changes are happening in the world economy. This crisis, however, has brought down the illusions that economic theory has found basic recipes for economic problems, that it has found the answer to preventing crises, that it has brought business cycles under control, in which they believed, in whole or in part, and some big economic names from today. Paul Krugman, for example, in the latest paper, which in free translation reads, "The return of depression economics and the crisis of 2008), nh? recalls nobel laureate Robert Lucas' address in 2003, given as president of the annual meeting of the American Economic Association, in which Lucas says "the central problem of depression prevention is resolved, for all practical purposes". What about the same work? recalls that one year later (2004), Ben Bernanki, Former Princeton professor, current head of the US Federal Reserve, argued in his speech, in a free translation titled "Great Moderation" that modern macroeconomic policy has solved the business cycle problem or more precisely, reduced the problem to a point of little discomfort, instead of a first-degree issue (nuisance than a front-rank issue). Given the fact that the world is experiencing this crisis today, these optimistic statements sound almost incredibly self-bending, bloated, Krugman says. Therefore, it is obvious that economists have not done their main job. The excitement and intrigue of economic science remains. And the request responds to the crisis that has already arisen confirm it. Trust brains from the world's central banks, scientific institutions, professional organizations, seek answers, apply therapies to mitigate and overcome the consequences of the crisis. That it will be overcome like any previous one is entirely certain. Only the time dimension and ability to reduce damage are at stake. But it is also certain that a cure for a repeat of the crises will not be found after this crisis. And, perhaps it is true that Nout Velink, the governor of the Central Bank of the Netherlands and chairman of the BANK's Banking Supervisory Committee, wrote: "At the most basic level, proximity is the result of the urges of living things that cause turbulent behaviour in the cycle and fear during the fall. This behaviour cannot be changed, but channels through which it manifests themselves can be discouraged." So the big challenge for economists in the world and in Macedonia remains. As you know, as the Central Bank is taking measures to prevent or minimise the consequences of the global crisis that, understandablely, could not bypass Macedonia either. Our contribution to depreciating the consequences of the crisis will be greatest if, in co-operation with the government, we preserve macroeconomic stability. Within those frameworks, we continue to believe that maintaining the stability of the exchange rate is crucial, and therefore the measures we have taken and will take are and will be focused, especially during this period, towards achieving that goal, as this best protects the stability of the entire financial system in the country. Of course, all the questions in this domain, all the questions and answers related to the economic crisis, the economic problems macedonia constantly faces are a major challenge to economic thought in our country. Working on them daily as an institution, we cannot escape the knowledge that the country's base of economic researchers should be qualitatively expanded and improved, why the economic challenges we face are undoubtedly both large and difficult. In addition, we are aware that a factor in this is a quality education system that is not a task, the jurisdiction of the Central Bank. But we also considered that we, as an institution working to improve the knowledge of our staff, precisely because of the character of the institution, we can try to participate more broadly in fostering knowledge and through that, involving more people who will work hard to demand better answers in economic policy-making and dealing with economic problems. Therefore, three years ago we introduced the "Annual Award of the National Bank for Young Researcher for Best Work in the Field of Macroeconomics". As with the previous two years, the ad for the 2009 National Bank Annual Award competition for a young macroeconomics researcher was published in several daily newspapers and professional journals, in accordance with the previously taken Decision by the National Bank Council on the way and procedure for awarding this award. In accordance with this decision, the incoming works of the competition were reviewed by the Evaluation Board, Composed of: Mr. Dimitar Bogov -Vice Governor, who is chairman of the Board, Dr. Goran Petreski, Associate Professor of the Faculty of Economics in Skopje and external member of the Council of the National Bank and Dr. Anetta Krstevska, Director of the Directorate of Research at the National Bank. The Board's report shows that of the seven papers that have arrived, one has the necessary characteristics and quality to receive the first prize in this year's competition. It is the paper "Investing in Infrastructure and GDP Growth: Metaregressive Analysis" by Author Dusko Joseski, which you will learn about in a very short time through the author's presentation of this work. I take the opportunity to congratulate him on receiving the Award and express hope that he will continue to work in this direction for both his and our own good. At the same time, I thank all participants in the competition for the effort made and the Labour Evaluation Board of the candidates for the award. Thank you all once again for today's presence at the commemoration of the Independence Day of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia and the annual award. And, as we planned, in the order of affairs, it now follows the satisfaction of hearing the Evaluation Board report to be presented to us by Mr Dimitar Bogov, vice governor at the NBRM, and then the presentation of the winner of the Annual Award. Thank you. Mr Petar Goshev Governor

Title: Address to the Annual Award of the NBRM and the 18th Anniversary of Monetary Independence, organised in Skopje
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Governor Petar Goshev's address to the Annual Award of the NBRM and the 18th Anniversary of Monetary Independence, organised in Skopje, 26.04.2010 Governor Petar Goshev's opening address on the awarding of the annual Award to the NBRM and the 18th Anniversary of Monetary Independence, organised in Skopje, 26.04.2010 Respected, Dear friends, Allow me, on behalf of all employees of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, to warmly greet you and express my huge gratitude to all of you for determining the time, today, on this important day, to be here together. A day on which the monetary history of the independent Republic of Macedonia began to be built exactly 18 years ago. Then, in fact, the Assembly of the Republic of Macedonia adopted the often mentioned laws: "The Law on the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia", "The Law on the Currency of the Republic of Macedonia", "The Law on the Use of the Currency of the Republic of Macedonia". They laid down the basic legal framework for the work of the Macedonian bank of banks, an entity that each country has. It was actually the beginning of the beginning. During that beginning, I was a member of the first pluralistic parliament of the independent Republic of Macedonia. So I was in the role of legislator. Of course, these were exciting and memorable moments. But I'm sure, no less exciting was the task for everyone who should have started their application. The challenges of the just established monetary authority were immense. From an ambition of hyperinflation and huge uncertainty, an ambition of low stable prices was to be created, and thus an ambition of acceptable, productive uncertainty. And the work begins. The employees at the time, a good part of them today, successfully laid the operational foundations of monetary policy, which will be able to continuously deliver price stability, of course, with the needed contribution to other policies that are not under the jurisdiction of the NBRM. At the same time, the work of building a stable banking system, healthy financial infrastructure, as a key condition for efficient, acceptable risks of taking a so-called temporary transformation of domestic and borrowed savings on the road to inventive investors is also intensively starting. In fact, the long, thorny process of building banking supervision begins; the continued strengthening of its capacity, the development and implementation of the regulations that will deliver, I reiterate, in conjunction with other irreplaceable important policies, stable, healthy, modern, financial ambition. And what can be said after 18 years? Without unnecessary modesty, I can say that the National Bank is today an institution that has clearly defined goals, a functional set of market-set instruments and an enviably successful record of achieving the objectives set. The history of low and stable inflation, the stable value of the domestic currency, the resistant and stable banking system is a feature that gives the National Bank a qualification of a quality and successful independent institution with deserved enviable credibility. The latest crisis, already "sung" as one of the world's longest and deepest recessions, is a test we can say we are successfully passing. This crisis has shown that we have the capacity to adequately appreciate the risks, take measures in time to remove obstacles to achieving our core objectives, and to adequately influence the expectations of domestic economic subjects. In this crisis, with roots in the financial system, the fact is that confidence in our banking system has not been violated, that the system has proved solid and stable enough and that in a short time it returns to the paths of moderate but steady growth. Respected, good results, especially in such areas, are not achieved overnight. Nor are there results that are good enough that they should not be better. The achievements so far are the result of continuous work at both individual and team level, the fruit of the productive confrontation of the views and opinions of the Bank's employees, the fruit of continuous learning and training in and mostly outside the country. This continuous learning and training is constantly embedded in the national bank's decisions, which have direct implications for the economy. But it is unnecessary to stress that the space to improve existing and analytical infrastructure will always be insufficiently filled. And precisely because that is the case, and precisely because crises continue to be an integral part of our action, roughly but sometimes harshly warning n? that knowledge in the world is far from necessary, the process of continuous learning and positive selection to enter the central bank and in the future will continue to be an extremely important preoccupation, as a process of the central bank that never ends. In fact, today, when we all sum up the consequences of the global financial and economic crisis, when we seek errors in the structure of systems and in policy steps, when we try to identify the main lessons of the crisis, we again understand that our knowledge and our skills were not enough to protect us from future tremors. William White, former chief economist of the BIS in his article "Modern macroeconomics is on the wrong track" lays out the reasons why, although warnings about the crisis existed, policymakers remained deaf to them. One explanation he offers is the problem of the existing macroeconomic paradigm, which leaves no room for crisis, of the kind we have recently experienced. But the simple promotion of the existing macroeconomic analytical framework, he believes, will not be enough to avoid future crises. He says her redesign is needed. The latest crisis, however, showed that models with the assumption of rational expectations failed, but also undermined the Keynesian models, which cannot assess the turning points in the economy, because the future, before? assess it over the past. The crisis also showed that the neglect of the financial component (such as the excessive debt of the corporate sector, population and financial sector) can be fatal, while stressing the need for deeper research work in the field of the functioning of the financial system. Blanchard, the IMF's chief economist, points out in his views on the lessons of the crisis in macroeconomic policies that "The crisis is not primarily caused by macroeconomic policy. But she showed the shortcomings of the pre-crisis policy framework, forcing carriers to find new policies during the crisis and forcing us not to think about the architecture of post-crisis macroeconomic policy." In short, he said, although the ultimate objectives remain a stable gdp gap and stable inflation, there should be additional objectives on the policymakers' map (GDP structure, real estate prices and financial assets and debt of economic entities). He also said the crisis pointed to the possibility of using a number of available instruments to meet the objectives of those used so far, and the combined use of traditional monetary instruments with regulatory measures and the better functioning of automatic fiscal policy stabilizers are some of the most commonly mentioned. Jean-Claude Trichet, the ECB's governor, sees the lessons of the crisis in perfecting and expanding the monitoring of the link between financial markets and macroeconomics. He says, "Financial risks need to be better identified and the growing potential for these risks to be transferred and obtained systemic dimensions." Some attempts to specify and simplify replacing some of the existing ones with new paradigms, as a result of the lessons of the crisis, systematize, for example, in this way: "Instead of a monetary policy focused only on price stability, we need a monetary policy focused on inflation, but also aimed at financial imbalances." "Instead of a microprudential policy focused on individual banks, we need a microprudential policy married with a macroprudential focus on systemic risk." "Instead of relying only on internal risk management, self-regulation and market discipline, the existing focus so far, it is necessary to focus on higher banking capital, better governance and an extended perimeter of regulation." "Instead of fiscal policy that does not care enough about financial stability, a clear countercyclical policy involving fiscal shock absorbers is needed." "Instead of just focusing on domestic targets, greater global coordination is needed." And evidently, it is not enough for everyone to arrange their own home. The connection of the world is dramatically increased. In fact, this suggests that financial stability needs monetary policy. However, it is not a question of whether monetary policy should target share prices, real estate and basic raw materials. The question is how monetary policy can be more symmetrical and directed against the walling of financial imbalances. Prudential policies, even both together, micro and macroprudential, are not enough to maintain financial stability. Without monetary policy participation, regulation would be overcrowded, overloaded, as the crisis has shown, without the necessary effect. Are central banks equipped for the new role - the role of supporters of financial stability? Some yes, some don't. Those who hold a supervisory function are in one state, with an excellent basis for performing and on such an additional mandate. Others are in a more difficult state and should seek other routes to contribute to that field. We as a central bank have been working on this issue in recent years and in our decisions the component of the contribution to maintaining financial stability has been present since. However, in any case, this issue raises a number of important issues for central banks' mandates, expertise (professional capacity), tools, immunities and governance structures. For example: What is the basis of central banks' mandate to take care of financial stability? Is there enough legal basis, is there enough public understanding of the responsibility to ensure financial stability? Do central banks have the necessary expert capacity and sources to do so? Do central banks have the tools they need? Do you need additional administrative and legal grounds? Is the existing independence of central banks adequate for such new responsibilities? What new arrangements in the management structure do a central bank need to succeed in this field, etc.? Respected, in fact, this crisis has shown that it is uncommon for subjects to behave within existing theories, so it is necessary to impose a request for changes in design and policy implementation, to invest additional energy to study this behavior and model new frameworks. As before, it is shown that knowledge and understanding of phenomena in the economy are dynamic categories, which must be constantly upgraded and improved. Globalization, contrary to all its contribution to the development of humanity, tests and denies many of the existing paradigms. Open new transmission channels for both growth and growth risks. Namely, with? The greater integration of our economy into the global economy does not make it highly exposed to global shocks and changes in the macropolicies of other countries. Their understanding, the assessment of their effects on the domestic economy, the monitoring of future directions requires us to invest in it. Without recognising the channels of crisis transmission, without assessing their intensity, as monetary policy holders we could not have conceived appropriate macroeconomic scenarios, we could not assess when and what changes we should take in monetary policy and in prudential regulation. That is why we are continuously working to improve people's analytical and research capabilities, and for ourselves and others I wonder if enough, are we doing it the right way? However, the introduction of the National Bank's Annual Young Researcher Award for Best Macroeconomics work we did four years ago was done with those motives. And after four years, we can say we didn't make a mistake. We met several young talented researchers, received valuable work, opened a channel for knowledge dispersion, and some of them enriched the professional capacity of the National Bank. This short experience says, keep going. And, of course, that's what we're going to do. As with the previous three years, this year the advertisement for the National Bank's Annual Award for Young Macroeconomics Researcher was published in several daily newspapers and professional journals, as well as on the NBRM website, in accordance with the previously decided by the National Bank Council on the way and procedure for awarding this award. In accordance with this decision, the incoming works of the competition were reviewed by the Evaluation Board, composed of: Dr. Sasho Arsov  associate professor of the Faculty of Economics in Skopje and an external member of the NBRM Council, also chairman of the Board, Mr. Anita Angelovska-Bejoska, Chief Economist at the National Bank and Mr. Ana Mitreska, Deputy Directorate of Research at the National Bank. The Board's report shows that eleven papers have arrived this year, with four papers entering closer competition. The general conclusion of the members of the Board is that all work that has entered closer competition has high quality, with differences between them, from the point of view of separate criteria, in some cases reduced to nuance. After the evaluation, the Board concluded unanimously that the work of author Blagica Nikoloska, entitled "Analysis of the role of the banking system in economic growth: the case of Macedonia", as a whole, taking into account all the criteria, can be considered the best in this year's competition and should be proposed for the award of the first prize of the competition. I therefore congratulate Blagica Nikoskai on receiving the award, without the dilemma that the author of the award-winning work, but also the authors of all other reported papers, will not stand here, but will continue to actively work in the field of macroeconomic research. Of course, I would like to thank all participants in the competition for the work invested, as well as the Committee for evaluation of the work of the candidates for the prize. Finishing, I thank you once again for attending this event, which also marks Monetary Independence Day and presents the Annual Award. I am pleased to invite Mr. Sasho Arsov, from whom we will hear the Evaluation Board report, followed by the presentation of the work of the author, winner of the 2010 NBRM Annual Award. Thank you. Petar Goshev, MD Governor

Title: Address to the Annual Award of the NBRM and the 19th Anniversary of Monetary Independence, organised in Skopje
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Governor Petar Goshev's address to the Annual Award of the NBRM and the 19th Anniversary of Monetary Independence, organised in Skopje, 26.04.2011 Governor Petar Goshev's opening address to the Annual Award of the NBRM and the 19th Anniversary of Monetary Independence, organised in Skopje, 26.04.2011 Respected! Welcome to the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia. Thank you for taking the time and year to mark it, in the already common way, the day of monetary independence of the Republic of Macedonia. And this year, as a few years earlier, a special event is the announcement of the winner and the awarding of the Annual Award to the National Bank to a young researcher in the field of macroeconomics. Today's commemoration is the 19th in a row, before next year's roundup, they would say jubilee, at the two decades, while the award ing is the fifth time. In the past, almost two decades, the Bank has overcome all childhood and youth diseases. Today it is a fully mature institution, capable of successfully fulfilling its constitutional and legal function. He studied quickly, studying the experiences of leading central banks through dynamic exchange of expertise and through not the very long but certainly exciting and challenging experience of his own. The results he has shown so far speak for themselves: an impressively long series of low and stable inflation and a healthy banking system, which was not destroyed either during the Great Recession. However, we all know that learning is never a completed process. Even more so if it is economic science, which not so few of its plumes say is not yet science. Therefore, from every crisis we get new lessons. After each crisis, questions follow: what has remained of the "truths" established before?, What have we missed learning?, what was missing from our instruments?, what should our role be, i.e. the mandate of the central banks?, what is lacking in their professional and operational capacity?, so that it can more successfully prevent the emergence of crises and with less costs to emerge from them. In other words, this crisis, from which we have not yet recovered, reupdated the issue of the role of central banks in preventing and managing crises. Or, more precisely, what the role of central banks should be after the Great Recession, the largest since World War II. And, as usual, some views are confirmed, withstand the test of time, others experience modifications and various adaptations, third, root changes. And here are some examples of that: 1. During the Great World Crisis, 1929-1933 and then, it is well known that many central bankers and other economists had the view that monetary policy should not be used to stimulate economic activity in a situation where the interest rate is reduced practically to zero. A condition that later became known as the liquidity trap syntagma. But as early as 1963, with the publication of the book "Monetary History of the United States", by M. Friedman and Schfartz, the economic profession, as a whole, began to accept the opposite view. Especially during the crisis, in many expert analyses and essays, we were reminded of Ben Bernanke's view from 1983, twenty years after the book mentioned, which says that the breakdown of the credit system was a key feature of the Great Global Crisis, i.e. much more than the very behaviour of the offer of money. In fact, according to Bernanke, the cancellation or inability to provide sufficient volume of loans, not the supply of money, in itself, was the primary cause of the breakdown of the monetary transmission mechanism during the Great Crisis. This view gathered many new supporters during the Great Recession, which began in 2007 with problems in mortgage markets in the United States. Perhaps that is why, sharing Bernanke's opinion, Paul Krugman wrote (2008) that there is no more suitable person at the time for the head of the US federal system than Ben Bernanke himself. The above opinion is actually the root replacement of one, with the other, the exact opposite view. 2. Although it is still too early to draw final lessons from the latest and still ongoing crisis, there is already greater consent on several important issues. But it is precisely the views especially on some of these issues that are reupdating the issue of the role of central banks after the crisis. For example, (1) reducing the reference interest rate to zero does not mean that monetary policy has been left without the possibility of an expansive response. In particular, until this crisis, economic textbooks said that if the reference interest rate reaches zero, monetary policy loses efficiency. And that in such conditions the only possible answer is fiscal policy (expansive, of course). After this crisis, we already know that is not the case. The so-called quantitative easing policy, the purchase of assets by central banks and when interest is zero (FED, BoE, in particular) came on stage. It is true that these purchases do not reduce the short-term interest rate, but undoubtedly increase liquidity. Through the purchase and then sale of long-term assets (so-called QE2), the central bank can affect long-term interest rates, which may have an additional effect on sectoral private demand for long-term assets, including mortgages and corporate investment. This is also a root change of view, but with influences on the position of central banks, accountability, governance. (2) Possession of a strong and robust financial system has been shown to be crucial. Of course, this is not a new knowledge. But his key role was once again confirmed by the events of the latest crisis. Countries affected by the crisis of their financial systems suffered incomparably higher GDP losses, unlike others who have more or less undergone standard experience of a business cycle. In the book, "This Time is Different", Carmen M. Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff) Reinhart and Rogoff convincingly document this. And, therefore, most of the ongoing discussion concerns the role of central banks in preserving financial stability, and we will later see that this is also the biggest reason for discussions on redefining, supplementing central banks' mandates, accountability, governance and transparency. (3) After this crisis, the syntagma "macroprudential supervision" (macroprudential policy) became one of the most exploited. There is no consensus on the definition yet, but there is a widely accepted view that it contains two key elements: (1) that it is a supervision concerning the total financial system; (2) that includes systemic interactions. The two elements, according to many analysts, were highly visible during the crisis. The much-apostropherole of so-called "shadow banking" and the effects of Lehman's bankruptcy are the most common examples used to apostrophe the characteristic of "systemic interactions". Therefore, we are talking about regulating the financial system at a very wide level, behind the boundaries of the banking system. We are also not only talking about supervising banking when considering macroprudential policy instruments, but much more broadly. And, as it is, when we talk about macroprudential supervision, we are actually talking about issues that require coordination between different regulators. Therefore, the terms macroprudential supervision and financial stability have the same scope of the financial system in its entirety. And that is why this issue can have strong impacts on the post-crisis role of central banks. (4) The issue of a borrower in the ultimate instance and "too big to go bankrupt" is simply inevitable. Various answers to this question also have different influences on the role and position of the central bank. The case where the central bank is a borrower in the final instance, in the face of temporary liquidity shortages, is clear. Much more complicated is the issue of a borrower in the final instance in the face of a solvency crisis. In the second case, restructuring interventions can cause a large and long-term financial cost to the public sector. In principle, the difference between liquidity problems and solvency should determine the measures and activities of the central bank and the government in the face of a crisis. In some countries, this difference is translated into their laws. In our country, when it comes to the second case, the problem of insolvency, the issue is completely open. The problem is even more complex because the difference between a liquidity problem and a solvency problem is rarely clear. What initially seems to be a liquidity problem (crisis) can very quickly prove to be a solvency crisis. Therefore, a percentage is taken at every stage of the financial crisis. The link to the issue "too big to go bankrupt" and moral hazard is a recurrence issue. That's the case during this crisis. In fact, moral gambit cannot be removed. The very existence of a "borrower in the ultimate instance" raises the issue of moral gambling. But, Therefore, it cannot be said that an optimal response would be to cancel the "borrower in the final instance" instrument, either when it comes to responding to liquidity deficiency and nor when it comes to a problem of insolvency, to an entity(s) whose collapse would have too much cost to an economy, i.e. for the people of that country. So, in deciding to intervene or not, it should always come from the costs imposed on the entire economy of a country, and in the globalised world and beyond. Ideally, regulators should have a system developed, a mechanism for resolving such cases, in an organised procedure and process. But so far, no one has been made that could serve as a satisfactory urn. Therefore, it is much better to think and act so that we do not find ourselves before the dilemma: to save an entity that is systemically important or not! In any case, the debate continues, but various possible solutions also have different consequences for the position of central banks. (5) The crisis re-updates the importance of the exchange rate for a small and open economy. The exchange rate is one of the two most important macroeconomic variables in a small and open economy. The other is the interest rate. However, there is no easy choice of managing the exchange rate. In any case, when we are on this issue, first comes to the agenda the choice of the system (regime) on the exchange rate, and then the level of the exchange rate. The choice of system (regime) is always related to the issue of control of capital flows. If capital flows can be controlled, then greater advantages are possible for the country that has fixed its nominal exchange rate. Macedonia has so far had no problems with capital flows that would jeopardise the application of the de facto fixed exchange rate strategy. In any case, it is in the majority that prefer a flexible exchange rate regime, with a more open capital account. But I canalmost not give opinions that the definition of "flexible" means a determination to cancel foreign exchange market interventions or that the capital account should be fully opened. All these issues, which certainly do not list the entire list, are deeply related to the issue of financial stability. More specifically, it depends on them, too, so we can say that they are her determinants (certainly not just them). The evolution of views on these issues is actually an evolution of the post-crisis role of central banks in achieving the desired objectives of economic policies. Although it is still too early to precisely define the post-crisis mandate and management arrangements of central banks, it is certain that: (1) their change-process has begun is open; and (2) some basic elements of their old-new position are already identified at this time. The main goal, keeping inflation low and stable in the medium term, remains an undisputed function, a task for central banks. But because maintaining price stability has proved not enough to provide and financial stability, the focus of the discussions is the role of central banks in preventing new crises from occurring, or on reducing their acuity, after a major recession, and of course how. The debates so far unequivocally show that central banks will increase interest in financial stability, which is actually already happening. The financial crisis showed that central banks were the first address to address as soon as it appeared. They (crises) not only end in high costs, but are also a major threat to the monetary policy transmission mechanism and the balance sheets of central banks. Central banks therefore have a long-term and legitimate interest in preventing them. Increasing interest in financial stability requires: (a) Increasing the capacity of central banks to create appropriate macro-prudential conditions. This assumes: (1) direct powers or clear channels to promote financial stability and independent monetary policy; (2) clear institutional arrangements, both to shape their own, and to contribute to the activities of others who have powers and control tools related to financial stability; (3) adequate capacity to participate in the design of regulation and macroprudential policy; and (b) Improvement of governance; increased direct or indirect power should necessarily be accompanied by greater accountability and an appropriate process of accountability and transparency. The new arrangements should protect the independence of central banks and at the same time encourage effective co-operation with other competent authorities in the process of preserving and improving financial stability. So, an intensive discussion process is underway and new responsibilities are being created by central banks: to create appropriate tools to achieve new obligations and to strengthen governance. Central banks are already receiving or strengthening mandates regarding financial stability. Monetary policy can and should promote financial stability more; act more symmetrically on financial imbalances and help alleviate their accumulation. Macroprudential policies do not eliminate the need for monetary policy to participate in achieving financial stability, although they may reduce pressure. However, it is not reasonable, even a clear distinction of instruments can be carried out. For example, to require interest rate policy to ensure price stability, while prudential and macroprudential policies ensure financial stability. This suggests that significant conceptual and operational challenges lie before central banks. Financial stability is inherently less suitable for precise specification and measurement than price stability. On the other hand, responsibility for dealing with systemic risk is shared with other competent institutions. The central bank must therefore act on a clear strategy for financial stability, with clearly formulated objectives and well-defined functions and responsibilities for it and for all other competent institutions. Without that, the danger of being dragged in an inappropriate way into the country's political discourse is high. What have we had so far? We have a new NBRM Law in which the obligation to contribute to financial stability is set to the Bank as a second goal. But mainly, the Law remains at that principle. We have a Memorandum of Co-operation with the Finance Ministry on financial stability issues, but as the title suggests, it is a formal co-operation process, without the hot question of precise specification of specific obligations in the event of a system solvency crisis or so-called entities that are too large to fail. We have memorandums of co-operation, mainly for information exchange and other financial sector institutions. Without a legal obligation, five years ago we began preparing and publishing an annual report on financial stability, following the example, then, of the smaller number of countries that have already done so, trying to raise awareness of issues of financial stability. These reports are available to the public for free, but the data, the key, from the central register, is not available to us for free for this nonprofit production required for the entire community. We have formed and developed a special department to monitor financial stability, whose capacity is increasing, almost on a daily basis. We believe that we have begun to influence the spread of awareness of the meaning of these issues. But reality in the country, as a whole, is far from desired. We need large-scale law-making to crystallize: clear mandates, clear objectives, clear responsibilities for the various participants in achieving the objectives of financial stability. In order for a central bank to play an important role in financial stability policy, appropriate tools and capacity to use them are also needs. One of the key issues, not only on this issue, is the achievement of an appropriate balance between discretionary decisions and built-in automatic stabilizers that can tailor systematic risk without further policy decisions. Fiscal policy, for example, acts countercyclically even in the absence of explicit changes in tax rates or discretionary cost changes, thanks to built-in stabilizers. Similarly, prudential rules can be designed in the function of stabilising purposes. Central banks should insist that macroprudential forces be given the appropriate weight in establishing macroprudential regulations. More elements of the BASEL 3 package, such as increased leverage ratio and capital margins, funding and liquidity requirements, both by designing them and calibration, can help reduce systemic risk. BASEL 3 requires for the first time minimum capital and minimum liquidity liabilities to be calibrated and applied according to so-called top-down macroeconomic studies, which link standards to economic activities. Of course, there are other available tools. Central banks can target the source of problems more precisely, for example, using the loan to value ratios ratios for mortgage loans, supplementing other measures that affect supply prices. The broader mandate in achieving financial stability assumes significant changes in the structure and operations of the central bank. The greater the volume of powers for financial stability, the greater the bank's preservation of the political process. Decisions related to financial stability require greater co-ordination and interaction with the government, as opposed to monetary policy decisions. How to organise and regulate such interaction in a way that will protect the autonomy of the central bank is a temptation that will come and will not be easy. In order to preserve autonomy in the face of increased interaction with the government, it will be necessary to develop a well-specified coordination mechanism. Arguments for independent monetary policy management, i.e. independence from the political cycle, apply equally to the sphere of financial stability. By contrast, it would also bring down independence achieved in the monetary sphere. Of course where she is elected. Only a clear definition of the central bank's mandate in the field of financial stability can lead to a clear definition of accountability, accountability and transparency.
