Therefore, respected, here is again a major megdan with new challenges for economic policymakers, for regulators, for supervisors, for researchers, including for the group for which we introduced the Annual Award of the National Bank.

Title: Twelve-Year Conference of the Macedonian Stock Exchange AD Skopje, in Ohrid
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Speech by Dimitar Bogov, Vice Governor of the NBRM, Twelve-year conference of the Macedonian Stock Exchange AD Skopje, 09-10 May 2011, in Ohrid Speech by Dimitar Bogov, Vice Governor of the NBRM, Twelve-Year Conference of the Macedonian Stock Exchange AD Skopje, 09-10 May 2011, in Ohrid Dear ladies and gentlemen, It is always a pleasure to attend the Annual Conference of the Macedonian Stock Exchange. It is undoubtedly the most important finance conference in Macedonia, which brings together all financial institutions and their regulators in one place. This is a good opportunity in my address to such a respectful auditorium for the first time to present my views on acting as governor of the National Bank. The governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia is undoubtedly the most responsible position in the financial sector. It is a great honor, but also an even greater obligation. The National Bank, in the 20 years of independent Macedonia, has built a reputation as a credible institution that successfully maintains price and financial stability. It has created quality staff and constantly upgrades its human and institutional capacities. It is a credit to the vision and work of all the previous leaders of the institution. I have the imperative to continue to build on the National Bank on the way to a respected, modern central bank, which in due course will become part of the system of European central banks. The main objectives are given in the Law on the National Bank. Therefore, I have no choice but to fully commit to achieving the basic objectives of the National Bank. I will allow the activities and citizens of the Republic of Macedonia to continue to enjoy the graces of price stability. I will work to strengthen the stability and competitiveness of the banking system by introducing best European practices in regulation and supervision. Not jeopardising the previous two goals, the National Bank will support the country's economic policy. In economic theory, there are no dilemmas that price stability is a necessary condition for economic growth. This does not mean that price stability will automatically bring growth. But without price stability, there certainly cannot be sustainable economic growth. When we talk about price stability, we imply that citizens and the business sector do not have inflation expectations. That is, they do not take into account inflation in making their business decisions. Central banks take care of maintaining the general price level over the medium term. But central banks cannot control the prices of separate products. Temporary increases at the general price level, as a result of shocks from the supply side of some products, do not mean that price stability is impaired. Central banks can control demand. Appropriately, they have the power not to allow price growth driven by demand. In this context, we should analyse inflation in Macedonia in the last three months. There is no doubt that higher inflation is a complete consequence of higher oil and food prices on world stock markets so far. To quote Trishe's Statement of 20 February: "We cando nothing against the growth of oil and food stock prices, but we must at all costs prevent price growth from passing on to other products." Or, as Bernanke says in April: "Inflation should be closely monitored to see evidence that stock prices have more than a temporary impact on prices. As long as inflation expectations remain stable and stock price growth slows, rising inflation will only be a short episode." Basic inflation that excludes energy and food prices is a good indicator of future inflation. Basic inflation in Macedonia is still low at 1.2%. By comparison, in 2008 basic inflation reached 2.8%. Given that basic inflation is low, while there is no pressure from wages and domestic consumption, the production gap is negative, food prices on world stock markets have been decreasing since March, early tightening of monetary policy could do more damage than good. In any case, the National Bank closely monitors inflation and inflation expectations and at the first signals that price growth is transferred to other products, I will not hesitate to react appropriately to preserve price stability. Dear ladies and gentlemen, The National Bank has been successfully maintaining price stability in the Macedonian economy for sixteen years by targeting a stable exchange rate of the denar. In addition, only once in 1997, at the very beginning of the implementation of this strategy, was forced to make a downward adjustment to the course. Since then, the exchange rate of the denar has been stable for the last fourteen years. Over time, a broader consensus has been built that a stable exchange rate serves the Macedonian economy well and that benefit should be maintained in the future. However, occasionally, considerations can be heard that it should be switched to a free fluctuating exchange rate or fluctuating course at a certain interval of /-5% or 10%. But I have not heard serious arguments so far as to why it would be a better strategy for the Macedonian economy. Contrary to such reflections, on this occasion I will elaborate on eight arguments as to why the stable exchange rate of the denar is still the best solution for the Macedonian economy. First, it is wrong to link economic growth to course policy. Economic growth depends on the quality of economic policies, not course policy. Has the 1997 devaluation improved economic growth in Macedonia? In the absence of quality economic policies, imbalances arise in the economy. In fixed-rate countries, imbalances manifest themselves at high interest rates, while in countries with a fluctuating course through exchange rate depression, or both if they try to defend it. Secondly, if small economies from the Baltic are looked at, through Central Europe to the Balkans (without Poland and Turkey that are large economies and cannot be compared to them), it will be seen that countries dominate a fixed-rate policy. These are the three Baltic countries, Croatia, Bosnia, Macedonia and Bulgaria. The fluctuating course is held by the Czech Republic, Hungary, Romania, Serbia and Albania. If the economic growth rates they have achieved in the last 10 years are compared, it will be seen that it is not at all true that fluctuating countries have achieved better economic results. Furthermore, apart from the Czech Republic, other small economies that have a fluctuating exchange rate constantly intervene in the foreign exchange market to prevent greater devaluation. So they can't afford a full, free fluctuating course either. The price for this is high interest rates, high inflation and loss of foreign exchange reserves. Look at Serbia's example. It currently has a reference interest rate of 12.5%, inflation of 14% and constantly intervenes in the foreign exchange market to prevent further currency depression. Romania has a reference interest rate of 6.25%, Hungary 6%, and Albania 5.25%. The average interest rates on local currency bank loans are currently about 14% in Serbia and about 12% in Albania and Romania. By comparison, the Reference Interest Rate of the NBRM is 4%, and the average interest rate of bank loans in denari is 8.9%. Third, the fluctuating course of denar and the very likely depression that would follow would not stimulate exports. Moreover, this was confirmed by the 16% devaluation in 1997. Macedonian exports include metals and textiles with a 50% participation. In their final product, import inputs participate by 80% to 90%. The only significant home input is the workforce. This means that there is very little space to reduce the production price of these two groups of products by depressing the denar. This reduction can only come from the largest domestic input -the workforce. And that, only if it is assumed that the depreciation of the exchange rate of the denar will not create pressure for wage surges, which is unlikely. Fourthly, in a highly euro-euroized economy, a fluctuating course would mean moving in a downward direction without a lower limit. 60% of the population deposits and 70% of company deposits are denominated in euros. Experience so far shows that with the slightest uncertainty and doubt about exchange rate stability, this percentage is rapidly increasing by creating pressure on the foreign exchange market. Moreover, in the three situations so far when the National Bank has been forced to defend the exchange rate of the denar, Spring 2001, autumn 2004 and early 2009, the greatest pressure did not come from the need for foreign exchange to carry out real transactions, but from the protection against risks ("hedging") of the denominational assets of all economic agents population, companies, banks. It is a clear message that economic agents in Macedonia are only prepared to hold denarii if they are guaranteed stability over the euro. Fifth, the high euroisation of the assets and liabilities of banks, companies and the population would imply high costs of the fluctuating exchange rate of the denar and certain exchange rate depreciation. 65% of companies' bank loans and 45% of the population's loans are denominated in euros. The banking sector as a whole has balanced foreign exchange asset and liability positions, the population has a high long foreign exchange position, while companies have a very short foreign exchange position. Even the population, although it has a long foreign exchange position as a whole, it is highly likely that the same households do not have foreign exchange demands and foreign exchange obligations to banks. Hence, the fluctuating exchange rate of the denar and certain depression would lead to the bankruptcy of a number of companies and households and the transformation of foreign exchange into credit risk in banks with the potential to jeopardise financial stability. Sixth, the analyses made by the National Bank on a regular basis do not indicate a reduction in the competitiveness of the Macedonian economy due to the ongoing parity of the exchange rate. Seventh, if devaluation is a solution to economic problems, why did Latvia not do so in 2010 and Greece in 2010? On the contrary, Latvia has avoided devaluation with great effortand sacrifice, and Greece is still struggling to avoid exiting the euro zone and devaluation. Instead of external currency devaluation, the two countries have undertaken exceptional reforms that essentially constitute internal devaluation by reducing fiscal expenditures, reducing public sector employment and wages, liberalising the economy. Devaluation is the easier way to solve problems, but without a guarantee that problems will not reappear. Restructuring the economy taken by the two countries is the harder way to achieve the same goal. The difference is that restructuring will strengthen the economy and make it more competitive in the long term. Eighth, the fixed rate requires more discipline than fiscal policy because in such a situation it is much more powerful in correcting imbalances in the economy. This is also the main reason why Macedonia has had extremely low budget deficits in the last 15 years. Dear ladies and gentlemen, What I said at the beginning about price stability can also be repeated for financial stability. If there is financial stability, it does not mean that there will automatically be economic growth. But there is no doubt that without financial stability, there can be no sustainable economic growth. The National Bank is the regulator and supervisor of the banking sector. But that does not mean that the National Bank should build relations with banks from a position of arrogance and power. On the contrary, banks are our partners. The main long-term goal of bank shareholders coincides with our goal. Our task is to make sure, at certain times, taken by the market struggle, that banks do not overcome the urge to make a quick short-term gain by taking too much risk, at the expense of a long-term stable return on capital. That is why the highest priority will be to upgrade the risk-based supervisory system. This implies an individual approach to each bank, identifying risks and taking appropriate micro prudential measures. When risks exceed individual banks, or are present in a number of banks, then macro prudential measures and monetary policy take the stage. I will also attach no less importance to the promotion of banking regulation. There is a great deal of room to simplify regulation and increase the speed and efficiency of the National Bank's operation. Without jeopardising the basic liquidity and solvency requirements of banks, as well as the eligibility criteria ("fit and proper") of shareholders. Dear ladies and gentlemen, The National Bank will support economic policies with its policies. But the National Bank will not stimulate economic growth by devaluation of the exchange rate of the denar, with high inflation or by stimulating excessive credit growth. It would not be a boost to economic growth, but to economic collapse. The National Bank will create conditions for sustainable economic growth by ensuring price stability, a stable exchange rate for the denar and a stable, competitive banking sector that will provide healthy credit growth. To achieve this, I will strive to pursue a policy at the optimal level of the reference interest rate and the optimal level of prudential banking regulation. At an optimal interest rate, I mean the lowest interest rate that provides stability at the denar exchange rate and price stability. Under optimal, prudential banking regulation, I imply regulation that will ensure the necessary liquidity and solvency of banks, but will not be an unnecessary regulatory burden on banks' balance sheets. Thank you for your attention.

Title: Speech in a stand at the Macedonian Chamber of Commerce
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Address by Governor Dimitar Bogov, stand at the Macedonian Chamber of Commerce, 14.9.2011 Address by Governor Dimitar Bogov, in a stand at the Macedonian Chamber of Commerce, 14.9.2011 Grandstand at the Macedonian Chamber of Commerce on "Monetary Policy in a Function of Accelerated Economic Growth" -Financial and Monetary Policy for Full Commitment of the Economy Dear ladies and gentlemen, It is a pleasure to be among you, who create our country's gross domestic product, create jobs and are exposed to market assessment every day. This is a good opportunity in my address before such a respectful auditorium to present my views on the link between monetary policy and economic growth. Because the document entitled "Monetary Policy in the Function of Accelerated Economic Growth" was offered as the basis for this stand today, I will polemise with some of those presented in it. Reading the document, I draw two conclusions. First, insufficient economic growth and a high trade deficit are due to restrictive monetary policy and low inflation that condition high real interest rates. Secondly, it is a consequence of defending the fixed exchange rate. Hence, we should learn the lesson that the fixed rate of the denar is all to blame. If we let it fluctuate freely, then there will be an unlimited offer of loans at low interest rates, the trade deficit will become a surplus, and at economic growth rates we will compete with China. And everyone will be rich and happy. Unfortunately, the reality is much more complex. In economic theory, there are no dilemmas that price stability is a necessary condition for economic growth. This does not mean that price stability will automatically bring growth. But without price stability, there certainly cannot be sustainable economic growth. When we talk about price stability, we imply that citizens and the business sector do not have inflation expectations. That is, they do not take into account inflation in making their business decisions. In that document, and sometimes in the media, I read the wording: "there should be stable prices, but with a higher level of inflation". It's like telling a lady she's a little pregnant. Impossible. It either has price stability or it doesn't. If inflation is six or ten per cent longer, then it will run out of control. Inflation expectations are created among the population and companies they embed in their decisions. Therefore, it is highly likely that inflation would escalate. Furthermore, it is wrong to link economic growth to course policy. Growth is influenced by many other major factors. Not only is it frivolous to put the economic growth rate in correlation with exchange rate policy, but also the examples underpinning the claim that countries with a fluctuating course have higher economic growth are irrelevant. Here, I will set an example that shows the exact opposite conclusion. A comparison of economic growth rates from 2000 to 2007 of all baltic countries to the Balkans shows that fixed-rate countries had a growth rate of 6.1%, while countries with a fluctuating rate of 4.8%. Is this enough argument to say that fixed-rate countries are achieving higher growth rates? Of course not. This is too serious a topic to use such lyrical arguments. Let's change, the next time someone says that countries with a fluctuating course have higher rates of economic growth, let them support it with an empirical study. Should we deal with the claim that Macedonia has restrictive monetary policy due to the fixed exchange rate of the denar? The average annual credit growth rate from 1996 to 2010, i.e. in the entire period in which we run a stable exchange rate policy, is 17.4%. This includes the years when we had external shocks. Without them, average credit growth would be 22.8%. Are those insufficient credit growth rates? There is no central banker in the world who would say that the credit growth rate of 17% is low. We saw what happened in 2008 after a few annual periods of annual credit growth rates of 50% and 100% in most Central and Eastern European countries. Believe me, no central bank will allow such rates of credit growth anymore. There is an unwritten rule that the credit growth rate should be twice the nominal growth of gross domestic product. We are here somewhere and we expect loans to grow at a rate of 15% to 20% in the coming years. Lessons from the financial crisis have not learned that higher growth than that would be risky and should be avoided. So credit growth had more than enough. Because average inflation during the same period was 2%, real loan growth was 15%. Now we come to the second question, at what price were those loans?! There are no dilemmas that for most of this period interest rates were quite high. But also the fact is that currently, bank loan interest rates in Macedonia are at their lowest in twenty years the denarii are 8.9% and foreign exchange is 7.5%. To come up with a solution as to how they are lower we need to see which factors affect the amount of interest rates on bank loans. The main factor is the price of the sources of banks' funds, i.e. the interest on deposits and foreign credit lines. This builds on a margin that depends on the customer risk premium, the operating costs of banks, the ratio of supply and the demand for loans. Alternative means of investing, such as treasury and treasury records, have their influence. Currently, the average interest rate on denominated deposits is 5.8%, and the exchange deposits are 2.7%. It's very high rates. But banks do not have much choice because the funds they can receive in financial markets are even more expensive. Hence, it is clear how bank interest rates can be reduced. By increasing austerity, reducing risks in the economy and reducing banks' operating costs. Can the National Bank contribute anything? Of course. Currently, the interest rate on treasury records is at a historically lowest level of 4%. The document notes that it is also high interest, in the euro zone it is 1.5%. If we play the course we will be able to lower the interest rate even further and thus contribute to lower interest rates on loans. Is that really the case? Let's see what happens if they had a fluctuating course. In a small, open economy with a high euroisation of the balance sheets of all economic subjects  the population, companies and banks, such as Macedonia, the announcement of leaving politics on a stable course would cause instability. In the absence of real pressures on the course, expectations of course depression would lead to depression. Everyone would seek to convert the denominations to euros, thereby pressuring the foreign exchange market. Because the exchange rate would be fluctuating, the National Bank would not intervene in the market. This would lead to a drop in the value of the denar and an additional wave of conversion of denarii assets into foreign exchange assets. The denar would be in free fall. Prices of imported products would rise, as would domestic ones, due to higher prices for imported raw materials. This would mean exceeding the inflation target and would require a monetary policy response by raising the interest rate and intervening in the foreign exchange market. But the credibility of the National Bank would be seriously impaired, which is why foreign exchange market interventions would have to be very large, as would the increase in interest rates. So the result would be, high inflation, high interest rates and loss of foreign exchange reserves. Let's not forget the reduction in living standards and increased payments for the repayment of foreign exchange loans, which would lead to the bankruptcy of a number of businesses and citizens. Those who think that a fluctuating exchange rate on the denar would have lower interest rates would refer them to Serbia. It currently has a reference interest rate of 11.25%, inflation of 10.5%, and its exchange market interventions are more common and higher than ours, although it has a fluctuating rate. The average interest rates on bank loans in local currency are currently about 14%. Domestic currency savings in Serbia are almost non-existent, more than 90% of deposits are in foreign currency. A change in course policy cannot be discussed, not given the high Euroisation and the 14-year stability of the denar. Economic agents are used to the acquired right to a stable currency and are appropriately dragging their moves. Moreover, in the three situations so far when the National Bank has been forced to defend the exchange rate of the denar, Spring 2001, autumn 2004, and in early 2009, the greatest pressure did not come from the need for foreign exchange to carry out real transactions, but from the protection of the denomination of all economic agents population, companies, banks. It is a clear message that economic agents in Macedonia are only prepared to hold denarii if they are guaranteed stability over the euro. I do not agree that the fluctuating course of denar and the very likely depression that would follow would drive exports. Moreover, this was confirmed by the 16% devaluation in 1997. Macedonian exports are dominated by metals and textiles with a 50% participation. In their final product, import inputs participate by 80% to 90%. The only significant home input is the workforce. This means that there is very little space to cheaper the production price of these two groups of products through depression of the denar. This cheapening can only come from the largest domestic input -the workforce. And that, only if it is assumed that the depression of the exchange rate of the denar will not create pressure for a rise in wages, which is unlikely. Although the exchange rate of the denar has been nominally stable for the last 14 years, according to analyses, the National Bank, in the last eight years for which we have consistent data, it has actually depressed by 10%, if measured by inflation, and by 40% if measured according to labour costs per unit of product. This means that the competitiveness of the Macedonian economy has improved in the last eight years. Moreover, that should be our goal. To increase the competitiveness of our economy not with nominal depression but with real, internal depression. Wages to grow slower than productivity growth, domestic inflation to grow slower than inflation among our trading partners. A seemingly simple solution, but to achieve this, complex reforms and dedicated work by everyone in the country are needed. Improving the services provided by public administration to citizens and businesses will save them time, resources and money. The increased efficiency of the judicial system will contribute to reducing interest rates and saving time, resources and money. Eliminating corruption will increase competition, efficiency, quality of products and services and save time, resources and money. Better education and health will increase the quality of human capital as one of the main factors of production. Better road and rail infrastructure will shorten the time and cost of transporting goods. Higher production of cheaper domestic energy will reduce production costs in other sectors. We at the National Bank can also contribute through the promotion of banking regulation. There is room to simplify regulation and increase the speed and efficiency of the National Bank's operation, without jeopardising the basic liquidity and solvency requirements of banks, as well as the criteria for shareholder eligibility. It will reduce banks' costs and create space for lower interest rates. The ultimate effect of all these reforms will be greater productivity and lower costs leading to a more competitive economy. The stable exchange rate of the denar is not a weakness of the Macedonian economy, but an advantage. He demands more discipline from fiscal policy, because in such a situation it is much more powerful in correcting imbalances in the economy. This is also the main reason why Macedonia has extremely low budget deficits in the last 15 years and low public debt. A stable course requires greater efficiency from the private sector, as it is the only way to increase competitiveness. There is no masking weakness with high inflation and currency depression. For me, the example with euro zone countries is much more insert. Long years before the creation of the monetary union, some countries, such as Austria and the Netherlands, pursued a fixed-rate policy with regard to the German brand. To import German stability, they had to build an efficient private sector and pursue disciplined fiscal policies. No coincidence, they are now among the several most stable economies in the eurozone. In contrast, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Greece led policies on a fluctuating course. This allowed them to cover their inefficiency with constant devaluations in relation to the German brand. Therefore, they entered the euro zone unprepared, continued their well-known policies, but no longer have the opportunity to conceal problems with the tried method. Dear ladies and gentlemen, The National Bank will support economic policies with its policies. But the National Bank will not stimulate economic growth by devaluation of the exchange rate of the denar, with high inflation or by stimulating excessive credit growth. It would not be a boost to economic growth, but to economic collapse. Thank you for your attention.

Title: Welcome speech at an International Seminar organised by the Association of Banking at the Stopna Chamber of Macedonia
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Welcome speech by Governor Dimitar Bogov at an International Seminar organised by the Association of Banking at the Stopna Chamber of Macedonia, 19.9.2011 Welcome speech by Governor Dimitar Bogov at an International Seminar organised by the Association of Banking at the Stopna Chamber of Macedonia, 19.9.2011 International seminar organised by the Association of Banking at the Stopna Chamber of Macedonia Dear ladies and gentlemen, It is a particular honor and pleasure to address this international seminar organised by the Association of Banking of the Republic of Macedonia and, on behalf of the National Bank, to welcome you to our country and to the successful course of the Seminar. The official admission of the Association of Banking to the European Banking Federation, as an associate member, is the result of the commitment of the leadership of the Association and especially Mrs Pantuchkova. Notice my sincere congratulations and respect for this achievement of yours. The benefits of the Association of Banking from membership of the European Banking Federation are undoubtedly very significant. The European Banking Federation is a forum where initiatives of its members are proposed and considered and issues of common interest to the entire European banking sector are addressed. She is a true representative and voice of all European banks. In order to ensure that banks' experience and views are taken into account, The European Banking Federation maintains a constant dialogue with the European institutions in devising policies relevant to the operation of banks, such as, among others, harmonisation of banking supervision, compliance with international accounting standards and other issues. The European Banking Federation supports the European unification process and represents, defends and promotes the interests of member states. The federation's activities are not limited within European frameworks. They also cover broader issues of importance to all European banks in relations with their business partners, as well as regulatory and supervisory authorities around the world. I would like to take this opportunity to highlight the excellent and extremely constructive co-operation of the National Bank and the Banking Association so far. I would particularly like to highlight the ongoing joint activities of the National Bank and the Banking Association in the following areas: -Co-operation in the preparation of regulation on the adequacy of banks' capital. The decision to amend and supplement the Decision on the methodology for determining the adequacy of capital was taken in early 2009, which provides for an obligation for banks, starting on 31.12.2011, to determine the corresponding amount of capital needed to cover operational risk. At the initiative of the National Bank, in March 2010, Within the Risk Commission of the Banking Association, a working group of representatives from five banks was formed, working on the development of a methodology for monitoring operational risk, i.e. a methodology for the appropriate division of the operation of eight business lines and for recording all revenues and expenditures along separate business lines. This methodology will form an appropriate basis for the preparation of the Guideline for implementing the Decision on the methodology for determining the adequacy of capital, which began in the third quarter of 2011. -Co-operation between the National Bank and the Commission for the Prevention of Money Laundering (AML) and compliance within the Banking Association takes place on a regular basis. Joint stands and seminars are continuously held, as well as exchange of suggestions and notes in the drafting of bylaws of the Law on the Prevention of Money Laundering and Other Yields of Criminal Offences and Terrorist Financing. The Administration for the Prevention of Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing, The National Bank and the Commission hold joint meetings, where indicators of risk analysis and recognition of suspicious transactions are updated on a regular basis, ideas are exchanged and proposals are made to remove possible disagreement of the regulatory framework with the practice in the field of preventing money laundering and financing terrorism. The National Bank highly appreciates and seriously considers the banking association's initiatives to improve regulation, whenever those initiatives are in line with the objectives of the National Bank. As a result of your last initiative for amendments to the Liquidity Risk Management Decision, a few days ago, the National Bank Council introduced a single liquidity coefficient instead of the previous special odds for denari and foreign exchange and recognised the appropriate percentage of term deposits that are delivered as long-term deposits. Dear ladies and gentlemen, In accordance with the National Bank Act, in addition to the main objective of achieving and maintaining price stability, the National Bank is responsible for maintaining a stable and competitive market-oriented financial system. To achieve this goal, currently, the National Bank is corrected before the challenge of completely rounding up regulation of Basel 2 standards by: -Making a new decision on the methodology for determining the adequacy of capital introducing new approaches to establishing the necessary capital (to cover credit and operational risk); -Adoption of the Guideline for applying the Decision on the methodology for determining the adequacy of capital; -Regulating basel 2's advanced approaches to calculating the necessary capital to cover risks. This obligation was also undertaken in the National Programme for the Adoption of European Legislation (NPAA), under which regulation should be prepared and implemented by 2013. In parallel, we are closely following the new standards that are set with Basel 3. Within these frameworks, we have already begun studying the new liquidity standards, establishing the necessary data to calculate the indicators established in Basel 3, and monitoring these indicators for banks in the Republic of Macedonia. These activities will be the focus of our attention in the coming period. But to successfully achieve these tasks, of course, co-operation with the Banking Association is more than necessary. I sincerely hope that the excellent and constructive co-operation of the National Bank and the Banking Association so far will continue in the future. Thank you!

Title: National Workshop on FDI Statisties in the Republic of Macedonia: Survey Methodologies in Collecting Data on FDI and TNC activities
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Speech of Anita Angelovska-Bezhoska, Vice Governor of the NBRM, for the unctad National Workshop on FDI Statisties in the Republic of Macedonia: Survey Methodologies in Collecting Data on FDI and TNC activities, December 19-21, 2011, Skopje Speech of Anita Angelovska-Bezhoska, Vice Governor of the NBRM, for the unctad National Workshop on FDI Statisties in the Republic of Macedonia: Survey Methodologies in Collecting Data on FDI and TNC activities, December 19-21, 2011, Skopje Dear guests and colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, It is my pleasure to welcome you today at the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, at the opening of the "National Workshop on FDI statistics in the Republic of Macedonia". This is the first event organized by UNCTAD in cooperation with the National Bank and I sincerely hope that this is a beginning of a long and productive cooperation. We strongly believe that we will all benefit in terms of strengthening the institutional capacity in the collection of data on FDI and transnational companies (TNCs), thus contributing towards a better assessment of FDI and activities of TNCs, as well as towards a better design and implementation of policies in this field. The intensive process of globalization in the last two decades has by now made capital flows a fact of life. Because of their features, FDI have proven to be a more desirable type of flows, as opposed to the much more volatile and uncertain portfolio and other flows. Indeed, the modern literature and policy-makers have no doubt that FDI have multiple beneficial effects on growth and development. One of them is certainly the provision of capital in countries where this production factor is scarce. As it happens, these are usually countries that register lower growth rates, but higher unemployment and poverty. By providing the necessary capital, TNCs help bring significant parts of population into employment, thus directly contributing to higher economic growth. Experience has taught us that the longer this process lasts, the more these effects reinforce and the more sustainable development becomes. When speaking of benefits of FDI, one must not overlook additional, less tangible, but equally or even more important ones. For instance, TNCs often bring technology and know-how which is not initially available in the host country. In the process of work, this knowledge is invariably transferred to the employees and commercial partners, which adds value not only to the company itself but also to the economy in general. Another indirect effect stemming from the usually more advanced TNCs (compared to local companies) is that they strengthen the competition in a market, which in turn often results in lower prices and higher quality products for all consumers. In addition, foreign companies can put pressure to improve business conditions, which often results in better institutions and governance practices. Despite the numerous benefits, FDI can often pose significant challenges for policy makers and economic agents. In the context of a fixed exchange rate regime, foreign capital flows usually raise the need for their sterilisation by the central bank, which often results in higher interest rates and entails certain costs. Moreover, macroeconomic management and bank liquidity can be affected by the uncertainty regarding the repatriation of earnings by TNCs, which is particularly an issue in cases of few big investors. I must emphasize that FDI are a particularly important issue in a small open economy such as the Republic of Macedonia. As is often the case with these economies, our growth is constrained by several well known factors, which were particularly relevant in the early years of transition, such as high unemployment, lack of domestic capital and low competitiveness of domestic companies. Therefore, we have chosen to rely on export growth and FDI as our main factor of growth. For almost two decades we have been witnessing the importance of FDI and their benefits through the channels previously mentioned. Consequently, we have been making great efforts in attracting foreign capital by maintaining a stable macroeconomic environment, enforcing structural reforms and promoting a better business environment. The increase of cross-border capital flows, particularly of FDI, the deregulation of markets and the continuous technological innovations pose numerous challenges to both compilers and users of external statistics. In addition, timely, accurate and reliable FDI statistics is an essential tool for policy makers trying to attract foreign capital. In fact, external sector statistics is vital for monetary authorities, as it sheds light on the country's transactions with the rest of the world, as well as on its international position of financial assets and liabilities, international liquidity and external debt. These are all crucial components for assessing current and prospective movements in the economic activity, inflation and particularly in foreign exchange reserves, exchange rates, external vulnerability and financial stability. Bearing this on mind, it is not surprising that in many countries the central bank is responsible for compilation of external sector statistics, including FDI statistics. In this context, the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia is the sole official institution responsible for the compilation, processing and dissemination of data on Balance of Payments and the International Investment Position. The methodological framework for FDI statistics is set in accordance with international standards such as the 5-th edition of the Balance of Payments Manual and the 3-rd edition of OECD's Benchmark Definition of Foreign Direct Investment. However, when implementing a compilation system for a certain type of statistics, the choice of data collection methods and data sources is affected by the existing institutional setup, data availability, the response burden imposed, the IT architecture and the implementation and running costs. Besides, one must also add specific national aspects, such as the size of the targeted population and the reporting practices. Consequently, the existing reporting system on FDI in the Republic of Macedonia is a by-product of all these factors, as well as of the changes introduced over time in order to catch up with the latest developments in the domestic market. Against the background of the the latest developments in the area of international and European statistical standards, we would like to point out that NBRM has been investing efforts to adhere to the recommendations in the new 6-th edition of the Balance of Payments Manual and the 4-th edition of the OECD Benchmark Definition of Foreign Direct Investment. In particular, we have been analyzing the possibilities for adjusting the existing FDI collection system to the new far more complex and demanding requirements. Therefore, we see this workshop as a possibility to enhance the capacity nationwide to further improve FDI statistics. We must stress that this is important not only in its own right, but even more in the context of national economic development strategies. We are convinced that the capacity to compile and use statistical data on FDI in a timely, accurate, reliable and effective manner will greatly enhance our ability to successfully implement these strategies in the future. On my personal behalf and on behalf of the Board of the NBRM, let me once again welcome you here and express my gratitude to the UNCTAD for organizing this workshop. I wish you a successful work.

Title: Welcome speech
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Welcome speech by the first governor of the NBRM, Borko Stanoevski, restaurant "Vodenica", 26.04.2012 Welcome speech by the first Governor of the NBRM, Borko Stanoevski, restaurant "Vodenitsa", 26.04.2012 Festive Academy -20 Years of Monetary Independence Dear guests, Dear ladies and gentlemen, I thank you most warmly for your presence and for the honor of giving us the celebration of the day when 20 years ago the Republic of Macedonia immortalised political sovereignty and independence, with the act of monetary independence and the release of the first Macedonian currency - the denar. Fate has determined me to be the last governor of the National Bank of Macedonia in Yugoslavia, which allowed me to gain experience in the field of central banking and then be the first governor of the National Bank in an independent and sovereign Republic of Macedonia. Therefore, I am also designated as one of the participants with the greatest responsibility in preparing and achieving this historic act. That is why I was honored and pleased, on this solemn occasion, to greet you and, with some memories, to remind you of those times. What happened on April 26, 1992 was a successful end to a long-preparing operation. Many individuals and institutions participated in the operation, and as the end approached, their numbers increased. This is a good opportunity to thank everyone and congratulate them on their successful work. At the same time, we have correctly participated in the work of the National Bank of Yugoslavia in the adoption and implementation of measures of the common and single monetary and foreign exchange policy. Banks in Macedonia used primary emission funds smoothly and bought foreign exchange from the foreign exchange market of the National Bank of Yugoslavia for the needs of the Macedonian economy. This allowed the Macedonian economy to survive the most difficult state it found itself in as the only Yugoslav market collapsed. However, when it became quite clear in March 92that Macedonia was ready to declare monetary independence in addition to political independence, the National Bank of Yugoslavia at the last March session of the Council of Governors declared itself incompetent on the territory of the Republic of Macedonia. With my consent, a joint commission is formed to ensure the agreed separation of the National Bank of Yugoslavia with the National Bank of Macedonia. Intensive preparations followed on 26 April 92nd by law, the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia was constituted in an independent issue central bank and the denar in sole payment funds. This happened in very unfavourable conditions for maintaining the stability of the denar. A monthly inflation rate of 86 percent. A high drop in production and exports. Doubled balance of payments deficit, reduced foreign exchange inflows and a minimum foreign exchange reserve level of only 19 million. However, the denar was accepted by the citizens with great joy and satisfaction. That n? encouraged and gave us hope that we had to succeed. And it was in those days, in the wake of the euphoria of the successfully completed monetary independence action that the director of the Oil Refinery visited me and brought me back to reality. He informs me that there is still an oil supply for about thirty days and that our banks cannot open an oil import credential. This was a huge threat to the stability of the denar in the near future. We had to find a way out of the unfavorable state that threatened us. At the time, the total ownership of the then Yugoslavia abroad, due to the war being fought, was blocked worldwide, and so-called mixed banks of the National Bank of Yugoslavia working abroad were blocked. The director of the Anglo-Yugoslav Bank in London has been good friends for a long time. I asked him to use all his acquaintances and authority and find an English or other bank that would open us an credential for 1 oil tanker. He made a counterproposal: to organise a visit to the Bank of England, and I would ask there to unblock the Anglo-Yugoslav Bank exclusively for lending banks from Macedonia. A 15-minute meeting with the Governor of the Bank of England, Sir Lein Pemberton, was arranged in 23 days. The meeting took place in May 1992. It was my first visit as governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia to a foreign central bank. The conversation with Sir Lein Pemberton lasted 1 hour and 15 minutes, as he became interested in the story of the events in Macedonia. A particular effect in him was left by the fact that Macedonia peacefully merged with Yugoslavia and did not participate in military operations, and attention was drawn to the way we teamed up with the National Bank of Yugoslavia and the samples of the value vouchers I gave him. He met all my demands: -First, they immediately partially unblocked the Anglo-Yugoslav Bank for working with banks from Macedonia alone, and for that purpose set a limit of 15% of the Bank's credit potential, which was about 60m. Later, on a visit by the President of the Republic of Macedonia to England, the limit was increased to 18%; -Secondly, they provided reception and training of staff from the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia in the domain of payment turnover with abroad and supervision of banks, at their expense; -Third, I received encouragement that he personally and the Bank of England, through its representatives, would help the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia join the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank and other international financial institutions as soon as possible. Thus, the threat to the stability of the denar in the first days of its release was overcome. A few years later, i sent Sir Lein Pemberton a letter to the Bank of England address samples from the wonderful third series of the Macedonian denar and once again warmly thanked him. Finally, let me express my satisfaction that in all those past 20 years the denar has remained stable. I also want to share my successor's expressed hope of witnessing the replacement of the denar with the euro soon. Dear guests, I hope I have not abused your patience. Thank you again and wish you a pleasant evening.

Title: Memories of the 20th anniversary of macedonia's first money
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Mr. Borko Stanoevski, Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia from 1986 to 1997 Memories of the 20th anniversary of macedonia's first money I. This text was first published 10 years ago, on the occasion of the 10th anniversary of the first Macedonian money - the denari, in the publication of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, titled "The Creation of macedonian Denar - Visions and Memories" published in Skopje in 2002. Ten more years have passed and now on 26 April 2012, we will celebrate the 20th anniversary of the first Macedonian money  the denar. It is a good occasion to remember the events of the time when the conditions for the beginning of the history of Macedonian money were created - the denominators, who defy all the challenges of the past 20 years, have basically remained a stable means of payment in the Republic. On the other hand, I describe in the article events and facts related to the process of creating the denar that are not processed in the regular reports of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, therefore not archived and as such, can remain unknown to the general public and unremembered. Furthermore, I feel the need to correct some errors made in the text from 10 years ago in quoting some facts (before all dates) and the interpretation of some events that occurred due to the short time I had at my disposal, as well as to supplement the text with some significant events that I missed in the first text. Finally, I hope that with edited and additional processing of some of the events I look back at, I will bring more light to their explanation and overcome the dilemmas of some authors regarding those events. II. I decided to start my memories with a quote from a speech that, at the invitation of the President of the European Parliament, I gave in the packed hall of the European Parliament in Brussels in mid-June 1996, when I presented to the world for the first time the spectacular results achieved after monetary independence of the Republic and the release of the first Macedonian money  the denars. Quote: "Dear ladies and gentlemen" More than a month ago, Macedonia celebrated an important jubilee  four years since its monetary independence was declared. In those four years, the following results were achieved: * When the Republic of Macedonia separated from the monetary system of then Yugoslavia in April 1992, the monthly inflation rate was 86%. Four years later, in April 1996, a monthly deflation rate of 0.7% was achieved. Cumulatively for the first five months of the year, the deflation rate is 1.5%; * In April 1992, the unofficial exchange rate of the denar was higher than the official exchange rate of the denar by about 70%. Today we have a single and stable flexible exchange rate on the denar in the only foreign exchange market. My ladies and gentlemen, allow me to briefly explain to you how these extraordinary results have been achieved with brief information about: 1. The monetary policy applied, 2. The structure and changes in the banking system, and 3. Relations with international financial institutions. 1. Monetary policy The Republic of Macedonia achieved its monetary independence on 26 April 1992, when the Assembly of the Republic of Macedonia adopted the following laws: * The Law on the Central Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, and * Law on the Currency of the Republic of Macedonia By the first law, the Central Bank of the Republic of Macedonia was established as an independent central bank. By the second law, the denar was introduced as a national currency. With the adoption of these two laws, the Republic of Macedonia has definitely separated itfrom monetary policy and currency of then Yugoslavia. These laws created the conditions for a single, independent monetary policy. When the Republic of Macedonia declared its monetary independence, hyperinflation admired hyperinflation, which reached 86% monthly in April 1992. To prevent this hyperinflation, we immediately began conducting restrictive monetary policy. As a result, the monthly inflation rate in May-December 1992 was reduced to an average level of 12.7%. At the time in the rest of Yugoslavia, the country we separated from, hyperinflation increased tenfold every month. After the first results of our own monetary policy were visible, the central bank decided on monetary policy reforms. The aim of these reforms was to remove inflationary instruments embedded in monetary policy. To that end, a monetary policy reform programme was prepared at the Central Bank of the Republic of Macedonia by the end of 1992. In the first months of 1993, the programme was adopted by the Government of the Republic of Macedonia, and during May of that year, implemented in appropriate laws. The central point of that programme was the elimination of so-called selective loans. They served as a basic long-standing and generally stereotypical and sterile instrument for monetary regulation. Instead of selective loans, the central bank began introducing other market-oriented monetary policy instruments. At the same time, the instrument already applied, the obligatory reserve of banks, modified, gained increasing application, and the central bank's essential rate gained its core function and tasks. Finally, the state's debt to the central bank was regulated by law, very restrictively. The consequence of monetary policy reforms was the introduction of daily and periodic auctions of deposits and securities by the Central Bank. They were the introduction of so-called open market operations, which were gaining an increasing role in regulating the liquidity of commercial banks. In parallel with changes in monetary policy, a reform programme in the country's foreign exchange and business system was also implemented. In this domain, the main orientation was the construction of an official foreign exchange market in the country and the introduction of a flexible exchange rate of denar. As a result of these changes, the so-called "black foreign exchange market" was soon destroyed, implying wild street shifters of effective foreign money, "protecting" foreign exchange and the like." * Completed citation In my further statement, I looked at relations with international financial institutions, the structure and efforts to sanitise banks in the country and the like. A discussion followed from several MEPs, who mainly expressed admiration for the results achieved and interest in more specific explanations for some parts of my statement. III. The introduction of denar into circulation and the conduct of its own monetary policy, although in extremely difficult and inadequate conditions, has indeed produced rapid spectacular results from the aspect of dealing with hyperinflation, maintaining the stability of the denar and exchange rate. Therefore, and also because Macedonia received its own money for the first time, it is interesting to clarify some of the circumstances regarding when it was born and how the idea of its own Macedonian money matured, in what conditions that this idea was born and, finally, how its fulfilment was carried out. I will look at some important events and events in which I was a participant or their carrier. Of course, there are many such events and events, and I will look back, in my opinion, on the most important. 1. In the first half of 1990, unlike the previous period after the publication of the reforms and the Stabilisation Programme of the Federal Government of Mr. Ante Markovic, the first major signs of financial indiscipline in both the financial and monetary spheres came forward, which announced the failure of the programme. In the financial sphere, indiscipline consisted in the increasing phenomena of non-settled republics' obligations to the federal budget, which is why the Federation's budget deficit was increasingly covered by primary emissions or by unsettled obligations to the holding based on exchange differences, export incentives and the like. In the monetary sphere, indiscipline existed in the use of the primary emission for selective loans and liquidity loans of banks. All of this fuelled inflation in the country, which had a steady trend of increase. However, the last blow that practically dismantled Yugoslavia's only financial and monetary system in 1991 was Serbia's incursion through the National Bank of that republic into Yugoslavia's monetary system. On 7 January 1991, the NBJ Council of Governors held an extraordinary session where we were notified that on 4 January, The Federal Executive Council received the "Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia - special magazine no. 14 of 28 December 1990", which published the Decision on the approval of liquidity loans to banks and the Law on the Debt of the Republic of Serbia to the National Bank of Serbia totalling 18.1 billion dinars, brought to the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia by the Joint Labour Council at the session held on 27 and 28 December 1990. On this occasion, the Council of Governors concluded to close the foreign exchange market and stop the further use of primary emissions until controls are carried out in all republics. Also, in the form of a conclusion, it was requested that the National Bank of Serbia refund the funds it eventually used on the basis of the acts of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia. Convinced that the National Bank of Serbia would not act on that conclusion and that it was the beginning of the end of Yugoslavia's only monetary system, I proposed to make a decision to approve the primary emission of all other republics, appropriate to participation in the primary show that each republic had in the previous year, regardless of possible hyperinflation and thus, neutralise the effects exploited by the Republic of Serbia by intrusion into yugoslavia's monetary system. Such a proposal was supported by the governors of Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Slovenia. However, on the grounds that the volume of the primary show under the SME Constitution and the NBJ Law is determined by the SME Assembly, not the Council of Governors, such a proposal with 4 votes in favour and 5 against was not adopted, and at the time the work in the SME Assembly, where such an idea could have been achieved, was already completely blocked. On 8 January 1991, I notified the Executive Council of the Republic of Macedonia of these events and the possible consequences of them, while submitting a draft law in which the Republic of Macedonia would intrude into the the SME monetary system, amounting to 5 billion dinars, explaining the possible positive and negative consequences of this. The key dilemma imposed on the issue of passing or not passing such a law was how the money made would be used in this way. It was quite clear that they would not be able to turn into foreign exchange, as the NBJ had already closed the foreign exchange market, and in the future access to the market was only possible on the basis of a positive report from the NBJ Control Sector, which employed exclusively citizens from the republics of Serbia-Montenegro. And Macedonia needed 150-200m a year, which it regularly achieved from nbj's exchange reserves. Therefore, the Executive Council of the Republic of Macedonia, by individual vote of each minister, and after previous extensive consultations with all experts from the Republic, decided not to accept the Draft Law on Intrusion into the Monetary System of Yugoslavia, and obliged the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia legally, through activities in the Council of Governors, to ensure adequate participation in the primary show, as in previous years and to provide foreign exchange to cover the payments needs of the Republic.1 1 To execute this conclusion more in the following text. On that occasion, the president of the Executive Council who voted to pass the Law asked me, "Is there a more secure way to secure some future similar intrusions into Yugoslavia's monetary system from the people's banks of Serbia or other republics?". I replied: "There is, and that is its own monetary system and its own money." Both the question and the answer were left without comment. First, no position on Macedonia's political future was yet built at the time. Secondly, the Executive Council was the body of the previous, one-party assembly of the Assembly of the Republic of Macedonia and did not feel competent to propose such fateful (historical measures). Therefore, that session of the Executive Council of the Republic of Macedonia did not discuss the issue of monetary independence and the release of its own money into circulation and no conclusion was reached.
