I mentioned only a few necessary conditions that would guarantee the success of the operation and which we do not yet have. I quote part of the transcript: "The introduction of its own money assumes absolutely physically closed borders of the Republic, with its own army, with its own customs officers. That border must not fly over without control, not pass trucks, trains, whole herds of sheep through the mountains, etc." In addition to the statement, I informed mPs that a variant was being prepared in case of the need for an urgent change in The U-dinars with Macedonian money. I informed that in the vault of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia we constantly kept new, unused yu-dinar banknotes worth 6 billion dinars and an appropriate denominationstructure, which, in case of need, by printing a dry stamp on them, would be transformed into temporary Macedonian money. However, no appropriate technical solution was found for the jigsaw, and there was a risk of certain political and other consequences, which is why that variant was finally rejected. I had a great desire to inform mPs about the visit of the paper factory in Radece and the agreement reached on the production of paper, however, I refrained, because although this part of the session was closed, many guests and officials attended it, so there was a possibility that the secret would go public, and that was not just our secret, but also the secret of the radece factory, to which I promised her maximum conspiracy. - I finally informed the Assembly why I asked for this part of the session to be closed to the public and why all this was the subject of debate around monetary independence and the introduction of Macedonian money in circulation should be treated as a state secret. Achieving one of the strategic objectives of economic policy in that year and early next depended on the loyalty of the Republic of Macedonia to the monetary and foreign exchange system of then Yugoslavia. The purchase of foreign exchange, which the Republic of Macedonia much needed, was only possible from the foreign exchange reserves of the NBJ if the Republic was within the monetary and foreign exchange system of Yugoslavia and if it did not show activities to exit those systems. And on this plan, this year (1991) we achieved outstanding results: - First, we have significantly increased our participation in the primary show of the NBJ. By 30 June 1991, Banks in Macedonia had used 2.458m dinars of primary emissions, or 9.4% of total emissions during that period, including the effects on primary emissions from all irregular intrusions of some republics into Yugoslavia's monetary system. In the second half of the year, due to the high liquidity of banks in Macedonia and hence, due to their disinterest in pulling funds from the primary nbj show, that participation decreased to 8.85%; - Secondly, in 1991 the republics - some started early, some later - did not pay their obligations to the federal budget. This shortage of funds in the federal budget was supplemented by borrowing in the NBJ (one of the reasons for the increasing hyperinflation). In the republics' total unpaid obligations to the federal budget, Macedonia participated with as much as 11.5%. Of those retained funds, for the first time this year, the calculated exchange differences and incentives of exporters were paid in full, satisfactory liquidity was achieved not only to banks, but also to a large proportion of export-oriented business entities; - Third, 181.5m was purchased through banks in the Republic, and 181.5m was purchased during the year in closed foreign exchange market conditions. That was 17.5% of NBJ's total sales this year. In addition, business entities from the Republic of Macedonia were paid all guaranteed and fixed obligations guaranteed by the Federation or payer agent was NBJ of over 130m. All of this was paid for by funds provided by the primary nbj show and at an official course that was significantly lower than the exchange rate formed in the black foreign exchange market. All this allowed us, in conditions when the SME was falling apart, and the Republic of Macedonia lived the first months of political independence, independence and sovereignty, without problems in the procurement of oil, medicines, raw materials and repromaterials. Completing his statement to the Deputies in the Assembly of the Republic of Macedonia, I once again stressed that we must not break ties with the Federation while they provide us with foreign exchange in such an amount and under such conditions and that therefore, further activities regarding monetary independence and the introduction of Macedonian money in circulation must be achieved in the strictest secrecy. Therefore, I asked the Deputies, everything that was said here, to remain here as a state secret. After several additional questions to which I gave short answers, my presentation, and that means my actions regarding the replacement of old yu-dinars with dinars with a new design, were fully accepted and confirmed. VIII. My main activities in early 1992 were directed, in addition to daily current affairs, in two directions: - first, completion of technical preparations for printing value vouchers, and - secondly, an effort by the Council of Governors of the NBJ to make the most of the rights to purchase foreign exchange as set out in the Quotas of the Federal Executive Council for the 1st quarter of 1992. 1. In the "Analysis of the possibilities and manner of introduction of Republic money" of November 1991, which was fully accepted by the Monetary System Working Group of the Government of the Republic, envisaged the introduction of republic money in circulation in two phases: first, to release value vouchers instead of real money, and after consolidating the situation in the holding to some possible optimal level, within no longer than one year, they should be replaced with real coins and banknotes. The two-phase introduction of Macedonian money in circulation was conditional on several moments. First, the production of coins and banknotes is a process that lasts at least 1.5 to 2 years (from design design, which requires a public competition, the production of special paper that follows, to printing, drying and, finally, treasury processing). We didn't have that much time. Secondly, the choice of design should go the way of competition  publicly, and we at the time, from the reasons already well explained, we had to carry out these activities in the strictest secrecy and in a short time. Third, the name of the currency has not yet been established, and this issue also required public debate, which we could not have at the time for the same reasons. Fourth, the Law on the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia has not yet been passed and the National Bank has not yet been constituted as an issue bank. The adoption of this law was possible only on the day of the declaration of monetary independence and the release of Macedonian money into circulation, which means that they had to be printed beforehand. Fifth, it was quite clear that the act of monetary independence and the release of republic money would be carried out in the face of hyperinflation and monetary chaos in the country from which we secede, then in the face of a significant decline in industrial production and a very low level of foreign exchange reserves, etc., which will all together have negative consequences for new money in terms of their rapid depreciation. For all those reasons, it was rated as good, and as the only possible solution, the release of the first Macedonian money will be in circulation with temporary value stamps, which will be printed in a short period, on paper of lower quality (and therefore cheaper), with simple markings and without the name of the national currency, which, after stabilising the situation in the national economy and, above all, in the monetary sphere (we practically did not know how much money in circulation there would be in the Republic on the day of the replacement of Yu-dinars with Macedonian money) will be replaced with real money, applying an appropriate denomination ratio. Because special colors and securities for value vouchers were ordered and their arrival in Skopje was a matter of the day, a priority issue i engaged on in the first days of 1992 was the issue of the design of vouchers. Almost every afternoon and on weekends in the first days of January 1992 I was in the printing house where the designers of the printing house together, before all a young talented boy, worked hard to realize various ideas about the possible design of value stamps. I have known from Yugoslav experience that the issue of money design is very sensitive, especially in countries with multinational populations and with different faiths, such as the Republic of Macedonia. Given that, as well as the short time we had to prepare, with the designers and the printing house director, who also honestly and maximised the issue, we came up with the idea that all value vouchers should be of the same design, and to differ only in colors, which for each depot will be different and the figures for the amount of the bon, which will be printed a little more impressively (large and strong) than usual. This reduced the time for preparations and rehearsals ten times, and also reduced the risk of errors in the choice of design motifs. We decided to make a basic character motif on the face of the vouch to be the Ilinden monument in Krushevo, which expressed the centuries-old struggle of the citizens of Macedonia for life in peace and freedom. The bona fides featured tobacco pickers who could be of any nationality. With samples of the samples carried out, I met all the senior managers in the Republic individually. Their reactions were very restrained. There was neither criticism nor support. I was aware that in the event of a poor reception of value vouchers, in terms of design among the citizens of Macedonia, all responsibility will be solely mine. On 14 January 1992, the printing house was ready to start printing the first Macedonian money in the form of value vouchers. Printing should have been made on a machine most appropriate for doing so, with which two workers, a married couple, worked. There was a solemn atmosphere and silence in the hall. When all preparations were ready, the machine numberer set to zero and the ordinary one replaced by special paper began printing the 10-unit value voucher around 11:00. When I saw the first tabac with the face of 24 banknotes, I felt my eyes filled with tears. Inorder to hide my weakness, I turned to the window wiping my eyes unnoticed. When I narrowed down a little, I turned back to the machine, which continuously printed the face of the banknote, after 24 copies of each tab, I saw that the eyes of the spouses working on the machine were also full of tears. And not only their, tears of joy were in the eyes of all who witnessed this historic act at that moment when the printing of the first Macedonian money began. Printing ended on 5.2.1992. On 7.2.1992, To the President of the Republic, the President of the Assembly and to the President of the Government of the Republic of Macedonia, I sent a letter (top secret number 5) informing them that in accordance with the Decision of the Government of the Republic of Macedonia of 19.12.1991, The National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia printed value stamps, namely 27,858,696 banknotes in denominators of 10; 25 and 50; 100; 500 and 1000 units of value totalling 8,433,647,700 units. I further informed them that the value vouchers were placed in the vault of the National Bank of the Republic Macedonia and that a plan has been developed to distribute them to all the headquarters of the Social Bookkeeping Service in 24 hours. I also informed them that for the release of value vouchers, i.e. to replace ju-dinars with value stamps, it is necessary to adopt in the Assembly of the Republic of Macedonia: the Law on the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, which will constitute it as an issue bank, the Law on the Monetary Unit of the Republic of Macedonia, which will determine the name and divisiveness of the Macedonian currency and the Law on the Use of the Currency of the Republic of Macedonia, regulating the use of value vouchers. I also informed them that the drafts of those laws are ready, as well as for the draft several decisions to be taken by the Council of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia: The decision to withdraw from the scope of the Yu-dinars, the decision to release the value vouchers, the Guidance on the way and conditions for removing ju-dinars with vouchers and more. The relevant managers informed them that the issue of the name of the currency of the Republic of Macedonia remains open. Remarkably, the total amount of the value vouchers printed was greater than the amount determined in the Government's decision obliged the National Bank to print value vouchers totalling 5 billion dinars. I did so on the basis of knowledge of the amount of money in circulation in Macedonia that we came to with the replacement of the old ones with new dinar banknotes from 26 to 31 November 1991, and after prior consultation with the Prime Minister and President of the Republic of Macedonia. However, as there was an increasing inflation month after month, we continued to print value vouchers and beyond, So on the day of the exchange of yu-dinars with value vouchers, on 26.4.1992, we had value vouchers of more than 18 billion dinars available, and two new banknotes were printed  with a modified design of 5 thousand and 10 thousand units. Despite these additional measures, after the exchange of the dinar with value vouchers, several times, there was a short-term cash shortage in payment turnover. In any case, with the first amount of value vouchers printed, which I notified the Republic's leadership on 7.2.1992, I fell a huge load off my back. From that day on, every day, if the circumstances sought it, the replacement of Yugoslav dinars with Macedonian money could begin. 2. Meanwhile, the NBJ Council of Governors waged a quiet war between me and the governor of the National Bank of Serbia. For the first quarter of 1992, the Federal Executive Council established a quota for the sale of foreign exchange reserves of NBJ's foreign exchange reserves of 298.2 million for current economic needs, of which 28.2 million were earmarked for the Macedonian economy (21.5m for oil imports, 3.8m for drug imports and 2.9m for agricultural needs). A quota for the repayment of loans abroad guaranteed by the Federation or nbj or NBJ is also established. Those obligations to the Republic of Macedonia for the 1992 quarter amounted to 38.4m dinars. Based on the two quotas, Macedonian banks were entitled to buy 66.6m, and the main condition for this was to respect Yugoslavia's only monetary and foreign exchange system, i.e. to remain loyal to those systems. The Governor of the National Bank of Serbia persistently, almost every session of the Council of Governors was aware that Macedonia had declared independence and was preparing for secession from yugoslavia's monetary and foreign exchange system and that it should therefore be shortened to use primary emissions and purchase foreign exchange from the NBJ's foreign exchange reserves and a number of other measures, previously applied against banks from Slovenia and Croatia. In addition, he often cited statements by the Prime Minister of the Government of Macedonia, who said on various occasions that the release of Macedonian money was only a matter of the day. Understandably, I have consistently argued otherwise, and the other members of the Council, especially the Governor of the NBJ, who was also in very poor relations with the leadership of the National Bank of Serbia and the governors of the people's banks of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Vojvodina, with whom I had an extremely good friendly relationship, believed in my statements and banks in Macedonia slowly exercised their right to buy foreign exchange within the established quotas. However, at the 419th session of the Council of Governors, held on 27.2.1992, a conclusion was adopted on the basis of which the National Bank of Macedonia was asked to give written notice on whether and when the Republic of Macedonia would introduce its own money. This conclusion was reached on the basis of a written request from the National Bank of Serbia, prepared together with the professional services of the NBJ, which stated the following: "It is obvious that Macedonia is also joining together and that it is becoming an independent, independent and sovereign state that expects international recognition. Many factors speak in addition to such a finding. Macedonia withdraws its representatives from the Federation, Long ago, it did not pay customs duties and contributions to the federal budget, banned the referral of recruits to the JNA. The SME presidency has decided to temporarily relocate the JNA from Macedonia and more, Macedonia is taking other measures and has taken decisions that go in favour of Macedonia's independence from Yugoslavia. These measures also concern the issue of the replacement of the dinar and the introduction of its own currency, which has otherwise been hinted at for a long time. In order to prevent economic damage and protect the economic interests of Serbia and its economy, decisions need to be made in a timely manner and measures taken, namely: ...". There are measures to be taken against Macedonia in the monetary sphere, payment turnover and the foreign exchange system. Faced with such a request, in which the above arguments could hardly be denied, because they were generally known, the Council of Governors reached the said conclusion. On 6.3.1992, I informed the Governor of the NBJ in writing that I had received a letter from the Government of Macedonia, the text of which I cited as a whole, which shows that the Government of the Republic of Macedonia will not take any measures in the monetary independence plan and the introduction of its own money in the next 1.5 to 2 months, and for a long period it will depend on many circumstances. I also presented a letter from the Assembly of the Republic of Macedonia confirming that no act of monetary independence of the Republic is in the process in the Macedonian Assembly. There was a similar statement from the Council of the National Bank of Macedonia. One of the sessions in the second half of March 1992 examined the governor of the National Bank of Macedonia's response, in which, by compromise, by forming two committees that were supposed to exercise certain controls, the answer was accepted as positive. Contrary to all the difficulties we had in the NBJ Council of Governors, all 66.6 million was used by the end of March 1992 based on both quotas. Commitments to abroad were paid as of 30.4.1992, and the oil crisis that seriously threatened us (we still did not have foreign exchange reserves in dollars for an oil tanker, nor did we have the chance to do so on loan from domestic or foreign banks) was postponed for the months that followed These foreign exchange, totalling 66.6m, were paid with funds received by banks from the primary nbj show by way of 3 See "Welcome Speech of the First Governor of the NBRM", Borko Stanoevski, held on 26.4.2012, on the occasion of 20 years of monetary independence of the Republic of Macedonia". selective loans or liquidity loans. In that period of three months, banks in Macedonia used 3,159m dinars, or 18% of the total emissionof the National Bank of Yugoslavia (which was then composed of four republics) broadcast during that period. If someone gives you money first and for that money allows you to buy foreign exchange, at an official, very undervalued exchange rate, and at the same time you do not fulfil any obligation to that common source of money and foreign exchange, all foreign exchange purchasers from nbj at the time could be treated as a gift. However, it should be stressed that Macedonia was no exception. Similar policies were pursued by other republics and used primary emission funds in the same way and purchased foreign exchange reserves from the NBJ's foreign exchange reserves, in which all republics participated in the previous creation, which is why they were equally entitled to use them. However, in April 1992, more and more facts talked about the republic of Macedonia's firm determination of monetary secession from then Yugoslavia and the release of Macedonian money in circulation instead of the Yu-dinars. For these reasons, the National Bank of Yugoslavia decided to close the foreign exchange market doors for banks in Macedonia and prevent them from accessing primary emissionfunds. Thus, the National Bank of Yugoslavia practically declared itself incompetent on the territory of the Republic of Macedonia, and its only interest remained to withdraw the dinars that were in circulation in the Republic of Macedonia. A joint commission was established to achieve this interest of the NBJ, which I accepted. Thus, in early April there definitely ceased to be the only and very important motive for the continued remaining of the Republic in the monetary and foreign exchange system of then Yugoslavia. Meanwhile, the JNA was withdrawn from the Republic of Macedonia, which was a very important limiting factor in the introduction of Macedonian money. At the same time, border crossings and customs controls were established towards the Republic of Serbia, as one of the very important assumptions about the introduction of their own money. In Yugoslavia, the inflation rate from month to month was increasing. In April 1992, it reached 86% per month. The Macedonian economy, which had an inferior position to some extent in relation to the rest of the Yugoslav economy, could have been completely devastated under hyperinflation. In addition, in the Republic of Serbia more than 100 products could only be purchased for foreign exchange, in no case with worthless Yugoslav dinars. These were the reasons why we should have run as soon as possible from the monetary zone of Yugoslavia. In mid-April 1992 In 2013, there was virtually no longer any reason why the monetary independence of the Republic of Macedonia and the release of Macedonian money should be postponed. Only waited for the completion of the first anti-inflation programme in the Government of the Republic of Macedonia and the determination of the day of monetary independence of the Republic of Macedonia and the release of the first Macedonian money in circulation. IX. On 26.4.1992, the Assembly of the Republic of Macedonia adopted the Law on the National Bank of Macedonia, the Law on the Currency of the Republic of Macedonia and the Law on the Use of the Currency of the Republic of Macedonia in a shortened procedure. The National Bank of Macedonia was constituted in an independent and issue bank. In accordance with Article 100 of the Law on the National Bank of Macedonia, until the election of the Council of the National Bank, decisions under the authority of the Council were made by the Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia. In accordance with that provision, I have made the decisions needed to withdraw Yugoslav dinars in circulation, to release the value vouchers that are given the name denar and with a special guidance I have prescribed the conditions for the time and manner of the replacement of the dinar with the denar. On 27.4.1992, the replacement of yu-dinars with denari began and successfully ended within the scheduled three days. There are detailed reports about how the replacement was carried out, and I will address two issues that are certainly not treated in those reports. The first question is about the creation of the name (name) of the first Macedonian money. The issue remained uncertain until days before the release of the value vouchers in circulation, although individual proposals for the name of the future currency occurred in early 1991, mainly in public voices. Thus, as early as 24 January 1991, an unknown author in Pulse promoted the name peon for future Macedonian money, according to the name of a missing people who lived in these spaces, the Peons. The article speculated that the news had passed from the National Bank, which was entrusted with the project to build its own monetary system. A little later that year, the "11 October" printing house in Prilep printed a prototype of Macedonian money called stater - a Greek name under which some ancient Macedonian rulers coined coins. However, when the Slavs came to the Balkans, the staters did not forge in Macedonia and were not in active use. One of the current political parties in various ways suggested the name lion, which also had no historical basis and was not taken seriously. The National Bank of Macedonia, as monetary independence day approached, used the name Macedonian dinar for future Macedonian money as a working name. A few days before the session of the Assembly of the Republic of Macedonia, held on 26.4.1992, I got a phone call from the then Finance Minister who introduced me to the proposal of academic Petar Hr. Ilievski, a prominent classical philologist who immediately seemed acceptable to me. The famous academic, based on his scientific research, came to the knowledge that at the time of the Slavs' arrival, Macedonia was a Roman province and circulated Roman money here. The main name of Roman money was denarius, from which the form dinarmon (dinar) was obtained through Byzantine Greek. The name denarius continued to be used to this day in the Balkans and the Mediterranean in two forms: less often denar and the prevalent dinar. For several reasons, the academic suggested the name denar. For this, in my opinion, only an acceptable name, I immediately informed the President of the State and the Prime Minister and because they agreed, we embedded the name denar in the Law on the Currency of the Republic of Macedonia. Later, this name was unanimously accepted in the Assembly of the Republic of Macedonia4. 4 The name denar can be read more in the daily Vecer from 1, 2 and 3 May 1992. The second issue is related to the very act of rereplacement of Yugoslav dinars with Macedonian denari. The act of replacement itself is a simple technical operation. However, it can have terrifyingly severe economic consequences, especially if it takes place in uncertain conditions in terms of the volume of money in circulation being withdrawn, especially if you have a fragile border with one of the neighbours where that money is an official means of payment. The second fact was particularly worrying, as the dinar in neighbouring Yugoslavia was devalued daily, it was in huge quantities, and many products could not be bought with it. So the replacement should have been carried out in very uncertain conditions: - first, the National Bank of Macedonia had no approximately accurate information on how much dinars there was in the macedonian area, as Macedonia was the only republic in the SME that did not it needed cash from the NBJ, but cash came with the sale of agricultural products on the markets in Yugoslavia. It was only known that from 26 to 31 December 1991, the old ones were replaced with new dinar banknotes worth 7 billion dinars. However, the period up to 26.4.1992 was relatively long to change the situation. The day of the replacement of the dinar with denari we welcomed it with value vouchers  denari totalling 18 billion denarii. Personally, I was not sure that amount would be enough for us; - secondly, it was not known which structure of citizens or legal entities possessed the largest amounts of money in cash. At the time, the grey economy and foreign exchange smuggling in the black market were very developed. These activities could only be carried out by citizens who owned large amounts of cash, but how much those amounts were and what their origin was difficult to check. The replacement was a good opportunity to "cut the wings" of those businessmen and the cash to return to regular payment flows or return from where it came from, i.e. in other areas of then Yugoslavia; - third, there was a real danger of many citizens of Yugoslavia, especially from the Republic of Serbia and the Autonomous Province of Kosovo, who in the face of hyperinflation and monetary chaos had large amounts of worthless Yugoslav dinars, whose further depreciation increased every day, to try those dinars, through their relatives or friends, to replace them for much safer Macedonian denarii and later turn them into material goods in markets in Macedonia or in foreign currencies. The same doubt applied to the countless representations of yugoslavia companies in Macedonia, which, in addition to cash, could manipulate jury money; - fourthly, certain manipulations could be expected to be organised regarding the replacement of dinars with denarii and the state structures of the republics that remained in Yugoslavia. Given all those circumstances, international experiences and recent experiences from Slovenia and Croatia, the day of the replacement of Yugoslav dinars with Macedonian denari I expected it restlessly and with a certain dose of fear. That was the moment, as I told lawmakers in the Assembly of the Republic of Macedonia, when we will perform the act of "salto mortale" with two possible finishes: in case of insufficient and poorpreparation, let's fall on our heads and break our heads or if we prepare well and prepare and we organize, fall to our feet and stay alive and well, albeit with minor injuries that can later be easily treated. Therefore, when asked about the replacement of dinars with denarii, I approached him with great seriousness. I made the instructions on the terms and manner of the replacement almost alone. In essence, the following criteria were established: only a citizen of the Republic of Macedonia over 18 years of age who is proven by ID can participate in the replacement, can be replaced in almost a maximum of up to 20 000 dinars, any larger amount can be paid into a savings book or in an current account which will later be separately controlled and, finally, the replacement deadline will last three days. The guideline provided many other details regarding the way and conditions of the replacement of dinars with denarii. A few days before the replacement (2 or 3 days, I do not remember exactly) the bills and acts regarding the impending replacement of dinars with denari were the subject of a review by the government group on the monetary system. At that meeting, the group president, a respected and respected academic, proposed that the limit for exchanging cash should be raised to 50,000 denari on the grounds that the amount of 20,000 denari is simply small and will mean unnecessary abuse of citizens. According to our estimates at the time, 20,000 denari could cover the one-week cost of a family of four, which is enough. I opposed such a proposal, pointing to the circumstances set out, confirming my proposal with examples from Slovenia and Croatia. In Slovenia, the replacement also lasted three days and amounted to 20,000 denari, and in Croatia much more restrictively, the exchange ended in two days and amounting to 10,000 dinars, although it was carried out three months later from Slovenia. In any case, the group accepted the president's proposal, and finally, although reluctant, I agreed on 27.4.1992 in the Instructions I signed and delivered to all the headquarters of the Social Bookkeeping Service, I found, in the capacity of the Council of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, a limit for the exchange of dinars in almost 50 000 dinars. However, the unrest and fear I felt from the uncertainty about the amount of dinars that would be replaced for denari i was growing. I spent the first day of the exchange visiting the headquarters of the Social Bookkeeping Service in talks with treasurers and following reports from all the headquarters of the Social Bookkeeping Service. Sometime after midnight I came to the following knowledge: first, on the first day of the exchange significantly more dinars were replaced for denari compared to our predictions; secondly, in Most of Macedonia, citizens change amounts to an average of up to 10,000 dinars, and in one part of Macedonia all family members over 18 years of age report en masse and change a maximum of 50,000 dinars. The night contradicts the second day of exchange, in the capacity of the Council of the National Bank of Macedonia, which has not yet been named (in accordance with Article 100 of the NBRM Law, The council's decisions were made by the governor, whose jurisdiction was the decision), and I decided the maximum possible replacement of dinars for denari was 20,000 dinars. On 28.4.1992, by 9:00 a.m., all the headquarters of the Social Bookkeeping Service were known for fax. Within less than half an hour, the ranks of the social bookkeeping service's counters in the regions where 50,000 dinars were changed en masse. At 10:00 the same day, I practically stormed the Prime Minister's Office and informed him what I did and the reasons why I did so. He briefly replied: "Okay, I hope you know what you're doing." X. Many authors in the publication "The Creation of Macedonian Denar - Visions and Memories" published in 2002, although insufficiently informed, comment on the time before the replacement of Yugoslav dinars with Macedonian denari, as a period when huge amounts of Yugoslav dinars were flowing into Macedonia, causing Macedonia great material damage. My fear of the existence of cash in circulation is also remarkable: whether we will have enough value vouchers printed to successfully complete the replacement, as our knowledge of the amount of cash in circulation is based on assumptions and estimates, not known figures. Causes of fear existed. It is known that in hyperinflation conditions (in April 1992 we had a monthly inflation rate of 86%) there is much more cash in circulation than would be in normal conditions. For example, in inflation conditions of 2% per year. Macedonia was the only republic in Yugoslavia that provided cash in circulation years by selling finished products - especially agricultural products - in other Yugoslav republics, especially in the second half of the year, and the National Bank of Macedonia was the only bank that, during each year, returned more than it needed cash from the NBJ vault. The fact is that the National Bank of Macedonia was the only central bank in Yugoslavia that did not have a book-logged debt for cash raised from the NBJ vault. We regularly returned damaged and poured banknotes more than we were in need of new banknotes. Finally, it was evident that in the face of monetary chaos and high inflation, fuelled by excessive primary money emissions, there was an invisible financial war in the area of the whole country, to materialise the excess cash, in which Macedonia was also dragged in. That financial war was particularly intensified with Slovenia's monetary independence and later Croatia. Aware of this situation as early as mid-1991, in co-operation with the government and the relevant ministries, we organised defence measures. Such was the case with the conversion of excess liquid money to banks in commodity reserves, foreign exchange buybacks and the like. The final answer to the question of whether there was much cash in circulation in Macedonia, for which someone bought foreign exchange or material goods, gave the act itself to replace Yugoslav dinars with Macedonian money. When all phases of the exchange ended, 23.8 billion dinars were raised in the vault of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia. According to the german brand's black exchange rate, which was formed on the black foreign exchange market at the time (June 1992) and which was about 650 denari for a German brand, the real value of that cash in circulation was about 37 million German marks. To compare and estimate the size of that amount, let the data serve that during the last year (2011) the amount of cash in circulation, on average, was about 25m euros, or about 50m German marks. This data is hardly comparable for at least two reasons, the first is the time distance of 20 years, and the second, due to the fact that inflation at the time of the exchange of Yu-dinars with Macedonian denari was 86% per month, which in itself withdraws a higher volume of cash in circulation, as opposed to inflation in 2011 from 2% annually, which in itself withdraws a smaller volume of cash in circulation. However, it can be concluded that the defence measures taken against the influx of devalued Yu-dinars at the time had a certain result and the volume of cash in circulation (Yugoslav denari) on the days of replacement was at a relatively normal level. Thus, theories that Macedonia was overwhelmed and ravaged by worthless Yugoslav dinars can be regarded as unrealistic.

Title: Fifth conference on "Payment and Securities Alignment Systems", June 4, 2012, Hotel Granite, Ohrid
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Address by Maja Kadievska-Vojnovic, Vice Governor of the NBRM, at the fifth conference on "Payment and Securities Alignment Systems", June 4, 2012, Hotel Granite, Ohrid Address by Maja Kadievska-Vojnovic, Vice Governor of the NBRM, at the fifth conference on "Payment and Securities Alignment Systems", June 4, 2012, Hotel Granite, Ohrid Dear colleagues from the Central Bank of the Netherlands and the Central Bank of Portugal Respected colleagues from the Central Banks of the Southeast European region and the Macedonian financial sector It is a great honor and a pleasure to address you today at the fifth conference on payment systems and securities alignment systems. First, I would like to welcome successfully established co-operation with the Central Bank of the Netherlands, and in the last two years, co-operation with the Central Bank of Portugal, without whose support this event would not have such a strong and significant character. Today's conference is held at a time when the Future of the Payment Services Market is being discussed and debated within the European Union. Namely, issues of digitisation of payment services, i.e. innovative payment models that gradually replace cash payments and traditional cashless payments and their regulation take up a greater place both in the efforts of payment service providers and regulators. This trend is consistent with changed consumer payment habits, i.e. continued growth in credit or debit card payments, the rise in ecommerce, the increased popularity of smartphones (smart) as new ways to make payments. Market integration in this area at European level is significant, and the European Commission launched the Green Paper on card, internet and mobile payments in January 2012. I would therefore like to welcome the move of our colleagues from the Central Banks of the Netherlands and Portugal, which at this conference opens the topic of the Green Paper on card, internet and mobile payments. The conference also presents topics related to major European Central Bank (ECB) projects relating to the integration of the European Union's internal market in both the field of payment systems and the domain of securities. Here I would mention the projects for: 1.TARGET2-Securities (T2S) -the future IT European Securities Alignment Platform. 2.Collateral Central Bank Management2 (CCBM2)-IT platform for Central Banks to manage acceptable provisions used in Eurosystem credit operations, and in accordance with the principle of decentralisation of access to loans. 3 Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) the European Union's integrated initiative to simplify and coordinate bank transfers, i.e. to establish a single European payment area. As is known, the proper functioning of payment systems and securities alignment systems contributes to the stability of the financial system, allows for efficient allocation of financial resources, reduces transaction costs in the economy, improves the liquidity of the financial market and facilitates monetary policy implementation. On the other hand, payment systems can be a channel for transmitting shocks from one part to another of the financial system, i.e. the economic system, and include significant exposure to participants, at financial risks. Such possible events have prompted central banks and regulators in the securities domain to build standards for work for systems in an international context. In this regard, I welcome the idea of presenting new standards for Financial Market Infrastructures (Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures) at this conference, which are a single set of standards that will replace previous standards for payment systems, securities alignment systems and Central Contracting Parties. These standards will also cause adequate adjustments by central banks in their practices with a more integrated approach to the implementation of standards, regulation and supervision of Financial Market Infrastructure. Finally, I would like to look briefly at the strategic objectives of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia in a period that follows. The strategic objectives in this domain stem from the RM's clear orientation to become a member of the European Union, and thus the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia part of the Eurosystem. In this regard, the following objectives are set out: 1.Increasing the degree of security, stability and efficiency of the MIPS system representing the REAL-time gross settlement (RTGS) system of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia 2. Adapting the existing framework for monitoring payment systems in accordance with changes in internationally accepted standards for the operation of payment systems, i.e. the adoption of new standards for Financial Market Infrastructure subject to observation at this conference. 3.Establishing new payment statistics in order to harmonise with the payment statistics of the European Central Bank. 4.Active participation in harmonising the legal framework for the payment systems of the Republic of Macedonia with the EU Directives in the field of payment systems, as well as considering the obligations of the National Bank that will arise from the integration process of the Republic of Macedonia into the European Union. Dear Sirs, at the end of my address I declare the fifth conference on payment systems and securities alignment systems open, and I wish President Mikhail van Doeveren a successful presidency of the conference. I hope the weather will be wonderful and you will enjoy the beauty of Ohrid and Lake Ohrid.

Title: Policy placement under different exchange rate regimes in central eastern and southeast European countries
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Anita Angelovska Bezhoska, Vice Governor, NBRM Ana Mitreska, Director of the Research Department, NBRM Policy Nexus under Different Exchange Rate Regimes in CESEE countries1 The main purpose of this note is to shed some light on the macroeconomic performance and mix of policies in CESEE countries2 in the period before and after the main wave of the crisis. Special focus is given to differences between the countries with fixed exchange rate regimes (peggers) and countries with floating regimes (floaters). The note aims at highlighting some commonalities and differences between peggers and floaters regarding the macroeconomic performances through visual data inspection and pinpointing some of the challenges that monetary and fiscal policies face with. Hence, the idea is not to draw any firm conclusions on the relations between the exchange rate regime, economic fundamentals and economic developments as averages could mask many issues and could not tell the story about many country-specific factors that might be of crucial importance in driving the economic developments. The optimal monetary-fiscal nexus has always been a thought-provoking issue. The traditional view on having proper monetary-fiscal coordination, to a large extent has boiled down to a consensus on allowing the monetary policy to focus on inflation and short-term business cycle stabilization and fiscal policy to focus on sustainable government debt and deficit. Expansionary fiscal policy may result in high real interest rates and suboptimal output. Yet, the optimal mix has to be analyzed in the context of the exchange rate regime. Pegged regimes, by their virtues, represent a constraint for the monetary policy especially under high capital mobility. However, the role of fiscal policy in output stabilization becomes also pronounced for flexible regimes under zero lower nominal bound. The recent crisis demonstrated that despite the aggressive monetary measures (including also non-standard measures), the fiscal policy played an important role in counteracting the impact of the financial and economic turmoil. Of course, the crisis emphasized again the critical importance of the initial fiscal space and the capacity for devising credible medium-term exit strategy. Both of them are perceived as critical for policy effectiveness, ensuring favorable expectations and credibility, potentially reducing the sovereign default risk, lowering interest rate, creating wealth effect and improving economic prospects (Agca, Igan, 2013). The occurrence of the crisis caught CESEE countries in a mode of solid growth rates amidst ample capital flows and rising vulnerabilities. Strong capital inflows (mainly in the form of external borrowing and FDIs) spurred credit growth that gave strong impulse to the 1 Mite Miteski and Katerina Suleva from the Research Department also contributed to the note. Special thanks to Dijana Janevska Stefanova, Neda Popovska Kamnar, Egzona Hani and Gani Ramadani for collecting and organizing the data used in the note. The note was prepared as a platform for discussion for the BIS Meeting of the Working Party on Monetary Policy in Central and Eastern Europe, Sofia, Bulgaria on 14-15 March 2013. 2 Includes: Macedonia, Serbia, Croatia, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Baltic States, Poland, Hungary, Czech Republic, Bulgaria and Romania. domestic demand. During 2004-2007, average growth rate for the whole group of countries amounted to 6.2%. This in particular refers to countries that were undergoing a kind of a convergence phase, where the buoyant capital flows led to a credit boom, which accompanied by strong confidence and high income expectations resulted in strong growth rates. For example, Baltic states in the run up to the crisis had growth rates close to 10%. However, in many cases the capital inflows were not primarily channeled in the tradable sector and resulted in high imports and consumption driven growth. Thus, strong growth rates were accompanied by high current account deficits and elevated external debt i.e., rising external vulnerabilities. Inflationary pressures in particular came to the fore during 2007 and 2008 when the global food and energy price shock was experienced. Given the conventional wisdom of exchange rate peg being an efficient tool for disciplining policies, the question is whether those countries entered the recent crisis with more superior initial conditions, both in terms of macroeconomic policies and in terms of their economic fundamentals. Simple visual inspection of the pre-crisis data averages of "peggers" and "floaters", points to some differences in performance between the two groups of countries. On average "peggers" had somewhat higher GDP growth rates (6.9% compared to 5.5% of floaters during 2004-2007), higher capital flows (13.5% compared to 9.2% of GDP of floaters), but also wider current account deficit (about 11.4% compared to 7.2% of floaters) and higher external debt (71.7% compared to 50.5% of floaters). An inference on the differences between the two groups of countries can be also drawn through the Macro Imbalance Procedure scoreboard of the European Commission (Annex 1). The scrutiny of these indicators reveals that countries with pegs appear to be better off in terms of the lower public deficit and debt. The state of their public finances appears more prudent, with lower headline and structural fiscal balances, and lower public indebtedness. Yet, dynamically observed, their structural fiscal deficits even before the crisis started to converge to the deficits of the countries with floating exchange rates. It indicated expansionary discretionary fiscal policy, potentially increasing the susceptibility to shocks. At the same time they enjoyed stronger growth rates, but on the back of higher current account imbalances, and higher private sector debt, domestically and externally financed. Yet, the deterioration in the external position and the credit growth were present and exceeding the thresholds in both groups of countries. Both groups of countries were also exposed to real appreciation, but in the run up to the crisis unit labor costs were increasing faster in countries with pegs compared with those in the floating regimes and were above the threshold, indicating larger erosion of competiveness. Large part of the gap between the floaters and peggers is created by the performance of the Baltic countries. This is expected, as the phenomena of EU prospect driven economic boom was perceived to be much more pronounced in this group, compared to other CEE countries. If the Baltic States are taken out of the pool, the performance of the peggers and floaters prior to the crisis is more or less similar, and the economic story as explained above still holds for the new group of peggers. Given that the peg in principle may act as a constraint for utilizing the monetary and fiscal policy in a strong countercyclical manner, the question is than, have these economies suffered much more compared to the "floaters", where the depreciation of the currency took part of the adjustment burden? The data analysis points to the fact that, on average, GDP drop in the acute phase of the crisis is larger in the "peggers" group and almost all countries in this group still haven't reached the pre crisis GDP level. The gaps between the two groups are much milder if the Baltic countries are excluded from the pool. Still, knowing the importance of the stable exchange rate in countries with pegs in determining confidence, and bearing in mind the severity of the externally-provoked crisis, most probably the peg underpinned the confidence and precluded panic, which could have yielded in a more inferior outcome that the actual one. Also, it is very important to note that the averages mask some important differences. For example Macedonia has a peg, but it went through a rather small GDP decline during the crisis (-0.9%) and its GDP is already above the pre-crisis level, explained by strong initial conditions in the run to the crisis and the ongoing structural changes occurring in the economy. Even within the Baltic countries, where strong internal adjustment under currency peg occurred, differences in post-crisis recovery are evident, with Latvia being furthest, and Litvania being closest to the pre-crisis level. Initial conditions, recovery of the main trading partners, the state of the banking system and institutions in general, i.e., countryspecifics are part of the solution of the "divergence puzzle". The occurrence of the crisis posed significant challenges for both groups of countries, but also brought to the fore the necessity for some divergence in monetary policy responses, and in some countries in terms of the time sequencing of the fiscal loosening. Fiscal policy in the crisis period The fall in economic activity and discretionary fiscal measures during 2008-2009 have had a significant impact on government balances and debt in both groups of countries. The average budget deficit in the countries with de facto fixed exchange rate increased from -1% in 2000-2007 to -3.8% in 2008-2009, with the largest deterioration being observed in Latvia, Lithuania and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The countries with flexible exchange rate recorded a smaller increase (though from higher level) in the average budget deficit, from 3.9% in 2000-2007 to -5% in 2008-2009, with the largest deterioration being observed in Romania, Serbia and Poland. In structural terms, the trend of deteriorating structural balances continued during 2008-2009 for both groups of countries reflecting the discretionary fiscal policy measures, though higher deterioration was observed for peggers. Rising fiscal deficits lead to a change in the public debt developments for both groups of countries, though more pronounced in the group of the peggers, where the initial debt level was also lower. Namely, the trend of declining public debt as a share of GDP was stopped when the crisis hit and it started rising. The debt accumulation was somewhat higher for the peggers though from significantly lower levels. Depreciation of the domestic currency posed additional pressures for some of the analyzed countries. As higher deficits implied higher external financing, the gross external debt to GDP ratios increased markedly in 2008 and 2009 in both groups of countries, though somewhat more in the case of floaters. The severe crisis implied a worsening of the financial conditions for CESEE countries, as illustrated by the development of CDS premiums for their government bonds. CDS premiums rapidly increased in 2008 and 2009, but the increase was more pronounced in the countries with fixed exchange rate which generally depend more on external financing. This implies that investors might have perceived peggers as riskier than floaters which resulted in rising financial costs and limited access to the capital market of peggers. However, we should not neglect the fact that within the countries with flexible exchange rate are well-performing countries like Czech Republic or Poland, whose strong underlying economic fundamentals prior to and during the crisis probably had a greater impact on investors' risk perceptions. Nonetheless, some of the countries that required financial support from the IMF, the EU or other financial institutions (Hungary, Latvia, Romania, Serbia, Bosnia) were floaters. Monetary policy in the crisis period It appears that stronger countercyclical responses by the central banks were seen in countries with floating exchange rates. When the crisis hit the region, most of the central banks were in a tightening stance of the monetary policy with upward interest rate cycle and prudential measures. However, when the growth path went downhill and the terms of trade considerably worsened, monetary authorities shifted their focus to a different type of challengestabilization of the economic activity. At the same time, they had to prevent excessive depreciation which might have fostered inflationary pressures again and could have adverse effects on financial stability. By the end of 2008 and the beginning of 2009, most of the countries with exchange rate flexibility, like Hungary, Poland and Czech Republic, started a process of monetary easing through a reduction of the key interest rate and use of prudential measures. They were quickly followed by the other floaters like Serbia, Romania and Albania. In some of these countries there were also significant depreciations of the currencies in this period. Bosnia and Herzegovina relaxed the reserve requirement in terms of rate and the basis for calculation and undertook other prudential measures to stimulate credit growth. The monetary policy in Macedonia, however, took an opposite stance at the end of 2008 and in 2009. Against the background of rapid loss of substantial part of the reserves (because of interventions), the Central Bank of Macedonia increased the interest rates, introduced liquidity requirements and raised reserve requirements on bank deposits. In Croatia the authorities also faced with the challenge of mitigating the impact of the crisis while protecting the kuna. In this light, the Central Bank intervened on the foreign exchange market, kept the key interest rate broadly stable and addressed the liquidity requirements by the banks through regulatory measures and repo auctions. If we look at the timeline of the monetary reactions in the CESEE countries, we see differences in the responses only during the first waves of the crisis, in 2008 and 2009. In this period, the spillover effects from the crisis were to a great extent conditioned on the structures of the different economies, their trade relations, their fundamentals and their accumulated buffers to defend them from shocks. But, as the economic slam deepened and broadened in almost every economy in the world, the hopes for possible recovery by the mid 2010 were quickly substituted with further negative outlooks and it became clear that the main focus of the macroeconomic policies in every country should inevitably be restoring the critical state of the real economy. In this respect, the monetary policies in all the CESEE countries acted in the same manner -towards stimulating the credit growth and thus recovering the real economic activity. Challenges ahead The recent crisis challenged the traditional view on the monetary-fiscal nexus, and to a certain extent blurred the boundaries between these two. "Over the past few years the combination of financial crisis and sustained fiscal imbalances has led to a substantial breakdown in the institutional framework and accepted barriers between monetary and fiscal policy... This pressure can threaten the central banks independence in conducting monetary policy and thereby undermine monetary policys effectiveness in achieving its mandate. (Plosser, 2012)". Although the blurred boundaries are more valid for countries outside the analyzed pool, still the statement of the necessary monetary-fiscal coordination and clear mandates for both policy makers should be considered as important, when discussing the future monetary policy challenges. The current experience with the European sovereign debt crisis, which raised issues about the sustainability of the monetary union, is a clear example of how important is the fiscal prudency in hard peg arrangements. What does MIP Scoreboard tell us about the current level of vulnerabilities in terms of fundamentals and policies? In general, vulnerabilities in terms of fundamentals for both groups of countries declined with peggers undergoing stronger adjustment. After the crisis started, the perception of the investors with respect to the countries with pegged exchange rates worsened much more compared to those with floating regimes. Capital flows reversed and declined more and credit growth slowed down more intensively, which led to a swifter and sharper current account adjustment and improvement in the international investment position. There have been also more pronounced adjustments in unit labor cost developments. So, current account deficit in countries with a peg is not anymore in the vulnerability zone, while floaters on average are still above the threshold. The credit growth went below the threshold in both groups of countries with a sharper adjustment in the group of peggers. However, fiscal stimuli lead to more vulnerable state of public finances. The estimated share of public debt to GDP at end-2012 is significantly higher compared to the pre-crisis period (15.1 p.p. higher for peggers and 16.4 for floaters). Given the initial lower levels of debt, the peggers currently appear to have lower level (estimated at end 2012 on average 34.6% of GDP compared to 56.6% of GDP of floaters). Some of the floater countries are very close to the Maastricht criterion, or even above it (Serbia, Hungary, Albania). A couple of aspects of the rising public debt need to be highlighted. Higher debt levels entail higher financing needs and higher refinancing risk. In many countries the current state of accommodative monetary policy and the risk-aversion of the investors provide room for the governments to borrow more extensively on domestic markets which may act as a potential disincentive for a more rapid fiscal consolidation. Despite the stronger accent placed on the development of domestic securities markets, the external borrowing is a key source of financing of the rising budget imbalances. This implies that susceptibility of countries to external financial shocks has increased. If no credible fiscal consolidation is present, a vicious circle might be opened. Foreign investors might "close the gates" or rise the risk premium to finance deficits or roll-over maturing debt (which was the case in the acute phase of the crisis). For the countries with a pegged exchange rate, the closure of the envisaged external borrowing would also entail risk of not accumulating reserves as much as planned, thus creating pressure for the monetary policy for defending the peg. This will consequently lead to higher interest rates and hamper the process of consolidation of public finances. The risk is even more pronounced in countries with less developed financial markets and where the short-term government debt is dominant. Short-term financing means fast translation of rising costs and increased rollover risk. Hence, probably for all the countries, bringing the public finances on a more sustainable path is the most important challenge, and for the peggers even more so. Medium-term fiscal consolidation seems needed to avoid fiscal dominance and provide a greater room for monetary policy. Large deficits add up to the current level of debt, which even though appears to be relatively moderate compared to other European economies, can be seen as a source of concern given that the sustainability threshold of their public debt is considered to be lower than for the more advanced countries. It is even more pronounced in countries with a pegged currency, as having healthy public finances is an important cornerstone of the monetary and exchange rate policy. A credible fiscal path increases also the probability of lowering the cost of fiscal financing, reducing the long term risk premium and paving the way towards longer-term government financing. In this light, further development of domestic government securities market can help diversify the sources of financing the budget deficit and decrease the rollover risk through extending the maturities. Consolidation plans are already included in the comprehensive medium-term budget frameworks of the governments of all CESEE countries. The reduction of the fiscal deficit should result in lower debt ratios of both peggers and floaters. Yet, this has to be done in a way that does not jeopardize the still anemic recovery of the real sector. The pace of consolidation will depend a lot on the structure of the budget expenditures, i.e., the discretionary spending room. In some cases the consolidation may require deeper reforms of the public spending and of the public finance management system in general. A challenging task for the monetary policy in the forthcoming macroeconomic constellation will also be combining the traditional monetary policy objective and the financial stability objective. The crisis made clear that "managing inflation is not an end in itself but a means to an end" (Stiglitz, 2011). Namely, the crisis was preceded by so called period of "Great moderation" pinpointing that achievement of price stability is not a guarantee for stable economy and that financial frictions can have a devastating effect on the business cycle. Thus, greater focus on financial stability and better coordination of monetary and macro prudential policy seem inevitable. The new regulatory reforms impose requirements that urge big banks to reshape their balance sheets and thus reduce their risky portfolio, while the sources for further increase in capital are quite limited. While the banks in the CESEE countries were able to remain well capitalized even during and after the crisis, the current balance sheet adjustments of the big European banks, highly present in this region, put significant constrains on the proactive approach in supporting the economic recovery. Even more, the general risk perceptions do not seem to change significantly in the next period, given the rising NPL ratios and decreasing quality of credit demand. In such an environment, the question is whether the policy interest rate, as main traditional instrument may further lose its effectiveness in the period ahead. The above analysis of the macroeconomic developments and policy mix in the CESEE countries in the period before the occurrence of the crisis, in the acute phase of the crisis and after it, points to some commonalities and differences between the two groups of countries. Of course, many country specific factors, including pre-crisis fundamentals, openness of the economy, structure of the main trading partners, pace of the structural reforms that increase the competitiveness of the economy, have to be taken into account to get a better and more comprehensive understanding of the different macroeconomic performance between them. In any case, it seems clear that sound policies and fundamentals in the run up to the crisis prevented excessive overheating of the economies and provided buffers for mitigating the shocks, regardless of the chosen exchange rate regime.
