Title: Discussion platform on a panel of the European Symposium "National Asset Liability Management", organized by Central Banking Publications, London
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Discussion platform of Maja KadievskaVojnovic, Vice Governor of the NBRM, on a panel of the European Symposium "National Asset Liability Management", organized by Central BankingPublications, London, 12-13 March 2015 Discussion platform of Maja Kadievska-Vojnovic, Vice Governor of the NBRM, on a panel of the European Symposium "National Asset Liability Management", organized by Central Banking Publications, London, 12-13 March 2015 1. What should the allocation of exchange reserves look like in the current environment? The global economy is facing a new challenge. The world's most influential central banks implement divergent monetary policies, according to the performance of their economies. Thus, the Federal Reserve in the United States and the Bank of England, led by a good recovery in economies in their countries, are ahead of a move to raise basic interest rates that will draw on an increase in yields and other financial instruments. On the other hand, the European Central Bank (ECB) has begun buying back government bonds and bonds issued by the public sector, in addition to the ongoing purchase of collateralised and securities secured by assets, while the Bank of Japan is already implementing quantum relief. Thus, these central banks apply non-standard measures to stimulate domestic economies when assessing unfavourable economic achievements and low inflation, and when they reach a threshold of basic interest rates of almost zero, they apply non-standard measures to stimulate domestic economies. The ECB's move to inject liquidity into euro zone economies will mean keeping it low, and in some countries negative yields of government securities, which will certainly have an effect on dimensioning strategies in the management of foreign exchange reserves, especially for countries where the euro is the dominant currency in the total portfolio. However, the current and future environment is only a continuity of low yield maintenance, which has been a feature of international financial markets for almost half a decade (since the 2009 rainfall). When it comes to what the allocation of foreign exchange reserves should look like in such an environment, my view is that the prudential approach should be followed and key elements (security, liquidity, profitability) based on the foreign exchange reserve management strategy should be respected. And they, in my opinion, have not changed in the past. Then, what's changed? The environment has changed. Before the crisis, the management of foreign exchange reserves reflected three decades of investments by central banks in fixed-yield instruments, mostly in government bonds. The premium for maturity and the difference in yields between different fixed-yield and different credit risk institutions were effective sources of excess yield. Achieving liquidity, security and profitability from the investments of the exchange reserves at the time was not an impossible mission. And then and now, a fundamental decision of each central bank, as an institution that manages the state's exchange reserves, is how to make optimal allocation of funds. The traditional strategy in the management of exchange reserves is based on several key issues: What is the role of exchange reserves? and What are the circumstances under which reserves are needed?. The traditional role of exchange reserves can be considered from several aspects. Exchange rate interventions by central banks serve as a means of mitigating exchange rate fluctuations, regardless of what exchange rate regime it is (exchange rate targeting, fluctuation smear, removal of instability or prevention of market failure, etc.). Then, holding foreign exchange reserves integrates an aspect of caution, i.e. they are a neutralizing zone for the current and financial account of the balance of payments in the event of external economic shocks and through them the confidence of the general public is built, i.e. reducing the likelihood of economic shock (for example, "sudden stopping of capital flows"). The other aspects of holding foreign exchange cuts are related to enabling regular servicing of the state's external debt, by improving the market perception of the creditworthiness of the overall economy and thus achieving a better sovereign rating and their role as guardian of the national wealth. It should be borne in mind that central banks are investors of a particular type, i.e. they face achieving specific objectives through the management of foreign exchange reserves. Preventing unforeseen economic events and the need to disposing of sufficient funds for short-term intervention with exchange reserves imposes the allocation of funds, taking into account the liquidity aspect of the markets and instruments in which the exchange reserves are placed. So uncertainty when foreign exchange reserves are needed, i.e. the need to stabilize potential negative effects of exogenous economic shocks, makes liquidity a significant principle in the management of foreign exchange reserves. In addition, the central bank's foreign exchange reserves are ultimately state property, so the state always appreciates a high level of their security. As a result, tolerance for reducing their value, and even temporarily, is extremely low. Thus, saving capital by placing it in low-risk instruments is also a key driver of foreign exchange reserve management policy. This makes central banks, in principle, averse to risk, i.e. correct them in the face of a significant institutional obstacle -reputational risk. Finally, minimising the cost of holding reserves or covering the cost of sterilisation focuses on the return on investment of foreign exchange reserves, which in the current situation becomes as important as the principle of liquidity and security. Given the above, the strategic asset allocation (SAA) should be set in a way that will ensure the achievement of key objectives in the management of exchange reserves, and that is: preserving capital, or ensuring the principle of security, fulfilling the principle of liquidity and ultimately achieving a return on the management of exchange reserves. So central banks are corrected to achieve multiple goals: security-liquidity-return. However, the priority of meeting these objectives is strongly correlated with certain specific factors, characteristic of each country: the exchange rate regime, the size of foreign exchange reserves, the size and depth of the domestic capital market and its sensitivity to volatility capital flows, the currency structure of the state's obligations to abroad, and the currency structure of external trade. After the crisis, achieving these goals became a major challenge for central bankers. In conditions of low yields of government bonds, in the case of impaired liquidity and high volatility of certain market segments, when restructuring regulation and imposing higher regulatory requirements for maintaining financial stability for market participants, central banks in addition to the new environment should also be guided by restrictions set by specific factors for the country. The reaction of many central banks to the new environment was, and is aimed at diversifying foreign exchange reserve investments in new types of financial instruments, beyond traditional investments in government bonds. Many central banks have expanded the list of allowed financial instruments, investing in securities issued by international institutions, local governments and agencies (SSA-Supranationals, Sub sovereigns and agencies), then in government bonds issued by Asian countries and other economies in the upswing (Asian bonds-excl. Japan and Other EMG's debt), in state securities protected from inflation, issued by the U.S. Treasury Department (TIPS-Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities), while at the same time shortening the possibilities for investing in securities issued by U.S. state agencies (US agencies), in securities provided by mortgage or other assets (MBS/ABS), in collateralized bonds, in corporate bonds (including bank bonds). At the same time, central banks have switched to the use of derivatives, securities lending and structured products. Investment in shares, although reduced in volume after the crisis, in current low yieldconditions and growth of stock indices is becoming an increasingly pronounced practice at several central banks. At the same time, central banks began investing in newly created instruments (ETF's -Exchange traded funds), and expanded the list of some of the previously excluded instruments. In addition to diversification by instrument, the process present since the crisis is currency diversification, which transcends sdr angry and even G10 currencies, i.e. increasing investment in currencies of economies in the upswing. The level and volume of further diversification is nevertheless limited by the excess reserves by a particular central bank. In this sense, central banks should strategically determine what the optimal level of foreign exchange reserves is, i.e. how many reserves are actually needed to deal with unforeseen shocks and at what level of liquidity. When they do so, central banks with a fixed exchange rate regime, such as in the Republic of Macedonia, bear in mind that reserves should be available at any time, and sometimes in significant amount, to intervene in the foreign exchange market. In this sense, under a fixed regime, reserve investment is realized in financial instruments characterized by high liquid markets. 2. Are there institutional and political obstacles to diversification outside traditional foreign exchange assets and, if so, how can they be overcome? In terms of institutional obstacles, diversification in new instruments and currencies has imposed a need for central banks to expand their skills and capabilities, with a particular focus on improving the process of strategic distribution, as well as adopting specific knowledge of different types of instruments and investment techniques, to improve the risk management system, and finally, but not least, to improve and increase the volume of research on economies and sectors that have not been the focus of strategies until then. From this point of view, in order to apply diversification, central banks are becoming increasingly similar to other institutional investors and more active in how they manage them and how they monitor their investments. This is the case with the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia (NBRM). In low-yield conditions, the review of the strategic allocation of foreign exchange reserves has gained significant dynamics. Thus, the NBRM joined the trend of other central banks, which, contrary to the application of static SAA, have switched to dynamic strategic allocation of funds (dynamic SAA). As part of this process, the NBRM, like other modern central banks, diversified currency placements other than traditional ones in the foreign exchange reserve portfolio, and diversification by instrument other than state securities. The NBRM applied currency diversification as early as 2012, mainly in so-called currency commodities, but also in currencies of countries that have better future economic prospects. In addition, diversification of instruments is carried out, but still within the basic asset class, i.e. within fixed-yield instruments. This requires expanding knowledge of economies and publishers of newly included currencies and instruments in our portfolio. The volume of measurement and monitoring of risks has increased, and the analysis of market movements has expanded. Moreover, in order to strengthen the institutional capacity of the NBRM in the management of foreign exchange reserves, in 2014 it joined the World Bank Advisory Programme (RAMP-Reserve Advisory Management Program). As for political obstacles to diversification into instruments different (such as shares) from fixed-yield instruments (e.g. government bonds) in some cases, as in the Republic of Macedonia, legal restrictions should be taken into account. Thus, in accordance with the Law on the National Bank, this type of instrument does not constitute an opportunity to invest the exchange reserves. However, the increasing number of central banks investing in shares due to significantly higher yields than those of fixed-yield instruments has prompted us to examine the experience of other central banks in this area. The analysis showed that central banks investing in shares had the opportunity or provided the opportunity to direct some of the investments in this asset by changing the legal regulation. This provided political and broader consensus. In general, these are central banks that have assessed that they have excess reserves above the required optimal level, but there are also those with a similar exchange rate regime and a level of foreign exchange reserves, as in our case. However, in order to treat this as an opportunity in our investment policy, we must again return to the main objectives available with the exchange reserves. This step will depend on the size of the reserves, the liquidity restrictions set by the fixed exchange rate regime, and the willingness of the general public to take such a step. 3. What are the pressures on central banks' balance sheets and capital from the traditional foreign exchange reserve strategy in the context of today's low-yield environment and what are the consequences for central banks? Managing the central bank's balance sheet in low yields in the investment of foreign exchange reserves, and in a strategy that needs to meet multiple targets and with increased sterilisation needs, is a significant challenge for many central banks. According to a certain record, in the last decade, 14 of the 19 central banks in economies in high-level foreign exchange economies faced a reduction in capital, which in some cases imposed the need to recapitalise central banks by the states. In just one decade, foreign exchange reserves worldwide have doubled, growth that is mainly led by the growth of foreign exchange reserves of rising economies. In search of yield, due to the low yields of financial institutions in highly developed economies, invaders directed capital into economies in the upswing, conditioning the growth of foreign exchange reserves in them. Central bank balance sheet growth, due to the growth of foreign exchange reserves (which are on the asset side), growth conditions and monetary liabilities of central banks, i.e. the supply of money in the economy and thus the state of instruments through sterilisation (withdrawal of issued liquidity), to protect against inflation. In addition, foreign exchange reserves have increased in the last decade due to the growth in the price of gold, for those economies that have a significant amount of foreign exchange reserves in gold and value it marketly. This contributed to an increase in revaluation reserves for gold. Activities aimed at carrying out the main objective of central banks, maintaining price stability, in the face of foreign exchange reserve growth, is inevitably linked to sterilisation costs (interest and compensation costs of used monetary instruments), which reduce the financial result of central banks, and can often generate losses. The performance of the central bank's tasks, and in a function of achieving its objectives, such as the preservation and management of foreign exchange reserves, are not always sufficient to compensate for the bank's total sterilisation costs, and especially not, in conditions of low yields in financial markets. In this context, the strength of the effect of low market yields, in the period of the crisis on the central bank's balance sheet, depends on the balance sheet of funds and liabilities in foreign and domestic currency. The longer the foreign exchange position, the stronger the effect of the negative interest rate range, at low yields of much of the asset and at the same time higher liability costs, expressed through the interest rates of monetary policy instruments. At the same time, market volatility, which meant increased market risks, due to a change in exchange rates and prices of securities and gold, conditions of high volatility in the market value (revaluation) of foreign exchange reserves. Here, the size of central banks' revaluation reserves for absorption of these shocks is certainly significant. In the Republic of Macedonia, foreign exchange reserves in a decade have increased more than doubled, from 1.1 billion euros in 2005 to 2.4 billion euros in 2014. Such foreign exchange reserve growth is the result of inflows based on foreign direct investment, while portfolio inflows, which are highly volatility flows, have had negligible significance, contrary to their importance in most economies in an upward trend that has shaken foreign exchange rates and monetary policy management. In addition, the country's foreign currency debt had a positive effect on the growth in the level of foreign exchange reserves in the Republic of Macedonia, but the state did not create sterilisation pressures on a net basis. Macedonia's economy, as a small and open economy, is significantly exposed to the euro because of its close trade ties with euro zone countries and other European economies with which trade is carried out in the euro, as well as due to the most significant participation of the euro and in the structure of the country's external debt. In such circumstances, and in implementing a monetary strategy of targeting a euro-bound exchange rate, the currency structure of foreign exchange reserves is dominated by the euro. Due to a certain percentage of the trade that is also done in the United States dollars, the second currency in the foreign exchange reserve portfolio is the US dollar. In terms of gold, the NBRM has a strategic determination to maintain it at a stable level, i.e. a possible increase in the amount of domestic sources. Thus, price movements in gold as well as the exchange rate movement between the dollar and the euro have an impact on the one hand on foreign exchange reserves, and on the other hand on the NBRM's balance sheet of success, which has an effect further through the distribution or coverage of the result affecting the NBRM's revaluation reserves for price and exchange rate changes. However, new market conditions characterised by low yields and even ongoing negative yields of instruments denominated in euros, especially to the government bonds of euro zone core countries where most of the foreign exchange reserve investments are allocated, conditions for the NBRM to redirect some of the funds to other currencies, instruments and issuers. The redirection of some foreign exchange reserves into other currencies, outside traditional currencies, was made in limited volume, and selected currencies have higher yields and a more stable outlook for the economies where it is invested. This contributed to an increase in current yields, while maintaining the euro's dominance of the total currency structure. The principle of security is achieved by investing in high-quality assets, government securities, but the maturity of investments has been extended in the longer term to achieve a positive yield. At the same time, the list of fixed-yield instruments was expanded with instruments issued by international institutions, local governments and agencies (SSA-Supranational, Sovereigns and Agencies), and bonds collateralised by state-guaranteed bonds were introduced and deposits were allowed in commercial banks. Additionally, strategic allocation also included some of the investments from the core of the euro zone to the peripheral countries of the euro zone, those with good economic indicators and the least investment rating. Here, I would like to point out that all these steps are in limited volume, so most of the investments of foreign exchange reserves are still kept in highly liquid government bonds or in bonds with an explicit state guarantee. At the same time, in order to protect against negative price changes in securities on the central bank's balance sheet, part of the portfolio in euros was classified as a portfolio of securities kept until delivery (Hold to maturity), an accounting principle in accordance with international reporting standards. In the run-up to the expected gradual normalization of the Federal Reserve's monetary policy in the United States and in the case of continued dollar preponderance, some of the exchange reserves have been redirected to a dollar portfolio, and according to tactical allocation, investments have a shorter maturity. Additionally, part of the dollar investment portfolio is classified as a portfolio of securities kept until delivery. At the same time, the NBRM has gone from passive to moderately active foreign reserve management, i.e. starting by taking tactical positions that allow yield transactions to be made under favourable market conditions and favourable trends. Any changes in the strategic and tactical allocation of foreign exchange reserves, by adding new debt instruments and new currencies to a certain extent, also meant increased exposure to credit and market risk to the foreign exchange reserve portfolio. However, diversification by instruments, currencies and issuers assessed the level of risk increase, which was also reflected appropriately in dimensioning the amount of funds subject to diversification. Thus, diversification allowed higher yields (other than zero) from the exchange reserve rankings, while preserving the basic principles in the management of exchange reserves. In this sense, the NBRM has undertaken numerous activities on the balance sheet asset side, within the management of foreign exchange reserves, in order to ensure the best balance between liquidity and investment security, and a positive return. On the balance sheet liability side, in the monetary bond section, in low inflation conditions and absence of exchange rate pressures, and in slow credit growth, the basic interest rate was brought to a historically lowest level. The monetary policy framework has been changed, with the addition of new instruments, allowing dispersion of the burden of sterilisation between the main instrument, treasury records, and new instruments, available deposits, intended for short-term liquidity management by domestic banks. In addition, the compensation paid to the obligatory reserve was abolished, a trend present in several central banks. To sum up, the environment of low/negative yields forced central bankers, such as the NBRM, to take a more active approach in the management of foreign exchange reserves, but within the established objectives. The NBRM managed to stitch up the bank's capital in such extraordinary circumstances. In this way, the most important principles  the institutional and financial independence of the central bank have also been achieved.

Title: Speech at the Eighth International Conference on Payment Systems and Securities Alignment Systems in Ohrid
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Speech by Maja Kadievska-Voynovic Vice Governor of the NBRM, at the Eighth International Conference on Payment Systems and Securities Alignment Systems in Ohrid, 10-13 May 2015 Speech by Maja Kadievska-Voynovic Vice Governor of the NBRM, at the Eighth International Conference on Payment Systems and Securities Alignment Systems in Ohrid, 10-13 May 2015 Respected, I am honored to welcome you to the Eighth Conference on Payment Systems and Securities Alignment Systems. This year, the conference is held organised by the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, in co-operation with the central banks of the Netherlands and Portugal, whose support and active participation have contributed to achieving and maintaining high quality at the Conference. Therefore, allow me on this occasion to welcome the traditional co-operation of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia with the Central Bank of the Netherlands and the Central Bank of Portugal. At the same time, I would like to express our great satisfaction with the presence of representatives from central banks from the countries of Central, Eastern and Southeast Europe, as well as the participation of the black sea and North African countries. Interest in attending this conference has been growing over the past few years, once again confirming the conference's significant contribution to the knowledge-enhancing and sharing of the experience of central banks representatives on a regional and international scale. And, of course, the Conference will not be the only treasure of knowledge and experience, without the presence of representatives from the domestic financial system, who, with their continued active participation, contribute to the Conference receiving a rounded, thematic whole. Dear colleagues from the financial sector from the country and abroad, allow me to give a brief look, summed up in ten points to be covered by the agenda in the coming days. First, the conference begins with a presentation of the 2015 UNCTAD Report, titled "Unlocking the potential of e-commerce for developing countries". As the theology progresses, this topic is becoming increasingly important for policymakers, given that the latest empirical research assesses the positive effects of the development of electronic trade on the productivity of companies. In this context, the report looks at the opportunities and challenges faced primarily by companies in developing countries that want to engage in electronic trade. Prepared from several thematic wholes, the report begins with a clear overview of the latest trends in the development of electronic trade globally with a wide range of official statistics, continues with the possibilities and barriers to the development of electronic trade in rural and low-income countries, and then with the percentage of countries' readiness to engage in electronic trade based on the constructed Electronic Trade Index. What gives it particular importance are recommendations for national strategies and policies to promote electronic trade in developing countries aimed at creating an environment to use the benefits of electronic trade, while reducing risks and costs. Opportunities for the development of electronic trade are a challenge and an attractive field of interest for both the Republic of Macedonia, as a small country in transition, and for this reason, a panel discussion is envisaged during today, encouraging the active participation of the Macedonian financial sector, regulators, as well as domestic and international experts in the field of electronic trade. Secondly, significant attention will be paid to the european union's integration payment processes and the ongoing development of the European Single Payment Area Project (SEPA). After 15 years of preparations, SEPA was successfully implemented in 2014 in terms of credit transfers and direct debts within the euro zone, allowing more than 2 billion transactions per month to be implemented in a standardised form. Introducing a single bank account for the execution of credit transfers and direct duties that can be used for cashless transfer of funds independent of the location of the customer or company making payments within the EU, "instant payments", as well as the development of payments in euros between customers via mobile phone, are only one part of the essential aspects that will be elaborated during the SEPA Payments Conference. Third, particular attention at the Conference will also be paid to the advances in the field of payment cards and payment innovation. From the point of view of integration processes within SEPA, the tendency is payment cards, despite the complexity of the overall infrastructure, to reach the same level of compliance and integration, as is the case with credit transfers and direct debts, hence the challenge of creating conditions for their greater use in the future, where risks and fraud will be minimally reduced. In order to contribute to tackling payment fraud, as well as strengthening customer confidence in the use of internet payments, The European Forum for Low Payment Security (SecuRe Pay) defines 14 harmonised European recommendations for the security of payments over the Internet, which contain minimum requirements for the performance of payment services over the Internet, which have been applicable since 1 February 2015. Fourth, this conference, in addition to payment news, traditionally covers trends in securities alignment systems. In this context, the discussions will focus on the realisation of the TARGET2 Securities (T2S) project, which is expected to provide cross-border alignment integration of real-time securities transactions on the principle of "delivery versus payment" by integrating transaction accounts and securities accounts on a single platform. Fifth, in the analysis of ongoing developments in security and liquidity management, the Conference will focus on monetary policy and quantitative easing within the euro zone. The latest measures from the ECB's Quantitative Facilitation Programme are aimed at reviving the euro zone economy, which are expected to contribute to reducing borrowing and easing credit conditions. In that direction, The ECB is in the process of purchasing 60 billion euros worth of securities from the private and public sectors every month, by September 2016 at the latest, allowing banks to use the additional liquidity of the Quantitative Easing Programme to approve loans and revive economic activity. Sixth, from the point of view of institutional changes, the Small Payments Committee in euros will be covered as the successor to the SEPA Council. The migration of credit transfers and direct debts in accordance with SEPA's requirements did not resolve all payment-related issues that will be imposed on the Committee's agenda. Currently, the Committee is focused on finding solutions to prevent fragmentation in the field of instant payments by taking advantage of integration and compliance achieved with the SEPA Project. Seventh, globally, financial inclusion has increasing importance and is of growing interest in economic policymakers, regulators and other parties concerned. Financial inclusion is already high in the Strategic Vision of the NBRM. In this context, the conference will discuss the benefits and effects of the financial inclusion of individuals and small and medium-sized enterprises on economic development. Favourable conditions for opening transaction accounts, expanding banking networks, especially in underdeveloped areas, new financial products and adequate financial education, are only part of the aspects that cover the problem. Eighth, financing trade through the use of instruments such as credentials and guarantees  supports almost a third of global trade flows and is one of the safest forms of funding that directly affects the promotion and support of the development of global trade. Analyses show that banks play a very significant role in supporting international trade by guaranteeing international payments, and this has an impact on reducing the risk in these transactions. Trade financing, as a process that evolves in line with market expectations and technological progress, will be particularly elaborate within this conference. Ninth, the European Commission has permanently taken initiatives in payment regulation at European level, in order to adopt proposals to revise and modernise existing directives and introduce new regulations on the European market. In this context, a discussion will be developed during the Conference on the proposal for a revision of the Payment Services Directive 2007/64 (PSD2), as well as the European Commission's proposal for interbank provisions for transactions made by payment cards In this context, of particular importance to representatives from the financial sector in the Republic of Macedonia will also be the presentation of the project leader "Further alignment with EU legislation in the field of free movement of capital and financial services -securities market and investment services". The project, which began in February 2015, whose benefits are of utmost importance for the development of the new legal framework in the field of payment systems, is funded by ipa 2010, and in its implementation, which will last a total of 18 months, the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia is actively participating. Tenth, the unhindered conduct of payment transactions requires the need to protect and improve the physical availability and accessibility of payment services to consumers and companies. A new era of digital payments, such as contactless payments and mobile phone payments, has led to a reduction in payments through bank branches and ATMs in favor of payments via the Internet and mobile phones. Global trends in the continued development and application of new payment technologies have ordered continuous co-operation between all parties concerned involved in national payment system forums to reduce the use of traditional payment instruments. Dear Sirs, at the end of my address, I declare the Eighth Conference on Payment Systems and Securities Alignment Systems open, and I wish President Michael van Douven and his colleagues a successful course at the Conference. Finally, I wish you a pleasant stay and bring with you fond memories of the beauty of Macedonia. I hope you will have the opportunity to visit the city of Ohrid in the afternoon and evening, which is one of the greatest testimonies of the existence of Macedonian spiritual culture and the history of these areas.

Title: First Regional Forum of Eastern Europe and Central Asia for Financial Inclusion
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Address by Governor Dimitar Bogov at the First Regional Forum of Eastern Europe and Central Asia for Financial Inclusion, 26-28 October 2015, Skopje Address by Governor Dimitar Bogov at the First Regional Forum of Eastern Europe and Central Asia for Financial Inclusion, 26-28 October 2015, Skopje Dear ladies and gentlemen, I am honored to welcome everyone here in Skopje, Macedonia. The National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia and the Alliance for Financial Inclusion, with the support of the Federal Ministry of Economic Co-operation and Development of Germany and the Secretariat for Economic Affairs of Switzerland, are organising the First Regional Forum of Eastern Europe and Central Asia (ECA) on financial inclusion policy. The aim of the meeting is to bring together regional leading policymakers and experts dealing with financial inclusion policy issues. Financial inclusion means improving the volume, quality and availability of financial services and products of subjects to whom they are unavailable, to those who are poorly available, or who are financially excluded. The definition of financial inclusion covers key principles that are considered particularly important for the delivery of a wide range of quality financial services and products. The first key principle is access, which means the availability of appropriate financial products, services and delivery channels, in order to provide universal access. Important steps have already been taken in this area and in previous years. Access should be complemented by the quality of financial services, which refers to how they are provided. Quality refers to the type of products and their delivery, which in turn improves the value of services. Access is of no use if customers do not use the product or service, so real financial inclusion should be accompanied by principle use. There are also other key principles, such as accessibility, under which financial services should meet customers' needs and ensure their protection and respect. We cannot exclude financial education from principles because it is a powerful driver of strengthening consumers' skills. It strengthens them with tools and knowledge of how to manage and work with their personal financial decisions and budget. Not only will consumers gain knowledge through financial education, but the most important thing is that they will receive fair treatment. This three-day forum will focus on financial literacy and consumer protection of financial services, financing of small and medium-sized enterprises, digital financial services and data, through the AFI platform for learning among members of the Alliance in order to improve financial inclusion policies in the ECA region. I think this region has many similarities in the area of financial inclusion in terms of the challenges of financial inclusion and regulatory barriers. There is a common view that the level and quality of financial inclusion in the economies of the region have a significant impact on the prospects for sustainable growth. Financial inclusion will also provide an opportunity for further progress for greater and more sustainable financial stability. A key point for ensuring financial stability is the financial capacity of consumers themselves, in the sense that they can take a significant part in the financial system. I hope that through enhanced co-operation and joint efforts between AFI member states in and outside the region, we will be able to progress in many areas of financial inclusion and build a strong and dedicated network. In 2011, the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia launched its financial education project, which constantly develops and covers many different activities including organising workshops for journalists, printing educational brochures, developing curricula and starting many other projects. The National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia has strengthened co-operation with regulators such as the Finance Ministry, the Insurance Supervisory Agency, the Capital-Funded Pension Insurance Supervisory Agency and the Securities Commission. Since 2014, efforts have been made to establish institutional arrangements in order for the authorities to jointly commit to clearly defined and measurable objectives in the field of financial education and financial inclusion. The result of these efforts is the Co-ordination Body of Regulatory Institutions for Financial Education in Macedonia. The main goal of this Coordination Body is to define national strategies for financial education and inclusion. I hope that this event will be an opportunity to gain knowledge, expertise and best practices in financial inclusion throughout the ECA region and to provide useful and fruitful meetings, interesting to all of you. Thank you!

Title: Meeting of the BIS Working Group on Monetary Policy in Central and Eastern Europe
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: PLATFORM FOR DISCUSSION EVENT: BIS Meeting of the Working Party on Monetary Policy Niko_Memo_Logo_Temno in Central and Eastern Europe DATE: February 11-12, 2016 NATIONAL BANK OF THE REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA LOCATION: Skopje, Macedonia info@nbrm.mk  HURDLES TO THE GROWTH AGENDA OF THE CESEE ECONOMIES Anita Angelovska Bezoska, Vice Governor Ana Mitreska, Director of MPRD1 1 Monetary Policy and Research Department. Hurdles to the Growth Agenda of the CESEE Economies The note will strive to tackle the growth issue in the CESEE region2, by scrutinizing the current growth performances, the envisaged growth outcomes in the period to come, and the extent to which certain growth drivers can act as boosters or hurdles to the growth agenda. The impetus for such a choice in our economic scrutiny is straightforward. Eight years after the onset of the global crisis, it does not seem that the question of how and to what extent economic growth should be reinvigorated lost any of its contemporaneity. It is on the top of the policy agenda in many countries. In the euro area in particular, as within the monetary union, growth momentum is difficult to be ignited. Of course, the CESEE region is not an exception in this respect. Most of the countries in the region are highly open economies with strong trade and financial linkages with the advanced European countries. Hence, external headwinds related to the euro area recovery and financial markets developments, as well as some country specific fundamentals might act as hurdles for the medium run growth prospects of the region as a whole. The process of gradual post-crisis economic recovery in the region continued in 2015 bringing the region slightly above its pre-crisis peak, on average. In most of the countries in the CESEE region, growth, although still modest, slightly accelerated with average growth rate projected to reach 2.4%. For the first time after the crisis, in 2015, all countries in the group were expected to register positive growth rates, with the highest growth rate being reported in the Czech Republic (3,9%) and the lowest in Croatia (0,8%). The average GDP level of the region is estimated to outpace the precrisis level of about 4%, with Macedonia, Albania and Poland having the strongest outperformance of around 19%. This group seems to be marked by country-specific growth boost factors  structural reforms, government stimulus, or sound fundamentals. The rest of the countries either are only slightly above, or are still below their peak levels. This prevalence of slowly growing economies in the region in the past several years is a first litmus to show that the factors in play, which should underpin growth, do not seem to proliferate recovery vividly enough. The growth structure did not change significantly in 2015, i.e. the trend of rising share of export and import, and declining share of investments and consumption, in GDP continued. The share of exports and imports in GDP continued to grow at a similar pace and thus the share of net exports remained broadly unchanged, but compared to the pre-crisis period, still there is a visible improvement explained by the faster growth of exports compared to imports. Apparently, despite the crisis, the export sector of the countries in the region managed to grow further, and it is particularly Includes Macedonia, Albania, Croatia, Bulgaria, Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Romania, Slovenia, Czech Republic, Poland, Estonia, Hungary, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia. pronounced in the case of the Baltics. The internal devaluation process in some of the countries and the structural reforms in the external sector in others, explain to a certain extent the improved export position. On the other hand, the share of investments continued to decline, falling from 30% (average for the region) in the pre-crisis period to about 23%, meaning a full reversal of the pre-crisis growth. The level of investment is much lower in all of the countries, with Poland and Macedonia being the only exception (in Macedonia the current level is by 40% above 2008, a result of foreign and public investments). As for the private consumption, its share continued to slightly decline and currently its level in most of the countries is somewhat lower compared to the pre-crisis period. The government consumption remained stable at the level of 18% of GDP. Chart 1: Expenditure components of GDP Eurostat; Authors calculations. The prolonged lackluster growth moves the region away from its previous trajectory in the real convergence process pointing to a new normal at a lower equilibrium. At the current juncture, it seems that on a medium-run, the pre-crisis mode of fast growth amidst liquidity glut and higher risk tolerance cannot be expected. The IMF baseline scenario for the next six years points to a further gradual acceleration of the growth to 3.2% in 2020, pointing to a significantly lower dynamics than in the pre-crisis period. In many of the countries, where the crisis revealed large deficiencies in their economic fundamentals, the distance to the pre-crisis growth dynamics is quite large. If we run a counterfactual analysis, applying the average pre-crisis growth rate to the GDP level in 2007 -before the crisis started, the simulated outcome is much higher compared to the current state. The simulated level is by 40% higher compared to the actual one (Chart 2, the second panel), but also significantly higher than the baseline forecast for 2020. Hence, this simple simulation clearly points to a new environment in which growth factors cannot return to the pre-crisis mode. Although, to some extent, this reflects an adjustment from an unsustainable boom-type of pattern, in the Baltic States in particular, there is still a room to pinpoint pale growth drivers in the period to come. Chart 2: Real GDP level, actual, forecast and counterfactual Source: International Monetary Fund, WEO Database, October 2015; Authors calculations. High and rising openness of the countries in the region with tight trade and financial linkages with the EU underlines the importance of the external demand as growth factor. After the sharp fall of the trade flows during the pick of the crisis, since 2009, the trend of rising trade openness has continued in almost all countries reaching 104% of GDP on average for the region (7 p.p. higher compared to 2008). The highest openness can be observed in the Central European countries of about 150% of GDP. Importance of the EU, as a main trading parting for the region, has continued to increase with about two thirds of the exports channeled to the EU. In particular, Germany seems to be an important trade partner accounting for about 17% on average of the exports with notable exposure of the Central European countries (close to 30% of the exports). European economy is expected to continue to recover, although moderately and thus it is not expected to provide strong boost to the growth dynamics in the region. The ECB quantitative easing coupled with weakening of the euro have contributed to improved growth prospects. Still, the potential growth of the euro area seems to have weaken, mirroring crisis legacies, demographics, and decline of the total factor productivity, which started even before the crisis.3 Notwithstanding the estimated slowdown in the potential growth, still the forecast for the next couple of years does not indicate a possibility for the euro area to close its output gap, and therefore, it will remain negative. The positive aspect is that the German recovery has been better compared to the average in the euro area with expectation of entering the zone of positive output gap. Chart 3: Growth and output gap in the euro area and Germany Source: IMF, World Economic Outlook, October 2015. Recent slowdown in some emerging markets (notably China) poses some challenges for the growth prospects of the region. The direct links between the CESEE counties and China are weak, as the share of domestic value added from the region consumed by China is less than 2% of CESEE countries GDP (with highest exposure of the Slovak and Czech Republics and Hungary). In this vein, IMF study estimates that the spillover effects of the Chinese slowdown via the real channel will be fairly small assuming that countries have fiscal and monetary space to act counter-cyclically. However, Chines slowdown may imply more general slowdown in emerging markets and subsequently stronger spillover effects on the European economy, particularly in the manufacturing sector of the German economy, and indirectly, in the CESEE economies. China is one of the top five export partners of Germany, accounting for about 7% of the German export. Also, having in mind the role played by China on international primary commodity markets, it poses risks for countries exporters of metals, but in the same time creates 3 For reference, see the IMF, World Economic Outlook, October 2015. positive risk for energy importing countries. Higher uncertainty may adversely affect investors confidence, risk premiums and result in spillover effects through financial channel, as well. Despite the post-crisis downward adjustment of the external financial exposure of some of the countries in the region, it remains elevated. The international investment position indicates that the strong rise in the gross external liabilities observed in the pre-crisis period was discontinued with the emergence of the crisis. The post-crisis downward adjustment was the largest in the Baltic States, while in the other two groups it continued to increase, but at a far slower pace than before. Yet, the external liabilities remain high mainly due to public sector borrowing, namely, in almost all of the countries, liabilities are more than 100% of GDP with sizable share of debt-creating flows-implying still high vulnerability of the region to any financial markets turbulences. Given the constrained external environment, it is of interest to shed some light on several domestic factors and to assess their impact in the context of growth. When it comes to the fiscal stance in the region, it appears that, despite the fiscal consolidation efforts, it is not yet complete and that it may continue to weigh on future growth. The trend of gradual narrowing of the general government balances has continued across most of the countries in the region, but at a pace insufficient to stabilize the public debt level. Thus, public debt continued to rise across the whole region with an exception of a couple of countries (on average, the public debt reached around 53% of GDP). In 6 countries, the level exceeds the threshold of 60% of GDP, and even more, the latest IMF forecast again does not point to room for a more significant adjustment. The issue of how to reconcile the fiscal consolidation with the need to boost the growth will remain as one of the key challenges in this regard. The scrutiny of the structural balances reveals that after 2009 fiscal impulse has been negative, and the latest IMF forecast shows that more or less the same pattern prevails in a medium run. Thus the need to further increase the growth friendliness of the budget structures remains. The IMF index that measures this budget dimension indicates that many of the countries managed to improve the budget structures in a way that positively affects the growth, though the progress was more visible on the revenues side i.e. shifting taxation away from direct to indirect taxes and property taxation. On the expenditure side, there has been limited progress in reducing high transfers and wage bills. Overall, public expenditure levels are still high and expenditure structure is similar to structures of advanced economies despite the lower income level. Chart 4: Fiscal profile4 4 Data for structural fiscal balances are not available for Albania, Macedonia, Estonia and Montenegro. Source: International Monetary Fund, WEO Database, October 2015; Authors calculations. The experience of the countries in the region regarding the role of the domestic credit finance in supporting growth is quite diverse, but generally many countries still struggle with anemic credit support. The average credit growth of the region in the last couple of years has been hovering around 1%, although there are high variations among countries. The intensity of the postcrisis downward adjustment was linked with the speed of the pre-crisis growth, and the sources of its financing. In those countries where pre-crisis growth was high, the post-crisis adjustment was also more intensive. This process was highly pronounced in the Baltic countries, while Montenegro, Croatia, Slovenia and Hungary can also been seen as part of a classical boom-bust cycle. In the rest of the region, although growing risks caused a slowing/decline in both credit supply and credit demand, the post-crisis adjustment was more moderate. Chart 5: Credit to the private sector Source: Central banks internet sites; Authors calculations. Taking into account the low rates of credit growth, on average, and the simultaneous challenge to accelerate the economic growth, the crucial question that arises is whether the banking system is in condition to intensify credit flows and thus support the economy as a whole. The screening of the key parameters indicates that the banking system in the region is generally sound. Although a slight decrease of solvency is evident compared to the pre-crisis period, in the last few years, the capital adequacy is more or less stable, averaging at about 17%, and thus exceeding the legal minimum more than twice. At the same time, the liquidity indicators point to the fact that the liquidity buffer is solid and that banks in the region are ready to absorb any potential liquidity shocks. The loan/deposit ratio dropped in all countries reflecting anemic credit growth thus pointing to a space for stronger credit support. Bank profitability is one of the points which certainly suffered serious consequences, after the onset of the global crisis. Taking into consideration that the income from interest on loans is the main source of income for the banks in the region, the slowdown in credit growth, even the decline in some countries, together with the environment of low interest rates, which creates pressure on interest margins, implied a decline in profitability of banks. Despite the solid state of the banking system that implies adequate buffers to intensify credit support, there appears to be some limiting factors. One of the key legacies from the crisis is the worsened quality of the credit portfolio that significantly inhibits new credit flows. The average level of NPLs is around 13%, and this average has been relatively stable in the last few years. Indirect market risk, due to the foreign currency exposure of banks balance sheets, and funding risk are part of these constraining factors. The financing risk is related to the so-called "forced" deleverage. The possibility of materialization of this challenge exists, and methods may vary, from the sale of banks that are systemically important for the countries in the region (outright divestment), to reduced financial support from parent banks, which in the absence of sufficient domestic resources, would mean reduction of credit support in the real economy. The introduction of the new Basel standards can also act as potential barrier for faster growth. It might reduce the availability of credit and increase the cost of financing. If on the backdrop of all these factors credit growth remains pale and thus act, as inhibitor of economic growth, there is high possibility the process of weak credit-weak growth to become self-fulfilling. Chart 6: GDP and credit growth in %; gaps as % of potential (average for the region) Source: IMF WEO database, October 2015 and central banks websites; Authors calculations. The risk of the vicious growth-credit-growth cycle can be depicted in a very simple manner, namely, by observing the degree of synchronization of the credit and economic growth. The general notion would be that their trajectory is fairly coupled, and on top, in the post-crisis period, the dynamics seems to be quite in line, as well. With all the deficiencies, due to the lack of a longer consistent data series, still, the first check on where the economic and credit cycles stand, points to two conclusions. First, there is more or less a co-movement in both cycles, and second, both credit and growth seems to run under their potential at the very moment. This brings us to the puzzle of how the prospects of the credit-growth puzzle would look like in the period to come. Although the banking system is in sound shape to be growth supportive, the other side of the coin is the private sector, i.e., the process of repairing of the balance sheet of the corporate sector. Despite the variations among countries, broadly, the trend of repairing corporate sector balance sheet through declining leverage that started with the occurrence of the crisis, continued in 2015. The emergence of the crisis interrupted the pre-crisis trend of sizable growth of the leverage of the private sector. In some countries, deleveraging of the private sector took place soon after the beginning of the crisis, reflecting financial and real sector constraints, somewhere as an effect of the growth in savings and fall in investment, and somewhere because of the faster economic growth. The most pronounced correction took place in the Baltic States that went through a severe boom-bust cycle. On the other end of the spectrum are a couple of countires that did not undergo adjustment at all, reflecting different country-specific factors. In some countries, capacity of payments or restructuring of the loans was insufficient, resulting in the persistence of debt. In others, the foreign investment cycle has not been terminated by the crisis (Macedonia for instance), thus the borrowing of the corporations from their parent companies increased. In some countries, the soundness of banking system was strong enough and the flows of lending to the corporate sector have not stopped. Chart 7: Private sector debt and distance from benchmark Source: Central banks web sites; Authors; own calculation. Distance calculated as difference between 2014 level and the benchmark. Although the current level of private sector debt in most of the countries in the region does not seem to be worrisome, still the process of deleveraging may proceed further and act as a limiting factor for the short-term growth prospects. For instance, it equals 113% of GDP in 2014, and is below the benchmark of the MIP scoreboard of the EC, which indicates private sector debt above 133% of GDP, as a threshold above which leverage becomes threat. Even more, if we control for the Baltic States, the average is much lower, i.e. around 100%, but still some of the countries are above the benchmark (Bulgaria, Croatia). On the other hand, some international institutions assess (IMF, for example) that the level of debt of the private sector in the region is currently high and not in line with its fundamentals. In addition, given that the debt of the private sector, in one part was financed through external sources, this process has had consequences for the rising external vulnerability of the region. Even though the changes in the debt in the post-crisis period are small, the rapid growth of debt before the crisis still represents a burden on the external position. Hence, the deleveraging of the private sector in the next period might be inevitable, and given the debt-growth nexus, this process could be a potential impediment to growth. The impact might be even reinforced, given the anemic external environment, the narrow policy space, and some bottlenecks in the banking system, the burden of NPLs in particular. If all the previously discussed issues are to be put in the growth context, it seems that more vigilant drivers should be found in the structural area, thus leading to rising productivity and competiveness. In that respect, it would be of interest to do a snapshot on the productivity data across the board. As productivity is a longer-term issue, we also deploy a longer-term perspective. At the same time, relative productivity is quite important for getting a more clear perspective to see how distant the region is, compared to a certain benchmark. As Germany is considered a good yardstick in this respect, we calculate the relative productivity of the region against Germany. Although the process of catching up in productivity in relation to Germany broadly continued, the speed significantly decelerated in the postcrisis period and currently, the productivity for the region as a whole accounts for about 62% of the German productivity. More favorable developments can be observed in Baltics, where internal devaluation process took place, and hence productivity improved mildly. Similar conclusion can be drawn by observing the data based on the growth accounting. By decomposing the GDP to contribution of the classical measured inputs, labor and capital, and the Total Factor Productivity (TFP), one can draw several inferences. First, before the global crisis, the TFP, which should be a vague indication of the efficiency and the technological growth, similar to Germany, was an important growth driver for the CEE and Baltic States, but less for the SEE countries, where the capital impact was prevailing. At the first stage of the crisis, TFP fell across the board. Subsequently, recovery was seen in all countries, but it was only the Baltics, similar to Germany, that benefited from the positive TFP impact. It is another facet, which gives an indication that the faster recovery of the region will require overcoming of many structural bottlenecks, thus boosting technological profile of the region, its efficiency and competiveness. Chart 8: Productivity in the region, relative to Germany (ratio) and growth accounting Source: The Conference Board. 2015. The Conference Board Total Economy Database, May 2015, /. Authors calculations. If we run the same counterfactual simulation, as the one for the GDP, by applying the pre-crisis average growth to the 2007 productivity level, we observe again much higher productivity level compared to the actual one. It indicates the spare capacities in the region, and gone productivity opportunities. Given that the loss in productivity is very similar to the loss in the output, this also pinpoints certain structural deficiencies in the region, as the counterfactual loss indicates only slow employment adjustment, and potential weaknesses on the labor market. The observation of the productivity dynamics across the countries in the region shows that all of the countries in the region are going through a productivity growth slowdown (Chart 9, panel 3). On average, the slowdown gravitates around 4 p.p, with only few outliers, i.e. the BIH and Estonia where the slowdown is more pronounced. Chart 9: Productivity from different angles Source: The Conference Board. 2015. The Conference Board Total Economy Database, May 2015, /. Authors calculations. The need to boost productivity brings us to another important issue for the region, which is the need to boost investment and increase the potential to grow. It is quite difficult task, given the current global economic circumstances, but it is unavoidable path if the growth is to become livelier. Traditionally, foreign investments have been a crucial source of additional capital in the region, which not only supplemented investments, but also provided boost to productivity and competitiveness to the regional economies. Fortunately, it is a source of inflows in the region, which was not completely discouraged by the burst of the crisis. Yet, particularly for the SEE group of countries that are lagging behind, FDIs remain an important challenge, if further rise in the economic potential is to be seen. Hence, again we are at a juncture where important issues in the growth context must reappear. First, the business environment in the countries must be friendly and competitive enough to attract financial flows. Second, financial flows should be allocated to productive, tradable sectors, thus boosting the growth of export. In other words, if another expansionary financial cycle occurs, a great deal of effort should be taken to ensure a proper allocation of resources, thus enabling rise in productivity and competitiveness. Historical data on inward FDI in the region point to a state where around two thirds of the inflows went to the non-tradable sectors, suggesting room for improvement in this area. Third, the strategy for tighter integration in the global supply chains, that has been an important growth driver for many CEE countries, might be a good solution forward for some of the countries that are lagging behind in this respect. Source: WIIW database. Cumulative inflows a sum of the annual inflows, data is not balanced, starting point different for different countries, conditioned on the data availability. Tradable includes agriculture and production. Non-tradable includes construction and services. In summary, policymakers will remain faced with the challenges to revive the growth and speed up the convergence process. Despite some differences across countries, broadly, the policy space has been used up, to a great extent implying limitations on the further fiscal and monetary policy support. In most of the countries, the process of dealing with crisis legacies such as high NPLs and balance sheet repairing is not yet over and will continue to be a drag on the credit flows and on the short-term growth. External environment is expected to remain fragile and uncertain, particularly in light of the possible slowdown of the emerging markets with possible negative spillovers through the real and financial channel, geopolitical risks as well as the ongoing refugee crisis in Europe. The countries where the recovery has progressed will have room to shift the focus from short-term stabilization of aggregate demand to medium-term structural issues that will increase the long-term potential of the economies, as well as rebuild internal and external buffers.
