Title: Annual Conference of the Macedonian Stock Exchange, March 29, 2016, Alexander Palace, Skopje
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Speech by Governor Dimitar Bogov at the Annual Conference of the Macedonian Stock Exchange, March 29, 2016, Alexander Palace, Skopje Speech by Governor Dimitar Bogov at the Annual Conference of the Macedonian Stock Exchange, March 29, 2016, Alexander Palace, Skopje How to a more efficient capital market in the Republic of Macedonia? First, congratulations to Ivan for the start of SEE LINK. I know he has made great efforts to achieve this idea. I think it's a great move in the right direction. And the direction is towards a more efficient capital market. But you're lucky Sasho Ordanovski has not heard of it yet. To know that you are opening a door for capital outflows, he will send protesters to the Stock Exchange immediately. As he threatened me to send it to the National Bank. Well, when Thelma asks you, and why right now? The joke aside, while some are sowing fog and making up conspiracy theories, some are working to improve the situation in the financial sector. The question is, what kind of capital market does Macedonia need? My answer is: effective. If I paraphrase the theory of efficient financial markets, the price of the action reflects all relevant information available for the true value of the action. In fact, the true value of the action is the current value of future cash flows that the owner of the action expects to receive. It is this opportunity to earn from the shares that makes investors buy and sell on the stock market. They are constantly in search of undervalued and overvalued shares. They constantly compare new information to those expected. Depending on whether the information is more favorable or unfavorable, the price that tends to move around the real price of the action also changes. Therefore, in an efficient market, investors, as a whole, cannot earn an extremely high return adapted to risk. That doesn't mean individual investors can't make much money and others can lose a lot. But on the whole, the long-term return on the stock market in developed efficient markets is slightly higher than the return on risk-free debt securities. That difference is the premium on the risk taken by investing in shares. So, in order to achieve high efficiency in the capital market, the role of information is key. Basically, it is three levels of information: 1. expectations for the environment; 2. Expectations for the industry in which the company that quotes the capital market operates; 3. what is the situation in the company, from the point of view of finance, the quality of corporate governance, the strategy for the coming period. The subjective factor is fundamental to the first and especially the third level, while the second level is, in some ways, given by global market movements that we cannot influence. The environment inevitably affects all companies, whether in a growing or declining industry, whether the company is good or bad. When the economy grows fast, it has positive effects on all firms. When there is political stability, it positively affects potential risks. As the National Bank is a monetary policy holder, I will take this opportunity to give our insight into the macroeconomic environment that investors on the Macedonian stock exchange can expect. Short -u2012low inflation below two percent, stable exchange rate of the denar relative to the euro, low interest rates, low current account deficit in balance of payments, solid economic growth. Inflation will be positive this year, about 1 per cent and close to 2 per cent next. Those underlying effects of the decline in oil and food prices on world stock markets are exhausted, so we expect inflation to normalise at a long-term level of 2 per cent. Exports will continue to increase and narrow the trade deficit and, accordingly, the deficit in the current account of the balance of payments. Therefore, no pressure is expected on the exchange rate of the denar. If we add the ECB's extremely expansive monetary policy to that, it is highly likely that the favourable monetary policy ambition will continue by maintaining a low interest rate. Economic growth, for three years in a row, is about 3.5% and the trend is expected to continue. But whether growth remains at that level, or whether we make a step up and exceed 4%, depends on political stability. Hence, political uncertainty also affects stock market movements. Of course stabilising political expectations and moving Euro-Atlantic integration would create a better environment for stock market investors. We create the business environment ourselves and we can do a lot to improve it, thereby contributing to creating a more efficient capital market. Much has been done to create and maintain macroeconomic stability. Significant progress has been made in the regulatory segment of the business environment. It is a process that should never stop and we should ascertain best regulatory practices. We have a lot of work to do to reduce political uncertainty. Information about the prospects of an industry where certain shares are located is the second level that is important for investors. Whether the industry is declining or is new, growing, whether the conjuncture is favourable or not. For example, low oil prices have lately contributed to the weaker achievements of oil companies and companies engaged in the exploration and development of new oil fields. Low metal prices pose a risk to many primary metal producers. On the other hand, some new industries based on the digital revolution offer huge growth opportunities. But cycles are spinning. Just a few years ago, oil and metals booked a big growth in profits, and let's remind ourselves that fifteen years ago, the dot com meurhappened. While we cannot influence the prospects of certain industries, we can direct investors to new digital industries. The fourth industrial revolution is based on digital technologies. Smart self-driving cars, smart household appliances that will communicate with each other, web platforms literally for every aspect of economics, culture, entertainment, etc. In this industrial revolution, the main resource is knowledge. Our education should be reoriented towards mass production of technicians, engineers, developers. Investors should form risky funds to invest in new IT businesses. Perhaps the Stock Exchange can report as a promoter of such events, where young "computers" will meet with their "waky" ideas with those who have money, and their only business idea is to build another hall, another business building where they will immediately put the inscription "issued". Perhaps television slots can buy out the hit series "Silicon Valley," instead of another Turkish or Indian series, or another reality show. At least the young will get some good business idea, instead of becoming "wolves", starlets, or crying brides. The third level of information is microlevel. There is an expression of the difference between good and bad companies. Investors need the most information here to distinguish between companies with good corporate governance, professional financial management, quality managers, clear corporate strategies and those without it. Because these are the elements that distinguish between companies in the same industries. There are companies in the growing industry with excellent performance and companies with modest results. There are companies with stable achievements in the declining industry and companies that are bankrupt. How many domestic equity companies in Macedonia have good corporate governance? How many public equity companies have good financial management? How many domestic companies have professional management involved? How many activist shareholders are there in Macedonia? (These are shareholders who buy a share package that allows them to enter the company's supervisory board without intending to take over and fight there to improve its achievements). How many companies have made an IPO? How many shareholders (where there is no overweight shareholder) where management does not try, at all costs, to avoid control from shareholders? How many shareholders are there where management cares about the cost of the action? How many public limited liability companies are there where management has been replaced due to poor results and an unsatisfactory return on shareholdercapital? As long as the answer to these questions is "no at all" or "there is insignificant", we cannot expect an efficient capital market. We can all do something to raise the efficiency of the capital market. But the companies themselves can do the most. For starters, they can show transparency, honesty and accountability to shareholders. Thank you.

Title: Final conference of the IPA project
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Speech by Mrs Maja Kadievska-Voynovic, Vice Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, at the final conference of the IPA project Skopje, 30/06/16 Speech by Mrs Maja Kadievska-Voynovic, Vice Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, at the final conference of the IPA project "Further alignment with EU legislation in the field of capital movements and payments and financial services -securities markets and investment services" Dear ladies and gentlemen, I am pleased to welcome you to the final conference under the project "Further alignment with EU legislation in the field of capital movement and payments and financial services -securities markets and investment services". This project, which consists essentially of two parts, one to align national legislation with EU legislation in the area of the capital market, and the other concerning compliance with payment legislation, as a whole, has great importance for the central bank. However, what is of particular interest to the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, and is in the context of one of the legal functions held by the central bank, is precisely the provision of secure and stable infrastructure for the execution of domestic payments, which ultimately means supporting overall financial and macroeconomic stability in the country. Allow me on this occasion to congratulate the excellent and fruitful co-operation of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia and the Finance Ministry with EU experts in the process of aligning Macedonian legislation with EU regulations in the field of payment services and payment systems. EU experts have made an outstanding contribution to the drafting of the new Payment Services and Systems Act, which also includes the Internal Market Payment Services Directive (PSD and part of the PSD2 provisions), the Settlement Finality Directive and the Electronic Money Directive. EU experts, in co-operation with the competent institutions in our country, have also developed appropriate bylaws regulating the licensing process for payment system operators, payment institutions and electronic money institutions, the opening and closing of payment accounts and the use of payment instruments. Respected, The National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia constantly monitors all the payment news that occurs in the common European market. A major contribution to "keeping up with the EU" is also the organisation of a regular international conference in Ohrid in the area, which has been in co-operation with two eminent EU central banks, the Dutch and Portuguese central banks for nine years. This conference and the visit of similar conferences abroad by employees of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia is a good opportunity to build the institutional capacity of the central bank in the field of payments with all the news that modern times bring. Thus, modern technical solutions in the field of payments and the use of sophisticated media and payment devices at global and European level have positive effects on the development of payment turnover in the country. In response to the era of digitisation, mobile and internet payments, in the Paid Turnover Act 2007, The Electronic Money Directive was installed, which achieved partial compliance with European legislation, and later introduced "micro-payments" in 2012 as a transitional solution for further development of mobile phone and internet payments payments. However, the changes to the legislative framework did not fully cover the significant aspects of European regulation relating to the opening up of the market for the entry of different types of payment institutions and new players in the field of payment systems, as well as ensuring greater protection for payment service users. Hence, the need to fully install the Payment Services Directive on the internal market, the Settlement Finality Directive and the Electronic Money Directive 2, which have now been introduced in the new draft Law on Payment Services and Systems, have been imposed. Our view is that, following the successful reform of payment turnover in 2001 in the Republic of Macedonia, this project of harmonisation of the legislative framework is a continuation of the reform process in the field of payments, which is expected to lead to: Incitement competition by allowing non-banking institutions to enter the market with innovative payment solutions; Strengthening the rights of payment service users to receive clearer and timely information; Lower payment service prices for payment service users; Increase financial inclusion and greater availability of payment services to consumers and companies; Further improving the stability of payment systems; Consolidation the applicable regulations currently covered by several acts related to payment services; Finally, but most significantly, establishing a legal basis for the faster integration of the Republic of Macedonia into the EU and inclusion in the Single European Payment Area (SEPA). Dear ladies and gentlemen, At the end of my address, I would like to express my sincere satisfaction and gratitude to EU representatives for the financial support for achieving this project, as well as to eminent EU experts and to the other parties concerned for the successful project, in anticipation and hope for further, future co-operation.

Title: Seminar on Applied Baesian Econometry, organized by the Bank of England and the NBRM, Skopje, 21-25 November 2016
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Address by Anita Angelovska-Bejoska, Vice Governor of the NBRM, Seminar on Applied Baesian Econometry, organized by the Bank of England and the NBRM, Skopje, 21-25 November 2016 Dear guests, dear colleagues, I would be very pleased to welcome you to the Applied Baesian Econometry seminar, which is jointly organised by the Bank of England and the NBRM. The world's latest monetary stimulus on the one hand, and the still weak recovery and dark growth prospects, on the other, have given the central bank community many dilemmas. Much of conventional knowledge has been reviewed to better understand the new reality and effectiveness of conventional and unconventional monetary measures. By contrast, the role of research and modelling is becoming even more pronounced, as they are expected to give some answers to current dilemmas, thereby improving the efficiency of the monetary decision-making process. I expect the knowledge gained from this course to significantly expand existing research tools and opportunities within our central banks. Baesian techniques take precedence over classical methods when applied to small specimens, which is the case with existing time series in transition countries, such as ours. In general terms, Baesian methods have additional advantages that make them extremely useful, such as models, design and research tools in the modern economy. Therefore, after several years of expansion and use of classical economic techniques, it is no surprise that we are seeking to expand the range with new tools, which could be used for both existing and new issues in economic research and modelling. Regarding the content of the seminar, I hope that you will find the right balance between theoretical lectures and practical exercises, which, in our experience, are especially useful for our employees. Although the course's duration of a week seems short, I believe it will give you the right basis, so that in the future we could expand and apply our knowledge of Baezian methods. The organisation of this seminar reflects our positive experience in co-operation with the Bank of England. So far, we have organised several similar courses in Skopje (in 2007, 2010 and 2012), which concerned Targeting Inflation and Monetary Policy, Economic Modelling for Central Bankers and Empirical Financing Topics. Our employees also often attend Bank of England courses in London, which regularly receive top training on key issues for research, modelling and design at central banks. With this seminar, we continue our practice of inviting other central banks from the region to join us. This reflects our view that we face similar challenges and that such opportunities allow for a significant overflow of knowledge, especially where we can learn from prominent experts, such as Mr. Gabor Pinter and Mr. Andrew Blake. Thus, we are really grateful to the Bank of England and appreciate the opportunity to be co-organisers of this event. In the end, let me wish you a successful job at the seminar, have stimulating lectures and discussions, which (I am sure), increase the knowledge of our central banks and help address the challenges that the central banking community faces today. I also hope that you will be lucky for the weather conditions to be beautiful so that you can at least take a little look at Skopje and enjoy it. Thank you.

Title: Promotion of the upgraded MIPS of the National Bank with the possibility of paying in euros through the ECB's TARGET 2 system
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Address by Governor Dimitar Bogov at the promotion of the upgraded MIPS of the National Bank with the possibility of paying in euros through the ECB's TARGET 2 system, Skopje, 28.3.2017 Address by Governor Dimitar Bogov at the promotion of the upgraded MIPS of the National Bank with the possibility of paying in euros through the ECB's TARGET 2 system, Skopje, 28.3.2017 Respected Finance Minister Minoski, Dear President of the Mitrovski Bank Association, Respected representatives from regulators and payment system operators and securities alignment systems, Respected representatives from the banking and corporate sectors, First of all, I would like to thank you on my behalf and on behalf of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia for your presence at today's promotion, at which we are presenting a significant project, from which the National Bank, the banking sector and the Macedonian economy as a whole will benefit. What is this about? Since the beginning of 2017, the National Bank has started working on the euro cross-border payment system by linking the Macedonian Interbank Payment System (MIPS) to the Eurosystem's Target 2 (Trans-European Automated Real-time Gross settlement Express Transfer system). To this end, an upgrade of the NBRM MIPS to make payments in euros was carried out and a link to the TARGET 2 payment system was established through italy's central bank. In doing so, MIPS has become a two-currency payment system for payments in denari and euros. The promotion of this capital project is, by its essence, a second generation of reforms in the field of payment infrastructure, following the first significant reform of payment turnover in 2001. The achievement of this project is proof that the National Bank follows the strategic determination of the Republic of Macedonia to join the European Union. Dear guests, For Macedonia, as a small and open economy, where most of the foreign trade is with countries on the European continent, the existence of correspondent channels for euro payments is important for trade relations. The population, but also our immigrants, need safe cashless transfers in euros. However, globally, including european soil, there has been a decrease in correspondent banking arrangements in the last period, primarily due to two groups of factors. The first group refers to economic factors. The installation of payment infrastructure for the single currency and the consolidation of the banking sector as a whole have caused a reduction in correspondent banking arrangements. The second group of factors is related to regulations to prevent money laundering and terrorist financing, which have imposed complex and expensive procedures for maintaining correspondent relationships. In such conditions, narrowing the possibility of maintaining correspondent banking relationships, the new established alternative channel for payments in euros through the National Bank is gaining increasing importance. The implementation of this project began as early as 2013, and is in line with the European Commission's recommendations, contained in macedonia's progress reports and in accordance with the National Bank's Needs Report, the IPA project implemented by representatives of the European Central Bank and the central banks of the Eurosystem members. In the process of implementing the solution, the National Bank co-operated with the Finance Ministry and banks. On this occasion, allow me to express my gratitude to the Finance Ministry for its positive approach to this important project, through amendments to the Foreign Exchange Act. At the same time, I would also like to express my gratitude to the representatives of the banks with whom we had active co-operation during the testing of the upgraded MIPS. Allow me to stress our assurance that setting up this alternative channel for cross-border payments through TARGET2 will be a market momentum for cheaper, faster and safer cross-border transactions in euros for Macedonian companies and the population. At the same time, the National Bank project will provide support for regional integration of capital markets, as it is expected to allow the monetary component to be aligned in euros in securities transactions in the future. Finally, no less significant benefit is the development of capacities in the National Bank and banks for future direct accession to target2, i.e. the future functioning of the Macedonian component of target2, in the membership of the Republic of Macedonia in the European Union. Respected fellow bankers, We call on you together to make this step even greater, through active use of this safe channel for payments in euros and together, and more easily and cheaperly, to enable all further steps of our payment and beyond, financial integration into the global world. Finally, I would like to thank the entire team of experts at the National Bank, the Payment Systems Directorate and the Information Technology Directorate, without whose strong commitment and teamwork this reform project would not have been possible. Thank you!

Title: Welcome speech at the sixth international research conference on Central Banking in the face of prolonged global uncertainty: The latest lessons while the "new normal" is sought
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Governor Dimitar Bogov's welcome speech at the sixth international research conference on Central Banking in the face of prolonged global uncertainty: The latest lessons as the "new normal" is sought, 5-7 April 2017 Skopje Honourable Minister for Finance, Excellency, Respected representatives of central banks, Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great pleasure to welcome you again to our regular, International Research Conference, which is traditionally organised to mark the anniversary of our country's monetary independence. As you already know, on April 26th this year, we celebrate the 25th anniversary of monetary independence and with this conference we will mark this jubilee with the introductory panel discussion on policies with the participation of senior representatives. We are particularly honored that in this jubilee year, we organised our conference as a joint event with the London School of Economics a survey of Southeast Europe, which I believe will contribute to extending the issues of discussion concerning the region and beyond. In the context of the topic of this conference and at our jubilee, I would like to mention some important issues that I believe will be thoroughly infuriated during the Panel Discussion on Policies and in the next two days. For some, the headline of this year's conference very clearly describes the current global macroeconomic environment. Central banks are still working in the face of prolonged global uncertainty, in an attempt to define and move towards a "new normal", while recognising and implementing the latest lessons from the global crisis. During this crisis period, we have undergone a relatively long process of correcting the shortcomings of the past, studying new experiences and strengthening capacities to better address future challenges. Although the global economy is gradually healing, uncertainty still exists, but it is of a different nature. Now, the world's attention is focused on the increasing likelihood of entering a new era of protectionism, the impact of Britain's exit from the European Union and increasing skepticism in the EU, as well as the geopolitical risks still present. The general economic debate concerns the impact of these risks on global economic recovery and, as regards the first issue, is debated primarily against trade barriers in the world. The expansion of world trade has contributed significantly to global economic growth ahead of the global crisis. At the same time, the principle of free movement of people, goods and services, capital and payments is one of the main pillars of the EU and, for now, contributes to strengthening the EU economy. As for the EU, it appears to be in a specific phase of "recreation". In general, without going into detail, the world is clearly at a crossroads u2012 phase in which stronger and internal consolidation and international co-operation are more than necessary. As for policy placement, low inflation due to low prices of basic products and the accompanying cycle of monetary policy facilitation in developed economies has ended or is approaching the end. As the US economy appears to be approaching its "new normal," for the EU economy it is likely to happen a little later. This would mean a return to normalising monetary policy and a sharp change in yield curves. Although the situation may vary from country to country, this still means that the world economy has functioned in low interest rates in a relatively long period of time that has already passed or almost passed. Although monetary policy has supported economic recovery in very specific circumstances, sustainable economic growth must still be based on deep structural reforms. Policymakers should therefore be brave in implementing reforms aimed at flexible labour markets, greater productivity, stronger competition and innovation. This will be a task not only for developing economies, but also for developed economies, but in a different starting position. "The alarm is on" and fiscal policy, which in many countries has become quite comfortable in low interest rates. It will also need to prepare for tightening financial conditions, making fiscal consolidation a bigger challenge. In the financial system, regulators around the world face challenges arising from new capital requirements in accordance with Basel III, which in turn contribute to preserving the security and stability of the banking system, not only in normal times, but also in times of stress. In Macedonia, we have just adopted this new package of provisions and now expect its smooth implementation, given the already strong position of the capital of the banking system. In an era of globalisation and digital technologies entering the field of financial services, regulators face increasing challenges. One of the lessons of the latest global crisis is that the development of the financial system must go hand in hand with the establishment of appropriate mechanisms to reduce risk and manage crises. Such dynamic and complex circumstances are an even greater challenge for growing economies understructural reform, a key prerequisite for a faster approach to higher income levels. Now that we are celebrating 25 years since Macedonia's monetary independence, we can say that we have witnessed various situations, We have dealt with several shocks  internal and external, we have learned a lot from others and ourselves, we have achieved many goals and in the end, we realized that we need to work even harder to achieve even greater results in the future. I would also like to mention in short that at the beginning of the transition we faced hyperinflation, low levels of foreign exchange reserves, macroeconomic imbalances, the need to restructure banks and companies, despite all this, a unilateral embargo imposed by a neighbouring country. We can proudly say that over the last twenty years, we have managed to maintain price stability with impressive average inflation of 2% and a stable exchange rate, as well as the stability of the banking system, which has survived many "real stress tests". As we tried to protect the economy in the stage of great growth before the global crisis, we experienced the opposite situation  we provided a monetary incentive for economic recovery after the impact of the global crisis, using conventional and unconventional measures. We believe that monetary policy has been and will be a stable component of macroeconomic policy in the country, which will contribute to maintaining overall macroeconomic stability. Such an environment has been shown to provide support for the implementation of structural reforms, which have produced visible results in recent years through a change in the economic structure towards the production and export of higher added value products, as well as a steady reduction in the unemployment rate, even during the global crisis. It is extremely important to mention that all these years, the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia has been constantly focused on strengthening institutional capacity in all areas of its operation, as a major prerequisite for carrying out new and different tasks arising from the above global environment. The transition process is a process of learning market principles and implementing them simultaneously in practice. I believe that all countries that have been through this process have experienced successful and less successful, satisfactory, unsatisfactory reforms and reforms that are still ongoing. Many years after the transition begins, it is useful to look back and see overall progress, to separate areas where the transition is completed or almost complete and others, where the transition lags behind. We should face our current position and speed up reforms in the future. Obviously, there are many different issues related to the transition process, especially in the face of changing the global economy. However, I would not owe any more and would give way to the Panel Discussion on Policies. It is a great honor to have distinguished lecturers today who will introduce us to the topic of the session dedicated to the region's transition process  that is Mr. Paul Thomsen, director of the IMF's Europe Department and the first head of the mission to Macedonia in 1993, gave us enormous support in dealing with the various shocks facing our economy at the beginning of the transition. The other participants in the Panel discussion are: Mr. Peter Sanfei, Deputy Director of Economics, Policy and Governance at the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, who is particularly involved in the activities of the EBRD in the region and Professor Vassilis Monastiriotis of the London School of Economics u2012Research of Southeast Europe. (I will join them in the discussion, too). The chairman of the Panel Discussion will be Mr. Gligor Bishev, former Deputy Governor of the NBRM and one of Mr. Thomsen's main colleagues in 1993. It also gives me great satisfaction that our Finance Minister Cyril Minoski is with us today. First, I will invite the Finance Minister to come on stage and give a welcome speech on the occasion of the 25th anniversary, and then Mr Thomsen with his opening lecture. At the same time, let me express our immense gratitude for their presence today. Finally, let me wish you a fruitful and interesting discussion during the Conference and a pleasant stay in Skopje. Thank you!

Title: Address on the opening of the exhibition in honor of the 25th anniversary of the monetary independence of the Republic of Macedonia
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Dimitar Bogov, Governor of the NBRM, Address ing the opening of the exhibition in honor of the 25th anniversary of the monetary independence of the Republic of Macedonia, Skopje, April 25, 2017 Dear guests, dear artists and friends of art, Tonight I have the great honor of opening the golden right guest exhibition of the Ljubljana family of artists: Biljana Unkovska-Spanzel, Rudolf Spanzel and Dorian Spanzel. At the same time, I give my gratitude to her curator, Dr. Andrei Semrov of the National Museum of Slovenia, because this exhibition allows the Macedonian public to become fully acquainted with the artistic work of three painters with extremely separate authorial scars, but which also characterizes a significant phenomenal intersection: design of and cash. In addition, I express no less gratitude to NLB Banka, AD Skopje for its selfless support in the realization of this art project in Skopje. Tonight, contrary to the day when the Republic of Macedonia rounded off its own monetary independence 25 years ago, this exhibition, and the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia as its host, undoubtedly reflects in one part the artistic evolutionary path of the Macedonian denar. 21 years ago, the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia printed the existing edition of Macedonian literary money, the design of which is carried by biljana unkovska's author's manuscript, as the first award-winning work of the Competition for an Idea Solution for a New Look of Macedonian Banknotes, called by our institution. Its creative design solutions also adorn all suitable gold coins and srebrenica issued by the National Bank between 1996 and 2004. I thank her for creating small works of art in which we are not only looking at because of the economic semantics of the figure used to indicate their nominal value. I would like to stress that it is a pleasure that the art dinner marks a significant socioeconomic process that constituted the independent Republic of Macedonia. Satisfaction, undoubtedly, is also because of the thought that this occasion has the potential to be another impulse for new and equally successful co-operation between our two friendly countries. Thank you. Gallery of photographs from the exhibition in honor of the 25th anniversary of the monetary independence of the Republic of Macedonia

Title: Conference organised by the Capital Funded Pension Insurance Agency (MAPAS) to mark Pension Awareness Day - September 15th, Hotel Continental, Skopje
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Anita Angelovska-Bejoska's speech as part of a conference organised by the Capital Funded Pension Insurance Agency (MAPAS) to mark Pension Awareness Day -September 15th, Hotel Continental, Skopje Respected, It is a particular honor and pleasure to be able to address this event, which is dedicated to a very important dimension in every individual's life, and that is awareness of our own role in creating our pension future. However, today I would like to look back on a broader concept, in which this issue undoubtedly belongs, which is the issue of financial literacy  why is it important to each of us, what is the level of financial literacy, whether efforts are being made and policies are being developed for greater financial education? It is more than clear that without understanding basic economic and financial concepts, people cannot make good financial decisions, or otherwise put it, they do not have the ability to make the right choice in terms of saving, investing, borrowing. Financial "ignorance" can impose large costs not only for individuals, but also for economies as a whole. The major economic crisis clearly pointed to insufficient financial education as one of the factors that contributed to the creation of the credit meur, which then dispersed with long-term consequences for the global economy. Understanding, however, of key financial concepts allows awareness, better risk diversification and finding better and (which is very important) sustainable investment alternatives. In fact, in the context of modern trends, the importance of financial education is steadily growing. As noted in the OECD report" the continued evolution of financial, economic, demographic configuration, as well as policies, increasingly conveys the risks of individuals and thus financial literacy turns it into one of the key life skills in modern societies" (OECD, 2016). In particular, what are these major changes, which increase the weight of financial literacy? It would set aside a few main concepts. First, it is the growing level of financial mediation and facilitated access to population lending, which in particular came to an expression in the period before the global economic crisis. The credit boom, which preceded the crisis, was supported by excessive confidence and irrational expectations of "infinite" growth in asset prices and low interest rates, which is, of course, due to insufficient financial literacy. The consequences of such behaviour by individuals, but also of banks, are well known to us, and it can be said that we still feel them. An even closer example to us of what negative repercussions may have insufficient knowledge of the risks, perhaps the episode of borrowing in Swiss francs in some of the countries in our surroundings. Low interest rates on this type of loan and exchange rate stability have led to higher borrowings in this currency, whose strong commitment in 2010-2011 increased the value of loans by as much as 30% and to a significant increase in the debt burden of credit beneficiaries, the inability to regularly settle liabilities and to deteriorate the quality of the banks' credit portfolio. Both examples show that financial literacy, and financial awareness, are not an important component only for individuals' personal finances, but are an important element of the stability of the entire financial system, and thus the overall economy. As Minehan notes, "economies are created by individuals and the more informed and knowledge-based decisions of individuals are, the greater the likelihood of economic prosperity". The second aspect is demographic, and refers to the process of aging the population, especially in Europe. While in 1990, the participation of persons over the age of 65 in the total POPULATION in the EU -27 was 14%, in 2016 it increased to 19%. This aging process certainly meant burdening pension systems, reforming insurance organised according to the principle of current funding (pay-as-you-go) and introducing private pension schemes. The increasing growth of private funds and the transition from defined benefits to defined contributions, of course, increases the responsibility of persons for good management of their own pension scheme, for providing sufficient finances in later life. Practice shows that in this domain, even in highly developed economies, understanding and knowledge of persons is not at an enviable level. For example, research in the Netherlands shows that as many as 58% of respondents have no knowledge of the size of their future pension income. Pension reforms in Macedonia have long followed concepts in developed economies, so that private pension insurance will become more significant now and in the future. This will also increase the need for financial education to properly plan pension schemes and increase financial well-being. The growing offer of complex financial products and services from new non-banking financial institutions is the third aspect, increasingly highlighting the risk of insufficient knowledge and uninformedness of persons in the use of new products. In this context, the term "fintek", which is a broad concept, relating to financial innovation supported by rapid technological development and which appear in various segments of finance  payment transactions, financial market infrastructure, investment management, insurance, but also the provision of credit support in the economy. All these innovations mean the possibility of greater efficiency and competitiveness of systems, but at the same time mean greater risks and the need for greater financial awareness, especially given the low level of regulation of companies in the fintech segment. Furthermore, another aspect is the need for greater financial inclusion, to which international institutions and policymakers are increasingly paying attention. Access to finance by most subjects, especially vulnerable groups in society, will on the one hand mean greater inclusion of growth and poverty reduction, but on the other hand, further emphasises the need for education. Unlike northern European countries where the level of financial inclusion measured through access to accounts in financial institutions is close to 100%, in some Eastern European countries, more than 50% of the population does not have access to formal banking services. In the case of the RM, about 72% of the population (over the age of 15) has accounts in financial institutions. Low financial inclusion is a combination of both supply and demand, with insufficient financial literacy considered one of the important reasons on the demand side for such low financial inclusion. Recognising the low level of financial literacy and the need for promotions in this regard, especially after the emergence of the global financial crisis, has also led to enhanced efforts by policymakers to improve financial education and better awareness. Some of these initiatives have a supranational character and refer to several EU directives that allow for greater transparency and knowledge and respect for consumer rights, responsible borrowing and management of mortgage debts and focusing on financial inclusion. Many European countries touch on the issue of financial education through national financial education strategies, which are joint documents and joint efforts by several involved parties, including central banks. Central banks are active participants and promoters of the financial education process in almost all countries. The reasons are multiple: 1)educated subjects better understand monetary policy, thereby increasing the effectiveness of monetary measures; 2)the better subjects understand the economy and finances, the more imperative the functioning of financial markets;3)higher education means less likely to take excessive risks, which is, in turn, directly correlated with the stability of financial systems and sustainable economic growth; 4)economic and financial education means promoting public good;5) good financial education supports the central bank's credibility and understanding of its activities. The National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia is actively involved in these modern trends in financial education of the public. Although this segment is still in its inception, the activity portfolio is steadily increasing. Increasing focus is on active engagement in the field of education for basic financial concepts of primary and secondary education students, given the need to start education in the early years. Hence, educational activities became part of our daily work. Increasing emphasis is on preparing various educational brochures and making educational films, enriching the set of available data and information to the public, organising seminars and workshops for target groups, and for the first time in the RM a pilot project for social and financial education by first-grade students has been implemented. As part of the 70th anniversary of central banking operations in the RM, a more extensive training programme was implemented for 4,330 students from 87 primary schools, and two documentary-educational films were produced for the purposes and functions of the central bank. At the same time, it recognises the need for synergies and jointcoordinated activity of several involved parties by concluding joint memorandums of co-operation with all financial regulators, the Bureau for Education Development and other institutions involved. Despite numerous long-standing efforts by policymakers to increase financial literacy, more recent research is pointing to a wide range of further promotions. The results of the new Standard & Poor's poll suggest that financial literacy is not at a low level only in developing countries, but is surprisingly low in countries with well-developed financial markets and high per capita income. In larger developed economies, only half of adults are considered financially written, and in developing economies the level is even smaller, with the RM estimated that only 21% of adults are financially written. Similar findings are from the OECD survey (a sample of twenty European countries) that suggests that 40% of respondents do not collect information at all before selecting certain financial products, over 80% did not request alternative offers at all, half of respondents did not set long-term financial targets at all. More generally, numerous polls draw several more important conclusions: still low financial literacy, Literacy levels correspond to education and income levels, respondents often assess that they have higher knowledge of the real ones and consider that there is a lack of easily understandable educational content and financial information that would help them in the decision-making process, which is particularly pointed out in the pension scheme information section. Hence, both globally and in our country, financial education, i.e. its proper measurement, guidance and evaluation, will continue to be a challenge for policymakers. Our positive experience so far motivates us to make further efforts in this field. In this regard, i would mention as more significant new future projects: the development of a national strategy for financial education, the introduction of indicators by which the level of financial literacy will be measured on a regular basis, and through the effectiveness of the measures, the support of the project for the introduction of an elective subject financial education in primary schools and the preparation of a separate national website for financial education. I hope that I have been able to capture some of the basic elements of the genesis of financial literacy, how present it is in global contexts, why it is significant and what the challenges are in the face of obviously rapid financial and technological progress. I would like to end up with a vision that Ben Bernanke, the former Fed governor, pointed out in a speech of his own  financial education is a constant, lifelong process. The financial decisions we make change during the life cycle  from paying tuition, to buying a home and planning pension schemes  hence, access to appropriate financial education is necessary in all different life stages. Thank you,

Title: Economic Forum,Astana, Kazakhstan
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Presentation of Maja Kadievska Vojnovic, Vice Governor of the NBRM, Economic Forum, 17-18 May 2018, Astana, Kazakhstan From 17-18 May 2018, Mrs Maja Kadievska Vojnovic, vice governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia participated in the prestigious Economic Forum in Astana, Kazakhstan organised by the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan, the Institute for Economic Research of Kazakhstan, the Breton Woods Conversion Committee and the International Strategic Parity Group (ISPG). The Economic Forum was held at a high level on "Ongoing Changes in the Global Economic Ambition", developing current topics related to current and expected movements in the global economy in the coming period with a focus on issues related to multilateralism in the modern multipolar world, protectionism, trade wars and the risks to global economic growth. Vice Governor Maja Kadievska Vojnovic participated as a panelist during a session titled "Trade Wars and Growing Protectionism: Risks to synchronized recovery of the global economy" along with Kazakhstan's finance minister, senior representatives from global banks and investment funds, professors and economic advisers and researchers. Several high-level speakers addressed the Economic Forum, including Mr. Francois Hollande, former President of France, Mr. Ban Ki-moon, former Secretary-General of the United Nations, Mr. Romano Prodi, former prime minister of Italy and former President of the European Commission, Mr. Steve Wozniak, co-founder of Apple and others. With vice governor Maja Kadievska Vojnovic's participation in this prestigious Economic Forum with top-level speakers, he contributed to strengthening the international position and reputation of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia.
