Title: Seminar "Dealing with Dysfunctional Loans in the EU: Regulatory and Supervisory Activities", 18.10.2018, Skopje, Macedonia
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Speech by Mrs Anita Angelovska-Bejoska, Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, at the seminar "Dealing with Sonyfunctional Loans in the EU: Regulatory and Supervisory Activities", 18.10.2018, Skopje, Macedonia Speech by Mrs Anita Angelovska-Bejoska, Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, at the seminar "Dealing with Dysfunctional Loans in the EU: Regulatory and Supervisory Activities" organized by the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, in co-operation with the European Banking Agency and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, 18 October 2018, Skopje, Macedonia Dear guests, Ladies and Gentlemen, I am pleased to welcome you to this regional seminar on "Dealing with dysfunctional EU loans: regulatory and supervisory activities" organised by the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, and in co-operation with the European Banking Agency and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. Let me first express my sincere gratitude and respect to our co-organisers who helped us organise this meeting here in Skopje, discuss the latest trends in dysfunctional loans, learn more about the latest policy initiatives at European level, especially eba's efforts to tackle dysfunctional loans, which are an obstacle to greater credit support and to look at best practices and regulatory frameworks in order to effective management of dysfunctional loans. It has been a decade since the outbreak of the global financial crisis, and the problem of increased dysfunctional loans and frameworks for dealing with dysfunctional loans is stuck in political debates and, in general, in the banking sector. This probably shouldn't surprise us. The root of the global crisis is in the financial sector, and dysfunctional loans are common side effects of the financial crisis and financial instability. Sometimes, they occur at a time when the credit upswing is turning into a decline, and in other cases they are just the effect of prolonged low economic growth or structural obstacles in the banking system. Regardless of the reasons, the consequences are common in the macronomy, they prevent loans from being placed in the economy because capital is tied to dysfunctional loans, jeopardising the potential for growth and even financial stability; at the microlevel, they are a burden on the profitability and efficiency of banks, increase the costs of financing and capital of banks; from the point of view of lenders, faster handling of dysfunctional loans is payable because they will avoid paying interest and provisions for funds they will not ultimately own. Given the size and duration of the latest crisis, dysfunctional loans have become a post-crisis problem across the board. It has come to the core of systemic and macrofinancial risks in very advanced and developing economies. The euro zone was no exception, where the rate of dysfunctional loans was tripled after the crisis, reaching 8% on average in 2013. The troubled balance sheets have prompted the adoption of common political measures at EU level, as well as strong efforts by separate banks to deal with dysfunctional loans. Driven by a gradual economic recovery, these efforts enabled a nearly continuous improvement in the rate of dysfunctional loans, which averaged 4.9% at the end of 2017. The improvement was on a broad basis, but the decrease was still slow and heterogeneous, and the ratio of dysfunctional loans remains at double-digit levels in some euro zone countries. Thus, dysfunctional loans remain an important obstacle to stronger and more diverse growth and to the proper functioning of the financial system. Although it is noted that the risks associated with high amounts of dysfunctional loans are primarily the responsibility of the banks and national authorities concerned, given the importance of the problem, it was recently placed at supranational level at the ECOFIN Council in July 2017, when finance ministers agreed on an Action Plan to deal with the state of dysfunctional loans in Europe and to prevent an increase in this risk in the future. Amid strong financial integration and the banking system's interconnection with the euro zone, the Southeast European region has not remained immune to these trends. Growing dysfunctional loans have become an important legacy of the crisis, but the spread of the problem has been of different intensity in different countries. It was more pronounced in those SEE countries that have gone through a cycle of ups and downs. These countries have gone from a credit boom driven by the finances of foreign parent banks financed in the pre-crisis years, to slow credit growth and the rise of dysfunctional loans in the post-crisis period. The sharp increase in the rate of dysfunctional loans (from almost 7% on average in 2008 to about 17% on average in 2013) and the reduction in income assets in banks, have consistently affected profitability and imposed one deduction behaviour on banks to take risks. In recent years, however, rates of dysfunctional loans have been decreasing across the region as a result of coordinated reforms in extrajudicial restructuring, regulatory write-off of dysfunctional loans and cyclical recovery. At the end of 2017, the rate of dysfunctional loans decreased to about 10% on average for the region still above pre-crisis level. Solving the problem of increased levels of dysfunctional loans was even more difficult, given the absence of markets for dysfunctional assets in the region. The sale of the portfolio of dysfunctional funds to private sector investors still plays a negligible role. Therefore, banks must deal with the increase in dysfunctional funds themselves, which should have engaged staff, money and time. Vienna's latest NPL monitor initiative suggests that the volume of dysfunctional loans has reached its lowest level in 7 years, which is largely due to stricter write-off policies and improved handling of dysfunctional loans, while transactions in dysfunctional loans are largely reduced, although there are signs of an increase in market activity in 2018. In the context of the complexity of the case, some countries in the region have begun adopting national comprehensive strategies for dealing with dysfunctional loans. Here, allow me to clarify the Macedonian case, as we have recently decided to develop a Strategy for resolving and improving the management of dysfunctional loans. The strategy includes several institutions, with a wide range of built-in measures such as changes to banking regulations, an increased focus of supervisors on banking internal capacities to deal with dysfunctional loans, adoption of specific regulation for the sale of dysfunctional loans, clarifications in the tax regulation on the trade in dysfunctional loans, exploring the possibility of publishing the largest dysfunctional loans, improving bankruptcy regulation, implementation, valuation, as well as the introduction of alternative investment funds. I must stress that in our case the strategy does not reflect the urgentness and severity of the problem of dysfunctional loans in Macedonia. In fact, at this point, Macedonia is compared perfectly well to the region in terms of the level of dysfunctional loans, and the same was the case when the crisis arose. Currently, the rate is 5.1%, compared to the highest rate of 12.6% in 2014, with adjustments reflecting solid economic growth in the post-crisis period and mandatory write-off measures introduced in 2016. More broadly, the lower rate of dysfunctional loans, compared to the region, represents a mixed effect of banks' prudential approach, a strong regulatory framework and the fact that banks did not rely on external ones, but on domestic sources of funding during the crisis. In addition, we avoided creating a large surplus of loans in the pre-crisis period, which protected us from a major deterioration in the outbreak of the crisis. Moreover, the problem is not generally accepted, but is quite concentrated in several large corporate exposures, hence well controlled. However, the experience of other countries has shown that there must be a suitable environment to prevent any serious increase in the danger in the banking system's credit portfolio. This requires a proactive approach by banks to manage dysfunctional loans, appropriate design and efficiency of the legal framework in which they operate, active markets and appropriate tax treatment. Therefore, a comprehensive and well-streamlined strategy can provide important takeovers and a solid framework not only to deal with, but also to remove the existing burden from dysfunctional loans. Finally, let me conclude, presenting the idea that the solution to dysfunctional loans is a complex process that requires a so-called "holistic approach". This means that only common private and public, coordinated and coordinated initiatives could yield sustainable results. The main responsibility is for the banks themselves, as they need to be proactive in providing an effective solution. The second layer is the public sector, which must provide a clear framework for reducing and preventing dysfunctional loans. This segment particularly wants faster progress, due to still adaptable financial conditions that cannot last longer. In this context, at this seminar, I am sure it will be particularly useful for banking regulators and supervisors from the region to take advantage of the experience of the European Banking Agency, especially supervisory guidelines and rules for managing dysfunctional exposures. The same applies to representatives of the EBRD, an institution that has been present in the region for a long time. Their views on the economic and regulatory environment in the region and the assessment of the current level of development in local markets for dysfunctional loans will provide further added value for regional regulators. Last but certainly not least, these events are a forum for sharing participants' experiences and policy responses on increased dysfunctional loans in their banking systems and exchanging opinions on the effectiveness of specific tools and measures and future plans to improve supervisory practices in relation to dysfunctional loans. With this address, I wish you a successful seminar and fruitful discussion. Thank you!

Title: Speech  to the Association of Banking at the Macedonian Chamber of Commerce  World Austerity Day
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Speech by Mr. Dimitar Bogov, Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Macedonia, the Pre-Association of Banking at the Macedonian Chamber of Commerce, on the occasion of October 31st  World Austerity Day Dear ladies and gentlemen, respected banking workers, respected guests, I am particularly pleased to address you on the occasion of the commemoration of World Austerity Day. This is the day we highlight the important role that austerity plays, not only from the point of view of its role as a source for financing individual banks, but also its immediate importance to the economy as a whole and to maintaining financial stability. Moreover, we have repeatedly had the opportunity, and you as bankers and we at the National Bank as regulators, practically make sure that the truth of the saying that maintaining the stability of banks is a reflection of the trust that savers have in them. This year, banks enjoyed the trust of the population, regardless of the adverse impact of domestic political events on the ordinary citizen and saver. Confirmation of this is also the latest available data on the movement of population deposits. As of September, population deposits show a very solid growth rate of 5.8%, an important indicator for stabilizing savers' expectations and views given the volatile ambition and restraint of economic agents from investment activity in the first half of this year. Positive movements in population austerity have also contributed to the growth of credit activity, so according to the latest available data from September 2017, loans grow by 4.3% on an annual basis, with solvency almost double the legal levels and volume of liquid assets that allow optimal daily operation. It must also be stressed that in addition to the political ambition, deposit growth, and thus trust in banks, have been achieved for some time in the ambition of historically the lowest interest rates, both in the financial markets in the euro area and in the domestic interbank market. On this occasion, I would like to note that in the coming medium term, banks' performance on the deposit market will require even greater efforts to modernise and increase their offer. We live in a global era of digitization, great progress in information technology and its daily greater use in the financial sphere. Innovation and the application of modern technologies are continually putting competitive pressure on traditional forms of banking and forcing banks to constantly adapt, be proactive and inventive and, by changing their business models to new phenomena and conditions, to seek their market success. Such processes will inevitably reach the operation of banks in the Republic of Macedonia. In perspective, the use of modern technologies will not only affect the market performance of banks, but will probably change their relationship with savers and other customers from the root. In fact, in this regard, even for countries such as the Republic of Macedonia, with relatively modest financial education of the population and low utilisation of modern technologies in the financial sphere, the issue imposed is not whether, but when the digitisation process will affect the domestic banking system. In this context, I would like to point out that the process of digitisation and the use of information technology should not be seen as a danger of increasing competition in banking, but as a new opportunity to bring financial services closer to as many customers as possible, and through that, to increase financial inclusion, the degree of financial literacy of the population and the better allocation of resources, as phenomena that have greater economic and social significance. On the other hand, the implementation of new technological solutions also brings changes in the range of risks taken by banks and managed in their daily operations. In addition to the conventional risks of a financial nature that banks deal with in their operations, such as credit risk, the risk of interest rate movements, currency risk, will gradually increase the importance of non-financial operational risks. The increased volume of use of modern technical solutions in operation will also mean greater importance of the risks associated with the security of information systems, data confidentiality, the preservation of information content, access and maintenance of payment systems. Finally, since the award of the best counter workers will follow, allow me on behalf of the National Bank to express my public gratitude for their daily and hard work in the branches of banks. Thank you for your attention and congratulate you on World Austerity Day!

Title: Promotional event on the conclusion of the Memorandum of Financial Education and Financial Inclusion and Global Money Week, Skopje, 20 March 2019
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Address by Dr Anita Angelovska-Bejoska, Governor of the National Bank, at the promotional event on the conclusion of the Memorandum of Financial Education and Financial Inclusion and The Global Money Week, Skopje, 20 March 2019 Respected Finance Minister, KHV President, MAPAS President (Capital Funded Pension Insurance Supervisory Agency) and Representatives of the ASO, Esteemed Representatives of the MBA and the Media, I am particularly pleased that the National Bank is hosting today's event, which we are organising together with other regulatory institutions to promote a new Memorandum that will continue to improve our co-operation in the field of financial education and financial inclusion, but also to bring our planned activities closer to the public in these significant segments. In the period after the start of the global financial crisis, financial education was among the new challenges and activities of central banks. The crisis period has addressed numerous vulnerabilities to the financial system, underlining the need to strengthen regulation and risk management by financial institutions, but also points to the need for a financially educated population, which understands the benefits of using different financial products, but also knows how to protect itself from the potential risks of using them. Consequently, central banks around the world already have developed various forms of financial education aimed at strengthening the population's ability to make the right financial decisions. Hence, the National Bank has been conducting activities in the field of financial education for many years, mainly targeting the youngest, who are still in the early stages of education and skills acquisition, by organising lectures and publishing various educational materials. Over the past six years, meetings have been held with about 9,000 primary and secondary school students and students, with specialised lectures on specific economic topics held for students, and the National Bank Museum educating its visitors about the history of money in these spaces. In the spirit of trends in this area, with the new memorandum of co-operation we sign today, not coincidentally, in addition to financial education, which was also covered by the previous memorandum, in the order of our activities we include support for as much financial inclusion as possible. The relationship between the two areas is more than obvious  the financially educated population has more knowledge of the benefits of using different financial services, which ultimately provides greater involvement of the population in financial flows and facilitated access to finance. The need to achieve higher financial inclusion is a global issue, given estimates that about 1.7 billion of the world's population do not yet have access to the banking system. Since access to finance is considered one of the key determinants for poverty reduction, the issue is gaining more and more importance. International indicators for measuring the degree of financial inclusion (the World Bank Index 2017) point to the need to make further efforts to increase the financial inclusion of the population and in our country. Although there is a solid financial involvement from the aspect of owning a transaction account (about 77% of the adult population has a transaction account, comparable to the European average of about 82%), however, several other indicators point to a significant gap: only 17% and 53% of the population own credit and debit cards, versus the European average of 35% and 71%, appropriate; only 37% of the population use the cards for purchase transactions, which is twice the European average (63%); Only 12% of the population use electronic access to accounts, and internet transactions make up only 17% of citizens, double the EU average. The need for greater financial literacy is particularly emphasised in the face of strong growth in the fintech industry. In recent years, there has been a proliferation of small companies offering technologically advanced financial products that are easily accessible to consumers. Moreover, one of the main advantages that this new wave of financial innovation brings is the easier access to new, more competitive financial products or forms of funding for the population and small companies, as additional sources of financing for economic growth. However, in addition to numerous benefits, this wave of innovation brings with it new challenges, both for regulators and financial institutions, but also for customers. Let's not forget one of the lessons learned from the crisis: easier access to financial services in the short term offers numerous advantages for consumers, but in the long term it can lead to too many risks, especially if there is an adequate level of financial literacy by the population. Greater financial inclusion in different segments of the financial system also requires joint engagement of regulatory institutions in terms of education and regulation, but also of private financial institutions in terms of providing greater availability and awareness of the financial services offered, including on accompanying risks. Therefore, I think it is particularly important that towards the end of last year, the National Bank concluded a Memorandum of Co-operation in the Field of Financial Education and Inclusion and with the Macedonian Banking Association, thus confirming its readiness for these aspects as the dominant segment of the country's financial system. The new, extended memorandum is not accidentally signed in the run-up to Global Money Week, in which, like in previous years, we plan more activities to raise awareness of the need for financial education and promote the benefits of greater financial inclusion. Over the next week, the National Bank will launch an educational caravan  we invited them and provided transport ation to students from several schools, mainly from rural parts of the country, who have not been to our institution before, to visit the National Bank and other regulatory institutions. On a visit to the National Bank, students will have the opportunity to submit educational presentations, receive educational materials that will allow them to educate financially appropriately at their age, and visit the National Bank Museum. Children from a kindergarten will also visit us, for the first time in the context of financial education, in an attempt to bring the youngest generations closer to the meaning of money. All that we achieve and achieve on the youth financial education plan is also our stake in the future. As institutions, we are obliged to carry policies for the development and support of the financial system and the economy in the long term. Through activities to enrich young people's financial knowledge, we contribute to building the capacity of generations that will be the main carriers of economic and financial flows in the country in the future. A special event in Global Money Week will be the national competition under the European Money Quiz, which will be held in our country for the first time. We started this activity late last year, at the initiative of the Macedonian Banking Association, in co-operation with the Securities and Science Commission, as part of the European competition in this area of children aged 13 to 15. We have already introduced the public to the Quiz and informed of the great interest and mass involvement of students from the country. During February, a preparatory meeting was also held at the National Bank, organised by the four institutions organising the Quiz, which is actually the first training of the teaching staff in the part of financial education. The national winners will be selected at next week's national competition, representing the country in the final it will hold in Brussels, organised by the European Banking Federation. We would also like to announce the publication of a series of short educational texts, called Economics for Everyone. As the name itself refers, it is intended for all segments of the population, including adults. Through these texts, in a simple language, we will try to explain certain terms or phenomena in the fields of macroeconomics, finance and banking. We hope that through this series of educational texts we will bring our work closer to the public and contribute to a better understanding of more economic issues that reflect everyday life, and are directly or indirectly related to central banking work. Let me at the end of my address, thank other financial regulators and business banks, for the co-operation in this area so far, but also to our colleagues who are committed to improving in this area and at the same time, to express my strong confidence that with our deepened co-operation we will continue to contribute to raising the quality of human potential, as a key prerequisite for prosperity in society. Each area has its own challenges, and in modern conditions, democratic societies advocate development and inclusivity in each sphere of social action  inclusivity in education, economics, inclusivity in enjoying general rights and freedoms. Our challenge as regulators is financial inclusion, which means access ing as much of the population as possible to the financial system, but in a sustainable way, without excessive risks, which in the long term should contribute to comprehensive economic growth whose benefits will be felt by all. Thank you!

Title: World Austerity Day
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Speech by Anita Angelovska-Bejoska, Governor of the National Bank, on the occasion of World Savings Day, Skopje, 31.10.2019 Revered Minister Angelovska, Revered Mrs Stevkova-Sterieva, Revered Mr Hadzhiev, respected employees of business banks, ladies and gentlemen, I am pleased to address today's event marking World Austerity Day and which is also a good opportunity to remind ourselves of the importance and numerous benefits that austerity brings to every economy. This year's commemoration comes at a time when the global economy is facing the challenge of continuing to maintain low interest rates, and in the face of a new wave of monetary loosening from the Fed and the ECB, as globally influential central banks. This has again fuelled debates about the possible negative effects of low and negative interest rates on the balance sheets of European banks, the stability of pension funds and insurance companies and, of course, on the savings of citizens in banks. Debates that on many occasions have relied on concerns that low and even negative interest rates in certain countries may reduce households' tendency to save in the form of deposits. Or, to cause excessive risks in search of a higher yield, which can negatively affect financial stability. Hence the question of how realistic such fears are. And can greater displacements in banks' deposit base as a result of low interest rates be expected? Eurozone achievements so far show that household deposits are steadily rising, despite low interest rates in the post-global economic and financial crisis. This growth in the last three or four years has accelerated and, according to the latest data, reached almost 6% year-on-year. Within the EU, deposits in banks (along with cash in circulation) participate with about a third of the total financial assets of households and this participation is relatively stable compared to the pre-crisis period. Are these low interest rate sensitivities of austerity, or are there other factors that have contributed to such movements? An analysis by the German Central Bank[1] of 2015 shows that the interest rate influenced, but was not a decisive factor for households' austerity decisions in the post-global economic and financial crisis. Other factors, such as the level and dynamics of disposable income and wealth, demographic structure, as well as the population's tendency to take risks and dispose of liquid assets, have largely determined household behaviour in terms of how much and in what form to save. This can probably be added to the fact that most European banks have, so far, basically not passed the cost of negative interest on savers[2]. Consequently, the effects of low interest rates on european banks' deposits have so far been assessed as moderate, with a lower likelihood of significant displacements in the coming period. In the domestic economy, interest rates have been decreasing for a long time, corresponding to global low interest rate trends and loosening monetary conditions within domestic frameworks. The fall in the price of loans contributes positively to economic growth, facilitating access to lending to households and the corporate sector. But it also withdraws lower savings yields as deposits are the main source of credit growth financing and their price is embedded in the price of loans. However, according to dynamics, the pace of adjustment is different, with the reduction in deposit interest rates significantly delayed in the last period. The last three four years have been characterised by a faster reduction in loan interest in terms of deposit interest, which contributes to a narrowing of the interest rate range. Compared to the European market, savings yields in the domestic banking sector are largely still competitive, and are basically relatively higher and compared to deposit interest rates in other countries in the region. The National Bank has taken several measures and activities to encourage banks to offer higher yields on long-term deposits, given the importance of longer-term austerity for the stability of the financing of the banks themselves, but also for the economy, as a source of financing for long-term investment projects. Our population's traditional penchant for saving in bank deposits has remained retained for the last decade, as confirmed through the steady growth of household deposits, which reached 9% year-on-year with August. The structure of austerity is also favourable. The trend of denarization continues, with about 60% of banks' total deposits now in domestic currency, a significant progress compared to the period of the global crisis when they were about 40% of total savings in denari. Our citizens still prefer to save in bank deposits, in front of other available instruments. As of the end of last year, bank deposits account for about two-thirds of the total financial assets of the population and this participation has increased compared to the pre-crisis period. The following are pension savings, which participate by 17%, while the total participation of investments in securities and shares in investment funds is 8%, and on life insurance policies just over 1%. According to the Vienna Initiative Report[3], the reasons for the conservative attitude of the domestic population towards other investment alternatives, and in conditions of declining interest rates, can be located in the still under-built investment culture, which leads to little interest in investment in the capital market. The shallowness of the market also has an impact, unpleasant experiencewith the fall in share prices from the not-so-distant past, and the limited supply of investment instruments that does not fully meet investors' diversification needs. An important factor in the development of the capital market, which is also highlighted in this Report, is the raising of the level of financial literacy of the average saver, which determines the propensity for risk and ability to make informed investment decisions. Recognising the benefits of a financial written society, the National Bank remains committed to working on financial education of the population, thus strengthening the capacity to invest responsibly and manage risks, with positive effects on maintaining financial stability. If we summarise, the ambition of low interest rates, which has been our reality for a long time, seems to linger in the next period. The fall in interest rates has so far not had a significant impact on our citizens' penchant for savings in banks, which is important for maintaining the overall financial sector. Given that in our economy deposits are the main source of financing for banking activities, it is important for domestic banks to maintain competitive austerity conditions in the next period. Given the stability of the balance sheets of the domestic banking sector, I think that can be realistically expected. Maintaining solid achievements over the long term, without destimulating effects on austerity, can be achieved by increasing the volume of private sector lending, improving productivity and operational efficiency, but also technological progress and diversification of revenues. At the level of the entire system, productivity of the domestic banking sector[4] has improved in the last period and it is important that this trend continues. A positive contribution in this regard can also be made by further consolidation and consolidation of the domestic banking sector, given the positive effects associated with such processes in order to improve efficiency and increase competition in the sector. Respected, Austerity is not only an economic phenomenon and a prerequisite for economic growth and well-being, but is also a factor in the individual's personal development. I hope that in our modernity, all in common, by raising the level of financial literacy and by fostering financial inclusion, we will contribute to strengthening awareness of the importance of austerity for each individual. As the famous researcher Thorton T. Munger has said, building austerity habits in itself is an educational process  strengthens virtue, develops a sense of responsibility and respect for order and discipline, encourages caution and predictability in behavior, thereby expanding intellectual visions. Finally, let me wash, and all employees in the banking sector, congratulate you on World Day of austerity, and wish you a successful further work that depends on maintaining a key social good  financial stability. Thank you for your attention! [1] German households saving and investment behavior in light of the low-interest rate environment, Deutsche Bundesbank Monthly Report, October 2015. [2] The exception is certain banks that have imposed negative interest on more property clients and higher provisions for managing corporate deposit accounts. [3] Vienna Initiative, Report by the Working Group on Capital Markets Union, 2018. [4] Measured according to the employee asset.

Title: Working meeting with the curriculum for the European Money Quiz
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Address by Anita Angelovska-Bejoska, Governor of the National Bank, at a working meeting with the curriculum for the European Money Quiz Dear Minister Angelovska, Deputy Minister Naumovska, President of the Macedonian Banking Association, Stevkova-Sterieva, representatives of the regulators of the financial system, valued professors and teachers, I am honored to welcome you and welcome you to today's event for the teaching staff, to prepare for participation in the upcoming edition of the European Money Quiz. After great success last year, when our country first participated in this significant youth competition, and our national representatives won second place in Europe, I believe that at this year's edition of the Quiz we all approach it with greater enthusiasm. This also confirms the fact that the number of registered departments and classes this year is significantly higher compared to the past, with schools from different parts of our country registered. And this year, the National Bank has strongly supported this MBA initiative, which moreover fully fits our long-term strategic goals to further improve the financial education of the population, including young generations. Today I would like, in this brief address of mine, to focus on a topic that is extremely important for the whole society, which is the quality of human capital. This topic is also important to you, as a pillar of society that acts on profiling young people, but also for us as institutions whose capacity depends precisely on the willingness of young people to integrate the labour market well, using their knowledge of the country's prosperity. In economic science, human capital  quantity, and even more quality is one of the most important prerequisites for raising the potential for growth of the economy. Some research suggests that 30% of income differences between countries are explained precisely by differences in human capital. This is particularly important for us, as an economy where per capita income is just over a third of income within the EU, which points to the need for a significant step up to increase growth potential. Comparative indicators of the quality of our human capital show that all of us as socially responsible institutions should make additional efforts to raise and move closer to more developed countries. One of those indicators is the World Bank's human capital index, which suggests that if comprehensive reforms in the field of the education and health system continue, children born during the current period when they turn 18 could be more productive by 50%. The index for the Macedonian economy is 0.534, versus the German economy, whose index is 0.795 and close to the maximum value of 1. A similar picture also gives us an indicator of the "years of education adapted to the results achieved", which for us amounts to close to 7 out of a maximum value of 13 in Singapore, which means that effectively acquired knowledge does not fully correspond to the number of years of education. A significant space for improvement is also visible on the employer side. According to the latest global competitiveness report, we are at 131. 141 countries after the volume of investment in employee training. These indicators give us a clear indication that our efforts, among other things, should also focus on greater symbiosis of theoretical knowledge and practical skills. This would also mean a stronger feedback between you  the education system and us, as institutions that absorb the workforce in the labour market. In this way, we can fill our gaps and improve the country's international position in this domain. This will contribute to a better and more competitive workforce and to increasing the productivity of our economy, which lags significantly behind the productivity of the European economy. Given the role of the central bank, as a pillar of the financial system, one of the important segments where we can proactively act with you is certainly financial education. There is no dilemma that a financially educated population manages personal finances better, acquires the ability to make sustained financial decisions and better protect against financial risks, which is in favour of maintaining financial stability. Financially educated clients take better advantage of existing financial products, which ultimately contributes to greater financial inclusion and sustainable economic growth. A survey on the financial literacy of the population, conducted in early 2018, found that the aggregate index for our country is 11.8 and comparable to countries in the region, although there is room for improvement. By comparison, in the Baltic countries, this index is above 13, and the average for OECD countries is close to 14. From the point of view of the components of the index, solid results are seen in the domain of financial knowledge. Thus, 45% of respondents showed solid knowledge of basic financial concepts, which contributes to enduring financial decisions. However, only 40% of young people aged 18 to 24 showed satisfactory financial knowledge, suggesting the need to further raise financial literacy in the young population. But I believe that the challenges in both general education and financial education are great, given that we all face new generations whose technological profile is changing very quickly. The labour market and financial product users are already actively involved in the so-called "millennials", or Generation Y. In fact, this is a so-called fintech generation that goes through the transition from classic financial products to using sophisticated technologies in finance and which requires speed of services, adapting services to their individual needs. A generation that lives with smartphones and communicates through instant messages, and that also mirrors it in its financial habits  avoiding going physically to a bank, using smartphones for financial transactions, etc. In your schools, however, you face an even greater challenge of the so-called "generation Z" (19952015), the only generation that was born in a almost completely digital context. Their profile, way of thinking and communicating, I believe, imposes a need to reconsider access to their education, a greater presence of digital technologies in the transfer of new knowledge, to retain their attention and thus to ensure quality educated young people. Globally, financial companies are particularly committed to offering financial services earmarked for this generation, but what has been identified as the main obstacle is the lack of sufficient financial education for this youngest segment. This global problem, along with World Bank data for our country, which shows that the population is seeing lower use of newer financial products clearly refer to the need for our common engagement in this field. Although awareness of new financial services is relatively higher in the younger population, according to World Bank data for 2017, the use of mobile phone or internet access to an account for young people aged 15 to 24 was represented by 17%, and the eurozone average was 45%. Given the world trends and needs in our country, the National Bank has further stepped up financial education activities in recent years. In March last year, a new Memorandum of Co-operation in the field of financial education and financial inclusion between financial regulators was concluded, and for the first time activities for greater financial inclusion were included in the order of our joint activities. At the same time, we at the National Bank began publishing series of educational texts and video materials, intended for all age groups of the population, including for young generations, through which in simple language and visualization we try to explain certain terms or phenomena in the field of macroeconomics, finance and banking. Last spring, as part of The Days of Financial Literacy, as central bank, we first made a public call to all interested citizens to attend educational presentations on various topics in the field of our work, which was of great interest. All these activities, including today's event, are aimed at further raising the level of financial literacy in our country. Today's event is just one step of bringing the financial sphere closer to the education system, for the sole purpose  to bring financial practice closer to educational programmes and to contribute to enriching the practical knowledge of students in this field. I believe we will contribute to successful preparations of the European Money Quiz, as well as for repetition, and perhaps to overcoming last year's results. Dear mentors, It is not a revelation that the future is a category that does not exist until we have created it in the present. You, the teaching staff, are active, key participants in creating the future of our economy. A wise thought dedicated to you, to educators, reads: "You can teach the student to master a lesson in a day; but if you can teach him to learn with curiosity, he will continue the learning process as long as he is alive." in conveying and mastering lessons on finance, students will learn about and explore new concepts with curiosity, and that curiosity about finances will persist long after the end of the annual european money quiz. It is in them that I see the future engines of our economic development and guarantors of our financial stability. I wish you and your students great success on the upcoming quiz! Thank you!

Title: BIS Monetary Policy Working Group meeting in Central and Eastern Europe
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: PLATFORM FOR DISCUSSION EVENT: BIS Meeting of the Working Party on Niko_Memo_Logo_Temno Monetary Policy in Central and Eastern Europe NATIONAL BANK OF THE REPUBLIC DATE: 20-21 February 2020 OF NORTH MACEDONIA info@nbrm.mk LOCATION: Becici, Montenegro MONETARY POLICY CONUNDRUM IN DEVELOPED ECONOMIES  IS THE REGION DIFFERENT? Ana Mitreska, NBRNM Ljupka Georgievska FSBRR1, NBRNM Gani Ramadani MPRD2, NBRNM 1 Financial Stability, Banking Regulations and Resolution Department. 2 Monetary Policy and Research Department. Monetary Policy Conundrum in Developed Economies  is the Region Different? Ten years after the global crisis, it is more than certain that the context for monetary policy making has not returned to the pre  crisis normal. Central banks, in advanced economies in particular, have deployed unprecedented measures to ensure proper functioning of financial markets, and to provide impetus to the economy. Despite the recent global recovery, uncertainties remain elevated and possible vulnerabilities come to the fore. At the same time, certain macro-economic linkages on which conventional monetary policy making was based on have been challenged. To streamline the matter, we will tackle few important issues, which as monetary policy makers we have been faced with. First, though the monetary accommodation helped the recovery, easy financing conditions might have encouraged excessive risk-taking and building of debt vulnerabilities. Second, inflation rate has been low for long, despite the wage growth in many countries, giving ground to the so called wage  price puzzle, and questioning the traditional Phillips curve concept. Third, given the lingering monetary accommodation, policy space has narrowed, thus constraining the room for reaction if severe shocks occur. In this note, we will make an effort to transpose these challenges to the countries of the CESEE region and asses how relevant these global matters are for them. Policy rates in advanced economies, in the US and the euro area in particular have remained low. The monetary policy normalisation was rolled-back in the US, with the new cycle of lowering the policy rate being opened. In the euro area, the accommodative stance of the ECB was strengthened, by further cutting the interest rates and relaunching the QE programme. These moves enabled for the already easy financing conditions to remain in place, and further easing to be expected as well. This environment in the global context has been conducive for behaviour of yield searching, thus potentially encouraging excessive risk-taking and building up of financial vulnerabilities. Conditioned on the specifics of the region/country, financial vulnerabilities are assessed to be located in different sectors across different countries. According to the financial vulnerability map of the IMF published in the Global Financial Stability Report, October 2019 it seems that the risks stemming for sovereigns are still visible across the board. Similar inference can be made by observing assessed vulnerabilities in nonbank financial sector and nonfinancial corporates, while the picture on households and banks is rather mixed. Chart 1: Financial vulnerabilities  heat map across sectors and group of countries Imes Source: Global financial stability report, IMF 2019. Low interest rates affect the cost for debt-service, thus being conducive for additional leverage in certain segments of the global economy. On the global map, sovereign debt levels remained elevated in some countries, euro area inclusive. As for the private sector debt, data do reveal that in some countries which were more resilient at the beginning, and entered the crisis with lower debt levels, vulnerabilities started to accumulate afterwards. This holds for the household debt, in particular, that proceeded to grow in some countries, raising concerns on the possible financial stability risks (Sweden, Norway, and Switzerland). Hence, it seems that in the global context, leverage issues seems to be on board, exposing some of the countries to risks in case of sudden tightening of financial conditions. In this case, debt level matters, as high levels can exacerbate the impact on growth and stability. How do countries from the CESEE region fit in the image? To answer the question we will dissect the debt data by providing perspective on both sovereign and private sector. In the matter of the sovereign debt, few years ago, it was diagnosed as one of the most vulnerable segments in the economies of the region. In most of the countries, the fiscal response to the crisis was countercyclical, asking for additional borrowing of the government and leading to sharp rise in the government debt level. The cumulative increase in the debt level since the beginning of the global crisis in 2007 until 2015 was close to 25 p.p. of GDP. In some countries, such as Slovenia, Serbia, Montenegro and Croatia, the shift was markedly above the average, with debt levels reaching between 70%-83% of GDP. After 2015, the debt level started to adjust, with a cumulative contraction of around 6 p.p. of GDP, visible in almost all countries in the region. The adjustment was supported through the cyclical recovery of the economies in the region, as well as fiscal discretionary measures, which allowed for fiscal consolidation and precluded further debt accumulation. Though public debt sustainability and vulnerability is a much more complex issue rather than a simple comparison with a benchmark criterion, still even the latter can provide certain guideline on the issues. Chart 2 *Region refers to all the countries in the sample from CEE, SEE and the Baltics. Source: World Economic Outlook, October 2019. The comparison of the public debt levels with the Maastricht Criterion as a benchmark reveals shift towards less vulnerable zone in most of the countries. In 2015, when the average government debt level reached its peak, it was below the accepted benchmark by close to 8 p.p. of GDP, while in 2019, the distance was widened to 14 p.p. and by 2024, it is expected to reach around 20 p.p. (according to the WEO, October 2019 forecast). This clearly indicates that in the last couple of years, despite the low interest rate environment, fiscal space in CESEE region was rebuilt thus reducing public sector exposure to sudden shifts in the sentiment at the global financial markets or reversal in the interest rate cycle. Still it has to be noted that the public debt level is still above the pre-crisis pone, and few of the countries, despite the adjustment, did not succeed in bringing the debt level below 60% of GDP (Albania, Croatia, Hungary, Montenegro, and Slovenia). Even more, in Montenegro the debt level has still been increasing, reaching above 80% of GDP in 2019, raising concerns related to sustainability issues. Private leverage in the region has been rising since early 2000s, albeit mostly from lower levels compared to advanced economies. After reaching the peak at the onset of the global crisis, gradual deleveraging occurred, but debt level remained elevated in comparison to the pre-crisis in many countries. At the outset of the global crisis, the average private debt level reached around 96% of GDP (2009), doubling compared to 2000. The post-crisis adjustment was mostly visible in the Baltic countries, where half of the pre-crisis rise was reversed. In the CEE and SEE countries, the adjustment was lesser. According to the latest available data (2017), given the decoupling in the speed of the post-crisis adjustment, private debt level in the different sub-regions started to converge. The average private debt level in 2017 stood at around 82% of GDP, with Baltics hovering at around 90%, SEE at 84%, and in the CEE region, standing at 75% of GDP. Chart 3. Total private debt Chart 4. Change in private debt to GDP ratios (in % of GDP) (in percentage points) 140.0 120.0 100.0 80.0 60.0 40.0 2002 2004 2006 2008 2010 2012 2014 2016 CEE SEE Baltics Region *Region refers to all the countries in the sample from CEE, SEE and the Baltics. Source: IMF Global debt database. The crisis accentuated the risks of high private sector indebtedness as important source of macro-financial vulnerability. In the CESEE region, some of these risks came to the fore in their banking systems, in the form of significantly rising NPLs during the crisis, following the years of high credit growth. Many countries came under the pressure to adjust their debt levels in line with the economic fundamentals that resulted in deleveraging process by households and corporates. The larger was the leverage build up pre crisis, the larger was deleveraging in its aftermath, in general. This particularly holds for the Baltics where private debt downscaled by 42 p.p. of GDP in 2017 from the peak in 2009. In CESEE region, deleveraging was most evident in Hungary and Slovenia, followed by Bulgaria as the most heavily indebted country pre-crisis. Yet, not all higher-debt countries managed to reduce their debt levels. Croatia, whose debt level rose substantially prior to the crisis, has only marginally deleveraged afterwards. There were also countries like Slovakia, North Macedonia, Poland and the Czech Republic, where the debt continued to rise further, yet, mostly from lower levels in the peak of the crisis. Chart 5. Change in private debt to GDP ratios, Chart 6. Private debt structure, 2017 2009-2017 (in percent of GDP) (in percentage points) *Region refers to all the countries in the sample from CEE, SEE and the Baltics. Source: IMF Global debt database. Cross-sector analysis reveals that the pre-crisis increase in private leverage was almost equally driven by corporate and household sector, as the context was conducive for rising debt across the board. Corporate debt on average rose by 25 p.p. of GDP in 2009 compared to 2000, but marked cross  country differences were visible. In some countries, such as Bulgaria, Croatia, Baltics, Slovenia corporate debt level was rapidly increasing, bringing the debt level very close to 100% of GDP. The higher the debt level, the more difficult the adjustment was, particularly given the soft post crisis economic recovery and hence the low capacity to reduce the debt burden. In fact, only Slovenia and the Baltic states managed to deleverage markedly, while in Bulgaria, the adjustment was slower and the debt level remained relatively high. In some countries such as Slovakia, North Macedonia, Poland and the Czech Republic, the corporate sector continued to accumulate leverage post-crisis. In the case of North Macedonia, the rise in corporate debt was predominantly driven by external borrowing, mirroring the expansion of foreign companies established in the Technological Industrial Development Zones (TIDZ) that mostly rely on external funding through inter-company loans from their parent entities. Corporate debt continues to account for majority of total private debt in most CESEE countries (close to 70% of total private debt on average). Loose financing conditions contribute to mitigating the risks to corporate debt sustainability. Chart 7. Bank credit to households and non-financial corporations (y-o-y change, in percent) Chart 8. Bank credit to households (structure, in percent, 2010-2018 average) (y-o-y growth, in percent, 2010-2018 average) Source: central banks websites. Household debt increased from a very low base in almost all countries in the region, as supply and demand factors kept this segment underserved. Given the pre-crisis context, marked with rising capital inflows, falling interest rates and strong confidence, household debt started to increase. By the beginning of the crisis, it reached around 30% of GDP, with very strong growth observed in the Baltics (reaching close to 50% of GDP). As the crisis occurred, the household debt adjusted as well, but the adjustment was mild, declining by only 5 p.p. of GDP after the crisis. It even continued to increase in some countries -Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Poland and North Macedonia  facilitated by loose financial conditions with the overall perception for this segment being more diversified, with less of a risk and higher quality profile of the overall portfolio. Bank credit extended to households generally grew faster than corporate credit in most CESEE countries post-crisis. Broken down by purpose, there is a growth in housing loans, but consumer loans have also expanded extensively in most of the CESEE countries. Strong growth in consumer credit warrants close vigilance by authorities, given the risks associated to consumer credit as typically unsecured loans with shorter maturity that increases the exposure to credit risk. Some countries implemented macro-prudential measures to curb consumer credit growth and mitigate potential risks from fast rising households credit to financial stability. These measures included tightening of debt service to income ratio (the Czech Republic, Hungary, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia) and/or loan to value ratio rule for housing loans (the Czech Republic, Poland, Romania, Slovenia), limits to the maximum maturity of consumer loans (Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia) and more stringent risk weights on households loans (Poland, Slovenia, North Macedonia). Chart 9. Share of households with a DSTI above 40% (% of all indebted households and 90% confidence interval) Source: Aleksandra Riedi Household debt in CESEE economies: a joint look at macro-and micro-level data, Focus on European Economic Integration, 2019, issue Q1/19 Recent OeNB study3 focusing on household debt in CESEE economies suggests that risks associated to households leverage have moderated post-crisis, but need monitoring in order to timely address potential vulnerabilities. The inference is based not purely on the level and dynamics, but some structural features as well, such as the currency and interest rate structure. Yet, estimated debt service to income ratio (DSTI)4 for all households in all CESEE countries is below 40%, as commonly used threshold in the literature for potential vulnerabilities related to household debt burden. Debt service burden is lowest in Hungary and the Czech Republic, while Romania and Albania stand out as 3 Aleksandra Riedi Household debt in CESEE economies: a joint look at macro-and micro-level data, Focus on European Economic \Integration, 2019, issue Q1/19. The analysis uses macro-level data and data from the OeNB Euro Survey conducted in fall 2017. The indicators we analyze here are based on data from the OeNB Euro Survey. 4 DSTI estimates (from Aleksandra Riedi Household debt in CESEE economies: a joint look at macro-and micro-level data, Focus on European Economic Integration, 2019, issue Q1/19) are based on the OeNB Euro Survey wave conducted in fall 2017, where respondents were asked to report the amount spent per month to service all loans held by household members (including interest and principal payments). Author relates these payments to the households monthly net income also reported by the respondent to calculate the ratio. countries with the highest DSTI. This particularly holds for lower income households as more vulnerable group of households. Romania has the highest share of vulnerable households (with DSTI above 40%) and potentially vulnerable households with low income and low educational attainment. In response to these developments, the National Bank of Romania undertook macro-prudential measures by setting up a cap on indebtedness at 40 percent of net income for leu-denominated loans and 20 percent for foreign currencydenominated loans starting January 2019. Measures are intended to address vulnerabilities associated with highly indebted borrowers and sustain financial stability in the country. Source: IMF Global debt database, IMF WEO database and IMF Financial development index database. Following the post-crisis adjustment, private sector debt to GDP ratio stands very heterogeneous across CESEE countries ranging from about 28% of GDP to 129% of GDP in 2017. In most CESEE countries, debt levels are below the European average which corresponds to the level of economic and financial development. Private sector debt ratios in most of the countries are below the threshold in the Macroeconomic Imbalance Procedure (133% of GDP for total private debt) and MIP based reference values for households and non-financial corporate debt. Favorable financing conditions and solid economic growth recently have alleviated debt sustainability concerns in the region. Yet, there are important differences across countries. In Albania, Romania and the Czech Republic, debt levels are well below MIP based vulnerability benchmarks with private debt having stabilized or decreasing in recent years. In other countries, such as Slovakia, North Macedonia and to some extent Poland, private debt remains moderate by international standards, but is growing post-crisis urging for close vigilance by authorities. There are also countries such as Bulgaria and Croatia where private sector is still highly leveraged and therefore is source of concern for macro-financial stability. European Commission5 notes high corporate debt in Bulgaria as potential drag on investment and growth over the medium term. Deficiencies in the insolvency framework are identified as important factor that slows down the reduction in private sector debt and the workout of nonperforming loans in the country. In its latest report on Croatia6 , the Commission has released the assessment showing that both household and corporate debt are within prudential levels, though still above the levels suggested by the economic fundamentals. The risks are moderating, but remain relevant mainly related to high concentration of corporate debt, exposure to currency risk and potential solvency risk for companies due to the high debt burden relative to corporate financial assets and equity. 5 European Commission Country Report Bulgaria 2019 Including an In-Depth Review on the prevention and correction of macroeconomic imbalances. 6 European Commission Country Report Croatia 2019 Including an In-Depth Review on the prevention and correction of macroeconomic imbalances. Chart 12. Private debt to GDP by countries MO,O Source: IMF Global debt database. Overall, private debt appears sustainable in most CESEE countries, though risks still remain. External environment remains challenging, making the region vulnerable to economic downturn, capital flows reversals and sharp tightening of financial conditions globally. In the event that monetary and financial conditions remain easy for too long, it may stimulate excessive risk-taking and build-up of financial stability risks. This calls for authorities in the region to maintain and further strengthen macro-prudential frameworks, if needed, to reduce vulnerabilities and enhance resilience to shocks. *** The second issue that we tackle in this note is the phenomenon of missing inflation and the wageprice puzzle. The issue became relevant in the last couple of years, in the euro area in particular, where despite the recovery and positive shifts on the labour market, inflation rate remains subdued and below the inflation target. Since 2014, notable improvements on the labour market have been observed, with employment growing on average at a rate of 1.3% in the last five years, compared to the average decline of around 0.5% in the 2009-2014 period. Unemployment rate has been declining steadily, reaching 7.7% in 2019, close to the pre-crisis rate minimum. As the economy gained momentum, the negative output gap began to close, and in the last two years, it has been estimated to be mildly positive. Despite the adjustment of the economy in general, and the labour market in particular, the inflation remained rather soft. In the last three years, the headline inflation rate has averaged 1.5%, thus undershooting the inflation target constantly. At the initial stage, it was related to the subdued wage growth (around 1.3% for the period 2013-16), but with wages beginning to grow at faster pace, the debate was opened and the so called wageprice puzzle was brought to the fore. Chart 13: Euro area inflation, output gap and Chart 14: Euro area headline inflation and core employment growth in % inflation (in percent) Source: IMF WEO Database, October 2019. Source: Eurostat. The debate focused on several important issues related to the labour-costs pass-through, whether it has weakened in intensity in recent years and reasons behind these potential changes. In general, the findings reveal that the impact of wages on inflation might be less pronounced than in the past and relates to three important cyclical and structural factors. The first one relates to more subdued inflation and inflation expectations. The second one relates to the corporate profit margins that tend to be pro-cyclical, with their capacity for absorbing the rise in labour cost changing across the cycle. The third one is a factor of a more structural nature, linked to the rising competitive pressures and overall rising globalization. The results from a study of the IMF (REO  Europe, November 2019) on a sample of EA 153 and the NMSs reveals that all these factors suggest that it is unlikely that the recent increase in wage growth will meaningfully spur inflation in the near term. These findings support the need for monetary policy in many European countries to remain accommodative for a longer period, but at the same time being vigilant as the prolonged period of accommodative financial conditions may have created an environment conducive to greater risk taking. Inflation in the region has been above the average compared with the inflation in the euro area, reflecting the convergence process, the greater exposure to shocks in primary commodities prices, and country specific factors. Yet, the overall inflation dynamics mimics the one in the euro area, given the tight trade linkages. The average headline inflation rate in the CESEE region in 2003  2012 period averaged around 4%, while the euro area inflation gravitated around 2%. In the last six years, a suppression of inflation rate was visible across the board, and in both regions (CESEE and euro area) it averaged around 1%. Some reversal to 2% is observed in the last two years, but it is debated how sustainable the pickup in prices is. Very similar is the pattern of the core inflation, which started decelerating in 2013, averaging around 1%, with converging dynamics in the CESEE and the euro area. The contribution of the core inflation and food and energy prices to the overall inflation rate in the countries of the CESEE region in the last six years on average is generally balanced, with core inflation weighing slightly more. In the euro area, 76% of the average inflation dynamics was driven by the core inflation, and the rest by the more volatile prices. Compared to the 2002-2012 period, on average, in the last couple of years, the importance of core inflation for the dynamics of the headline inflation is much more pronounced, both in the region and the euro area. It either indicates that demand pressures and cost-push factors are becoming more prevalent, or that the pressures from the global commodities prices are becoming lesser. Source: IMF WEO Database, Eurostat and National Statistics. Source: Eurostat and National Statistics. The contribution of the monetary policy relevant inflation rate  core inflation to the overall inflation in the countries in the region has gained weight in the last couple of years. Still, the overall dynamics of the core inflation remains soft, with average growth at around 1%, very close to the growth in the euro area. Given the fundamental relation between the demand and the dynamics of the core inflation, the first area to be scrutinized is the dynamics of the output gap, which can provide for information on the cyclical position of the economy. The precrisis data reveal strong positive output gap, which in 2005-2008 averaged around 5% of the potential GDP. The economies in the region went under strong economic adjustment, as the crisis emerged and their growth was undershooting the potential, leading to negative output gap for much of the postcrisis period except for the past three years. Apparently, despite the post-crisis economic recovery, the momentum gained was not strong enough to lift the output gap away from the negative territory. In the last two-three years, turning point in the cycle can be noticed, though its strength and length is not strong enough to create pressures on the core inflation. Chart 17: Output gap in CESEE region and Euro area (percent of potential GDP) Source: Authors calculation for most of the CESEE countries and IMF WEO Database for Euro Area. The other important concept, which can be linked to prices are the wages, unit labour costs in particular. Although labour costs only account for some 20% of the cost structure of manufacturing firms, and for 40% in the case of firms in the services sector, these figures rise to almost 90% excluding inputs. Accordingly, when value added deflators, which exclude the cost of inputs, are analysed at aggregate level, changes in unit labour costs (that is, employee compensation corrected for productivity gains) are understood to be a fundamental determinant of future changes in prices (Bank of Spain, Economic Bulletin, 2/2019). After the drop in the midstream of the crisis, unit labour costs in the region started to rise moderately until 2017-2018 when sharp rise was noticed, supported by the cyclical upturn, as well as the rise of wages in public sector and minimum wages in some of the countries. During 2011-2016, the overall growth of ULCs in the region averaged around 2%, while in 2017 and 2018 the y/y growth picked up to 5% -very close to the pre-crisis average growth. The sharp rise of the productivity adjusted wages should translate into higher core inflation. Yet, it only supported the disposable income and the rise in private consumption, while price pressures remained subdued. This disconnect between unit labour cost and inflation might indicate probable time lag between the two. Or there might have been structural changes to the way firms incorporate costs into their pricing decisions that has affected the relationship between wage growth and inflation. If firms and workers expect low inflation going forward, for example due to the improved credibility of the central bank, firms may be reluctant to raise their prices even when faced with higher wage costs as they expect increases in costs to be only temporary. In such a situation, the pass-through of higher wages to prices would be muted due to lower expected persistence of cost and price changes. Alternatively, the rise in competition, either domestically or from abroad, may have limited the ability of firms to pass cost increases to consumers for fear of losing market share. Another important consideration of a more cyclical nature is firms profitability, which determines how much and how fast wage growth feeds into prices. To the extent that firms have buffers -comfortable profit margins -they may be able to absorb higher wage costs without increasing prices (IMF, REO -Europe, November 2019). Chart 18: CESEE and Euro area unit labor cost Chart 19: CESEE and Euro area labor productivity (change in percent) per person employed (change in percent) In this note, we will shed some light on the third issue, related to corporate profit margins. As discussed before, we will approximate the change in the profit margin as a difference between the GDP deflator and the change in the unit labor costs. Profit margins are thought to be pro-cyclical, with rising buffers during expansion, and their depletion during downturn, though this cannot be fully confirmed with the data that we have. What can be observed through the data is continuous downsizing of profit markups in the region since 2012, on average at around 1.3%. Apparently, the profitability position of the corporates was comfortable enough to allow for continuous compression across countries and time, thus absorbing the rise in ULCs without passing them through to prices. Despite the adjustment, according to the latest IMF Regional Economic Outlook for Europe, November 2019 the level of the corporate profitability for part of the region that we scrutinize, the NMSs in the EU, is assessed as comfortable at the current juncture. It seems that after-crisis, pass-through from the rising wages to inflation weakened. The IMF study in the REO, November 2019 reveals that inflation expectations, rising competition and profitability buffers can explain the broken link in the euro area and NMSs of the EU. According to our estimates, profitability buffers seem to play role in the region as a whole. This gives more comfort for the central bank in pursuing an accommodative monetary policy. Yet, cautiousness is needed, as once the profitability breakeven is crossed, prices can respond stronger to the overall cycle and wage pressures. Hence, central banks have to be cautious in accommodating, as not always this is warranted by low inflation. Low prices might be a reflection of a more structural features (competition for instance), or cyclical ones (such as profitability). In the first case, the impact of the central bank is constrained, while in the second case  once the impact of the profitability cushion wanes  the monetary accommodation can add to stronger inflation pressures than acceptable. Source: Eurostat, SEE Jobs Gateway Database, National Statistics and Authors calculation. Conclusion In the last couple of years we have dealt with the issue of the impact of the monetary policy normalisation, of the ECB in particular, on the region. At the current stance, not only that normalisation is distant, but rather stronger accommodative approach is being employed. The prolonged monetary expansion has called for greater vigilance in the context of excessive risk taking and debt build-up. At the same time, more scrutiny has been put on the causes of the low inflation that might possible disclose a need for cautiousness in providing monetary stimulus. We have tried to transpose these challenges to the countries in the region, as in some of them economic boundaries for the monetary policy are lesser compared to the ECB, given positive policy rates. Our simple analysis shows that financial vulnerabilities, observed through the leverage of the public and private sector, seem to be contained, despite the loose financial conditions. Sovereign debt has decreased in the last couple of years, indicating that countries use the benign financial conditions for creating more fiscal space. Private leverage is well below some of the accepted benchmarks. Yet in many of the countries, given the low interest rate environment, household credits are on a rising path, and potential risks are addressed through macro-prudential measures. Hence, some vigilance is needed, with respect to build-up of financial vulnerabilities, though they seem to be much lesser in the region compared to the more advanced economies. Inflation dynamics and its drivers seem to resemble those in the euro area, asking for more profound scrutiny of prices, before proceeding with monetary loosening. At the current juncture, it seems that despite the monetary policy space which exists in part of the region, further policy cuts should be carefully calibrated and considered in the context of country specific assessment of future financial and inflation risks.
