The latter is prerequisite to preclude devaluation of the data, and statistics plays a critical role in preserving the value of data. In the new era when we have open access to multiple sources of information, it is not enough official statistics to be disseminated more effectively, but it has to be accepted, understood and trusted by the general public. Good official statistics, as dramatically shown during the Covid-19 crisis, can be crucial to provide a first line of defence against misinformation (Biancotti et al., 2020)[2]. High quality and reliable statistics is the weapon against fake news and divisive messages. More than ever as policy makers we are faced with misinformation, fake news and speculations that can undermine our ability to act effectively. The digital environment, the growing role of social media and absence of clear regulatory framework propelled the dissemination of the so called mal-information. For example, we as a central bank, faced ungrounded speculations against the exchange rate on a couple of occasions. Keeping us 24/7 alerted is the least damage that this type of irresponsible behaviour implies. But the social costs, the damage to the public and the confusion it creates, the harm to the integrity of the institutions and their credibility is enormous. Uninformed agent can base their financial decision on unsound grounds, thus incurring personal economic losses. And we as institutions might suffer erosion of our credibility that could hamper us in delivering on our public goods. What can be done to mitigate the impact of misinformation in the modern world? Let me refer on this note on the Study on Societal Costs of Fake News in the Digital Single Market[3] and transpose it to economics. First, it is the selfregulation of the industry  raising awareness of misinformation, costs that it can entail for the society and need of factchecking. Second is the regulation  creating clear and transparent rules of game. Third, education -media and information literacy can lead to increased public awareness and capacity to critically asses the news, including fake news. Against this background, how can we as producers of statistics contribute in this regard? It appears that adequate communication of our data to the public can help crowd out low quality statistics. We need to consider how to bring closer the statistical products of our work to the public. It is true, that we as central banks have provided to the public a vast portfolio of statistical data, with many dimensions, metadata and public explanations. However, the data, or the explanations may not count if they do not reach the public and do not influence their decisions. According to some estimates, by 2025, 463 exabytes of data will be created each day globally. This means huge generation of data that can blur the official statistical information making it difficult for people to read and understand it. Obviously, to bring statistics closer to the public we need to place further focus on aspects such as putting numbers in perspective so that they can be easily understood by the wider public, language simplification, that sometimes is not an easy task for experts that are used to statistical taxonomy, segmentation of the audience (communicate not only to financial analysts and journalist, but to the broader audience, although through different channels), as well as creation of relatable content that considers what matters to the public and at the same time is educational and entertaining[4]. Along those lines, the National Bank, recognizing the importance of communication, engages in quite an array of activities. At the end, I feel that it is appropriate to conclude my address with the motto of the European Statistics Day 2021 Statistics, a vaccine to protect democracy and combat the virus of disinformation. [1] Survey of National Statistical Offices (NSOs) during COVID-19,World Bank and the United Nations Statistical Division (UNSD), brief, July 6 2020. [2] Biancotti C., Borin A., Cingano F., Tommasino P., Veronese G., The case for a coordinated COVID-19 response: No country is an island, 18 March 2020 [3] Prof. Dr FRAU-MEIGS D., Societal Costs of Fake News in the Digital Single Market, University Sorbonne Nouvelle, Paris, France, European Parliament's Committee on the Internal Market and Consumer Protection, January 2019 [4] Nunes L.M, Colaco A., Marques R., Oliveira M., When reaching is no longer enough: 8 tips to engage with Central Banks data users, Banco de Portugal, ISI, 63 World Statistics Congress, 2021

Title: World Austerity Day organised by the Macedonian Banking Association (MBA)
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Address by National Bank Vice Governor Anna Mitreska to mark World Austerity Day organised by the Macedonian Banking Association (MBA) Respected Minister of Finance, Mr Fatmir Besimi, Respected Director of the Deposit Insurance Fund, Mr. Amir Shabani, Respected President of the Macedonian Banking Association, Mrs Maja Stevkova-Sterieva, Dear colleagues, I thank you for the invitation and the opportunity given on behalf of the central bank to address this event, which marks World Austerity Day. Going back to genesis and the essence of marking this day, it is interesting to see that its basis is the understanding of "austerity as an expression of the maturity of individuals, but also societies as a whole". Many aspects are based on this thesis, such as the financial literacy of each individual, trust in institutions, the development of the economy and the capacity to save, the responsibility of those who manage savings and direct them for productive purposes to increase the potential of the entire economy. World Austerity Day, the second year in a row, is marked in pandemic conditions and from there I will stick to several main issues that are particularly relevant due to the prolonged health crisis. First, what are the consequences of the pandemic on the volume of austerity and its structure? Second, do the new circumstances change the investment behaviour of the population and what consequences can it have on financial stability? Third, what are the processes that have accelerated and surfaced because of the pandemic, and what are the possibilities for productive use of austerity and financial support for sustainable projects by the financial sector? Unlike other episodes of crisis, the pandemic actually increased austerity and this process is a global phenomenon. In developed countries, the estimated surplus of savings in 2020 was close to 7% of GDP, showing that more was saved in the pandemic than in normal circumstances. In the Western Balkans region, domestic austerity rates measured as a difference between income generated and total private sector and state consumption saw a slight decrease of about 3p from GDP, but in conditions of strong fiscal spending to support economies. This means that private sector austerity, despite a major recession, is highly likely to have remained relatively stable or growing. There are three reasons that contribute to such a phenomenon. First, despite the recession, the available income did not suffer a reduction, in part because of the fiscal momentum to support wages and jobs. Furthermore, given the nature of the crisis, restrictive measures and movement restrictions, some of the population has faced a forced reduction in consumption, primarily the consumption of various services, which is characteristic of people with higher incomes and with greater capacity and propensity to save. Thirdly, since all future economic flows are conditional on an extremely uncertain epidemiological curve, in such an ambition, the motive of caution plays a major role in the behaviour of savers. Both the European Commission and us and the Western Balkan countries show that the surveys of respondents in 2020 and 2021 are in favour of the view that due to the economic situation during this period, austerity is a more favourable decision, compared to past years. At the same time, surveys by our Statistical Office show a decrease in the use of savings as a source of income during 2020. What has been happening to saving in the banking system in our country since the beginning of the pandemic? Deposit potential increases at a relatively solly intensity of over 8% on an annual basis, making the increase dynamics very similar to that of 2018\u20122019. Such dynamics do not resemble events during the global financial crisis, when deposit growth slowed in a short time, which of about 20%, decreased to about 7% year-on-year. These trends show that the propensity to save and retain funds in the banking system remains high. Population austerity is growing dynamically, within historical trends. However, the unique character of the crisis leaves consequences for its structure. Given the unpredictability, the propensity for long-term savings is decreasing, and the participation of these deposits in total population deposits since April last year has decreased by five percentage points so far. On the other hand, in the corporate sector, growth rates are significantly above the historical average, with refrain from investment activity and asset growth. Past crisis episodes have been characterised by a reduction in corporate deposits, which shows that the crown crisis encourages different behavior. Due to the pandemic, the propensity to hold liquidity and austerity increases, in conditions of pronounced and prolonged unpredictability. In addition to the growth in savings in banks, in the face of a pandemic, the growing propensity of the population to invest in real estate is remarkable. In fact, in low interest rates conditions, relatively stable disposable income, reduced opportunities and consumption needs, change in working models, globally there has been an increase in demand for real estate and real estate prices. Unlike a number of economic indicators that collapsed during the pandemic, real estate prices are growing. In EU countries, in the first half of this year, real estate prices have seen an average growth of close to 7%, versus growth of about 4% in the past few years. In our country, price growth is more moderate than about 4.4% during this year, but with signs of acceleration. Throughout the region and in our country, housing lending is accelerating and growth rates are more dynamic than consumer credit growth. For now, real estate market movements appear to be moving in line with shifts in supply and demand, and price pressures exist, but it is not as pronounced as it is in European Union countries. However, this "pandemic syndrome" should be closely monitored, as the banking system's exposure to the real estate market is increasing. Hence, there is a need for strengthened monitoring of this part of the portfolio and the preservation of banks' capacity to deal with possible future shocks. Banking systems, both in the region and in our country, pass the test imposed by the pandemic crisis, and the challenge of maintaining credit support capacity while maintaining stability will remain in the next period. Indicators of solvency, liquidity, bank profitability and credit portfolio quality remain stable, and some of them have improved further. But the crisis is gaining a prolonged dimension and can leave lasting consequences and impose a need for restructuring in some sectors of the economy. Currently, disruption of global supply chains and cost growth are creating disruptions in certain industries and are one of the greater risks to the expected economic recovery. Hence, the priority at the moment is to monitor all risks in a timely manner and identify them in a timely manner, due to a reduction in the burden on banks' balance sheets. According to the latest EIB poll, some banks in the wider CEE region expect a some increase in dysfunctional rankings in the coming period. Upward shifts are possible in our country, but for now stress tests show sufficient resilience to the banking system, under a solid regulatory framework, cautious behaviour of banks and signs of economic recovery. The central bank's policy has been loosened for now, contributing to favourable financing conditions and economic recovery, in conditions where we have enough comfort in foreign exchange reserves to respond to possible shocks. Of course, given the uncertain ambition, we constantly and closely monitor the trends of all indicators relevant to monetary policy. Currently, almost all countries, with austerity growth, sources are increasing to finance banks and their capacity to support the economy, especially at points that will respond to new post-pandemic demands and increase growth potential. The transition to a green economy is undoubtedly one of the issues that, with the pandemic, from the margins, has shifted to the core of priorities. The preferences of both consumers and global investors are changing and the "appetite" for so-called green technologies and business models is increasing. In such fundamental, global structural changes, and our competitiveness as an economy will depend on the ability to rapidly transition to infrastructure that will provide green-stamped products. Otherwise, the opportunity to be competitive in both product markets and access to financing will be low and costs high. Financial support from the banking system can significantly accelerate this transition and help increase the competitiveness of the domestic economy. Probably faster than expected, the world is at a crossroads when structural changes need to accelerate, accelerate the transition to a digital and green economy, allow for sustainable, post-pandemic global recovery. The role of the financial sector in this regard is great, as its stability and readiness for financial support will largely depend on the capacity of the entire economy to tackle new challenges. Finally, allow me on behalf of the National Bank to congratulate Austerity Day, and special congratulations to this year's plaque winners u2012recognitions for achieved special results in the performance of the work tasks. Thank you! Skopje, 29 October 2021

Title: Concluding remarks on the 8th Research Conference, Aneta Krstevska, Chief Economist, National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Concluding remarks on the 8th Research Conference, Aneta Krstevska, Chief Economist, National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia I will try to make a short wrap up of the discussion during these two days, by mentioning the main points that came out from the conference. In a period when one shock is replaced by another one, policy makers are facing multiple challenges. During the last several months we have seen how quickly inflation can rise, triggered mainly by commodity prices. However, the central banks are fully aware of the current risks. It seems clear that the global economy is moving towards monetary policy tightening (although, as we have seen today there is still ongoing debate), currently mainly to stabilize inflationary expectations and second round impact of rising commodity prices. The key to higher sustainable growth is to strengthen the productive capacity of the economies, therefore the structural changes need to continue, more than ever. The ongoing de-globalization requires urgent improvements in the infrastructure, faster and low-cost linkages between trading partners in order to avoid disruptions in value chains, transition to green economy and therefore energy sector transformation and support of green finance, sustainable agriculture, and finally digitalization and consumer protection in order to increase financial inclusion. The financial sector went relatively well throughout corona crisis, however vigilance is still needed in view of prolonged uncertainty and the new geopolitical risks. In view of higher financial inclusion, the banking, but also non- banking sector should continue to provide options for easier access to finance, especially to SMEs. On the other side, improving managerial practices in SMEs should also contribute to meet eligibility criteria for financing. Special attention is needed on private sector indebtedness, having in mind the ongoing or expected tightening of the financial conditions and in some countries the increase in housing prices. In the new age, the Central Banks must find the right balance between the current and new Central Banks challenges regarding digitalization, green finance and financial inclusion. In this view, the cooperation and appropriate involvement by the private and non-government sector is crucial. Regarding climate risks, as globally important topic, we realized that private sector initiatives certainly provide support to the climate agenda of the policymakers. We need to pay attention on the nearshoring potential of the region in a really critical moment of international environment, calling upon appropriate policy action in favor of FDI attraction. As a conclusion, having sound policies and prudent and proactive management in place should make easier to face any unexpected shock and will build more resilient economies across the world, that was actually the main topic of the conference. In the last couple of years, the macroeconomic and financial topics changed a lot - from taking lessons from the last global financial crisis to facing and managing new crisis and new risks. I hope we fully accommodated to the changed agenda of policy makers currently and that you found the conference and the overall discussion useful. Let me thank to EIB for being co-organizer of this event, for their overall support and engagement. Many thanks to all panelists, presenters, moderators and discussants and the overall organizing team. Many thanks to all of you who came here and all of you who joined us on-line. Hope to see you again, on our next events. Thank you!

Title: Chief economist Krstevska at the M6 Educational Centre "Step Forward": The difference between our inflation and EU inflation is a reflection of domestic structural factors
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Chief Economist Krstevska at the M6 Education Centre conference "Step Forward": The gap between our inflation and EU inflation is a reflection of domestic structural factors Scotland, 24 November 2022 "A global shock hits all economies, but domestic structural factors in each of the economies determine the intensity of inflation ... The dependence on imports and the degree of trade openness of our economy are significantly higher compared to the European Union. Openness and dependence on imports are reflected in imports and their structure, further on the structure of consumption and, consequently, on domestic prices. These structural factors largely explain the difference between domestic inflation and inflation in the euro area," noted Aneta Krstevska, Chief Economist of the National Bank, who presented the latest macroeconomic projections to the business community, at the M6 Education Center conference titled "Step Forward in the Macedonian Economy in Double Shock  Where Are We Heading?" She noted that further geopolitical tensions from the military invasion of Ukraine, in conditions when the world is still suffering the consequences of the pandemic, have contributed to the deterioration of the global environment, adversely affected the economic outlook and created additional pressures on world prices of basic products. Central banks around the world have responded by tightening monetary policy due to the amplified and prolonged growth in global inflation, which is reflected in financing conditions. "Global movements have also affected the domestic economy, with lower growth compared to April projections. Inflation for this year has been revised upwards, given the higher performances so far, but it is important to stress that next year the inflation rate is expected to slow down, which will be 8-9% in 2023, with price pressures gradually easing from import prices, subsidising the price of electricity for the food industry and tightening monetary conditions." Krstevska stressed that inflation, according to the National Bank's projections, will continue to stabilize, coming down to the levels of 2.4% and 2% in 2024 and 2025. All the measures taken so far by the National Bank in relation to inflation were explained to the business community, through various instruments. At the same time, it was emphasized that the approach of gradual but steady tightening of monetary policy is already having effects in certain segments, and further effects are expected, to the extent possible in this type of inflation  cost inflation. "The National Bank is resolute in dealing with inflation and inflationary pressures, given that price stability is a basic prerequisite for economic growth," Krstevska concluded. At the conference held within the framework of the project "M6 Step Forward", the short- and medium-term challenges of the Macedonian economy were discussed by representatives of the institutions and the business sector.

Title: NB Chief Economist, Krstevska: Through stimulation of savings to inflation stabilization
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: NB Chief Economist, Krstevska: Through stimulation of savings to inflation stabilization Skopje, 24 July 2023 "Central banks around the world are in the phase of conducting a tighter monetary policy, to deal with pressures on inflation and inflation expectations. Reduced or delayed consumption in periods of increased interest rates, amid simultaneous stimulation of savings, contributes to returning price stability in the long run, which is critical for the standard of living of the population. At the moment, global inflation slows down, but the risks are still present and there is a need for further vigilance, said the Chief Economist of the National Bank, Aneta Krstevska, in an interview for Bloomberg Adria. Krstevska explained that the tightening of the monetary policy by definition means lower consumption, in order to reduce inflation and inflation expectations. "We believe that in periods of higher inflation, we all better understand the importance of price stability, i.e. of low and predictable inflation rates. Constant inflation is caused mainly by global factors - the prices of food and energy, but with indirect effects on other prices and inflation expectations, she said. Referring to the domestic context, Krstevska emphasized that inflation has been slowing down for eight months, while in the last few months it is also accompanied by a slowdown in core inflation, and there are positive trends in the dynamics and currency structure of deposits. Inflation is currently in line with the latest forecast of the National Bank, according to which this year inflation would be 8 - 9%, on average, annually (compared to 14.2% last year), and it will slow down also next year. Concerning the foreign exchange market developments, the Chief Economist of the National Bank pointed out that they were stable, and the foreign reserves were at a solid level. Regarding the monitoring of the monetary signals by the banking system, Krstevska pointed out that according to the Bank Lending Survey of the National Bank, the responses received from the banks suggest an increased influence of the monetary policy on the policies of the banking sector. These responses correspond to the upward changes in the bank interest rates, including deposits, which enabled an appropriate acceleration in the deposit growth. Changes in newly approved loans and newly received deposits were more significant, but in the course of time, that change became visible in total loans and deposits. The changes in deposit interest rates are gradual, but constant for several months, which indicates appropriate caution of banks for the interest yield of deposits, as their main funding source. In any case, the National Bank made gradual changes to the monetary policy, in order to avoid sudden changes in the economy, Krstevska says. Amid global uncertainty and increasing interest rates, same as in many other countries of the region and beyond, the credit growth from the beginning of this year slightly decelerated, but remains moderate (6.5% annually in May). The National Bank made efforts also in these conditions to improve the structure of lending, by encouraging green loans to banks in order to support the energy transition of the economy. For this purpose, the National Bank in the past period adequately adjusted the set of available instruments, i.e. it continued to use the reserve requirement for unconventional purposes (release from reserve requirement for loans for renewable energy sources), followed by expansion of the banking portfolios with green loans, said the Chief Economist of the National Bank.

Title: Angelovska-Bejoska for MIA: Denar is stable, changing denari in foreign exchange is an unnecessary cost to citizens
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Angelovska-Bejoska for MIA: The denar is stable, converting denars into foreign exchange is an unnecessary expense for citizens March 13, 2022 With all responsibility, the National Bank stands behind the fact that the denar is stable and will remain stable. "There's no reason to change course, it's not going to benefit anyone," National Bank Governor Anita Angelovska-Bejoska said in an interview with MIA. She points out that the National Bank has the capacity and tools to defend the exchange rate of the denar if necessary, as evidenced by the past almost three decades, when the stability of the domestic currency has been successfully maintained through many crises. Foreign exchange reserves are high at 3.4 billion, or double the level of 2008, which was the year of the global financial crisis, and the stability of the denar has been successfully maintained. Regarding the information that there is no foreign exchange in the market, the governor says that this is not true and appeals to citizens not to succumb to such speculation. - I have to address this issue, because in reality these speculations are causing material damage to the citizens. We are witnessing that, at a time when we are talking about a crisis, still some citizens are resorting to converting savings into foreign currency or buying foreign exchange cash. In addition, there is speculation that there are no currencies in the market, which is absolutely not true. In this way, unfounded panic is created and citizens, based on speculation, pay a higher price for changing currencies and lose funds, the governor stressed. In the interview, the governor also revealed whether there will be double-digit inflation and whether the National Bank is planning measures similar to those during the health crisis when there was a temporary delay in the credit obligations of citizens and firms. Governor, the Russia-Ukraine crisis is clearly affecting the economy. While there are no direct effects on our economy, the rise in food and energy prices on world stock markets is also being felt by us. The cost of living is rising every day. Some experts predict that double-digit inflation is not expected. How realistic are these expectations?  The direct exposure of our economy to the Russian and Ukrainian economies is admittedly small, but from the very beginning, before the conflict escalated, we indicated that indirect effects were expected through energy and food prices and through reduced growth of the European economy. This comes from the fact that our economy is an open con-European economy (77 percent of our exports are to the EU), and the European economy is exposed to the Russian and Ukrainian economies. Exposure is particularly high towards Russia through energy imports, given that Russia is the EU's main supplier of crude oil, natural gas and solid fossil fuels. Hence, the main risks to Europe, and through it to our economy, are higher inflation and lower economic growth. In fact, higher inflation alone is expected to halt the trend of gradual recovery in personal consumption which will adversely affect growth. According to the ECB, the eurozone inflation projection has been revised upwards and is expected to stand at 5.1 percent this year, before easing to the 2 percent level the central bank is targeting. In some scenarios, it could be as high as 7.1 percent this year. On the other hand, the eurozone growth projection has been revised downwards. In this context, the ECB has not yet tightened monetary policy, i.e. it has not taken a decision to raise interest rates, and has continued to inject liquidity into the economy, albeit with a slightly lower intensity than previously expected. In terms of inflation in our country, upward price movements are present  a phenomenon present in all countries right now. This phenomenon is mainly a reflection of rising world prices of primary products (food and energy), but also generally rising import prices of other products. This is especially evident in economies that are import-dependent, i.e. where a significant proportion of consumption is imported, such as our own economy. In fact, we are the most open economy in the Western Balkans region, and in the Central South East Europe region, we are the most open economy. The ECB's latest projections for inflation in the EU, as our most significant import partner, as well as upward revisions of global energy and food prices, point to higher inflation in our country this year and then a gradual decline next year. However, we should keep in mind that lower economic growth will mean lower demand for goods and services. Hence, the assumptions change, there are several factors that may act on inflation in the coming period, and what their impact will be depends a lot on the further development of the crisis, the intensity, duration, new sanctions, etc. Also, the fiscal measures taken should mitigate the short-term effects. If there are more pronounced demand-side pressures, there should be no dilemma that the National Bank will react promptly with the tools at its disposal. We monitor events at home and abroad daily. At least once a month, the monetary policy setup is fully reviewed. International financial institutions assess that the National Bank is pursuing an appropriate monetary policy. In short, all we have to do is do it. We are making every effort to maintain macroeconomic stability while contributing to favorable interest rates for individuals and companies, and the economy. Russia's invasion of Ukraine has created fears of a devaluation of the denar. As a central bank, you came out with information that the denar is stable. Can a central bank, with all the instruments at its disposal, guarantee that the national currency will remain stable?  Categorically, with all responsibility, the National Bank stands behind the fact that the denar is stable and will remain stable. There's no reason to change course, it's not going to benefit anyone. We have the capacity and we have the tools to defend the exchange rate of the denarius, if the need arises. The momentum speaks volumes over the past nearly three decades, when the stability of the domestic currency has been successfully maintained through many crises. As for the instruments, although we have more instruments at our disposal, I will highlight the most important one  foreign exchange reserves, which are high, 3.4 billion euros, or at twice the level compared to 2008, the crisis year, the year of the global financial crisis, when we also successfully maintained the stability of the denar. And the IMF's latest country report, released last month, indicates that the level of foreign exchange reserves is appropriate to the exchange rate policy we apply. In the report, the Fund finds that the level of the exchange rate is fully compatible with economic circumstances and policies and there is absolutely no need for any change. In addition, the central bank has access to a special repo line, i.e. additional foreign exchange liquidity in the amount of 400 million, which the European Central Bank made available to us back in 2020. This means that the National Bank has additional room for quick and effective action if it is necessary to mitigate possible negative effects on the domestic economy and financial markets, given the uncertainty of the current global economic and geopolitical crisis. Recently, speculation has become more frequent regarding the demand for foreign currencies, specifically the euro, in the domestic market. I have to address this issue, because realistically these speculations are causing material harm to citizens. We are witnessing that, at a time when we are talking about a crisis, still some citizens are resorting to converting savings into foreign currency or buying foreign exchange cash. In addition, there is speculation that there are no currencies in the market, which is absolutely not true. This creates baseless panic and citizens, based on speculation, pay a higher price for changing currencies and lose assets. Consequently, I would again point out, the National Bank remains committed to maintaining the stability of the domestic currency and has sufficient funds to provide foreign exchange liquidity. Given the new situation, can we expect that the Macedonian economy will reach the growth projections or will the National Bank come up with a correction of the projections? "We ended last year with growth that was almost entirely in line with our latest projections, in which we forecast growth of 3.9 percent for both last year and this year. However, those projections did not anticipate developments in Ukraine, which are causing turbulence in global markets. Escalating conditions are exacerbating pre-existing problems from slow supply chains, and we are all witnessing the volatility it causes in energy, food, and other resource prices. The diurnal oscillations in both the upward and downward directions are extremely large. This shows that we are currently facing volatility and unpredictability, which make forecasting difficult. Under such circumstances, subjects' expectations change, and reluctance to spend and invest may increase. Hence, the risks to economic growth are downward, and to what extent the impact of all these factors will be expressed will depend, among other things, on further developments in Ukraine, which are currently very uncertain. For us, a significant factor is the developments and growth prospects of the EU, as our most significant trading partner, and of course the growth of import prices, in line with their impact on foreign and domestic demand. In line with the ECB's latest estimates, the outlook for economic growth in the euro area has deteriorated as a result of the effects of developments in Ukraine on energy prices, confidence and trade, which is why economic growth projections have been revised downwards for 2022 (by 0.5 percentage points) and minimally for 2023. These expectations of the ECB are based on the assumption that the ongoing disruptions in energy supply and the negative effects on confidence associated with the military conflict are temporary, without a more serious impact on global supply chains. Given the high uncertainty of military developments, we assume two alternative scenarios  an adverse scenario, in the event of the introduction of tougher sanctions against Russia, which would also affect global supply chains, and second, an extreme scenario, in the event of a more pronounced reduction in energy supply and thus a stronger reaction to energy prices and financial markets and more pronounced price pass-through effects  according to which growth in 2022 would be lower in an interval of 1, 2 to 1.4 pp relative to the baseline scenario. The spring cycle of macroeconomic projections is underway, within which new information and risks will be discussed in detail, after which the National Bank will come up with new observations for the next period. The banking sector has proven to be resilient during the health crisis and has shown to be resilient even in times of crisis. You assure that he is still stable and ready to respond to the challenges arising from the Russian-Ukrainian conflict. How powerful are domestic banks in such complex conditions to respond to the needs of companies and citizens?  As you yourself stated in the question, the banking system, as many times before, has proven to be resilient to shocks and has successfully dealt with the challenges of the health crisis. At the same time, what is particularly important, and I would like to emphasise, is that throughout this period the banking sector has been able to provide solid credit support to the real sector, which is a significant impetus for the economic recovery. It is through this channel that relaxed monetary policy has been and is a major contributor to supporting the private sector in times of crisis. These have been our assessments and expectations since the beginning of the pandemic and the same assessments we have now. We look at a number of indicators for the banking sector, which the National Bank monitors regularly, some of them on a daily basis. They show that the protective capacity of the domestic banking sector has not only been maintained but has been further strengthened during this period. The system has an adequate level of capitalization, with a capital adequacy rate of 17.3 percent, which is a higher level compared to before the onset of the corona crisis. The loan portfolio is healthy, with a non-performing loan rate of 3.3 per cent and marking an improvement over the pre-pandemic period. Lending has continued to grow since the beginning of this year and stood at 8.6 per cent in January, with loans being granted to both the population and the corporate sector. This is supported by further growth in deposits, which are up 8.5 per cent since January. We do not expect developments in Ukraine to have a significant direct impact on the domestic banking sector, due to the very weak financial ties it has with Russia and Ukraine. An additional factor is the absence of capital from these two countries in the domestic banking sector. Also, regular stress tests show that the banking system as a whole is resistant to possible shocks. These are all facts that speak to the soundness and stability of the domestic banking sector. And this is not only our assessment, but it is also noted in the reports of international institutions. So, to summarize my answer to your question  yes, the domestic banking system has the capacity and complex conditions to respond to the needs of citizens and companies, and this was best confirmed during the pandemic. The latest data shows that this time around, too, it is prepared to deal with risks, should they arise, and has the capacity to support the economy. If there is a deepening of the crisis, is there any possibility that the banking sector will temporarily defer the loan obligations of citizens and firms, following the example of such a measure at the beginning of the health crisis?  Regulatory easing allowing for temporary deferral of credit obligations was enacted in response to the specific shock of the pandemic, to mitigate liquidity pressures on the private sector, which were very pronounced at the time and could spill over into solvency, with a permanent impairment of creditworthiness for a large number of clients. This also protected banks' balance sheets from possible over-stockpiling of bad loans in a short period of time, which would limit lending activity. Seen from today's perspective, the measures have yielded results by easing the financial burden on the population and the corporate sector. Almost two years after the introduction of such a measure, banks' loan portfolios are of good quality. I would note that even without regulatory relief and in accordance with existing regulation, banks have the option to restructure receivables, i.e. to change the contractual terms of a loan or reverse credit exposure to close an existing one, of a customer who has a deteriorating financial condition or has signs of a deterioration in his financial condition, as a result of which he cannot or could not comply with the agreed terms. This is a regular opportunity, in line with international and European standards that are embedded in domestic regulation. Of course, we, as the central bank, will continue to monitor developments and react accordingly if necessary, with measures that will most appropriately respond to the overall situation, of course with the priority of maintaining macroeconomic and financial stability, which is the basis of the National Bank's actions. (MIA) Biljana Anastasova-Kosti photo: Frosina Naskowi

Title: Address by National Bank Governor Anita Angelovska Bejoska at the presentation of the EBRD TransitionReport 2021-2022
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: OGpakahte Ha ryBepHepKaTa Ha HapoflHaia 6aHKa AHi/iTa AHrenoBCKa BeKOCKa Ha npe3eHTai_njaTa Ha TpaH3m4HCKMOT M3BeLUTaj 2021-2022 Ha EBOP Presentation of the EBRD Transition Report 2021-22 Opening of the event Anita Angelovska Bezhoska, Governor National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia 24 March 2022 Dear colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, At the beginning let me thank you for the kind invitation to address you at the launch of the latest Transition Report that analyses and measures the progress of transition economies on their way towards higher income levels. It is indeed my privilege. For us, in the transition world, the Report has always been an important guideline, both with respect to advices on how to address the deep-seated structural issues, but on cutting edge maters as well. In the current context, it even gets more prominence by providing valuable insights in the extent to which the unprecedented shock have derailed policymakers from structural agenda, which is a key precondition for faster transition. Similar to most of the countries in the world, the emergence of the pandemic has hit Macedonian economy severely. Although it caught us on a strong footing with solid economic fundamentals and absence of any significant disequilibria, the economic activity plunged by 6%-which has not been observed in the last two decades. Despite the rebound during last year, not all economic losses were recovered. The economy is still below the pre- pandemic level, and even more importantly, the growth outlook is under new threat in the midstream of the recent upheavals in Ukraine. Subsequent shocks and the need to respond in crisis management mode increase the risk of distancing from structural policies that provide impetus to a faster transition and more productive growth. However, growth decomposition exercise reveals that even before the health crisis, the growth of the Macedonian economy, similar to the growth of other CESEE transition economies, was not predominantly driven by innovative and efficient sources. The average growth in the decade preceding the pandemics gravitated around 2.5%, somewhat above the CESEE average, with the contribution of total factor productivity (TFP), as a measure of economic efficiency and innovation, being relatively marginal. Although two thirds of growth dynamic was capital driven, the impact of the ICT capital was rather small. Labour had also positive contribution to the growth, but it was predominantly due to labour quantity, and less due to labour quality. During the pandemics, the bulk of the adjustment in fact went through the TFP which declined close to 5%, as the overall context was barely conducive for innovative decisions. In this context, global competitiveness index in terms of innovation capabilities and ICT adoption locates us at the 97th and 70th rank (out of 152 countries), similar to Western Balkans peers, but much further from the advanced Europe. Jointly with several countries in the region, we were positioned in the group of efficiency enhancers, meaning that reforms must be intensified to increase the growth efficiency and quality. Increasing the technological readiness was one of the identified priorities. Thus, in the last decade, the Macedonian productivity level has been staggering to around 40% of the level of advanced economies, such as German economy. This clearly points that if we want to grow at stronger pace and in a more sustainable, green and inclusive way, we need to continue intensively addressing the structural hurdles for the key long-term determinants of the growth: labour, capital and productivity. Let me focus on productivity. At this point, I think I can bring in the highlight of the latest Transition Report, i.e., innovation and digitalisation of the economies. The adoption of digital technologies can unleash productivity revival and possibly counteract some forces that act as drag on growth, such as adverse demographic and emigration trends that dampen the labour supply. What is the pace of digitalization of the Macedonian Economy? The new EBRD digitalization index points to a progress in both segments that are captured by the index - first, the preconditions for the use of digital technologies (digital infrastructure, skills, regulation, provision of government services), and second, the actual use of digital technologies by individuals and companies. The progress is particularly visible in the area of regulation and provision of government services, where score has more than doubled. Still, overall we are scored about 59% for digital preconditions and 48% for the actual use of digital technologies, which is close to the regional score, but still far from the frontier of 100. I think that the scores are useful guidelines on where the policies should be focused on. In our case, it is clear that efforts should be concerted in setting a more adequate digital infrastructure, but even more in raising digital skills. On the latter, as noted in the report, significant efforts should be employed in enhancing digital training by employers and limiting digital brain drain. The more limited digital skills are, the more difficult it is to use new technologies and more limited are the growth prospects, in the world of rising digital intensive sectors. In this overall context, as a central bank we have our eyes laid on the financial sector. Obviously, advancement in technology opens the door to innovative financial services, but to unlock its true value for businesses and consumers, we as regulators have a role to play. Against this background, we have embarked on many activities in this area, including setting up an Innovation Hub in 2019, which interacts and supports companies that are willing to pursue innovative business. Last year we conducted a broad based survey, with an aim to map the ecosystem, as a base for policy calibration. The survey revealed that 90% of the respondents recognize the need for digital innovation in the financial sector and 72% are already in the process of implementing some form of digital transformation. There is an agreement among respondents that regulation can sometimes be a barrier for a swifter innovation. To eliminate regulatory barriers, a new Law on Payment Systems has been prepared and is currently undergoing a parliamentary procedure. We have already drafted the First National FinTech Strategy, which will soon be shared with other stakeholders. Tomorrow, under our initiative, all financial regulators will sign a Memorandum for setting up a FinTech Committee with a view of promoting digitalization in the financial sector. To recap, there are no doubts that faster and inclusive income convergence calls for strengthened efforts to lift the growth potential, and perhaps even more importantly to lift the quality of growth. In this context, we would like to express our gratitude to EBRD for supporting us for almost three decades with more than EUR 2 billion total investment to date aimed at supporting competitiveness, trade integration and green transition. Despite the current headwinds which put economic growth at risk and require immediate policy focus, we should not lose sight of a longer term structural agenda, including digitalization. As Andy Rooney said, Everyone wants to live on top of the mountain, but all the happiness and growth occurs while youre climbing it. So, let us keep climbing. Thank you. Closing of the event Anita Angelovska Bezhoska, Governor National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia 24 March 2022 At the end, let me thank the colleagues from the EBRD for the highly insightful presentations on the state of the economy and the main challenges of the WB region as well as the main findings of the Transition Report, which primarily focuses on digitalization. This does not come as a surprise knowing that digitalization has been significantly boosted during the pandemics, bringing a number of benefits to the societies, including support for faster transition and income convergence. Despite the efforts, income gap of the Western Balkan economies in comparison with the EU still remains wide - regional income is only about 38% of the European income. This largely correlates with the level of productivity in the region that significantly lags behind the EU productivity. And, the increase in productivity can be achieved only by structural and institutional reforms, including digitalization that can lead to more efficient allocation of resources. Thank you

Title: Note of the Governor of the National Bank: 30 years of monetary independence
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Governor's Note: 30 Years of Monetary Independence Friday, April 26, 2022 Today we mark an important jubilee, a monument to the building of our country. Thirty years ago, under the baton of the Monetary Empowerment Commission, our national currency, the denari, was introduced. At the same time, the institutional framework of the monetary system was established  the National Bank began to function as an independent central bank. Although a relatively young central bank, over the past 30 years, the National Bank has faced a number of challenges, which it has successfully answered. The first years of monetary independence were marked by periods of hyperinflation, recession, insufficient foreign reserves, persistent depreciation of the domestic currency, and general macroeconomic instability. In response, in October 1995, the monetary strategy of a stable exchange rate of the denar against the Deutsche Mark was introduced, while since January 2002, the exchange rate of the denar has been pegged to the euro. For the fixed exchange rate strategy, both then and now, there is a consensus that it is one of the key pillars of the stability of the Macedonian economy. The stability of the denar and financial stability were preserved even in the wake of the most acute economic crisis, caused by the Covid-19 virus pandemic. The National Bank was one of the pillars that kept the entire economic system stable, achieving its mandate goals, supporting the economy through appropriate policies and measures. I will not be wrong if I say that after this crisis, both the economy and the institutions that are part of the economic system have become stronger. The National Bank has reiterated its commitment to maintaining the stability of the denar and it will continue to be "anchored in the stability of our economy" in the future. We constantly maintain foreign exchange reserves at a comfortable level, guaranteeing the stability of the currency. The banking system is set up on a fully market basis and is stable, liquid, and sufficiently capitalized to provide credit support for economic activity. In terms of the framework for the operation of the banking system, we have received significant recognition from the European Union, which has placed us on the list of only 26 other countries in the world whose banking regulation and supervision meets European standards. The victories won over the past 30 years, in crisis and periods of economic growth, would certainly not have been possible without the National Bank's most valuable asset  human capital. Over the years, the central bank's efforts have always been aimed at recruiting quality staff, upgrading them, and continuously learning throughout their institutional careers. I will not be immodest if I say that our cadres set standards for work, not only in the country but beyond, which has been marked by numerous accolades over the years. Here, I would like to thank you for the strong support we have from international financial institutions, which, together with our dedication, allows us to have a high-quality core of professionals. This year's jubilee  30 years of the denar and 30 years of the central bank's independence  should be a national pride for all of us. What we can say as a central bank is that we will otherwise be upright in facing all future challenges, guaranteeing the stability and prosperity of our society.

Title: Address by Anita Angelovska Bezhoska, Governor of the National Bank, at the presentation of the EBRD Transition Report 2021-22
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Introduction speech by Anita Angelovska Bezhoska, Governor of the National Bank, at the marking of the 30 years of monetary independence Skopje, 28 April 2022 Distinguished Minister of Finance, Respected members of the Government Dear guests, Distinguished President of the Republic of North Macedonia, Distinguished Prime Minister of the Republic of North Macedonia, It has long been said that history is a witness to the past, example and lesson to the present and lesson and warning to the future. Therefore, the celebration of the thirtieth anniversary of a momentous event, such as the monetary independence of the modern Macedonian state, is not just an honor and a motive for celebration. It is also an obligation, standing before the generations of devotees who have invested in what is today our modern monetary history, but also before the generations to whom we owe the future. the great Goran Stefanovski once said, "Identity is a story about who we are, why we are, and what we want." Monetary independence and our currency - the denar are the central chapter in our story - an essential element of our identity. In 1991, the dream of an independent, sovereign and autonomous, modern Macedonian state came true. Yet, without the monetary independence that happened these days in 1992, without an independent central bank and without a national currency, our would not have been complete. We must not forget this, neither today nor at any time in the future, not only to valorize the past, but also to be able to make now our contribution to the future of our authentic story. What is more, we must never forget that we have an obligation to continue the story in this chapter, because as Stefanovski said, "identity is both work and responsibility." It is the work and the responsibility that have been the exact postulates of the National Bank over the past thirty years. A lot of work, with full commitment, independence and professionalism in overcoming challenges and achieving goals under various, not always easy circumstances, in historical turmoil and milestones. Not only as an occasion, but essentially we must keep reminding ourselves where we started off thirty years ago. At the beginning of this crucial monetary chapter of our story we started with almost zero foreign reserves, hyperinflation which in 1992 reached close to 1700%, recession, permanent depreciation of the domestic currency and general macroeconomic instability. The effect of all this was experienced by the citizens and all stakeholders in the economy, which was flagging until 1996. We must never forget it, because when the memory of historical events is lost, the potential for critical observation and making the right decisions in the present moment is lost as well. But we do remember! We also remember the series of bold and decisive steps of the then policymakers towards macroeconomic stabilization, further supported by international financial institutions, especially through the first arrangements with the IMF and the World Bank back in 1993. The results were gradual inflation drop to single digits, enhanced foreign reserves, control of monetary aggregates, and consolidation of the fiscal sector. Crucially, in 1995, the monetary strategy of stable exchange rate of the denar was furnished - a strategy that is an anchor of stability of the Macedonian economy today. The same year, soon after the adoption of the bank regulation and supervision, the banking system was rehabilitated, and later on transformed on a market basis. Six years later, the payment system reform was introduced, along with the building of other central bank capacities, including in the field of statistics, financial market operations, treasury operations and, of course, research as a significant support for the monetary decision-making. All this created preconditions for the 25-year long monetary chapter of our story to be engraved with macroeconomic stability and compliance with international and European standards. For many years now, the European Commission, in its annual progress reports on monetary policy, has noted a high level of compliance with the European legislation. However, in recent years, besides the constant improvement, we have also confronted and responded to a series of challenges, both domestic and global. Just to recall the crisis episodes of 2001, 2008 and 2016, when we as a central bank had to deal with a crisis of confidence, unfortunately prompted by numerous speculations. In all these episodes, we faced pressures on exchange rate and foreign reserves. As an example, during the 2008/2009 Global Financial Crisis we lost as much as a third of them. There were also periods of bank runs. For example, during the 2001 crisis, the deposits dropped by as much as 8% in a very short period of time. Unfortunately, even in the recent period we have not been spared from serious challenges. The pandemic brought about economic losses, again required the use of foreign reserves to maintain stability of the domestic currency, as well as financial policies to support economy and maintain the banking system stability. This pandemic crisis, for various reasons, has made the issue of inflation relevant again, putting it in the focus of central banks. And the still ongoing pandemic was followed by another major shock - the war in Ukraine, which is not only a human tragedy, but also produces economic cost in the form of inflationary pressures and slowdown of economic recovery. All these crisis episodes remind us that the denar stability is a public good?benefit and crucial for the general economic stability. This illustrates how great our responsibility is as an institution that has a mandate to preserve its stability. But all other incumbents in society also have a responsibility to make their contribution, because we all benefit from the macroeconomic stability. Unfortunately, we know that in these turbulent times, speculations have occurred more than once and caused nothing but harm to you, us, the entire economy. On this special day for us, when we celebrate a jubilee that is important not only for the National Bank, but also for the homeland and the entire nation, standing in front of you, I once again declare - the denar stability is guaranteed! Dear guests, We must always appreciate and respect the achievements of the past thirty years and to praise highly the contribution of all those who have been part of the central bank and managed to build and maintain an institution that is independent, transparent, highly professional, and esteemed in the international community. But I also thank all the incumbents of our society who have been fully aware that an independent central bank is a prerequisite for the future of our story. On behalf of the National Bank, allow me to express my genuine appreciation to the international financial institutions that lent our central bank a hand after the monetary independence and to this day have constantly supported us in our efforts to do our utmost for the Macedonian economy and citizens. Just as an illustration and example, I would like to remind you that in early 2019, we adhered to the highest statistical data dissemination standard of the IMF, as the eighteenth country in the world and last year, the European Commission adopted a Decision assessing that the banking regulations and supervision implemented by the National Bank are in line with the standards of the European Union. This puts us on the list of only 26 countries in the world that adhered to these standards. Still, regardless of the commitment and the standards, without the trust and contribution of the citizens, no central bank can fully achieve its goals. That is why we are committed to transparency, both to them and to all economic agents, which is why transparency is one of our strategic goals. The National Bank is the second central bank in the world for which the IMF made an assessment according to the latest Transparency Code and we are glad that it found that our bank is implementing advanced transparency practices. Dear guests, Each historically significant anniversary puts us at a crossroads, and depending on what has already been achieved, requires from us to figure out which direction to take. Therefore, I must emphasize that regardless of how the country's European integration process will proceed, the European standards will continue to be our guide to the European family of central banks. And then, when the European chapter of our story is completed and the denar remains our historical symbol of stability, I believe that it will be confirmed once again that as a central bank we have walked down the right path. Since the 2008/2009 Global Financial Crisis and the experiences of the COVID crisis, in a time of accelerated changes on the world stage as a result of globalization, digitalization and financial innovation, the mandate of central banks has been constantly changing and expanding with new functions. All current and new functions and activities of modern central banks that protect the public interest are already part of our vision, but not as an activity that we forecast for the time future and distant, but as something we are already working on. Among other things, we are particularly dedicated to financial education and inclusion given the importance of increasing knowledge about financial services, especially at a time of rapid fintech development, which would eventually provide easier access to finance for citizens and companies. In support of the fintech development, we drafted the first version of the national strategy, with a view of making our story a regional leader in this area as well. Following the example of the European Central Bank, this year, when we celebrate thirty years of the introduction of the denar as our currency, we initiated activities to consider the introduction of a digital denar. If the analyses show that there is a need for introduction of a digital denar, hopefully, during some of the next celebrations of the day of monetary independence we will talk about the digital denar as an official means of payment in the country. Dear guests, The great Goran Stefanovski, whose words inspired me to open my address tonight, also reminded us that stories are the core of our lives and that they are not something that is planned, but something that is created and won every day - just like the freedom. Therefore, the National Bank will continue to write and add to the monetary chapter of our story, working professionally and responsibly for the benefit of the citizens, guided by the European central banking principles. Congratulations on the anniversary and the celebration of the stable denar which is something that belongs to all of us, the citizens, the present and future generations!

Title: Address by Governor Anita Angelovska-Bejoska to mark the opening ceremony of the exhibition "V/VALUES AND VALUES"
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Address by Governor Anita Angelovska-Bejoska on the occasion of the Opening Ceremony of the exhibition "IN/VALUES AND VALUES" Scotland, 8 July 2022 Dear President of the Republic of North Macedonia, Honourable Members of the Government, appreciate Excellencies, representatives of the judicial authorities, guests from academia and institutions that preserve and nurture culture, Ladies and gentlemen, The independence of our country is the greatest benefit to all of us who live on this piece of land. By undermining statehood, we have created a shared future based on historical facts, on records, on aspirations, as well as on cultural differences and historical intersections. In 1991 we realized our dream of an independent, sovereign state, but our nationhood would not be complete without monetary autonomy  an independent central bank and its own currency. The monetary chapter of our story began on April 26, 1992, when the first Prime Minister of our country, Nikola Kljusev, showed the first Macedonian money from the pulpit of the Assembly. But money is not just a symbol of our monetary sovereignty, it doesn't just talk about the face value that is inscribed on it, it talks about the values created in the past, about our history and culture. The design of the first transitional edition of paper money is the work of the team from the printing house "11October", and the banknotes bear artistic solutions from Macedonian history. Speaking of the character of the coins that are in circulation today, it is inevitable to mention the work of the Macedonian artist Biljana Unkovska.The 200 and 2000 denar banknotes are the author's work of graphic designer Lasko Dzurovski. The artistic eye and sense of belonging and pride of everyone involved in the crafting process contributed to our banknotes carrying the beauties of the Macedonian soil. In doing so, the fundamental value of money is added to the preserved value of cultural wealth, the designation of the region, the contribution of our ancestors. It was by creating the image of money that we showed that from time immemorial this little piece of land of ours values were valued, zealously committed to a better tomorrow. Centuries passed, cultures were networked, historical and cultural values were created and remained. Celebrating this year's jubilee  the 30th anniversary of monetary independence, the National Bank, as the holder of the exclusive right to print and issue our currency, had an obligation to remind of these great values of the Macedonian soil, values of the past that have been passed on to us and left to future generations of preservation and nurturing. Today, before us and in front of the Macedonian public, here at the Museum of the National Bank, we have the opportunity to see the story of Macedonian money, to witness the beauty of the values selected and placed on the front and back of the Macedonian currency. Together, we commemorate the art of Macedonian money, whose name, denoting Roman silver coins, was used in this territory more than 2,000 years ago. Look at the money. You will see some of the most significant archaeological discoveries, icons, frescoes, architectural buildings from centuries ago, which reflect the multiethnic character of our region. You will sail back to the early sixth millennium B.C., at a time when on this soil the artistic creation and beliefs of prehistoric man created the extraordinary Great Mother. In the third and second centuries B.C., when the valuable artisan hands of ancient Lychnid made sumptuous gold jewellery, among it was the gold studded earring, now represented by the tenden-day earring. You will see the colorful peacock of the mosaic at Stobi, before you will pour out the beauties of fresco painting, of architectural buildings, of the Colorful Mosque, of the ceiling rosette of an Albanian house from Debar, of the copper vessels  saani, of the golden mask. You will see that our Macedonian money bears witness to priceless wealth and urges us to continue to explore and nurture this treasure. I am glad that, as a result of the efforts of the author of the exhibition, our colleague Kateryna Hristovska and her team from the Museum, as well as the support of other cultural institutions, today each of us has the opportunity to directly witness a part of this priceless treasure, for which I express my great gratitude. Our museum, which this year marks two decades of its existence and support for culture, once again reminds us that history does not and must not forget its greatest values. Dear Readers, It has long been said that at the moment of creation, state sovereignty, including monetary sovereignty, is an idea, a longing, a dream come true, and a nation's dream come true, but in every moment thereafter, it takes a lot of work, responsibility, and wisdom to preserve and develop. Hence, as a central bank, we have a responsibility and honour to continue to maintain monetary stability as our primary objective, but also to support the protection of our numismatic heritage and the study of the long and complex monetary past on this soil. And one day, when we become part of the European family, the denar will remain our historical symbol of stability, and new generations will write a new chapter of our authentic story. In the end, to enjoy art which, as the German artist Paul Klee put it, does not produce the visible, but makes it visible. You're thankful,

Title: Address by Governor Angelovska-Bejoska at panel discussion number: "Measurement of values - economic visions"
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Governor Angelovska-Bejoska's Keynote Address at the Panel Discussion: "Measurability of Values  Economic Considerations" C/Values and Values \u2012 Debate on Fundamental Values in the Contemporary Social Context \u2012 National Bank Museum, 2 \u2012 5 September 2022 Good afternoon everyone! Distinguished participants in today's debate, Academicians Bexheti and Fiti, Professor Popovski, Mr. Hajredini, former member of the Council of the National Bank, Professor Mojsovska, distinguished representatives, heads of public institutions, financial institutions, honourable ladies and gentlemen. As individuals, we create and leave a mark on values throughout our lives. We carry that stamp everywhere, in our personal and professional aspirations, in all our attempts to build, create, and actually heed Einstein's advice "to strive not to be success, but to be worth." All of our individual attempts, aspirations, and actions are the foundation for the creation of collective, societal pillars, pillars that can withstand the burden of future challenges, and will be malleable enough to be upgraded and strengthened by future generations. In the past three decades of the state's independence, for many actors in society, these postulates have been the guide for creating, building and facing all the challenges of one of the greatest economic transformations. The transition to a market-oriented economic system, the stabilization of the economy, the integration into global and financial flows, the establishment of its own monetary system and its own currency  all these were extremely serious steps that required vision, uniformity in strategic directions and value setting. I think that in the field of central banking, we have managed to steadily go through the process of transformation and with integrity and professionalism to maintain existing and build new values. Only three years after monetary independence have we managed to tame the inevitable hyperinflation and stabilize the exchange rate by establishing macro-financial stability, which has been continuously maintained for two and a half decades. In fact, unlike some other transition countries, we have succeeded in trying to provide a strong institutional framework and stabilize inflation from four to single digits since the initial wave of transition. And that's how we set the foundation. I will not speak again about all the efforts made at the central bank over the past three decades in which we have grown and matured into an institution that can be compared to the most modern central banks. There are many achievements and confirmations from relevant international and European institutions that speak about it. But I want to point out that in all of these efforts and decades there is one constant that has been tested  high professional responsibility and commitment! Because the responsibility in decision-making in monetary policy is extremely great, because they are crucial for the nation, for every citizen, for the homeland and for its future. That is why in all the past 30 years, every move and every decision of the National Bank, both in episodes of crisis and in calmer times, has actually been and is at stake in the future  in the time when the homeland belongs to the next generations. As a central bank, despite numerous crisis episodes, for more than two decades we have successfully ensured one of the key prerequisites for economic growth  macroeconomic stability. But to raise the quality of life for each of us and to increase well-being, it is not enough. It is generally known that in the long run, the drivers of growth may not be monetary factors, but rather structural factors, such as human potential, physical capital, and productivity. Our income level of only 38% of Europe's, as well as the slow progress in closing this huge gap (only 3 percentage points in the past decade) alarm that serious changes are needed in structural segments such as good governance, the rule of law, in the quality and quantity of human potential, to prevent demographic decline, to find ways to grow efficiently and innovatively. Because it is actually the "gateway" to faster, but more importantly, to better develop society. Unfortunately, the challenges in these structural segments continue to be numerous. In the decade before the pandemic, our economy was growing at an average rate of about 2.5%, which is slightly higher compared to the countries of Central and South Eastern Europe, yet this growth did not stem from productivity, as an indicator of innovation and efficiency. Our productivity has stagnated for a long time at a low level of only 40% of Germany's productivity level. It is good that investments have also made a solid contribution to growth, given the fact that our capital volume is only 43% of European capital, however, there is little participation in investment in innovative capital, i.e. innovative technologies. Human capital has also made a positive contribution to development over the past decade, but mainly as a result of quantity, not quality, of labor. The severe shocks that the world has been facing over the past few years, including our economy, are bringing to the surface structural weaknesses and the overwhelming need to reform and expand the economy. In addition, according to some estimates, the pandemic shock alone has reduced the growth potential of economies  for the countries of Central and South Eastern Europe  by an average of 1 percentage point. The pandemic and now the war in Ukraine are creating a different world and order. The geopolitical order is changing, we are witnessing rapid polarization, rapid changes in the behavior of economic subjects, economic disintegration and deglobalization. The global value system is changing. The economic consequences of all these developments are great, inflation in the world and at home is rising, under the pressure of sharp and unprecedented growth in the prices of basic resources. We are facing a long-unseen combination of rising prices on the one hand, and downward risks and prospects for the economy on the other, the risk of stagflation. This is particularly challenging for economies such as the UK, which have not yet fully recovered and returned to pre-pandemic levels, while at the same time having high trade openness, which means greater vulnerability to external shocks. In this context, the challenge for policymakers is enormous  how do we stabilise inflation, which is primarily caused by supply-side factors, while not significantly disrupting the recovery of economies? It goes without saying that we, like other central banks, are consistent with the primary mandate that we have, which is to maintain medium-term price stability with all available instruments. However, it is of paramount importance that there is a good interaction between monetary and fiscal policies, which, by their very nature, can contribute more directly to alleviating price pressures, but also provide support to the most affected citizens and sectors of the economy. However, given the limited fiscal space, as well as the need for a prudent fiscal stance and beyond without creating additional demand-side pressures, good prioritisation and setting of fiscal targets is required. It is clear that in times of crisis, macroeconomic policies are the first line of defense, but their room for maneuver is not unlimited. Hence, in times when we deal with crises, usually by taking swift and short-term macroeconomic measures, we must not lose focus on structural measures that reduce the vulnerabilities of economies, increase growth potential, and thus provide room for macroeconomic policy maneuver. But it is obvious that it takes a lot of effort, dedication and generational responsibility for this kind of reform. Let's recall an example from university textbooks, in which we were taught as students that the most important disparities facing our economy in the 1990s were the backwardness of energy, the backwardness of the raw material complex, the backwardness of food production, the backwardness of traffic, etc. Unfortunately, three decades later, these findings about the imbalances, i.e., structural weaknesses, of our economy are still similar. Indeed, the strength of this current economic shock is also the result of a lack of commitment to these segments over the past period. Given the complexity of dealing with disparities, it reminds us once again of the historical responsibility we have today  what values we will affirm and create with our current decisions, how much we will build on the experience gained and the lessons learned from the past, and how much we will show a clear vision of the future. Let's go back to the end of the concept of values. In the times we live in, it seems increasingly difficult to come up with a single definition of what "value" is in the true sense of the word. If we consult interpretative dictionaries, we will often find two meanings in them: first, an assessment that something should be considered important, and second, principles or standards of behavior, decision-making, and evaluation. It seems that one meaning does not exclude the other, because whether we make a correct assessment that something should be considered important depends on what principles or standards of behavior and valuation we have, both as individuals, and as institutions, but also as a society, nation, and state. It depends not only on what attitude we have in valuing what our predecessors have left behind, but also on what values we will create in our present.
