The result of what has been achieved by our predecessors is more than visible  preconditions have been created for 25 years of macroeconomic stability and the introduction of high international and European standards  stable money, stable prices and a stable banking system, but also built awareness of both citizens and policy holders about the importance of this stability, for the nation and the state, for the present and future generations. These are some of the most important values that the National Bank has built into our economy. But it has succeeded precisely because of the principles of behavior, decision-making, and valuation, which are both institutional values  dedication, responsibility, independence, and professionalism. It is our obligation and responsibility, as the current generation of the central bank, to do our part by adhering to those institutional values. It is in this context that I would like to quote George Bernard Shaw in the end: "We become wise not only by remembering our past, but by taking responsibility for our future." Thank you!

Title: Speech by Ms Anita Angelovska Bezhoska, Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia, at the 14th Conference on Payments and Market Infrastructures, 4-5 October 2022
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Speech by Ms Anita Angelovska Bezhoska, Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia, at the 14th Conference on Payments and Market Infrastructures, 4-5 October 2022 Flourishing Digital Payments Future Your Excellences, Dear Governor Tabakovic, Ms. van Dijk, distinguished speakers, Ladies and gentlemen, It is my great pleasure and honour to welcome you at our traditional Conference on Payments and Market Infrastructures, which is organised for the fourteenth time in collaboration with the Dutch central bank, which we deeply appreciate. Given the perpetual changes in payments industry, the conference has always served as a valuable platform for discussion on the latest trends, innovative ideas, as well as new risks that innovation brings. There is no doubt that the process of dramatic transformation of financial industry, which has been in place for years and significantly accelerated by the pandemics, continues. At the forefront of this transformation are the payments, where new payment systems, new payment methods and new players are shaping the payment landscape. We are witnessing a proliferation of fast (instant) retail payment systems across the world, making payments more convenient, easily available and fast. According to BIS, currently fast retail systems operate in 45 countries, with expectations for this number to climb to 60 in near future. Payment methods are evolving as well. Payments are becoming increasingly cashless, thus being one of the main drivers of stronger financial inclusion worldwide, supporting the development of digital economies and driving innovation. According to the latest Global Findex survey of the World Bank (2021), two thirds of adults around the world made or received at least one digital payment. In high-income economies, 95 percent of adults did so, compared with 57 percent of adults in developing economies. Although a gap between developed and developing economies is visible, yet in the latter group major positive shifts have been taking place in recent years. The share of adults involved in digital payments has grown rapidly-by 22 p.p.in the last seven years. These trends are also present in the Macedonian economy where 74% of adults were involved in digital payment, an increase of 20 p.p. in the last 7 years. Even more importantly, according to PwC analysis, global cashless payment volumes are set to increase by more than 80% by 2025, and to almost triple by 2030. This innovation in payment methods is significantly underpinned by proliferation of newcomers in the payments landscape, which have significantly increased the competition to the benefit of the consumers. According to BIS, non-bank players that provide payment services now account for a quarter from all payment institutions, up from only 14% six years ago. There is also an increase in e-money providers, but to a lesser extent. This significantly affects the environment in which banks as traditional players operate, bringing threats, but also new opportunities. Although new players have advantages, as they are less robust and less regulated, the big data analytics and Al are providing to the banks opportunities to keep pace with the transformation. Recent EBRD Survey indicates that dominant part of the banks consider fintech to be more of a threat than an opportunity pointing to a strong competition in the area of digital payments. Still, it is encouraging that banks identify digitalisation as one of the top priorities. In fact, 46 per cent of the surveyed banks pointed that digitalization will have profound bearing on their business over the next 25 years. The Survey conducted by our central bank points to a similar conclusion - banks awareness and focus on the digital transformation appears to be accelerated by the pandemic. All of the banks declared their plans to increase their investment in digitalization and 38% intend to increase their investments in fintech companies/startups. Which are the major forces that have been shaping this digital revolution in payment industry in terms of new payment systems, new methods and new players? More broadly, there are three groups of factors defining the digital era in payments - technological advancement, regulatory environment and evolving consumers preferences. Safety and efficiency of transactions remain the main underlying of the modern payments system, but speed and convenience are becoming equally important requirements by consumers. No doubt that the COVID pandemic and related lockdowns influenced the consumer behavior and preferences markedly. The share of non-cash payments in total GDP sharply increased across the globe (BIS, 2021) and according to one of the latest surveys on banking, fintech and payments organizations (PwC, 2021), 90% of respondents agreed that the shift towards e-commerce would continue to increase, requiring significant investment in online payment solutions. Looking forward, it is clear that these factors, namely, technological progress, consumer preferences and regulatory environment will continue to shape the future of payments. In addition, we should not lose sight of CBDS initiatives, which in essence are policymakers response to the digital revolution. In fact, the digital currencies of central banks are predicted to have the most disruptive impact in the payment system in the next 20 years. According to the latest data, 105 countries, comprising 95% of the global GDP are researching on the various aspects of digital currencies, while this number in 2020 was only 35. We as a central bank have also envisaged a medium-term project to explore the benefits that digital currency can bring for the Macedonian payment system and more broadly for the overall economy, but also to explore the risks that it may imply for the financial stability and monetary policy. CBDC are expected to be in particular beneficial for financial inclusion, which in turn, as documented by many empirical studies, have positive effects for growth prospects. Worldwide there has been significant progress in recent period, but still around 1.4 billion of people remain unbanked. Also, in the Macedonian economy, there has been a notable progress in financial inclusion, measured through access to credit and debit cards and bank accounts - 85% of adult population has a bank account, which is above the world average of 76% and 71% for developing economies. Still, despite the progress gaps to advanced economies remain, gender and age group gap, in particular. It is critical to build on these encouraging trends, especially given the current headwinds - accelerated inflation and decelerated growth that hurt poor the most. Evidence shows that households and businesses that have better access to financial services are better able to withstand financial shocks than those that do not. Overall, it is apparent that tectonic changes are occurring in the payment and financial industry in general. It is confluence of many factors and many involved parties. These include central banks, government, traditional finance industry, and new players. Therefore all the efforts must be coordinated, inclusive and based on a strong mutual partnership. In this vein, we as a central bank have already embarked on a number of activities for setting the stage for faster penetration of innovation in finance. We established the Innovation Gateway in 2019, as a platform for a dialogue with Fintechs to facilitate the entry of new technologies in finance. Furthermore, two years ago we conducted a thorough survey to landscape the development of the fintech sector and to assess the opportunities and barriers for faster innovation, which clearly pointed to regulatory and small market size barriers. Meeting the challenge with full enthusiasm leads us to another joint journey with other financial regulators - preparation of our first National Fintech Strategy. These highly coordinated institutional efforts are expected to create synergetic effects in the design and implementation of the envisaged concrete steps. With the new Law on Payment Services and Payment Systems, that was adopted this year, we as authorities have created a regulatory framework, which hopefully will catalyse Flourishing Digital Payments Future to be written successfully in our country as well. Having in mind the small size of our economy, we highly appreciate regional initiatives conducive to faster and cheaper domestic and cross border payment services such as the ongoing initiative to connect Western Balkan economies with the Target Instant Payment System (TIPS) of ECB. Also, thanks to governor Tabakovic and her team, we are currently exploring the possibility of deepening our excellent cooperation by connecting with payment system operated by the National Bank of Serbia. These regional efforts mean additional step in connecting our businesses, our citizens, and more broadly our economies supporting each other in our mutual strivings to higher income convergence. I believe that during the Conference we will see, learn and hear about Flourishing Digital Payments Future, which will change the payment behavior and experience for all of us and build a more convenient, safe and accessible payment world, as this is a new and highly innovative world in which what is now proved, was once only imagined - William Blake. I wish you an enjoyable and rewarding virtual conference. Thank you.

Title: Speech by Dr Anita Angelovska-Bejoska, Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of Northern Macedonia, on the occasion of World Austerity Day
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Speech by Dr. Anita Angelovska-Bejoska, Governor of the National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia, on the occasion of World Savings Day Dear Attendees, Ladies and gentlemen, It is my pleasure to address today's World Savings Day event, where we are reminded of the benefits that savings brings, both for each individual and for economies as a whole. Domestic savings are particularly important for small, lower-income economies because savings depend on investment, and without investments that increase long-term growth potential, higher income levels are possible. Indeed, one of the key reasons for slower economic growth and slowed convergence in the CEE region in the decade before the pandemic is precisely lower investment in the context of reduced domestic savings and reduced foreign capital inflows. Domestic savings, as the difference between total income created and consumption, is particularly important in the context of tightening conditions in international financial markets. After a decade of low inflation and extremely low interest rates, the global landscape has suddenly changed this year. Inflation has accelerated significantly, reaching historically high levels, and the answer to this is a synchronized cycle of monetary policy tightening. This basically leads to more difficult access and a significantly higher cost to foreign sources of financing (foreign savings). Thus, Eurobond yields of countries in the region have suddenly risen since the beginning of the year (by an average of 500 basis points), which led to a decrease in the amount of government securities issued by about 55% compared to last year, and instead more attention is paid to domestic markets (domestic savings). Savings in the form of bank deposits is one of the most traditional, and therefore the most common, forms of savings in many countries, including our country. About 60% of households' financial assets are in the form of bank deposits. Viewed over the years, household deposits have grown almost steadily at solid growth rates and with only occasional oscillations and transient reactions to economic and political developments. This indicates an established tradition and enduring trust of the beneficiaries, including in the past few years which have been marked by strong succession, which are reflected in household disposable income and its potential for savings. What more specifically does our experience so far show us about the dynamics of austerity in developed and less developed economies? In developed countries, austerity has seen high growth during the pandemic. In the euro area, the household savings rate reached an all-time high of 25% of GDP in the second quarter of 2020, driven mainly by bank deposits. Analyses[1] for the eurozone show that the main factor behind such movements is so-called "forced" austerity in the face of introduced safeguards that have limited consumption, as well as extensive fiscal stimulus to support income. There is also caution due to the uncertainty caused by the pandemic. According to surveys, the majority of households were still unable to increase their savings during the pandemic. Savings were concentrated in 20% of the population, mainly among the wealthier and older segments of society. Such a structure reduces the role of these savings in mitigating the energy shock, as households that have been saving are generally less sensitive to the energy crisis. According to data from the beginning of this year, the savings rate in the eurozone is decreasing and is expected to fall to pre-pandemic levels by the end of the year[2]. In the CE countries, deposits also saw growth during the pandemic period, but weaker compared to the eurozone. According to a study by the Austrian Central Bank[3], the savings rate (measured by the participation of savers in the total population) was stable on average during the pandemic, i.e. about 50%. The Macedonian economy is among the countries that have seen a decline in the number of savers. However, the pandemic has impacted the ability to save. Between 40 and 50 percent of respondents reported that they had saved less during the pandemic, and a smaller proportion (under 20 percent) had used their savings to mitigate the shock. As in developed countries, anti-crisis measures have mainly targeted lower-income households that do not have savings to protect against shocks. The analysis also examines the factors influencing savings, and finds that the leading factor on which the state and growth of savings largely depend are expectations for the future economic condition of the country. In addition, the analysis suggests that elevated inflation expectations and, to a lesser extent, negative past experiences (hyperinflation, banking crises, deposit freezes) reflect adversely on new savings. If we analyze the most recent year-to-date movements, they clearly show a slowdown in deposit growth in both developed and less developed economies. In the domestic economy, growth in total deposits has also slowed, largely stemming from corporate deposits, while in households, movements have been more stable. The average annual growth rate of household deposits in the first nine months of this year was 5.1%, which is close to the previous year's average (5.6%). Compared to previous crises, the growth of household deposits in this period is weaker relative to the global economic crisis, but is several times higher than the average growth achieved in 2016 (1.8%), a comparable period given the prevailing speculation about the stability of domestic banks and the exchange rate of the domestic currency. As then, so now, speculation was short-lived, and expectations stabilized relatively quickly. The stability of the exchange rate was successfully maintained, which once again confirmed the credibility of the fixed exchange rate strategy. We have also taken more targeted measures to encourage denar savings through amendments to the reserve instrument. The latest data, especially from the third quarter, give early signals of the impact of these measures, i.e. the contribution of denar deposits to the growth of total household deposits. Long-term deposits are also on the rise, after a longer period of decline since the start of the pandemic, which is supported by banks' proactive approach by offering new deposit products with higher interest rates. To stimulate savings, the stability of the banking sector is extremely important, which has been successfully maintained even after multiple shocks and has actually been further strengthened since the beginning of the pandemic, with banks being better capitalized, maintaining solid liquidity, and reducing the share of non-performing loans below pre-pandemic levels. All of this is indicative of the banking sector's solid resilience to shocks. However, we are facing major global shocks, high uncertainty, and a cycle of rising interest rates that can again test the resilience of the real economy, especially when fiscal support space is limited and the banking system becomes resilient. Hence, the National Bank acted preemptively and enacted a macroprudential measure, which introduced a countercyclical capital shield rate, which would further strengthen the capital strength of domestic banks. In fact, one of the lessons we have all learned from the global economic crisis is that the most important thing is to make a thorough assessment of the risk being taken, to identify the appropriate value correction at the first sign of its realization, as well as to raise capital to maximize the power to mitigate possible losses, especially in the face of a solid rate of profitability of the banking system. Finally, financial education plays an important role in savings, especially in the context of the dynamism and innovation of the financial system, which emphasizes the importance of proper understanding of financial concepts and reliable information when making financial decisions. This is particularly important in banking systems such as ours, where so-called "small savers" predominate  94% of individuals' deposit accounts (including transaction accounts) are made into deposits worth up to EUR 5,000. Hence, financial education and financial inclusion are important both for the stability of existing ones and for fostering new savings. In this context, the National Bank has been investing more and more in this sphere in recent years, and with the adoption of the first National Strategy for Financial Education and Financial Inclusion, our country has stood out among the first in the region. Dear Readers, We live in a time of extreme geopolitical and economic uncertainty, as well as structural shifts in the global economy, caused by climate change and increasing digitalization. At a time when the concept of frugality is becoming even more meaningful, understood in a broader sense  from prudent consumption and use of resources to investments in renewable energy sources and environmentally sustainable projects. Of course, the most important thing for the transformation of economies is the support of the financial system, and its capacity is based precisely on the savings of citizens. In this context, I would single out a quote from the great thinker and philosopher Aristotle, who talks about money in general, but I would depict saving: "Saving is a guarantee that in the future we can have what we want. Although we may not have any need at the moment, austerity provides us with the opportunity to afford the need when it arises." I congratulate you on World Savings Day, and I congratulate the winners of the Best Bank Clerk Plaques for their success. Thank you! Title: Address by Governor Anita Angelovska-Bejoska in the stand "Economic journalism from independence to the present day - journalists and the National Bank in the direction of informing and financial education of the public"
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Governor Anita Angelovska-Bejoska's Address at the Panel "Economic Journalism: From Independence to the Present - Journalists and the National Bank in the Direction of Information and Financial Education of the Public" "Public Communication and Transparency of the National Bank Over the Years: Priority, Challenges and Achievements" Long gone are the days when the motto "central banks should talk as little as possible" was a generally accepted convention. There is now a clear consensus that clear, effective and simple communication with central banks is one of the key tools in fulfilling its mandate. Through their communication, central banks act on expectations, reduce uncertainty and create a more predictable environment, thus making the reactions of economic agents more predictable. Hence, not only through concrete measures, but also through communication with the public, central banks affect the efficiency of meeting their goals, strengthen their credibility and public confidence. Let me briefly address the key reasons that have led over time to the evolution of transparency and central bank communication. First, the emergence of rising inflation in the 1970s, when central banks began to actively manage inflation expectations through clearer and more open communication in the direction of stabilizing and thus calming inflation. Second, the introduction of the inflation targeting strategy in the 1990s, which implied the public announcement of a quantitative inflation target, and over time led to almost all central banks announcing their targets, macroeconomic projections, and some central banks even the future trajectory of interest rates. Third, in recent history, it is the emergence of the global financial crisis that was a catalyst for tectonic shifts in the way central banks communicate. The disruption of monetary signaling, the introduction of a flurry of unconventional measures at that time by multi-central banks, including ours, in a short time imposed the need for more frequent and clearer openness of central banks to the public. Global central banks have also embarked on so-called "forward guidance", announcing in advance the trajectory of interest rates, the timing point to which they would keep low, the volume and dynamics with which they would continue to inject liquidity into the economy before starting withdrawals, and the like. Perhaps the best illustration of the changes in central bank communication is a comparison of Jean-Claude Trichet's famous mantra "we never before commit" to Mario Draghi's 2012 "whatever it takes" statement, which shows a complete shift in the openness of central banks. It is good to see trends in openness and central bank communication through the prism of concrete indices that try to quantify transparency[1]. One of the most comprehensive indices, it contains five dimensions related to central bank transparency. The first is about the openness of central banks to policy objectives, the second dimension is economic and refers to the economic information that central banks communicate (the data on which decisions are based, policy projection and evaluation models, and the forecasts themselves), the third is procedural, i.e. it shows whether there are explicit rules and strategies and mechanisms for decision-making, The fourth concerns how quickly central banks announce their decisions, along with an appropriate explanation of the causes and consequences of the decision, and the last concerns whether central banks publicly disclose information about possible problems and obstacles to policy implementation. The overall index increased significantly from 1998 to 2019 in almost all countries, including the leading central banks. For example, in the case of the eurozone, this index increases from 8 to 12, while for the Fed the change is from 7 to 12.5. What is important is that our central bank's index increased from 5 in 1998 to 9 in 2019, with the biggest positive moves in terms of data, models and projections communicated in the context of decision-making, as well as in terms of speed of publication and reasoning related decisions. A major change in recent years has also taken place in relation to the target group of central banks  the perimeter is expanding from financial markets and experts to the general public. Why is this happening, and why is our outreach to the general public imperative? Firstly, we have been living in periods of crisis for a long time (the financial crisis, the Covid crisis, the war in Ukraine), which is why we are forced, in addition to the standard ones, to react with "unconventional" measures that have not been applied before, but also to be present in public much more often and more focused than before. For example, in the Covid crisis, we and many other central banks have introduced a series of measures to mitigate the effects of the pandemic. Apart from monetary easing, it has resorted to other measures that have not been the way central banks react so far. For example, temporary moratoriums on loan repayments to firms and households have been introduced, temporarily easing the burden on firms and households in times when the economy has had to hibernate. Secondly, the mandates of central banks are gradually modifying, from the introduction of financial stability in our perimeter to green finance, for which, for example, in 2021 about 63% of central banks declared that they should be their mandate, due to the impact of climate change on the achievement of basic goals. This means that our goals, instruments, measures are becoming more complex, related to specific issues that are of direct importance to the general population, and this requires a simpler, easier, faster and more direct way of communication. The name itself suggests that this crisis has an impact on every individual in societies, which further emphasizes this need to be "understood" by the general public, to act on expectations for the future in order to reduce pressure on prices, and in our case in particular, to "narrow" the space for speculation and destructive statements that cost additional societal damage. How do central banks try to get closer to the general public? One of the more visible changes is the channels of communication, but also the increasing focus on economic and financial education. The new channels include websites, social media, and the organization of various events. A survey conducted at the end of 2021 on a sample of 75 central banks found that 80% of banks use the Internet as a communication module, with some banks having "layered communication"  the same concept has simple but also very complex explanations according to the target audience. For 40% of banks surveyed, economic/financial education is directly referenced as an area of websites, and over 90% of banks surveyed use a Twitter account for short, clear, indirect communication. A large percentage of banks (over 80%) use communication and a YouTube channel, and about 40% of banks organize special meetings and events with the general public. Similarly, in this year's survey on central banking, although traditional channels of communication (press releases, press conferences) remained the dominant and key instruments, central banks indicated that just over 50% of the messages they send to the public are sent through social networks, where there is both interaction with the public and the ability to gauge opinion/sentiment about the central bank. Where are we as a central bank in these attempts to increase transparency, but also to redesign the way we communicate, in order to be simpler, more understandable, and able to effectively send messages to the public? I mentioned that our transparency is growing, much like with other central banks. The assessments are positive in line with the IMF's recent mission, under a pilot project to assess our profile under the new Central Bank Transparency Code, through which we have also received guidance on which we are working to raise communication and transparency to a higher level. We increase our presence through traditional channels of communication. For example, to illustrate, the number of press releases from about 50 announcements in 2013 reached over 200 announcements in 2022. We are also seeing the efforts we are making to diversify the channels of delivery of our messages  in addition to regular tools, we are increasingly using social media, simplifying information, using visualization tools. On one of these most used networks, from 2018 to 2022, there was a 23.4% increase in posted accounts of the National Bank. In order to communicate the activities of the National Bank through these channels of communication, intended for the general public, the language and concept of the content have been significantly simplified. We also started by using custom illustrations to encourage audience interaction with the posts. It is evident that central banks are constantly working to increase their transparency and change their communications. Changes that mean not only a greater presence of the central bank in the information space, but also a change in the quality of communication, adaptation of communication to new waves of digitization, and greater rapprochement with the general public. These steps are necessary in a world where central banks face delicate challenges, mandate expansion, and changes in instruments to meet their targets. Moreover, the broader communication of central banks is gaining weight as a necessary tool in the battle against false and false news, speculation, irresponsible statements that can jeopardize the achievement of the goals of the central bank, which are the public good. Unfortunately, in recent times we have seen such speculative and irresponsible attacks and statements become very common, causing social harm and undermining the foundations of some issues on which we should have a social and professional consensus. Hence the need to go above and beyond traditional target groups and through traditional channels, to take a bigger step forward and send messages that are relatable, understandable and, most importantly, relevant to the general public. In any case, regardless of the mode of communication, the need for messages to be clear, consistent, and transparent remains. Only in this way can we have effective communication, manage expectations appropriately, and achieve our goals because, as Michael Woodford points out  "For not only do expectations about policy matter, [...] but very little else matters. Title: Note of the Governor of the National Bank: 2022-A jubilee year, but also a year of challenges and ordeals
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Note of the Governor of the National Bank: 2022-A jubilee year, but also a year of challenges and ordeals Skopje, 31 December 2022 As we countdown the last hours to the New 2023, we remember all the events that marked the passing year and the things we will remember it for. In 2022 we marked the 30th anniversary of monetary independence, 30 years of building one of the pillars of the statehood. In conditions of numerous crisis episodes and historic ordeals that we have witnessed in the past three decades, the monetary sovereignty maintenance undoubtedly required great commitment, professionalism and leadership by the central bank, as well as support from other social stakeholders. Following the acta non verba principle, we built this institution step by step, investing in its human potential, without which the monetary stability maintenance and strengthening would be impossible. We maintained the denar stability, one of the symbols of our statehood and the anchor of stability of our economy. Just as there are two sides to a coin, every period has its good and bed sides. Thus, unfortunately, the year of 2022 will be historically remembered as another crisis year-a year in which a war started on European soil, a year of energy crisis, a year in which the world registered one of the highest inflation rates in the past few decades. Therefore, all central banks, including ours, changed the long-time course of monetary policy and started the cycle of its tightening. The aim of these changes is to stabilize the price growth, to prevent a decrease in the citizens purchasing power and to ensure predictability in making decisions. In fact, we have done this successfully in the past three decades, a period that registered higher inflation rates in our country only on few occasions. These episodes, like the current one, were mostly a reflection of external shocks which affected our small, open and energy dependent economy, as well as of structural weaknesses of the economy that were not given adequate attention in the past decades. Over the years, the National Bank has successfully responded to these challenges and with its measures and policies consistently adhered to its goals- a stable currency and stable prices. We are closely monitoring this crisis situation and we are prepared to undertake further steps to ensure the medium-term price stability, which is also a prerequisite for sustainable economic growth and better life of citizens. Next year we expect a gradual slowdown of the inflation, which would return to the historic rates of around 2% in the medium term. In concluding I would like to point out that this year has taught us that we should think and act one step further- the world faces and will face major changes, among other climate and energy challenges, as well as digitalization. It is more than obvious that the main emphasis should be placed on sustainability- sustainable energy, sustainable agriculture, sustainable finance. This requires structural reforms which will strengthen the economic resilience, hence we, the policy makers, should think and act responsibly, strategically and sustainably. I wish you all a successful and much better 2023!

Title: Address by Governor Angelovska-Bejoska at the Workshop for Journalists on the topic of the Law on Payment Services and Payment Systems, Ohrid 3-4 March 2023
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Address by Governor Angelovska-Bejoska at the Press Workshop on the Law on Payment Services and Payment Systems, Ohrid 3-4 March 2023 Dear Media Representatives, I welcome you to today's workshop, organised by the National Bank and supported by the European Fund for South Eastern Europe (EFCE). The workshop is thematic and dedicated to the new Law on Payment Services and Payment Systems, which came into force at the beginning of this year, and in general, to the concepts of digitalization and innovation in the field of payments. Digitalization is becoming an indispensable part of our daily lives, including in the financial sphere. Globally, the transformation of financial systems, supported by digitization, is proceeding at an extraordinary speed. The principles of charges, the way of securing credit and financing in the economy, the way of savings, investment advice, etc., are changing. And we are no longer familiar with the concepts of digital wallets and payments via mobile phones, artificial intelligence-based financial advisors, and peer-to-peer crowdfunding platforms. New technologies are not only changing the nature of the financial services offered, but they are also changing the structure of financial service providers. Traditional financial institutions are increasingly facing competition from new fintech and bi-tech companies that offer a range of services that until recently were part of traditional bank functions. More recent data concerning, for example, the group of eleven major technology companies (biktech) shows that all of them already provide payment services, two-thirds provide banking and credit services, and not a small number of companies that provide asset management, insurance, and crowdfunding services. At the heart of these trends are large and sustained investments in research and development. Amazon, Google, and Apple are three of the top 10 companies in the world that invest the most in R&D. Innovation is evident in all spheres of finance, but the most pronounced is the transformation of payment services. Payment systems and payment services play a vital role in an economy, and their rapid digital transformation enables extremely fast, efficient, and secure payments. According to some estimates, the rate of adoption of the digital payment method is so high that the scenario of a global cashless society no longer seems so far away. According to some estimates, cashless global transactions are expected to grow by 80% from 2020 to 2025 and triple by 2030. Several factors are contributing to this revolution in the field of digital payments. First and foremost is technology. According to some statistics, mobile wallets, for example, are one of the major factors driving the development of global digital payments. The second factor is the desires of customers, who are increasingly looking for the ability to make payments anytime and anywhere. Of course, it is also important to adapt payments regulations to encourage market opening, attract new entrants, modify traditional entrants, and develop new services. Such trends in payments and innovation by new entrants to the payment system create pressure for greater competitiveness among traditional providers of these services  banks. According to an EBRD report, banks perceive the fintech sector as a potential threat mostly in the area of payments, to which they respond proactively. Namely, about 40% of the surveyed banks already use digital wallets, biometric identification or sophisticated algorithms to assess the profile of their customers, and a large number of banks are in the process of introducing such solutions. Moving the payment services market through increased competition in both providers and service types brings many advantages, one of which is better access to financial services and greater financial inclusion. There are a lot of positive changes in this area. World Bank data shows that globally in 2021, 74% of adults had a bank account, compared to about 47% in 2011. In 2021, this percentage was 80%, but it was also relatively high in 2011 when it was 72%. The results of digitization are also striking, given that globally, in 2021, 64% of the population made or received a digital payment, while in 2014 this percentage was only 44%. In our country, this percentage is higher in 2021 at 74%, versus 54% in 2014, which is a significant shift. These indicators clearly point to increasing financial inclusion and financial digitalization. However, these trends in the payments sector, in addition to advantages, also carry certain risks. Modern technologies impose greater risks than traditional solutions. The risk of fraud, unauthorized accesses, cyberattacks, insufficient protection of personal data, insufficient knowledge of consumer rights are some of the risks that innovative financial technologies bring with them. The risk of cyberattacks in particular is gaining weight, and according to a recent report by Blackrock, this risk is second most important on the global risk map, with a high probability of occurrence. These attacks are increasing in scope, frequency, and sophistication, increasing the possibility of damage to the economy and financial markets. This requires a great effort to increase digital literacy, but also to build a good regulatory framework and infrastructure. Their relevance to our economy is becoming more and more important, as digitalization is gaining momentum in the financial industry, and new regulations in the payments sector are opening up this market to new entities and new services. Our role as a regulator of this market is to foster competition, which should contribute to increasing competition, enriching services, and thus fostering the process of financial inclusion of citizens. We expect that the new Payment Services Act, which embeds the highest European standards in this area, will achieve precisely these goals. Consumer protection is at the heart of trust and is therefore one of the key prerequisites for the revival of the market. The new regulatory framework clearly regulates the obligations of payment service providers in the segment of consumer protection. Title: Governor Angelovska-Bejoska's interview on "Marili": Despite successive crises, the continuity of stability and reform processes has been maintained
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Governor Angelovska-Bejoska's interview with Marilee: Despite successive crises, continuity of stability and reform processes has been maintained Friday, March 8, 2023 Interview with National Bank Governor Anita Angelovska-Bejoska. The Governor spoke about all the measures taken by the National Bank during the several successive crises, the Covid and post-Covid period, the energy and food crisis, the price shocks and the measures taken to reduce high inflation. Angelovska-Bejoska also spoke about the new Law on Payment Services and Payment Systems, which came into force in January this year, about encouraging green finance, protecting banking service users, as well as the risk of deglobalization. MARILLI: The Macedonian economy has faced multiple crises in the past, what is specific to the last one, and how do global price shocks affect our economy, which is import-dependent? ANGELOVSKA-BEJOSKA: As you point out, the Macedonian economy as a small transition economy has faced multiple shocks that we have successfully dealt with while maintaining macroeconomic stability as a result of the institutional capacity of the central bank, the broad monetary instrumentation, the support and good coordination with other macroeconomic policies, as well as the expert public, which has been particularly important in dealing with the numerous exchange rate speculations, The banking system, etc., which, as a rule, occurred in all crisis episodes, further burdened the already difficult environment. There is no dilemma that dealing with each crisis is a major challenge, but what is specific in the current context is that we are talking not about one, but several successive crises that have been going on for a long time, crises of unprecedented proportions. These are shocks that are largely on the supply side and therefore simultaneously cause a slowdown in economic growth and an acceleration in inflation. As soon as inflation accelerates, the space for macroeconomic policymakers to support the economy narrows. This is very different from crisis episodes, when in conditions of low inflation there is room to implement looser monetary and fiscal policies in order to cushion the blow to the real economy. Given that we are a small and open economy, which is significantly dependent on imports, and especially in terms of energy supply, it is understood that the current geopolitical developments, supply disruptions and uncertainties that have gripped the global economy and which have a strong impact on international markets are also being passed on to our economy. World food prices reached a historic high in March last year (60% growth compared to the pre-pandemic period), and energy prices in August last year when the price of electricity was 650% and gas 250% higher than in late 2021. Increasingly high energy prices on world markets have quickly passed on to our country and driven up domestic inflation and caused a significant widening of the trade deficit. Last year, average inflation reached 14.2%, of which about three-quarters were the direct effect of import pressures on food and energy prices. At the same time, the trade account deficit widened significantly, mainly from energy, whose imports increased by about 2.1 times in 2022 compared to the previous year. This situation has further brought to the surface decades-old structural weaknesses in the domestic economy and the need for accelerated implementation of structural reforms that will strengthen fundamentals and increase resilience to external shocks. MARILLI: What is the NBA doing to curb inflation and maintain monetary stability? ANGELOVSKA-BEJOSKA: After a long period of low global inflation, inflation hit historic highs last year, especially in less developed economies. Thus, in the region of Central and South-Eastern Europe, annual inflation is about 13%, on average. This necessitated a response from central banks. In the context of an unstable external environment and increasingly higher price pressures, the National Bank has been making changes in monetary policy since the end of 2021. First of all, we have started with appropriate changes in liquidity, and from April last year until now, through an increase in interest rates.Monetary policy tightening aims to stabilize inflation expectations and thus contribute to maintaining exchange rate stability and stabilizing inflation in the medium term. Additional measures have also been taken, such as the mandatory reserve instrument, to strengthen monetary signals, while supporting the process of denarization of the economy and encouraging savings in the domestic currency. Given the monetary strategy of a stable exchange rate of the denar against the euro, the changes in domestic monetary policy reflect the changes in the monetary policy of the European Central Bank, although our reactions started earlier in relation to the ECB  the ECB made the first interest rate hike in July last year, and announced a reduction in liquidity for March 2023. The National Bank has taken additional systemic measures to further strengthen the resilience of the banking system, which is the pillar of financial stability of our economy. MARILLY: Are stimulus measures being taken to transform the economy and what are the concrete steps that the NBRM is taking to encourage green finance? ANGELOVSKA-BEZOSKA: A significant part of domestic inflation last year was due to the rise in prices in the energy component, which includes household electricity, fuel, heat, etc. With regard to electricity prices, this component covers only the direct effect of changes in electricity prices on the regulated market for consumers, but not the indirect effects of the increase in electricity costs for companies, which are passed on to the final prices of other products and services. There is no dilemma that deeper and faster reforms and strengthening the sustainability of the domestic energy sector can significantly alleviate price pressures from the energy crisis, but also alleviate trade deficit and foreign exchange market pressures. Central banks, by their mandate, do not have a direct role in this process. However, the National Bank is making efforts to provide a more favorable environment for investment in renewable energy sources. To this end, changes to the mandatory reserve instrument are aimed at encouraging financing investments in renewable energy sources and energy sustainability. It is a non-standard measure that encourages lending to projects related to domestic generation of electricity from renewable sources. I would also point out that we are in the final stages of drafting a Strategy to encourage green finance and its systemic approach from the point of view of maintaining financial stability. The strategy will encompass systemic measures to raise awareness of climate change and the need to mitigate it through financial sector activities, while maintaining its stability and unhindered credit support for economic activity. MR. MURPHY: Last year you celebrated 30 years of monetary independence. With the exhibition "Values and Values" at the NB Museum, the Bank has shown that it cherishes cultural heritage. How much, in your opinion, is the Macedonian bit invested in our money, which is of a specific design in which cultural heritage is a universal feature that gives the banknotes priceless value? ANGELOVSKA-BEJOSKA: The National Bank is an institution that has been involved for more than two decades in the collection, preservation and protection of the Macedonian cultural heritage, in particular a segment of the magnificent cultural treasury of our country. The National Bank Museum plays a very important role in the protection of our numismatic cultural heritage, which is not only of special, common cultural and historical value, but is an indispensable source for understanding and reliable interpretation of various aspects of our long monetary and economic past. The exhibition that we organized last year in order to commemorate an important state-building event in the recent history of Macedonia had a really great response in the general public. This is probably so because the exhibition very directly revealed to us the real cultural, historical and artistic values that served as inspiration for the creation of the design of contemporary Macedonian money. In fact, we had the opportunity to see some of the artifacts that are depicted on our banknotes in one place. Throughout the entire period of our monetary independence, the National Bank has been working ruthlessly and devotedly to build confidence in our national currency, so I can say that with last year's exhibition we also showed that the denar is indeed a wonderful blend of exceptional cultural ornaments, and at the same time a currency that provides economic security for our citizens. Or, in the words of the immortal Virgil of the Aeneid, "decus et tutamen," denarote our adornment and protection in economic, social, and cultural terms. MARILLE: The new Payment Services and Payment Systems Act went into effect in January. One of the important segments of the bill is consumer protection. What is different about this law in terms of consumer protection? ANGELOVSKA-BEJOSKA: Opening up the market to new payment service providers and expanding the range of payment services that will offer significant benefits to our economy from the new Payment Services and Payment Systems Act. This creates preconditions for the offer of new, innovative payment services and products, which will allow citizens and companies to execute payments faster and more efficiently, and on favorable financial terms. But these changes are also accompanied by appropriate regulatory requirements to protect consumers. Thus, there is an obligation for the provider to inform the consumer in advance of the terms under which it can use payment services, before concluding a contract, as well as to inform the fees for the most commonly used, i.e. the most representative services related to the payment account. In addition, the National Bank has issued a list of 11 most representative services related to the payment account, for which it will regularly collect data on fees from each payment service provider and publish them on its website in a comparative context. The first publication of the fees on the National Bank's website is scheduled for the end of September this year. In this way, citizens will have quick and easily accessible information about fees when deciding which payment service provider to use with. Also, a novelty in the Law is the definition of an account with basic functions for citizens, through which they will be able to carry out regular payment transactions with cash, debit cards and credit transfers, within the funds at their disposal. For these services, the fee charged by payment service providers will be limited to 0.1% of the average net salary paid, or about 31 denars. In addition to this limitation on the cost of maintaining a payment account, the Act provides that banks and savings banks will not charge fees for using the account with basic functions for consumers of vulnerable categories (beneficiaries of dependents, social security assistance, temporary unemployment, child allowance and the like). The law provides for other types of consumer protection, such as in the event of unauthorized payment transactions and the like. MARILLY: What other actions is the National Bank taking to better protect banking service users? ANGELOVSKA-BEJOSKA: In recent years, the National Bank has been constantly working to strengthen its activities in the field of protection of users of banking services, as well as to further strengthen the financial education of the population as an important prerequisite for greater financial inclusion and at the same time greater awareness of the advantages and risks of using financial services. Since last year, a special organizational unit has been launched at the National Bank  the Directorate for Consumer Protection and Financial Education, which confirms our commitment to further financial education and greater protection of consumers  natural persons who are users of services in the banking sector. In the first year of its operation, the Directorate worked on reviewing and supplementing the existing regulations in the field of consumer protection, data collection and analysis of the position of banks in the domain of consumer protection, and during this year will begin regular dedicated inspections of banks in this domain. A circular for banks containing best practices in this area is in the final stages, which should further promote transparency and access of banks and savings banks to their customers, including access to complaints received by them. Since 2021, in order to increase transparency, banks have started publishing standard tables with basic data on the loans and deposits they offer, which are also available on the website of the National Bank. The National Bank, in cooperation with other financial regulators, has been working for some time on the preparation of the Draft Law on the Financial Ombudsman, which regulates the resolution of disputes between natural persons as users of financial services and financial institutions. All these activities should allow for a significant improvement in the consumer protection framework in the financial sector. MR. MURPHY: There are certain opinions that we are currently facing the risk of deglobalization. How would this process affect small and trade-dependent economies like ours? ANGELOVSKA-BEJOSKA: There were some signs of slowing globalization in the pre-pandemic period when a slowdown in world trade was visible, but the pandemic and the war in Ukraine are considered the biggest stress test for the further course of these trends. The Global Connectivity Index, which measures globalization through trade in goods and services, through international financial flows, but also the flow of technology and people, shows a downward shift during the pandemic, but there has been some improvement since then. In any case, one cannot ignore the risk that the subsequent crises we face, in the medium term, may lead to changes in the scope, structure and geographical dimension of globalization. The harms of an eventual setback in this process can be significant, with longer-term consequences, especially for less developed, open states (such as our own and countries in the region), as trade, financial and technological fragmentation can increase costs, reduce efficiency, and slow down the growth of these economies. Indeed, the region's increasing trade and financial integration into the European economy has been seen as one of the key drivers of economic growth over the past decades. This is particularly relevant for the Macedonian economy, which has the highest degree of trade openness in the Western Balkans region at 140% of GDP. In the current context of already slowing economic growth as a result of successive global shocks and with an acute need to respond to new challenges related to digital transformation, energy efficiency and diversification, and climate risks, it is more necessary for the countries of the region to further strengthen, rather than decrease, ties with developed economies. MR. MURPHY: In the run-up to Women's Day, let's look at the state of women's economic participation in our state. In July 2022, the British think tank OMPHIF reported that the National Bank ranks first in the world among central banks and financial institutions in terms of representation of women in leadership positions. Is that an advantage in guiding the policies of the National Bank and are you taking action to increase the involvement of women in the economy? ANGELOVSKA-BEJOSKA: We are proud to point out that the National Bank stands for equal opportunities and strengthening the role of women. In the total number of employees in the National Bank, women are represented by 55.9%, while in the management structure by over 70%. This was also noted by the British think tank OMFIF, which pointed to this achievement of the National Bank given that globally, women are represented by 29% of women in leadership positions on the boards of financial institutions. Here I would emphasize that the basis for employment and participation in the management structure of the National Bank is first and foremost expertise, knowledge and willingness to give the maximum in the work, regardless of the gender of the employee. In this system of equal opportunities, women's natural predispositions to greater pragmatism, greater caution of risks, and pronounced thoroughness have come to express, which are significant contributions to the success of policies. The state of the economy is a little different. According to the latest data, the percentage participation of women in the total number of employees in the state is a satisfactory 42%. Similar conditions are observed in financial institutions, where women are represented by only about 28% in decision-making bodies. But it would be one-sided if we viewed gender equality only through the prism of the representation of women employed in managerial functions. It is imperative to strengthen women's financial management capacities, provide them with adequate access to the financial system, and give them the necessary support to increase their opportunities for social inclusion. Unfortunately, the data showed that a significant proportion of the female population is still not actively involved in the labor market (only 41% of women, versus 59% of men), and about 45.4% of women are beneficiaries of loans, versus 54.6% of men. It should be emphasized that the National Bank is working intensively in this area as well, with financial education and inclusion being one of our priorities and part of our strategic goals.

Title: Address by Governor Anita Angelovska-Bejoska at a workshop for journalists to use the NBStat statistical tool
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Governor Anita Angelovska-Bejoska's address at a press workshop on using the NBSat statistical tool Dear Media Representatives, As always, the opportunity for direct discussion and cooperation with journalists and the media is a particular pleasure for us. As an institution, we believe that our mission can only be accomplished by clearly and objectively communicating our views, views, and decisions to the public, and this is nearly impossible without your support from the media. The occasion for our meeting today is statistics and data  the basis of policy-making and decision-making.The National Bank has continuously, including over the past few years of multiple crises of unprecedented proportions, continued to strengthen its institutional capacity in the field of statistics. This is evident through an exceptional commitment to further enriching statistics and advancing the quality of statistics. Just as an example, I would cite the publication of financial account statistics, which was first launched in 2021, which provided users with detailed information on the financial assets and liabilities of individual sectors, as well as on the interconnection of the financial relationships of the sectors. As of last year, we have also begun publishing a new set of debt securities data. In doing so, the National Bank continues to contribute to strengthening the decision-making process of economic actors, especially when adopting policies to maintain macroeconomic stability. In addition, given that the risk of climate change is gaining increasing precedence  according to the latest report of the Global Economic Forum this risk along with the cost-of-living crisis and economic fragmentation are the three most significant global risks, last year we began collecting and publishing data on green finance by the banking system. Also, in order to foster greater gender balance in the economy, which according to numerous studies brings great benefits to the economy, we have started collecting data in payroll statistics and on the gender dimension  women's access to payroll accounts, the use of electronic banking, etc. Nowadays, it is increasingly a priority and necessity to structure statistical databases in order to make them more usable and useful by users. That is why almost four years ago the statistical web portal of the National Bank, NBStat, was launched  the specific topic of today's workshop. This tool allows users to quickly and easily access reliable and detailed statistics. It allows for independent data selection, time series, display in multiple forms of visualization, and download in different formats according to the user's needs. This significantly expanded the possibilities for data analysis by users. This practice of self-retrieval and management of data, which is characteristic of most central banks of European Union countries, is a kind of confirmation of our continuous efforts to comply with the highest European and international standards. It is in the context of this strategic determination of ours  the production and dissemination of statistics in accordance with the highest standards  that I would be reminded of our membership in the SDDDS plus the IMF standard. Thanks to many years of efforts and investments, in 2019 we became one of only 18 Member States to apply this standard.Meeting this highest statistical standard is significant not only from the point of view of policymakers, but also from the point of view of the perceptions of potential domestic and foreign investors in our economy. Finally, I want to emphasize that statistics do not achieve their goal simply by producing quality and internationally harmonized data. Transparent and clear communication with the public is just as important. Guided by this principle, we were the second country in the world to participate in the IMF's pilot project to assess the transparency of the National Bank under the latest central bank transparency code. Positive ratings are our motive for further investments to establish more receptive communication with the public, such as a tool for downloading data from users, regularly posting press releases, or posting brief information on social media about new statistics. We strive to bring statistics closer to users through better visualization, relevant content, and simpler language. In fact, this workshop is one of a series of activities we are undertaking towards better collaboration and communication with the public. And the public is central banks' most important ally in maintaining macroeconomic stability, especially during periods of extremely high uncertainty and numerous challenges of unprecedented proportions. Thank you and wish you a successful job!

Title: Anita Angelovska-Bejoska, Governor of the NBRSM European Money Quiz  AWARDING APPROPRIATE MBA Awards, June 12, 2023
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: Anita Angelovska-Bejoska, Governor of the NBRSM European Money Quiz  MBA Awards, June 12, 2023 Honourable Minister, Honourable President of MBA, Honourable Teachers and Professors, Dear Students, As Nelson Mandela said, knowledge is the most powerful weapon for changing the world. Therefore, marking the 5th anniversary of the European Money Quiz, I am honored to point out that the National Bank has been an active participant and supporter of educational events, including the European Quiz from the very beginning. From today's perspective, we can be proud of the five-year run of results achieved in this European competition for 13-15-year-olds, with us having twice European runners-up. This clearly shows that our country has great human potential, which policymakers must upgrade, preserve and use for higher economic growth. The effects of organizing this money quiz aren't just seen through the success of the competition. Let's not forget that the participation in the final of the European Quiz of a team of two students is preceded by preparations involving a large number of students. Over the past five years, from 500 to 900 students per year were covered in preparatory activities on topics in the field of finance, all of them had the opportunity to get acquainted with the basic topics and terms in the field of money and finance, to gain additional knowledge about the management of personal finances, as a basis for further strengthening the level of financial literacy of young people. Most importantly of all, we will feel that we have achieved our goal with this competition if we succeed in bringing all participants, students and their mentors, closer to the importance of financial education for everyday life and the need to start with it at an early age. The latest measurement of financial literacy in our country indicates that youth aged 18 to 29 have 54% of the total financial knowledge scores, which is slightly below the regional average of 56%.Consequently, there is room for improvement through educating the youngest from school benches, collaborative efforts both by financial regulators, the private financial sector, and the private financial sector. And so it is for educational institutions. The first national strategy for financial education and financial inclusion, which the National Bank and other financial regulators adopted in 2021, among other things, envisages activities for greater representation of financial education in formal education, for which cooperation and support from the competent ministry will be of paramount importance. The experience with the European Money Quiz shows that the increasing investment in the financial education of young people gives visible results, both through the increased interest of young people in acquiring knowledge in the field of finance, and by raising the level of their financial literacy. In a survey conducted by the National Bank at the preparatory event for the European Money Quiz 2021, 53% of registered students declared that they participate in the competition because they are learning something new, and at the same time a significant proportion of them (40%) find the quiz interesting. This data assures us that young people's interest in the European Money Quiz will persist in the future. On the said survey, the students stated that the results of this contest benefited both from the exercises of the Kahut application used in the competition, as well as the preparation of mentors, lectures to financial institutions and available educational materials. Financial education is especially important in today's dynamic environment, as a factor that significantly affects access to new innovative financial products, i.e. financial inclusion. The National Bank will continue to work on affirmation of financial education among young people, through its regular educational lectures for all interested schools, but also by constantly modernizing the manner and format of presentations and educational materials, keeping in mind that digital channels are also more attractive to youth. Finally, I would like to congratulate the annual national winners from Resen, the second-placed team from Bitola and the third-place finishers from the Municipality of Ilinden, their mentors, as well as all the participants of the national competition, because you had the courage, the desire to learn and gain new financial knowledge. Continue on that path that I believe will lead you to a prosperous future. As the Greek philosopher Diogenes said, "The basis of the prosperity of every state is the education of its youth." Thank you!

Title: Nacevska for MIA: Payment services market opens, competitiveness increases and compensation reduces
CentralBank: National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia
text: On MIA: Opening up the payment services market, increasing competitiveness and reducing fees --StuRat (talk) 05:05, 5 February 2023 (UTC) The new Payment Services and Payment Systems Act is expected to introduce new payment service providers to increase market competitiveness which in turn will contribute to enrichment of services, digitalization and reduction of fees charged to citizens. In addition to banks, savings banks and specialized institutions will now be able to provide payment services, which will need to obtain permission from the National Bank and meet a series of strict criteria. - In the case of new payment service providers, in a similar way to banks, citizens and firms will be able to open payment accounts through which they will make payments for various purposes using electronic banking or initiating them at the suppliers' workspaces, use payment cards, mobile phones and other smart devices to initiate payments at physical points of sale or over the Internet, as well as withdrawing and depositing cash into their payment accounts using ATMs or counters. Moreover, given the experience of countries where such institutions are present, it is expected that new payment service providers will offer innovative ways to facilitate the initiation of charges and their faster execution, says National Bank Vice Governor Emilia Natsevska in an interview with MIA, which is published below in full. She stresses that citizens' and companies' money with these service providers will not be treated as deposits, but will be protected so that it will be held in a separate account and in the event of bankruptcy or liquidation will not go into the bankruptcy estate. - The funds of citizens and companies at payment institutions and electronic money institutions are for the purpose of executing payment transactions and do not constitute deposits, as is the case with funds held by banks and savings banks which, according to legal regulations, are subject to indemnification by the Deposit Insurance Fund in the event of bankruptcy or liquidation of the depository institution. and for their protection, payment institutions and electronic money institutions under the new regulatory framework will be obliged to allocate the amount of money in payment accounts that citizens and firms have not used to make payments, into separate accounts and must not be confused with their own funds that they use for their regular business, Natsevska points out. The National Bank, as it emphasizes, will carry out field and extra-field supervision over the operation of new payment service providers in order to monitor their compliance with applicable regulations. The interview in full: The new Payment Services and Payment Systems Act came into force in January. It opens up the opportunity for new players to enter the payments market. What are the new types of payment service providers that we can expect and what kind of payment services will they offer? - One of the significant benefits arising from this bill is the opening up of the market to new payment service providers and the expansion of the range of payment services offered in the market. Thus, in addition to banks, savings banks will also be able to provide payment services, and as new players, there will be specialized institutions for providing payment services and/or issuing electronic money with which payments will also be made. New institutions, as well as savings banks, should obtain permission to provide payment services and/or lend electronic money from the National Bank, for which they must meet the relevant conditions that are clearly prescribed by the Law and bylaws. In the new payment service providers, in a similar manner to banks, citizens and firms will be able to open payment accounts through which they will make payments for various purposes using electronic banking or initiating them at the suppliers' workspaces, use payment cards, mobile phones and other smart devices to initiate payments at physical points of sale or over the Internet, as well as withdrawing and depositing cash into their payment accounts using ATMs or counters. Moreover, given the experience of countries where such institutions are present, it is expected that new payment service providers will offer innovative ways to initiate charges more easily and execute them faster. Of course, an additional benefit for citizens and businesses will be the ability to make payments using electronic money issued by payment service providers. In such a competitive environment, it is expected that existing payment service providers will offer new, innovative payment services and products to make payments more efficient and faster for citizens and businesses. When are these new providers expected to start? - A new regulatory framework has been in place since the beginning of this year. Hence, interested entities can submit applications and appropriate documentation for obtaining permission to provide payment services, i.e. issue electronic money to the National Bank. If applicants meet the stipulated regulatory requirements, they will be able to start providing payment services after obtaining permission from the National Bank. What is the guarantee that the new providers will operate in accordance with the law and what if any of them fail? Will the assets of citizens and companies be protected? - The funds of citizens and companies at payment institutions and electronic money institutions are for the purpose of executing payment transactions and do not constitute deposits, as is the case with funds held by banks and savings banks which, according to legal regulations, are subject to indemnification by the Deposit Insurance Fund in the event of bankruptcy or liquidation of the depository institution. And for their protection, payment institutions and electronic money institutions will be required under the new regulatory framework to allocate the amount of money in payment accounts that citizens and firms have not used to make payments into separate accounts and must not be confused with their own funds that they use for their regular operations. In addition, payment service providers are obliged to notify the National Bank of any changes in the method of protection of funds used for payment transactions, i.e. the use of electronic money, with appropriate evidence and documents within the legally prescribed period. In the event of bankruptcy or liquidation of a payment institution or an electronic money institution, the funds so allocated to citizens and companies on special accounts will not enter the bankruptcy estate of the entity, i.e. they will be protected and placed at the disposal of the owners. The National Bank will carry out field and off-site oversight of the operation of new payment service providers in order to monitor their compliance with applicable regulations. One of the novelties in the bill is that citizens are offered a basic payment account as an option. What kind of account is it and how does it differ from the payment accounts that citizens now use? - A payment account with basic functions, according to the Law, will be able to be opened by consumers, i.e. citizens.An account with basic functions can only be in denars and, similar to other payment accounts, can be used to pay bills for utilities and other services, public fees, various other payments and transfers of funds, deposit and withdrawal of cash, or for purchases at physical points of sale or over the Internet with debit cards. The difference with other payment accounts is that through these accounts citizens will be able to make payments only within the funds available in the account, i.e. they will not be able to use contractual overstepping and enter the so-called "minus balance" to make payments. It is because of this restriction that a bank or savings bank may calculate and charge a total monthly fee only up to a reasonable amount, which shall not be higher than 0.1% of the moving average monthly net salary paid in the country for the preceding 12 months. According to the announcements by the State Statistical Office, the calculated monthly allowance would currently amount to about 31 denars. This fee includes monthly account maintenance, an unlimited number of payment transactions for depositing or withdrawing cash directly at the counter at the provider's office or through its network of ATMs, an unlimited number of debit card transactions, and the execution of a minimum of five payment transactions by credit transfer, including a durable order, or by direct debit transferring funds to other customer accounts of the same provider payment services. In addition, it is important to note that consumers belonging to the group of beneficiaries of legally defined rights, such as for example, social security assistance, temporary unemployment, child benefit, scholarship or the like, arising by law, for the use of said payment services through a payment account with basic functions, a bank or savings bank or savings bank are not allowed to calculate and charge a fee. According to the above, the key difference between the existing payment accounts held by citizens with banks in terms of the payment account with basic functions is in the limitation of the fees that citizens will pay for the use of payment services through this account and the possibility for persons with legal rights to use it without charge. If someone wants to open such an account, does it mean that they will be able to use all existing accounts in parallel? - Citizens who want to use a payment account with basic functions will be able to have only one payment account in denars at all banks and savings banks. Hence, if citizens currently have multiple payment (transactional) accounts in denars, they will have to close them, and they will be able to transform one of them into a payment account with basic functions. If citizens want to open a payment account with basic functions with a bank or savings bank where they do not currently have a payment (transaction) account, then they will need to close all payment (transaction) accounts in denars with other banks and savings banks that they have opened in the past. On the other hand, at the same bank or savings bank, citizens will be able to use a credit card for which they will have to enter into a separate agreement, as well as have an unlimited number of payment accounts in foreign currency.
